    PART 1 / UNIT 03 / CHAPTER 3.2

    A secure request, one round trip at a time

    Prerequisites: 3.1 · Addresses, sockets & transports5 original figures
    Read the labels and caption with each figure. Boxes show parts or states; arrows show how they are connected.

    The first page takes longer to open than the next, although the server does the same work. What happened before the first request could be sent?

    Let us find the site, protect the connection, and add up the time spent along the way.

    3.2.1 · Find an address from a name

    We know the name tasks.example. How do we obtain its IP address? The Domain Name System, or DNS, provides records associated with names.

    The browser, or the operating system on its behalf, asks a resolver, a service that finds DNS answers. If the resolver has no usable saved answer, it follows DNS information to a server responsible for the name. That authoritative server supplies the published record. The resolver can then return the address to the client.

    A cache saves a result for reuse. Suppose the returned record permits caching for 60 seconds. This permitted lifetime is its time to live, or TTL. A lookup ten seconds later can reuse the saved answer. After its permitted lifetime ends, the resolver normally needs a new answer before reusing that record.

    Now change the published address. Existing caches can still hold the earlier answer until it expires. Clients with an open connection may not perform another lookup at all. DNS can also cache negative answers, such as “this name does not exist.” This is why changing a DNS record does not move every client at once.

    3.2.2 · Protect the conversation with TLS

    The browser has found a server. It must check that the server really represents tasks.example and protect messages as they travel. HTTPS uses Transport Layer Security, or TLS, for this purpose.

    A certificate is a signed statement linking a name to a public key. The public key may be shared; its matching private key is kept secret. A digital signature made with a private key can be checked with the matching public key. Changes to the signed data make that check fail.

    The certificate carries its issuer’s signature. The browser checks a chain of these signatures leading to a certificate authority it trusts. It also checks the requested name and the certificate’s validity. During this initial exchange, the server proves it holds the required private key and the peers establish traffic keys.

    The traffic keys protect later HTTP messages. Encryption makes their contents unreadable without the relevant keys. Integrity protection allows alteration to be detected. The identity check is authentication: establishing who the peer is.

    This protection ends where TLS ends. If one server decrypts a request and forwards it, the next connection needs its own protection. The application must also check whether this user may read task 42. That permission check is authorisation. A protected connection alone cannot answer it.

    3.2.3 · Carry several HTTP exchanges

    Our page needs a document and two images. These are three HTTP exchanges: each has a request and a response. A header is a named field carrying information about an HTTP message, such as its content type.

    HTTP/1.1 can reuse connections, but an earlier slow response can hold up later responses on the same connection. Browsers commonly use several connections. HTTP/2 divides messages into smaller frames and labels them by stream, so data for several exchanges can share one connection. This sharing is called multiplexing.

    HTTP/2 normally carries those frames over TCP. If a missing TCP byte blocks delivery, frames for several streams can wait behind the same gap. HTTP/3 uses QUIC streams, so loss in one stream need not block delivery in another. All three versions still use HTTP meanings such as GET and 200 OK. They change how messages travel, rather than what those operations mean.

    3.2.4 · Use a connection again

    A connection lets both ends keep information about an ongoing transport conversation. A new TCP connection normally begins with three messages, called a handshake.

    First, the client asks to connect and announces its starting byte-sequence number: SYN. The server acknowledges that message and announces its own starting number: SYN-ACK. The client acknowledges the server: ACK. Both ends now have the starting information for sending and recognising stream data. For HTTPS over TCP, TLS setup adds the protection described earlier.

    Once the task page has arrived, the browser can use the same usable connection again. A request needing fresh setup is often called cold; one reusing setup is called warm. An idle connection can be closed, so reuse lasts only while the path remains usable. Replacing a failed connection does not tell us whether its last request already ran.

    3.2.5 · Add up the waiting time

    A round trip includes travel to another participant and back. If one exchange must finish before the next starts, their waiting times add.

    Assume this simplified cold request needs 20 ms for DNS, 40 ms for TCP setup, 40 ms for TLS setup, and 55 ms for the request, server work, and reply. The elapsed totals are 20 ms, 60 ms, 100 ms, and finally 20 + 40 + 40 + 55 = 155 ms.

    If the next request reuses the lookup and secure connection, the assumed setup work disappears. The same request-and-work stage remains: 55 ms. Its travel is already included, so we do not add another round trip to it.

    These are teaching inputs, not measured timings or fixed handshake costs. The calculation shows why a short server calculation can still be part of a much longer wait.

    Remember: A request can spend time finding the site and setting up communication before the server handles it. Reusing completed setup can shorten a later request.

    Try applying it: Which parts of our 155 ms example are saved when the next request uses the same secure connection?

    PART 1 / UNIT 03 / CHAPTER 3.3

    Intermediaries & persistent connections

    Prerequisites: 3.2 · A secure request, one round trip at a time4 original figures
    Read the labels and caption with each figure. Boxes show parts or states; arrows show how they are connected.

    Our application has become busy, so we run three copies. A request now needs to reach a suitable copy. We also want new tasks to appear without repeatedly reloading the page.

    We will follow the components in front of the application, then compare ways to send updates.

    3.3.1 · Forward a request through a proxy

    A proxy receives communication and forwards it on another party's behalf. The names forward and reverse tell us which side it serves.

    A forward proxy serves clients. A browser sends its request to the proxy, which contacts the destination on the browser's behalf. An organisation might use this arrangement for staff internet access.

    A reverse proxy fronts a service. Visitors contact it as the site's public server; it forwards requests to an application server behind it. Such a destination is often called a backend. The reverse proxy can handle TLS and select a destination by the requested path.

    Forwarding information also needs a trust rule. If the application accepts a “user 7” header, a public caller must not be able to invent that identity. A trusted proxy must verify the identity and remove or replace untrusted versions of that header. The application must also control who can reach it directly.

    3.3.2 · Share traffic and check common rules

    Suppose three copies of our task application can answer requests. A load balancer chooses which copy receives traffic. It might send successive requests to A, B, and C so that one copy does not receive all the work.

    An API is an interface through which programs use application operations. An API gateway can perform common checks before requests reach those operations. For example, it may check a sign-in credential or enforce a quota, an allowance such as a maximum number of requests.

    Follow a request for task 42. The gateway checks who is calling. The balancer selects application B. B then checks whether that user owns task 42 before returning it. These are separate decisions, although one product may perform both gateway and balancing work. All three application copies may still depend on the same database.

    3.3.3 · Route by port or by path

    A balancer can choose a destination using different parts of a request. The familiar labels Layer 4 (L4) and Layer 7 (L7) refer to the transport and application layers of a network model.

    An L4 rule can use IP addresses and transport ports. It can select a server for a TCP connection without reading the HTTP path. Traffic on that connection generally continues to the selected server.

    An L7 rule reads application messages. It can send /tasks to the task service and /images to an image service. To read an encrypted HTTP request, the routing component commonly ends the TLS connection and decrypts the message. The useful distinction is the information used for the choice: transport information or application content.

    3.3.4 · Send updates to the browser

    Our task page needs to show new changes. With polling, the browser repeatedly asks whether anything has changed. If 1,000 clients ask every five seconds, the average rate is 1,000 / 5 = 200 requests per second, even when there are no updates.

    With Server-Sent Events (SSE), one HTTP response stays open and the server sends a sequence of events through it. With WebSockets, either end can send messages over the established channel. Both can avoid repeated empty polls, while keeping connections and buffers in use. A buffer is memory holding data while it waits to be handled or sent.

    Suppose a client receives event 20, disconnects, and misses events 21–23. Reopening a connection does not recover them by itself. The application must send retained events after 20, or send a fresh task list. Small heartbeat messages can help discover a broken idle path; they do not replace that missed-update recovery.

    Remember: A proxy forwards traffic, a balancer chooses a server, and a gateway performs common API checks. Updates still need a recovery path when a client disconnects.

    Try applying it: A browser last received event 20. Which information would let it recover after missing events 21–23?

    PART 1 / UNIT 03 / CHAPTER 3.4

    Discover, route & survive the network

    Prerequisites: 3.3 · Intermediaries & persistent connections5 original figures
    Read the labels and caption with each figure. Boxes show parts or states; arrows show how they are connected.

    The browser asks to add a task. It waits, but no reply arrives. Is the task missing, or is only the reply missing?

    We will follow the request and its return path, then see how addresses, cached copies, time limits, and reusable connections affect the result.

    3.4.1 · Follow traffic out and back

    A laptop may use private address 10.0.0.7 inside its local network. To reach an internet service, its traffic may pass through network address translation, or NAT, which changes address information.

    For example, a NAT device can replace source 10.0.0.7:51000 with external source 203.0.113.5:62000. It remembers the mapping. When a reply arrives for the external address and port, it uses that mapping to forward the reply to the laptop. These are illustrative addresses. If the mapping expires, an old connection may no longer have a working return path.

    A firewall applies rules allowing or blocking traffic. NAT changes addressing; a firewall decides which traffic is permitted. One device can do both.

    Ingress means traffic entering a boundary; egress means traffic leaving it. Our request is egress from the laptop's network and ingress to the server's network. The reply travels the other way. Checking both directions helps explain why a listening server may still receive no usable connection.

    3.4.2 · Find a service whose address can change

    Our task application may need a file-conversion service. Its instances can be replaced, so their addresses can change. Service discovery finds the current destinations for a service name.

    An instance can register its address and port in a registry, a list of service instances. The caller obtains the list, selects instance A, and connects. DNS or a deployment platform can also provide this information.

    Now let A stop after the caller receives the list. The saved list still names A, so the call can fail. The caller needs to refresh the list and handle an unusable destination. Discovery finds a possible place to call; the operation's own rules decide whether a failed call can safely be retried.

    3.4.3 · Reuse a nearby copy

    The task page includes a public help image. Its original server is called the origin. A content delivery network (CDN) keeps permitted copies at serving locations near users. These locations are called edges.

    The edge looks for the requested image in its cache. Finding a usable copy is a hit. Otherwise it is a miss: the edge fetches the image from the origin and can save a copy for later requests. A cache key identifies which saved copy to look up. Different image sizes need distinguishable keys.

    Reuse reduces some travel and origin work. It also needs a freshness rule saying when the copy may be used. A public help image can be shared widely; a private task page cannot be shared just because its URL looks similar. Permission and content differences must be preserved when deciding which requests may share a copy.

    3.4.4 · What does a timeout tell us?

    Our client asks to add “Read” and waits one second. No reply arrives. Reaching the waiting limit is a timeout. It tells us the reply was not received in time.

    Consider two sequences. In the first, the request never reaches the server. In the second, the server saves task 7 but its reply is lost. The client sees the same timeout in both. Repeating the request as a new operation could add “Read” twice.

    Give the first request an operation identifier, op-9. The server saves the task and records “op-9 created task 7” in the same database transaction. If the client resends op-9 with the same request, the server returns that recorded result. The operation identifier recognises the request; the task identifier names the created task. A status lookup can also reveal the result.

    Set an overall deadline, the latest time the caller will wait, so retries do not restart the full allowance. Packet loss means a packet did not reach its destination; a transport may recover it. A network partition prevents some participants from communicating even though they may still be running. A timeout alone cannot distinguish these causes from a stopped or slow server.

    3.4.5 · Borrow and return connections

    Opening a database connection has a setup cost. A connection pool keeps connections ready for reuse. A request borrows one, performs its database work, and returns it so another request can use it. If every connection is borrowed, the next request waits.

    Assume twenty connections, each held for an average of 50 ms, or 0.05 seconds. One continuously busy connection can complete about 1 / 0.05 = 20 borrowing periods per second. Twenty give an ideal rate of 20 × 20 = 400 operations per second, assuming one operation per period and no other limit.

    This calculation uses the assumed hold time. Keeping a connection longer lowers the rate. Failing to return one removes a slot from the pool, even when the database is healthy. Returning borrowed connections on success and error therefore matters as much as creating them.

    Keepalive probes are small checks sent on an idle connection to help discover that it has broken. Reusing an HTTP connection, also sometimes called keep-alive, is a different use of the term. Neither tells us whether a particular application operation completed.

    Try the mechanism in code

    The following Python code adds the four times in our example. The dictionary stores a name and duration for each stage. On the warm path, the earlier setup is reused, so only the request-and-work stage remains.

    Python · arithmetic model

    cold = dict(dns=20, tcp=40, tls=40, request_and_work=55)
assert sum(cold.values()) == 155
warm = dict(request_and_work=55)
assert sum(warm.values()) == 55

    The first assertion checks 155 ms. The second checks 55 ms. Both use assumed durations; the code performs arithmetic rather than measuring a network connection.

    Download the executable mechanism collection ↓ · Follow the connected complete design →

    Think further · Our application used to call a local function. Now it calls a service in another region. What new events can affect the result?

    The request must travel to another machine and the reply must travel back. Setup and travel add time. The server can finish while the reply is lost, leaving the caller uncertain. The interface now needs a waiting limit and a way to recognise or find the original operation when repeating it could cause another effect.

    Remember: A timeout means the reply did not arrive in time. Recover the original operation instead of assuming that the server did nothing.

    Try applying it: After “add task 7” times out, what could the client ask that would avoid creating another task?

    PART 1 / UNIT 04 / CHAPTER 4.1

    The runtime owns your resources

    Prerequisites: Introduction to System Design5 original figures
    Read the labels and caption with each figure. Boxes show parts or states; arrows show how they are connected.

    Our task application can now receive files. One upload waits for storage while another needs processing. What is running, what is waiting, and where do their bytes stay?

    Let us follow the program, its threads, and the resources they use.

    4.1.1 · Start a program and follow its threads

    Our task application now accepts file uploads. The instructions saved on disk form a program. When we start it, the operating system creates a process, a running instance with memory and resources such as open files. The operating system is the software that manages these resources and access to the processor.

    Start the same program twice. We now have two processes. Each has its own running state and its own view of memory, called an address space. Ordinary variables in one process are not automatically variables in the other.

    Inside a process, a thread is a path of execution: a sequence of instructions that can be run. One thread might receive an upload while another works on an earlier file. Threads in the same process can share data. This helps them cooperate, but also lets them interfere with each other's changes.

    A source-code module is a way to organise instructions. It need not be a separate process. Several modules can run in one process and stop together if that process crashes.

    4.1.2 · Keep data alive while it is needed

    An upload arrives in a buffer, an area of memory holding its bytes. A reference lets the program refer to that buffer without making another copy of all its contents.

    The call stack records unfinished function calls and where execution should return. When handle_upload calls read_file, a new call record is added. When read_file returns, its call record is removed. A record can hold local values and references to objects.

    Dynamically created objects are commonly kept in an area called the heap. Suppose handle_upload gives its buffer to background work and then returns. Its call has ended, but the background work still holds a reference. The buffer must remain available until that work stops using it.

    Languages manage this storage differently. A runtime is the supporting code that carries out language operations. In a runtime with garbage collection, memory can be reclaimed when the program can no longer reach an object through the references it keeps. A background task’s reference therefore keeps our buffer available, even after the handler returns. That does not promise prompt closure of a file or database connection. Those resources need a clear close or return step when their use ends.

    4.1.3 · Let threads take turns

    The CPU, or processor, carries out program instructions. A core is an execution unit within it. Assume our available core runs one thread at a time. If two threads are ready, they take turns. The operating system's scheduler chooses which ready thread runs next.

    Suppose A begins reading an upload from storage and must wait. The scheduler can run B during that wait. When the read is ready and A is selected again, A continues from where it paused.

    Changing the running thread requires saving enough information to resume it and restoring the next thread's state. This is a context switch. Switching itself takes work. If both A and B need continuous calculation, taking turns does not give them a second core. More waiting threads may help use idle time; more ready threads competing for a busy core also add waiting and switching.

    4.1.4 · Find out whether work calculates or waits

    An upload can spend time calculating or waiting for data. Input/output (I/O) moves data between the program and something such as a network connection or storage. A workload is I/O-bound when these operations are its main limit. It is CPU-bound when calculation is the main limit.

    Assume 1,000 independent uploads each wait 100 ms for storage and need negligible calculation. Handle them one at a time: 1,000 × 100 ms = 100 seconds. Allow fifty waits at once: there are twenty ideal groups, taking 20 × 100 ms = 2 seconds.

    The second calculation assumes all fifty waits overlap without making storage slower. Actual bandwidth, overhead, and storage capacity can increase the time.

    Now let each file need compression instead. A core must execute the compression instructions. Overlapping more waiting operations does not supply more computing power. First ask where the time goes: calculation, I/O, or both. That tells us which resource needs attention.

    4.1.5 · Start now and receive a result later

    Suppose the caller asks our service to convert a file. With a synchronous interface, the call returns the result or an error before the caller continues past it.

    With an asynchronous interface, starting the operation and receiving its result are separate. The caller can receive a way to obtain the later result, do other work, and wait for completion when it needs that result.

    This describes how completion is presented to the caller. A separate question is whether a thread is held waiting underneath. An asynchronous operation can still use a library call that blocks its thread. To understand the behaviour, we must follow what the actual call does while it waits.

    Remember: A process is a running program; its threads execute work and can share data. Follow how long data and other resources remain in use, not just how long a function call lasts.

    Try applying it: An upload handler returns while another task still uses its buffer. Why must the buffer remain available?

    PART 1 / UNIT 04 / CHAPTER 4.2

    Tasks, threads & event loops

    Prerequisites: 4.1 · The runtime owns your resources4 original figures
    Read the labels and caption with each figure. Boxes show parts or states; arrows show how they are connected.

    A file read is unfinished. Must the thread remain idle until the bytes arrive?

    We will follow two uploads to see how work can pause, let other work run, and resume. Then we will give waiting jobs a limited number of workers.

    4.2.1 · Wait without holding the thread

    A thread calls read to obtain the next upload bytes. If no bytes are available, a blocking read keeps that thread waiting inside the call until data or another ending condition is available. The scheduler can run another thread meanwhile.

    A nonblocking read can return “not ready” instead. The program arranges for a notification when reading may make progress. The thread can then do other work rather than remain in that read. When notified, the program tries the read again.

    The next read may supply only part of the file. Reading a few bytes and finishing the entire upload are different events. Some platforms instead report completion of an operation submitted earlier. In either arrangement, repeatedly checking without waiting for a useful notification can waste CPU time. Nonblocking I/O helps because unfinished waits leave the thread available for other work.

    4.2.2 · Distinguish overlap from simultaneous work

    Upload A starts and waits for storage. While A waits, one core runs B. Later it resumes A. Both uploads are in progress during overlapping periods. This is concurrency.

    Now let two cores execute work on A and B at the same instant. This is parallelism. Concurrency is about overlapping progress; parallelism is about simultaneous execution. One core can provide the first without providing the second.

    Taking turns can still cause interference. A might read a shared completed-upload count and pause before writing it. B can change the count before A resumes. We will follow that sequence in Chapter 4.3. Shared data needs coordination even when the threads do not execute at the same instant.

    4.2.3 · Follow a task through an event loop

    A thread carries out instructions. A task represents a piece of work that can pause and resume. A future represents a result that may not yet be available; it later holds the result or an error. Languages also use the name promise for objects representing later results; their exact interfaces differ.

    An event loop runs ready pieces of work in turn, often on one thread. A callback is a function arranged to run when an event occurs. The loop runs a callback or part of a task, then moves to other ready work.

    Follow two uploads. Task A starts a read and reaches await, which waits for its result. If the read is unfinished, A pauses. The loop runs B. When A's read completes, its future receives the result and A becomes ready to continue. The code that resumes A is its continuation.

    Ready does not mean running. If B keeps calculating for two seconds without yielding the loop thread, A waits for its turn even though its bytes have arrived. An await on an already available result may not pause at all. What matters is when the running work actually gives the loop a chance to run something else.

    4.2.4 · Give workers a bounded waiting queue

    Let a job mean “convert this uploaded file.” A worker is a thread or process that takes a job, does the work, and takes another. A worker pool is a fixed set of these workers. A thread pool uses threads for that role.

    Suppose eight workers are busy. New jobs enter a queue, a collection waiting to be taken. Eight workers limit active jobs to eight; they do not limit the number waiting. Give the queue its own limit too.

    Keep the file bytes in storage and place small file references in the queue. A waiting job then need not keep the whole upload in memory. In our example, a full queue causes the service to reply “busy” instead of accepting another job.

    This queue is held in process memory. A restart removes its entries. If “accepted” must mean that processing will survive a restart, save a job record as well as the file, so a replacement worker can find the unfinished work.

    Remember: Work can overlap while one thread takes turns. A ready result still needs execution time, and a worker limit needs a separate limit on waiting jobs.

    Try applying it: A read completes while the event-loop thread is calculating. When can the waiting task continue?

    PART 1 / UNIT 04 / CHAPTER 4.3

    Shared memory & coordination

    Prerequisites: 4.2 · Tasks, threads & event loops4 original figures
    Read the labels and caption with each figure. Boxes show parts or states; arrows show how they are connected.

    Two uploads finish, yet the completed-file count increases by only one. Let us follow the reads and writes to find the missing increment.

    We will then use locks and other coordination tools, and see how waiting for those tools can itself prevent progress.

    4.3.1 · Share a value or send a message

    Two workers finish uploads and need to increase the same completed-file count. With shared memory, both can read and change that count directly. They need a common rule for taking turns during an update.

    With message passing, one owner keeps the count. Worker A sends “one file finished.” The owner takes that message, adds one, and can reply with the new count. It then handles B's message. The workers request changes instead of changing the owner's count themselves.

    This arrangement helps only if the owner really controls the state. Passing a reference to a mutable object does not make it private when other callers can still change it. Across a failure, a message may also be repeated or its reply lost. Message passing changes where coordination happens; the chosen delivery and recovery rules still matter.

    4.3.2 · Follow a lost counter update

    Start the completed-file count at zero. A reads zero. Before A writes, B also reads zero. A adds one and writes one. B adds one to its earlier value and also writes one. Two completed files have produced a count of one.

    This is a lost update. The result depends on how the operations take turns, so it is a race condition. The error begins with the shared old read, before either final write.

    A critical section is the part that must be protected from interfering access. Here it includes reading, adding, and writing. With the same suitable lock around all three steps, A changes zero to one; B then reads one and changes it to two. Locking only the assignments leaves both earlier reads unprotected. Every caller changing this protected count must follow the same rule. This is an illustrative interleaving; language memory rules also govern which shared accesses are allowed.

    4.3.3 · Choose the right coordination tool

    A mutex is a lock held by one caller at a time. A acquires the mutex, updates the count, and releases it. B waits to acquire that same mutex before entering the protected section. Separate private locks would not make A wait for B.

    A semaphore manages a number of permits. With four permits, the first four uploads can enter; a fifth waits. When one upload returns a permit, another may proceed. Four permits limit resource use but do not give exclusive access to a shared counter.

    An atomic operation is indivisible for its specified action. An atomic increment combines reading, adding, and writing as one operation for that counter.

    Separate atomic actions do not automatically form one larger action. If transferring ten changes balances from 100,100 through 90,100 to 90,110, another observer can encounter the intermediate pair. One repair uses the same lock for both changes and for readers of the pair, so a reader cannot enter halfway through the transfer.

    A condition variable lets a worker sleep until shared state may have changed. The worker locks the queue, finds it empty, and waits. Waiting releases the mutex. A producer can then acquire it, add a job, notify a waiter, and release it.

    The worker reacquires the mutex and checks the queue again before taking a job. It checks in a loop because another worker may have taken the job first, and some interfaces permit wake-ups without a relevant state change.

    4.3.4 · When work stops making progress

    A holds the file lock and waits for the counter lock. B holds the counter lock and waits for the file lock. Each waits for the other to release something, so neither can finish. This is deadlock.

    Require every caller to acquire the file lock before the counter lock. B can no longer hold the counter lock while waiting for the file lock. This removes the illustrated circular wait. The order must apply to every path that takes both locks.

    In starvation, one caller keeps missing out while others make progress. For example, A repeatedly obtains a lock before waiting B gets a turn. B can remain stuck even though the system keeps completing A's work.

    In livelock, callers keep acting but finish nothing. Suppose A and B each take a different lock. Both fail to obtain the second, release the first, and retry in exactly the same pattern. They are active, unlike deadlock, but remain unable to complete. A retry needs to change the failed coordination, rather than repeat it forever.

    Remember: Protect the whole update with a common coordination rule. Then examine the waiting sequence too: a correct lock must also be used in an order that permits progress.

    Try applying it: Both callers lock only the final counter assignment. Why can the completed-file count still be wrong?

    PART 1 / UNIT 04 / CHAPTER 4.4

    Visibility, cancellation & overload

    Prerequisites: 4.3 · Shared memory & coordination4 original figures
    Read the labels and caption with each figure. Boxes show parts or states; arrows show how they are connected.

    A request ends, but its child work still holds a file and a large buffer. Another worker has data ready to share.

    We will see how workers safely share values, limit waiting work, and release resources when an operation ends.

    4.4.1 · Make a completed value visible to a reader

    A creates an upload record, sets its title, and shares a reference with B. We want B to see the completed title. Merely knowing that A ran earlier does not establish that guarantee.

    A language's memory model gives rules for which writes another thread is allowed or guaranteed to observe. A compiler translates program code into instructions. It and the processor can arrange execution and memory access in ways that an unsynchronised reader cannot safely infer from the source’s line order. A log's timestamps do not add the missing synchronisation.

    Consider a mutex with the language's required visibility guarantees. A acquires it, sets the title and shared reference, then releases it. B later acquires the same mutex and reads the record. The release-and-acquire relationship makes A's earlier protected writes visible under those rules. The Go memory model specifies such an ordering for mutex unlock and later lock operations.

    Happens-before names the ordering relationship used to reason about effects like these. It connects program order with the language's synchronisation rules. The writer's initialisation then happens before the reader's use. This safe publication matters even when nobody will change the record afterward. Other languages require their own documented memory-model guarantees.

    4.4.2 · Keep shared data safe to use

    A task record that never changes after construction is immutable. Two workers can read that record without competing to change its fields, once it has been safely shared with them.

    Now put immutable records into a mutable dictionary. Adding or removing an entry still changes the dictionary. The records' immutability does not protect those dictionary operations.

    An object is thread-safe for a stated use when permitted concurrent calls preserve its required behaviour. For our completed-file counter, two allowed increments must leave the correct count. A suitable lock or atomic increment can provide that behaviour. For a collection, its own access rules must protect lookup, insertion, removal, and any combined operation the application needs.

    Ask which part changes and who controls it. Keeping state private to one owner, returning copies, or sharing immutable values can reduce competing changes. Returning a writable internal collection lets callers bypass that protection.

    4.4.3 · Slow arrivals when workers cannot keep up

    Assume 150 jobs arrive each second and workers finish 100. With no rejection or abandonment, unfinished work grows by 150 − 100 = 50 jobs per second. After ten seconds, 500 additional jobs remain. Once workers are busy, this excess waits in the queue.

    Those jobs retain memory or other resources. Continued growth can cause resource exhaustion: the service runs out of something it needs. A larger queue delays the problem without changing the extra fifty arrivals each second.

    Now limit the queue to 100 waiting jobs. When it fills, the service can reply “busy,” and the producer can slow down before trying again. Or a producer can wait for queue space before sending more work. This effect on the producer is backpressure: downstream capacity limits upstream work.

    A queue limit protects space; the response and the producer's reaction make the feedback useful. Also observe how long jobs wait. Even a queue that fits in memory can contain work that is already too old to be useful.

    4.4.4 · End related tasks and release their resources

    One request starts two child tasks. One reads the uploaded file’s name and size; the other makes a preview. The request-handling task is their parent. With structured concurrency, these related tasks belong to a scope, a block of work whose parent must account for its children before leaving. The scope keeps track of their completion and failure.

    Suppose the request's time limit ends. The parent requests cancellation: it asks the children to stop. A child reaches a stopping point, closes its file, releases any borrowed resources, and ends. The parent accounts for its children's termination before leaving their scope. A blocking call that cannot respond promptly can delay this sequence; cancellation is not an instant kill.

    Stopping the connection does not reverse work already saved. If the service accepted a job that must continue after the request ends, give it a saved job record and an owner beyond this request. Request-scoped children can then stop and release their resources while a later worker resumes the accepted job.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Let us connect the worker pool to a definite acceptance rule. This pseudocode stores each upload as a temporary file and tries to add its identifier to a queue. A full queue returns “busy”; it does not accept that job. An accepted entry is queued for this process run.

    The queue holds at most 100 waiting identifiers. Fifty copies of worker run. try_put adds an identifier only if there is space; take waits while the queue is empty. convert either finishes or raises ConversionError. The finally block releases that job’s resources on either exit.

    These limits cover conversion jobs. The service also needs separate limits on file sizes and simultaneous upload reception, since accept saves the file before checking queue space.

    Pseudocode · fifty workers and at most one hundred waiting jobs

    waiting = bounded_queue(capacity=100)

def accept(upload):
    file_id = save_temporary_upload(upload)
    if not waiting.try_put(file_id):
        delete_temporary_upload(file_id)
        return "busy"
    return "queued for this run"

def worker():
    while True:
        file_id = waiting.take()
        try:
            convert(file_id)
            record_success(file_id)
        except ConversionError:
            record_failure(file_id)
        finally:
            close_job_resources()
            delete_temporary_upload(file_id)

start_workers(worker, count=50)

    When fifty workers are busy and one hundred jobs are waiting, the next attempted queue insertion fails. That upload’s temporary file is removed and its caller receives “busy.” When a worker finishes, it takes another waiting identifier.

    This example assumes the shown storage and cleanup operations succeed. Its queue is in memory, so restart loses queued entries. To promise restart recovery, store a job record before reporting durable acceptance and let replacement workers find unfinished records.

    Download the executable mechanism collection ↓ · Follow the connected complete design →

    THE WORKBENCH · TRY CHANGING THE INPUTS

    What happens when jobs arrive faster than they finish?

    Start with 150 arrivals and 100 completions each second. The extra jobs must wait or be rejected. Increase the queue limit: does it make workers finish faster, or only let more jobs wait? This model starts empty and treats jobs as a steady flow; it does not simulate individual threads or storage.

    Compare waiting with calculation

    Assume 1,000 independent files each wait 100 ms for storage and need negligible calculation. One at a time, they take 100 seconds. Fifty waits at once give twenty groups of 100 ms: an ideal two seconds. For this calculation, ignore startup, transfer limits, and other overhead.

    The same assumed I/O work, with different ways to run and retain jobs
    ArrangementIdeal elapsed timeWhat needs a limit?After process restart
    One upload at a time100 sOne active file; waiting work elsewhereA saved job record is needed to resume
    50 threads doing blocking I/O2 sThreads, buffers, connections, and waiting jobsMemory-only jobs are lost
    Nonblocking I/O, 50 files in progress2 sTasks, buffers, connections, and waiting jobsMemory-only jobs are lost
    Saved job queue and 50 workersAt least 2 s, plus queue workAccepted jobs, waiting jobs, and active workersSaved records identify work to resume

    Now change the work: each file needs 20 ms of CPU time and negligible I/O. The total is 1,000 × 0.02 = 20 CPU-seconds. One executing core needs at least 20 seconds. Eight cores sharing the work perfectly need at least 20/8 = 2.5 seconds. An event loop does not supply those extra cores; the runtime must permit actual parallel execution.

    A saved queue preserves job records. It does not remove processing time or prevent every repeated effect during recovery. These calculations compare stated assumptions, rather than measured systems.

    Think further · The client disconnects after an upload job is accepted. Should processing stop?

    First decide what acceptance promised. If the job must continue, its saved record and a worker outside the request scope own the remaining work. Request-owned children can stop and release their resources. If cancellation of the job is allowed, record that decision so later workers can obey it. Closing the connection alone neither deletes the saved job nor reverses work already completed.

    Remember: Share data through the language’s synchronisation rules. Bound waiting work and give every file, connection, and child task a clear end to its use.

    Try applying it: When a request ends, which child resources should be released, and which saved job may still need to continue?

    PART 2 / UNIT 05 / CHAPTER 5.1

    Model behavior with objects and values

    Prerequisites: Introduction to System Design5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    One payment class reads an HTTP request, checks an order, calculates fees, creates a provider client, and stores the result. A fee change and a provider change both send us into the same class. Dividing it into files will help only if we also decide which rules and details each part owns.

    We will use this payment to distinguish abstraction, encapsulation, polymorphism, and inheritance, then compare inheritance with composition. We will give the gateway a behavioural contract and follow a likely change through the design. By the end, we should be able to explain how each boundary helps and where SOLID offers a useful question to ask.

    5.1.1 · Abstraction, encapsulation, polymorphism, inheritance

    Imagine one payment class that checks an order, creates a client for a payment provider's software library (SDK), calculates fees, and writes audit records. A fee change and a provider change both require editing it. Let us separate the work, beginning with what the application needs from a provider.

    The application wants to request a charge and receive an outcome. It need not know the provider's JSON field names or connection setup. A gateway offers an operation such as charge(command); a provider adapter translates that request into the provider's protocol. Presenting the useful operation while hiding those implementation details is abstraction. The operation's contract must still explain what its result means.

    Now consider the payment's own state. Suppose any caller can set payment.status to “paid.” It can bypass the check that a charge actually succeeded. Encapsulation controls access to internal state so that changes pass through operations that enforce the rules. An operation that records verified approval can check the current state before allowing the transition. Hiding a field helps only if the permitted operations preserve the rule.

    We may have two provider adapters offering the same charge operation. The payment service can call either through the gateway contract, without choosing a different calling procedure for each provider. This ability to use different implementations through a common contract is polymorphism. Both implementations must preserve the meanings callers rely on, including the distinction between decline and uncertainty.

    Inheritance creates a specialised class from a base class, reusing or overriding its behaviour. It can support polymorphism when a subclass fulfils the base class's contract, but it is not required for abstraction, encapsulation, or polymorphism. Composed objects and functions can also provide those capabilities. Keep these questions separate: what operation is exposed, who may change the state, which implementations callers can use, and whether a class hierarchy helps express that relationship.

    5.1.2 · Composition vs inheritance

    Suppose callers use an Account contract that permits withdrawal when sufficient funds are available. A ReadOnlyAccount subclass that always rejects withdrawal changes an assumption those callers rely on. Sharing balance fields through inheritance has not established a valid behavioural relationship. A subclass offered in place of its parent must preserve the parent's contract, including the operations callers are allowed to request.

    Composition builds behaviour by connecting collaborators. A payment service can receive a fraud policy and a gateway, then call each for its own part of the work. To change the fraud policy, we supply another policy while keeping the gateway. To change providers, we replace the gateway while keeping the policy. Inheritance that combines both choices can lead to a subclass for every policy–provider combination.

    The inheritance-versus-composition figure shows the same issue with content and delivery channels: two independent choices need not become one growing hierarchy. Composition adds wiring and contracts, so use it where those variations are real. Inheritance remains useful when the specialised object consistently fulfils the inherited contract. Judge that relationship by what callers may do, rather than by similar fields or convenient code reuse.

    5.1.3 · Interfaces and contracts

    What does charge(100) mean? It might mean one hundred dollars, one dollar expressed in cents, or another currency entirely. An interface describes the operations available to callers. Its contract must also explain their inputs, outcomes, and failure behaviour.

    A clearer operation might accept amount_minor=100, currency=USD, and operation_id=P7. The amount and currency identify one dollar in this representation; the operation identifier names this intended payment. The contract must explain how repeated use of that identifier is handled. Merely passing an identifier does not make a provider recognise duplicates.

    The result also needs a precise meaning. “Accepted for processing” leaves different work for the caller than “captured.” A payment may be approved, declined, or uncertain, with a provider reference when available. A timeout after submission is uncertain because the provider may already have charged. The caller needs a supported way to obtain further evidence before deciding what to do next.

    This behavioural contract lets the application replace adapters without silently changing payment meaning. Test the real adapter as well as a substitute: a fake returning “approved” cannot establish how the provider handles lost replies or repeated operations.

    5.1.4 · High cohesion and low coupling

    A fee rule belongs with related payment rules. An SMS receipt formatter has a different reason to change. If adding SMS requires editing ledger arithmetic, the responsibilities are entangled. Move receipt formatting into a formatter so that a new layout has a clear place to change, while fee calculations remain with the fee policy.

    Cohesion describes how closely the work inside a module belongs together. Coupling describes its dependencies on other modules. A payment module still needs a provider, but depending on a narrow gateway contract requires less knowledge than constructing provider requests throughout its code. Provider field names can then change inside the adapter.

    Test the arrangement with likely edits: where would a new receipt format, fee rule, or provider go? The cohesion/coupling figure follows these changes to their owners. Some changes still cross boundaries: adding a new payment outcome may require both the adapter and its callers to change. Avoid dividing work so finely that a simple action becomes difficult to follow. Extract a module when it protects a rule, hides changeable details, or gives a real change a clear home.

    5.1.5 · SOLID principles, including their limitations

    Suppose we add a second payment provider. Which code should change, and what must remain true for callers? SOLID gives us five related principles for examining this change. Each asks a different question about responsibilities and dependencies.

    Single responsibility asks whether a module has a focused reason to change. Provider request formatting and fee policy can change independently, so give each a clear owner. This does not require a separate class for every method; several operations may serve the same responsibility.

    Open/closed asks whether a useful variation can be added through an established extension point. If the service already uses a gateway contract, we can add a provider adapter without rewriting its payment decisions. The contract itself may still need to change when the business requirements change. No design can anticipate every future variation.

    Liskov substitution asks whether an implementation can replace another without breaking the promised behaviour. A replacement gateway must preserve amount units and outcome meanings. Turning every timeout into “declined” would violate that expectation even if the method signature stayed identical.

    Interface segregation asks whether callers depend only on operations they need. A checkout caller that needs charging should not have to depend on unrelated provider-reporting operations. Dependency inversion asks which way code dependencies point: the payment policy uses an application-owned gateway contract, and provider adapters implement that contract. At runtime, the policy still calls the chosen adapter; it simply no longer needs the provider's types and error codes.

    These principles help judge a design, rather than prescribe an interface around every class. Apply them to a concrete change or testing problem. An elaborate extension system can cost more to understand than a direct edit when the supposed variation never occurs.

    Think further · Which payment rules should remain the same when objects are replaced by pure functions?

    Currency, units, allowed state transitions, operation identity, and the meaning of uncertainty remain requirements regardless of representation. For the same inputs and observed provider outcomes, the new design should make the same business decisions. Tests can check these decisions through explicit function inputs and outputs.

    The separate effect coordinator still needs authorisation, durable progress, transactions for local changes, provider identity, duplicate handling, and reconciliation. Replay should recompute decisions without blindly repeating external effects. Moving methods into functions changes the representation, not the obligations of a payment system.

    Remember: Give payment rules and provider details clear owners. Distinguish the operation exposed, access to state, replaceable implementations, and inheritance; judge their contracts by what callers can rely on.

    Try applying it: When a provider renames a request field but the payment rules stay the same, which part should change? Which amount, outcome, and retry meanings must its gateway contract preserve?

    PART 2 / UNIT 05 / CHAPTER 5.2

    Principles under pressure

    Prerequisites: 5.1 · Model behavior with objects and values4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Our payment code now has separate collaborators. We still need to decide what to share, what callers may know about internal objects, and who should enforce a reservation rule. A shorter expression or an extra wrapper does not settle those questions.

    We will examine repeated business knowledge, a chain of object lookups, and an account reservation. Then we will separate operations that report information from operations that request effects. The aim is to apply each principle to a concrete dependency or rule, including the coordination needed when two callers act at once.

    5.2.1 · DRY, KISS, YAGNI

    Suppose every gateway contains a copy of the same currency-conversion policy. When that policy changes, updating only one copy makes providers calculate different amounts. This is duplicated knowledge: the concern behind DRY, “Don't Repeat Yourself.” Give the shared policy one maintained definition that the relevant callers use.

    Similar-looking code need not represent the same knowledge. Two forms may both reject blank text, while one checks a postal address and the other checks a product description. If their rules change independently, merging them can create a dependency between unrelated policies. Ask whether the checks must agree for the same business reason.

    KISS asks us to keep the required design understandable. A direct fee function may be enough; a configurable rule engine needs a stronger reason. YAGNI, “You Aren't Gonna Need It,” discourages building speculative features before there is a need. Together, these ideas suggest a practical approach: share a rule where it has one meaning and owner, and add structure when a real requirement makes that structure useful.

    5.2.2 · Law of Demeter

    Consider order.customer.account.settings.currency. The caller now knows the shape of several objects. Changing the account's settings representation may force that caller to change too, even though the caller still needs exactly the same information.

    If the caller wants the payment currency, its contract can ask for that through order.paymentCurrency(). The object that knows the representation performs the lookup. Callers then need to understand the payment-currency operation, rather than the route through customer, account, and settings.

    The Law of Demeter encourages limiting such knowledge of distant collaborators. Its value here is reduced dependence on internal structure. Counting dots is not the objective: a fluent builder, whose chained calls deliberately construct a result, or a traversal of plain data can be clear. A forwarding method is useful when it hides a meaningful representation decision; adding layers of forwarding without hiding such a decision only makes the call harder to follow. Ask which details callers would otherwise have to understand and maintain.

    5.2.3 · Tell, Don't Ask

    A caller reads an account balance, decides whether money is available, and writes a new reserved balance. It has taken responsibility for a rule that belongs with the account. Another caller may implement the rule differently. “Tell, Don't Ask” suggests requesting reserve(amount) from the owner of that rule instead.

    Suppose the balance is 1,000 minor units and no money is reserved. A reservation of 500 can succeed, leaving 500 available. A later reservation of 600 must fail under the rule that reserved money cannot exceed the balance. The operation gives the owner a place to check this rule and perform the change together. Reading a balance for a report remains a useful query.

    The method boundary organises responsibility, but simultaneous callers still need coordination. If two processes both observe 1,000 available and each reserves 600, separate checks can let both proceed. The actual shared storage boundary must make the check and update atomic: other writers must not slip a conflicting change between them. Moving the method onto an object does not supply that guarantee. Keep the business rule and the mechanism enforcing it under concurrent use explicit.

    5.2.4 · Command-query separation

    A call named payment.status() should report the payment's state. If reading status unexpectedly charges a card, drawing a screen can create a financial effect. We should be able to repeat the status query without intending to change the payment.

    Command-query separation distinguishes queries, which report information, from commands, which request state changes. An operation named payment.capture(operation_id) clearly requests an effect. The strict formulation keeps commands from returning values. Many practical APIs let a command return information about its effect, such as an operation identifier; document that convention while keeping the effect explicit.

    This separation helps a reader predict what a call can do. It does not imply that two status reads must return the same value: another operation may change the payment between them. CQRS, Command Query Responsibility Segregation, goes further by giving commands and queries different models where their needs justify it. Ordinary command-query separation does not require separate databases, services, or event histories. Begin with clear operation meanings before considering a larger architecture.

    Think further · Which payment rules should remain the same when objects are replaced by pure functions?

    Currency, units, allowed state transitions, operation identity, and the meaning of uncertainty remain requirements regardless of representation. For the same inputs and observed provider outcomes, the new design should make the same business decisions. Tests can check these decisions through explicit function inputs and outputs.

    The separate effect coordinator still needs authorisation, durable progress, transactions for local changes, provider identity, duplicate handling, and reconciliation. Replay should recompute decisions without blindly repeating external effects. Moving methods into functions changes the representation, not the obligations of a payment system.

    Remember: Share knowledge that has one meaning and owner. Limit dependence on internal representations, keep rule enforcement with its owner, and make the difference between queries and effects clear.

    Try applying it: Two callers each try to reserve 600 from an account with 1,000 available. How does reserve(amount) help organise the rule, and what must shared storage enforce for only one reservation to succeed?

    PART 2 / UNIT 05 / CHAPTER 5.3

    Side effects, domain models & collaboration

    Prerequisites: 5.2 · Principles under pressure4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A payment keeps its identity while its status changes. Its amount and currency have value of their own, and a provider call can create an effect outside our application. Treating all three as ordinary mutable fields makes the payment difficult to reason about.

    We will separate calculations from effects, distinguish entities from value objects, and follow checkout's conversation with inventory and payments. We will then test the observable outcomes, including decline and uncertainty. By the end, we should be able to identify what each collaborator owns and which claims need evidence from a real storage or provider boundary.

    5.3.1 · Immutability and side-effect management

    Suppose several helpers edit the same payment summary. To understand its final value, a reader must track every mutation, or change to that value. An immutable value cannot be changed after construction. We calculate a new summary and leave the old one available for comparison.

    For example, let amount=100 and fee=3, both expressed in USD minor units. A calculation can return a new summary with total=103 without altering its input. A pure function depends only on its explicit inputs and produces no externally visible effects. This makes the arithmetic straightforward to check: the same inputs produce the same result without contacting a provider or database.

    Keep such calculations separate from effects, including provider calls and database writes. The trace shows the calculation, a new value, the gateway effect, and storage of the outcome as distinct work. The local storage transaction does not include the provider's remote charge. Immutability also has a limited scope: an immutable command can still be executed twice, and it cannot undo a charge. Execution still needs authorisation, operation identity, and duplicate handling. Measure copying and allocation costs where they matter.

    5.3.2 · Domain models, entities, value objects

    Payment 42 is still the same payment after its status changes. Its identity matters, so it is an entity. Creating another payment for the same amount does not replace payment 42: the two payments have different histories.

    Money has a different meaning. Two Money values with the same currency and minor-unit amount can represent the same value without separate identities; they are value objects. Replacing Money(USD, 100) with another equal Money value is usually harmless. Replacing payment 42 with another payment for that amount is not. Immutable representations are useful for values, although identity and immutability answer different questions: an entity can also be represented by successive immutable snapshots with the same identifier.

    A domain model expresses business concepts and their rules. Money arithmetic should reject incompatible currencies unless an explicit conversion rule applies. A payment transition should preserve its required amount and currency rules. A domain service can express a business rule involving several values or entities when no single entity naturally owns it; the gateway adapter still handles provider communication.

    Put important rules where callers can consistently use them. Simple transport data need not become an elaborate object model, but scattering payment invariants across controllers makes them difficult to preserve.

    5.3.3 · Object collaboration

    During checkout, an orchestrator coordinates a sequence: it asks inventory to reserve items, asks payments to authorise, and records the order's progress. Each collaborator owns its own rules and returns an explicit result. An object collaboration describes this conversation, including responsibilities and returned information, rather than only the fields each object holds.

    Follow one exchange. Inventory returns a reservation identifier. Checkout records that identifier so it knows which reservation belongs to the order. If payment is definitely declined, checkout can request release of that reservation. Inventory should not quietly edit payment records, and checkout should not infer a reservation's identity from unrelated stock changes.

    An uncertain payment needs a different recovery path from a definite decline. Checkout must retain the payment's identity and seek evidence; it cannot assume that the charge failed. Releasing inventory, refunding, or cancelling may themselves require tracked operations. Returning an error does not undo earlier effects.

    Also consider where calls run. Several small in-process calls may be cheap. Moving the same conversation across a network adds waiting and partial failures, where one participant succeeds while another cannot communicate. Design a remote contract for that boundary rather than automatically copying the object interface.

    5.3.4 · Testability and design for change

    To test a declined payment, give the service a test gateway that returns “declined.” The test can then check the order's resulting state without contacting a real provider. Controllable inputs and visible outcomes make such tests useful.

    A useful test calls the payment operation and checks that the decline was recorded, the order did not become paid, and shipment was not initiated. Another test supplies an uncertain outcome and checks that the order remains pending for investigation. These checks express the behaviour the user depends on, even if the service's private methods are rearranged.

    A test that only expects a particular sequence of private method calls can fail after a harmless refactor while missing a business error. Prefer checks of required results and state. Keep integration checks for the real boundaries: request encoding, transactions, timeouts, and resource cleanup. A substitute gateway helps test orchestration but cannot establish the actual provider's behaviour. For example, testing local code with a canned timeout cannot establish whether a real provider recognises repeated operation identifiers. Choose evidence appropriate to the claim being checked.

    Think further · Which payment rules should remain the same when objects are replaced by pure functions?

    Currency, units, allowed state transitions, operation identity, and the meaning of uncertainty remain requirements regardless of representation. For the same inputs and observed provider outcomes, the new design should make the same business decisions. Tests can check these decisions through explicit function inputs and outputs.

    The separate effect coordinator still needs authorisation, durable progress, transactions for local changes, provider identity, duplicate handling, and reconciliation. Replay should recompute decisions without blindly repeating external effects. Moving methods into functions changes the representation, not the obligations of a payment system.

    Remember: Distinguish identity from value and calculation from effect. Follow the collaborators and their returned results, then test both required business outcomes and the real boundaries those outcomes depend on.

    Try applying it: A test gateway returns uncertainty and the order stays pending. What has this established, and what evidence is still needed about actual provider retries and database persistence?

    PART 2 / UNIT 05 / CHAPTER 5.4

    Design for change, testing & functions

    Prerequisites: 5.3 · Side effects, domain models & collaboration4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    We want to improve the payment class without changing what its callers can rely on. Moving code can still introduce a serious error: a provider timeout might become a decline, or an amount might acquire different units. The revised class diagram would not reveal either mistake.

    We will make small structural changes and check the same success and failure histories after each one. We will also express payment decisions as pure functions and leave effects to a coordinator. The aim is to choose a clear representation while preserving business rules, outcome meanings, and recovery responsibilities.

    5.4.1 · Refactoring and recognizing code smells

    Before reorganising a large payment class, capture its important behaviours: successful payment, decline, timeout, and storage failure. In particular, keep an uncertain provider outcome distinct from a definite decline. Refactoring changes internal structure while preserving the required observable behaviour.

    Extract fee calculation first and compare its results on the same inputs. Then extract provider communication while keeping result categories unchanged. Run the behavioural checks after each move. Small steps make it easier to locate a mistake because fewer decisions have changed at once.

    A long method, duplicated rule, or repeated conditional is a code smell: a sign that deserves investigation. It is not proof of a defect or an instruction to add a design pattern. Ask what change is difficult and which responsibility or dependency causes that difficulty before choosing a repair.

    Tests focused on outcomes allow code to move without preserving every old private call. If the existing behaviour is wrong, changing it is a separate behavioural change that needs an explicit explanation and checks. For example, correcting a timeout that was formerly reported as decline is necessary work, but it should not be hidden inside a claim that the refactor preserves behaviour.

    5.4.2 · Functional programming alternatives to object-centric design

    We can express payment decisions using functions as well as objects. A pure function decide(state, command) can return a new state, events describing a decision, or requests for external actions. Another part of the application carries out any database write or provider call. This arrangement is often called a functional core with an imperative shell: calculations at the centre, effect-performing code around them.

    For example, given a pending payment and a recorded provider timeout, a decision function can return a pending state and a request to check the provider later. It makes no remote call itself. An outer coordinator records and performs the requested work, then supplies the observed result to the next decision. Inputs and outputs expose the reasoning without hiding communication inside it.

    Because the decision function has explicit inputs and no hidden effects, it is easier to test and replay. Replaying its output must not blindly repeat external actions. The effect-performing part still needs durable progress, ownership, authorisation, and duplicate handling. Calling a pure decision function twice is different from charging a provider twice. Choose functions and objects according to which makes the rules and collaboration easiest to see; they can be used together in the same design.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · injected collaborator

    class RecordingGateway:
    def __init__(self): self.calls = []
    def charge(self, command):
        self.calls.append(command)
        return "uncertain"

def pay(command, gateway):
    return gateway.charge(command)

gateway = RecordingGateway()
assert pay({"amount_minor":100,"currency":"USD"}, gateway) == "uncertain"

    The recording gateway receives the command, appends it to calls, and returns “uncertain.” The pay function returns that result unchanged, so the assertion passes. Inspecting gateway.calls would also show the supplied USD amount of 100 minor units. Passing the gateway as an argument lets us exercise this behaviour without contacting a provider.

    This example isolates the collaborator boundary. It does not validate money, supply an operation identifier, persist progress, or reconcile a real charge. A complete payment service needs those responsibilities and tests of its resulting business state. Preserving the uncertain result here matters: the caller has not been given evidence of either approval or decline.

    Download the executable mechanism collection ↓ · Follow the connected complete design →

    Think further · Which payment rules should remain the same when objects are replaced by pure functions?

    Currency, units, allowed state transitions, operation identity, and the meaning of uncertainty remain requirements regardless of representation. For the same inputs and observed provider outcomes, the new design should make the same business decisions. Tests can check these decisions through explicit function inputs and outputs.

    The separate effect coordinator still needs authorisation, durable progress, transactions for local changes, provider identity, duplicate handling, and reconciliation. Replay should recompute decisions without blindly repeating external effects. Moving methods into functions changes the representation, not the obligations of a payment system.

    Remember: Refactor in small steps while preserving observable behaviour, including uncertainty. Objects and pure functions can express the same rules; executing their requested external effects still needs explicit recovery and duplicate handling.

    Try applying it: A refactor moves payment decisions into a pure function. Which test would catch a timeout being reclassified as decline, and why must replaying a decision remain separate from repeating a charge?
