    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.1

    Dependencies, inversion & composition

    Prerequisites: Object-Oriented and Modular Software Design6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Our notification service creates an email provider inside its own code. Testing a notification rule therefore starts by dealing with provider configuration, even when the test only needs to see which message would be sent. We will move construction to startup and follow how the service receives its sender. This gives us a concrete way to distinguish dependency injection, inversion of control, and dependency inversion.

    6.1.1 · Dependency, dependency direction, and inversion

    Suppose our notification service calls an email provider's software library, or SDK. To send a message, the service builds that library's request object and interprets its status codes. Its code depends on the SDK: a change to the provider's types can require a change to the service.

    We can give the application its own Sender contract, with an operation such as send(message). A provider adapter implements that operation by translating the application's message into an SDK request and translating the response back. The notification service now uses the Sender contract; the adapter knows both the contract and the provider's details. This arrangement is called dependency inversion because the application policy no longer has to depend directly on the external implementation.

    Distinguish two kinds of arrow in the diagram. A source dependency says which interface a piece of code must know. A runtime call says which object executes next. At runtime, the service still calls the concrete adapter, which reaches the provider. Reversing the source dependency has not reversed that call. Check the values and errors crossing the interface too: provider-specific meanings can keep the policy dependent on the SDK even after its import moves elsewhere.

    6.1.2 · Inversion of Control (IoC)

    In a small script, our main function decides when to call send_receipt(). In a web application, we usually register a request handler and let the framework decide when to invoke it. We provide part of the behaviour while another part of the program controls when that behaviour runs. This is Inversion of Control, or IoC.

    An event loop provides another example. We register a callback; when the relevant event is ready, the loop invokes it. The callback still contains application decisions, but it no longer owns the surrounding dispatch loop. This division lets the framework provide shared connection handling and scheduling without copying those mechanisms into every handler.

    To use this arrangement correctly, learn when the framework considers a callback finished, how it reports errors, and what happens to work started by the callback. These rules determine where cleanup belongs. A framework may also construct handlers and supply their dependencies. Dependency Injection is one technique used in such arrangements; IoC is the broader idea of handing control of part of the execution to a coordinator.

    6.1.3 · Dependency Injection (DI)

    Our notification service needs a sender. One version creates EmailSender inside its constructor. Every service instance then makes that construction choice for itself. In another version, startup code first creates sender = EmailSender(config) and then creates NotificationService(sender). Supplying a needed collaborator from outside is Dependency Injection, or DI.

    During a notification operation, the service calls the supplied sender's send(message) method. It does not have to choose a provider or load its configuration at that point. In a test, we can create RecordingSender and pass it to the same constructor. The test sender records the requested messages so we can inspect them; the service needs no special testing branch.

    Constructor arguments, function arguments, and ordinary assignment can supply dependencies. A DI container is optional. What matters is that the receiver gets the collaborators it needs through a clear contract. Passing a large infrastructure object containing dozens of unrelated services still leaves the receiver with a broad dependency. Supplying a focused Sender makes both its needs and the permitted interaction easier to see.

    6.1.4 · Constructor, property/setter, and method injection

    A notification service cannot send anything without a sender. Constructor injection supplies that required collaborator when the service is created. Once construction succeeds, callers can expect the service to have its sender. This helps prevent an object from appearing usable while a necessary field is still missing.

    Property or setter injection supplies a collaborator after construction. For example, a service might accept an optional observer through set_observer(). Its contract must say what happens before the observer is supplied and whether replacing it during use is allowed. If a setter supplies a mandatory dependency, some additional rule must prevent calls while the object is incomplete.

    Method injection supplies a collaborator for one operation, such as render(message, formatter). The receiver can use the formatter for that call without retaining it afterward. This is useful when the choice varies by call or the dependency has a shorter lifetime than the receiver. Choose the form by asking when the dependency becomes necessary and how long the receiver may keep it. A long-lived service can use a request's database session during an allowed call, but must not store it for use after that request ends.

    6.1.5 · Dependency inversion principle vs DI

    Consider NotificationService(provider_sdk). Another part of the program supplies the SDK, so the service uses dependency injection. Yet its methods may still build provider-specific requests and catch provider-specific exceptions. Switching providers still requires changing the notification policy's code.

    Dependency injection answers how a collaborator reaches an object. The dependency inversion principle answers a different question: which abstractions should important policy depend on? We can define an application-owned Sender contract with the message and outcomes the policy needs. The provider adapter then converts between this contract and the SDK. Both application policy and adapter refer to the application contract, while provider details stay in the adapter.

    The two ideas often cooperate. Startup code can construct the adapter and inject it as a Sender. But the presence of a constructor argument alone does not establish dependency inversion. Inspect the request values, result meanings, exceptions, and resource handles that cross the boundary. A manually assembled application can respect the principle, and an application using a DI container can still depend heavily on provider details.

    6.1.6 · Composition roots and DI containers

    Before the notification application handles requests, it needs actual objects. Startup code can create a repository from a database path, create an email sender from provider configuration, and pass both to NotificationService(repository, sender). This is the composition root: the place where we choose concrete implementations and connect them into a working application.

    The service can then concentrate on the notification operation. It receives ready collaborators instead of deciding how to build them each time. Reading the composition root tells us which repository and sender this application uses and which objects they share. A request or background job may also have a defined boundary where its shorter-lived collaborators are assembled.

    A DI container automates some of this work. We register how to obtain each contract and how long its objects should be reused. When asked for a service, the container follows those registrations to construct its dependencies. For a large set of relationships, this can reduce repeated assembly code. It also makes registration and lifetime rules part of the design. Validate them early, define who releases resources, and keep broad resolution near the assembly boundary. For a few collaborators, explicit construction may be easier to understand.

    Think further · A notification job runs after both the creating request and the user session have ended. How should it obtain resources, and which authority should permit its action?

    Save durable job data and identifiers instead of capturing a request connection or session object. When execution begins, create a job scope, obtain current resources under a documented owner, load the required state, and release those resources when the job finishes or fails. The request and job now have separate ownership boundaries.

    The application must also choose an authorisation policy. Some jobs represent work validly accepted earlier; others must recheck current membership or permission before acting. Make that decision explicit and retain only the necessary context. A long-running job must not silently treat an expired user session as continuing authority.

    Remember: Supplying a collaborator is dependency injection. Choosing an application-owned contract can invert a source dependency. The composition root connects the concrete objects that carry out the runtime calls.

    Try applying it: The service receives an SMS SDK through its constructor, but every method still interprets that SDK’s status codes. Which problem has injection solved, and what additional contract would keep notification policy independent of those codes?

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.2

    Lifetimes, ownership & cleanup

    Prerequisites: 6.1 · Dependencies, inversion & composition6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A request creates a background job and passes it an open database session. By the time the job starts, the request has finished and closed that session. We will trace when objects are created, which callers reuse them, and who releases them. These steps explain why having a reference is different from having permission to keep using a resource.

    6.2.1 · Transient, scoped, singleton, and framework-specific lifetimes

    Suppose two parts of one request need the same database session. They should receive one shared session for that request, and a different request should receive a different one. A scoped lifetime provides this reuse within a defined boundary. If request one receives A twice and request two receives B twice, the identities are A,A and B,B.

    With a transient lifetime, each resolution creates a new instance, so two resolutions can produce C and D even within one request. With a singleton lifetime, resolutions reuse one instance within the container or application boundary stated by the framework. Both requests may therefore receive S. These rules describe when instances are created and reused; the relevant boundary must always be stated.

    A second process can have its own singleton. Also, a shared object may receive concurrent calls, so its implementation must support the permitted concurrent use. The word singleton supplies no such safety guarantee. Frameworks differ in registration, scope, and disposal rules. Check those rules before choosing a lifetime, and ensure that any resource the object retains remains valid for every use.

    6.2.2 · Request scopes, session scopes, and custom scopes

    A web request opens a scope, obtains a database session, and creates a background job. The response ends, so the request scope closes its session. If the job retained that session, its next query uses a resource whose lifetime has already ended. Keeping a reference did not keep the session valid.

    Give the job its own lifetime. The request saves the necessary job data and passes durable identifiers, such as a notification identifier, to the background worker. When the worker runs, it opens a job scope, obtains a current database session, loads the data, performs the work, and closes its scope. Resource use now fits the operation that owns it.

    A request scope normally ends with one request. A session scope may span several requests, and a custom scope can cover a job or another explicit activity. Longer scopes also retain objects and possibly user data for longer, which affects memory and privacy. A scope describes ownership and reuse; it does not automatically start a database transaction. Nor does retaining user context establish that the user's permissions are still current when later work executes.

    6.2.3 · Object creation vs object ownership

    A factory returns a database connection. Before using it, the receiver needs to know whether it owns the connection or is borrowing it. An owner is responsible for releasing a resource at the agreed boundary. A borrower may use it under the contract but must not close a resource that other components still need. Creation and ownership can belong to different parts of the program.

    For example, a factory may create a new stream and transfer ownership to its caller: the caller must close it. Another factory may return an application-owned shared sender: the caller must leave it open. Both return an object, but the responsibilities are different. Writing the ownership rule into the contract avoids both leaks and premature closure.

    Returned values can also depend on resources indirectly. A repository's lazy query result fetches rows as the caller reads it, so it may still need an open connection. Closing the repository before traversal ends can make the next read fail. For a bounded result, the repository can fetch the records before returning and release the connection. For a stream, return an explicit resource whose owner knows when and how to close it.

    6.2.4 · Disposal, cleanup, and resource lifecycles

    Assume a pool has ten connections. A request borrows one, encounters an error, and exits without returning it. Nine connections remain available. If this happens repeatedly, healthy requests eventually cannot obtain a connection even though the database itself is working. Cleanup preserves the application's capacity as well as releasing individual resources.

    Arrange acquisition and release together. A structured resource scope or finally-style block runs cleanup when an operation succeeds, fails, or is cancelled. Depending on the resource, cleanup may return a connection to its pool, close a stream, release a concurrency permit, or roll back an unfinished transaction. The owner should perform this work at its declared boundary.

    Memory garbage collection reclaims memory according to the runtime's rules. It does not guarantee that a scarce external resource will be released in time for the next request. If cleanup itself fails while another error is already being handled, preserve the original problem and record the additional failure. Otherwise, the error that caused the operation to fail may disappear behind an error from its cleanup path.

    6.2.5 · Lazy initialization

    A report generator needs an expensive template compilation, but many application runs never request a report. We can postpone construction until the first report request. This is lazy initialisation. It avoids unused startup work, while moving the construction delay and any construction failure to the first caller.

    The application needs a controlled first-use sequence. A caller discovers that the generator is absent, constructs it, and makes the completed object available to later callers. If two first callers arrive together, an uncoordinated check can let both construct it. Publishing a reference before construction finishes can let another caller use an incomplete object. Use the runtime's supported coordination and safe-publication mechanism to enforce the intended behaviour.

    Define failure too. Should later callers retry construction, or receive the stored failure? Can an unsuccessful attempt leave resources that need closing? For a resource essential to ordinary requests, constructing it before advertising readiness may give clearer behaviour. Lazy creation changes when construction occurs; ownership, cleanup, and safe concurrent use still need their usual rules.

    6.2.6 · Dependency cycles and captive dependencies

    Suppose NotificationService needs DeliveryPlanner during construction, while DeliveryPlanner needs NotificationService. We cannot finish either constructor first. This is a dependency cycle. Examine which responsibility requires each link: shared work may belong in a third collaborator, or a separate coordinator may be responsible for the sequence. A global lookup can delay the failure until execution while leaving the underlying relationship unclear.

    A different problem appears when construction succeeds but lifetimes do not fit. A singleton service stores a request-scoped unit of work. The request ends and disposes that unit of work, while the singleton remains available to later requests. Its next operation uses an expired dependency. This is a captive dependency: a longer-lived object retains a dependency intended for a shorter lifetime.

    The operation can instead receive a currently valid collaborator for the call, or use a narrow factory that opens an appropriate scope and defines cleanup. The chosen scope must also carry the correct user and tenant context. Container validation can detect some invalid relationships, but the requirement is broader: every actual use must occur while the dependency and its context are valid.

    Think further · A notification job runs after both the creating request and the user session have ended. How should it obtain resources, and which authority should permit its action?

    Save durable job data and identifiers instead of capturing a request connection or session object. When execution begins, create a job scope, obtain current resources under a documented owner, load the required state, and release those resources when the job finishes or fails. The request and job now have separate ownership boundaries.

    The application must also choose an authorisation policy. Some jobs represent work validly accepted earlier; others must recheck current membership or permission before acting. Make that decision explicit and retain only the necessary context. A long-running job must not silently treat an expired user session as continuing authority.

    Remember: Choose object reuse and resource ownership together. Every use must fit the resource’s valid lifetime, and cleanup must run when its owning operation succeeds, fails, or is cancelled.

    Try applying it: A request queues a job that may run an hour later. Which identifiers should it pass, and where should the job create and close its database session?

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.3

    Injection, locators & factories

    Prerequisites: 6.2 · Lifetimes, ownership & cleanup4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A service receives a container and looks up whichever collaborators it needs. The constructor is short, but the service's actual needs are now scattered through its methods. We will compare this arrangement with explicit dependencies, then introduce a narrow factory for a choice that really must wait until a notification arrives.

    6.3.1 · DI vs service locator

    Compare NotificationService(sender, repository) with a service whose send method calls global_registry.resolve(Sender). The constructor tells us what the first service needs before it runs. For the second, we must inspect its methods and the registry configuration to discover its dependencies. Such runtime lookup is called a service locator.

    A missing constructor argument is apparent when we assemble the service. A missing locator registration may remain hidden until a particular branch executes. Tests of that branch may also need global registry setup, and one test's changes to that registry can affect another. Explicit collaborators make these requirements easier to assemble and inspect.

    A locator can have a deliberate role at a framework integration boundary. Resolve the needed collaborators there or at the relevant scope boundary, then pass their focused contracts into application code. Merely injecting the entire container does not make those needs explicit if methods still request arbitrary services from it. The design question is what the receiver is allowed to obtain, when it obtains it, and who owns the resulting resources.

    6.3.2 · DI vs factory pattern

    If every notification uses email, startup code can create one email sender and inject it into the service. Now suppose each notification chooses email or SMS. The appropriate choice is not known until the command arrives. We can inject a SenderFactory with an operation that obtains the sender for that channel.

    During the operation, the service reads the command's channel and calls the factory. The factory selects or constructs the concrete adapter and returns it under the Sender contract. DI supplied the factory to the service; the factory makes a creation or selection decision later. They can therefore be parts of the same design.

    The factory must explain what it returns. Is this a fresh sender the caller must close, a shared application-owned sender, or an object borrowed from the current scope? That rule determines what the service may retain and dispose. The factory can hide provider configuration while still exposing meaningful construction failures and ownership. A narrow factory for a real runtime choice is easier to review than permission to resolve arbitrary objects from a whole container.

    Think further · A notification job runs after both the creating request and the user session have ended. How should it obtain resources, and which authority should permit its action?

    Save durable job data and identifiers instead of capturing a request connection or session object. When execution begins, create a job scope, obtain current resources under a documented owner, load the required state, and release those resources when the job finishes or fails. The request and job now have separate ownership boundaries.

    The application must also choose an authorisation policy. Some jobs represent work validly accepted earlier; others must recheck current membership or permission before acting. Make that decision explicit and retain only the necessary context. A long-running job must not silently treat an expired user session as continuing authority.

    Remember: Name known collaborators explicitly. When a runtime choice requires a factory, give it a focused operation and state whether its result is owned, shared, or borrowed.

    Try applying it: A SenderFactory sometimes returns an application-owned email sender and sometimes creates a new SMS sender. What must its result contract tell the caller so neither sender is closed at the wrong time?

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.4

    Creational patterns

    Prerequisites: 6.3 · Injection, locators & factories6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    An exporter must choose a writer. A notification may need a renderer and template that agree, or several settings that must be checked together. We will follow five creational patterns through these different construction problems, including the ownership rules of copied and shared objects.

    6.4.1 · Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype, Singleton

    A direct constructor is often enough to create a valid object. More varied construction can raise separate questions: who chooses the concrete writer, how do we obtain a compatible renderer and template, or how do we validate several optional notification settings? Creational patterns provide names for arrangements that answer these questions.

    Factory Method varies a creation operation; Abstract Factory creates a compatible family; Builder assembles a value in stages; Prototype copies a configured instance; Singleton restricts instance access within a stated boundary. Their individual treatments below follow the actual creation steps. Choose according to the variation needed, while keeping the resulting object's validity and ownership clear.

    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Factory Method

    An exporter has a stable job: obtain a writer and ask it to write the rows. A CSV exporter needs a CSV writer, while another exporter may choose a different format. We can put that construction decision in make_writer(). The shared export operation calls it and then uses the returned writer through the writer contract.

    Factory Method makes this creation operation a point that a concrete creator can customise. In an inheritance-based implementation, a specialised exporter overrides make_writer(); in a smaller design, a supplied creation function may express the same needed variation. The processing code does not have to name each concrete writer.

    Use this arrangement when the creator genuinely needs a construction choice. A direct constructor call is clearer if the choice never varies. Also define the returned writer's ownership: if it holds an output stream, someone must close it after writing. Abstract Factory addresses a related but larger choice, producing a compatible family of objects rather than customising one creation operation.

    export(rows):
    writer = make_writer()
    writer.write(rows)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Abstract Factory

    An HTML notification needs a renderer and a template that use the same content model. If the application chooses each independently, it could accidentally pass a plain-text template to an HTML-specific renderer. The two objects form a compatible family.

    We first select HtmlNotificationFactory. The client asks that factory for renderer() and template(), then passes the template and data to the renderer. A plain-text factory can supply the corresponding plain-text family through the same product contracts. Abstract Factory keeps these related creation choices together, so clients can switch families without assembling each combination themselves.

    The arrangement is useful when complete families really vary. Its maintenance cost appears when we add a new kind of product: every supported factory may need another creation operation. If one stable renderer and template are all the application needs, direct assembly can be clearer. The family's contracts must still explain compatibility and any resource ownership; using one factory does not by itself validate every possible input.

    family = HtmlNotificationFactory()
renderer = family.renderer()
template = family.template()
renderer.render(template, data)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Builder

    A notification needs a recipient and a template. A caller may also choose its locale and expiry. With a Builder, the caller records these choices in stages: set the recipient, select the template, and optionally set an expiry. The builder holds the unfinished choices until build() is called.

    The build step checks required fields and their relationships. For example, it can reject an expiry earlier than the permitted send time, or a template that does not support the chosen locale. Only after those checks does it return a usable notification. The partly configured builder is therefore distinct from the completed value; code should not send it as if it were already valid.

    Builder is helpful when staged assembly makes a complicated set of choices easier to express. It solves a different problem from Abstract Factory, which selects compatible kinds of products. For a small notification value, a constructor with named arguments may collect and validate every field just as clearly. Add the stages when they help the caller construct a valid result.

    builder.to(recipient).template(template_id)
notification = builder.expires_at(deadline).build()
# build rejects missing recipient or incompatible fields
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Prototype

    A report layout already contains carefully chosen margins, sections, styles, and a title. We want a second layout with most of those settings and a different title. Prototype creates it by copying the configured instance, then allowing the copy's owned values to change.

    Follow what happens to a nested editable section. A shallow copy of the layout may leave both layouts pointing to the same section. Editing that section through the copy then changes what the original sees too. A clone operation can copy the mutable values that should belong to the new layout while retaining references to suitable immutable data, such as shared font definitions.

    The copying contract must identify these choices. A deeper copy is not automatically correct: copying a connection handle does not create another independently owned connection. Resource ownership needs its own rule. Prototype is useful when copying configured values is clearer than reconstructing every setting; fresh per-request state built from immutable configuration may be simpler when the ownership rules would otherwise be difficult to follow.

    layout = prototype.clone_owned_values()
layout.title = "Monthly report"
# Shared immutable font data remains shared
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Singleton

    Suppose the application loads immutable configuration once at startup. Each service can receive the same configuration object because they all use the same values and none changes them. A Singleton arrangement restricts access to an instance within a stated program or container boundary.

    State that boundary explicitly. Process A can have instance S1, while process B has S2. Neither is a single object shared across every host. A container-managed singleton describes a reuse lifetime; a class that constructs its own sole instance and offers global access also determines how callers obtain it. These are related arrangements with different effects on visibility and testing.

    An application-owned instance can be passed to its users through ordinary injection. Its owner remains responsible for any required cleanup. Sharing mutable request data in one instance is riskier: concurrent callers can interfere, and tests can retain one another's state. A singleton lifetime does not make an object safe for concurrent use or make its shorter-lived dependencies valid indefinitely.

    configuration = load_immutable_configuration()
service = Service(configuration)
# One application-owned instance; no hidden global lookup
    Think further · A notification job runs after both the creating request and the user session have ended. How should it obtain resources, and which authority should permit its action?

    Save durable job data and identifiers instead of capturing a request connection or session object. When execution begins, create a job scope, obtain current resources under a documented owner, load the required state, and release those resources when the job finishes or fails. The request and job now have separate ownership boundaries.

    The application must also choose an authorisation policy. Some jobs represent work validly accepted earlier; others must recheck current membership or permission before acting. Make that decision explicit and retain only the necessary context. A long-running job must not silently treat an expired user session as continuing authority.

    Remember: Choose a creational pattern for the construction decision it expresses: one product, a family, staged assembly, copying, or restricted sharing. Define when the result is valid and who owns it.

    Try applying it: A notification has three required fields and two optional fields that a named-parameter constructor can validate together. What additional need would justify introducing a builder?

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.5

    Structural patterns

    Prerequisites: 6.4 · Creational patterns8 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    We add timing to a sender, translate an SMS provider's status, and simplify notification submission for a caller. All three changes can involve wrappers, yet they change different relationships. We will trace seven structural patterns by asking what each object adds, translates, shares, or controls.

    6.5.1 · Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy

    Our notification service may need to translate a provider's interface, add timing around send(), or control who can read a result. Each change places an object between collaborators, but each has a different purpose. Structural patterns describe useful ways to arrange these objects.

    Adapter translates interfaces, Bridge separates two independent kinds of variation, and Composite treats leaves and groups through a common operation. Decorator adds behaviour, Facade offers a focused entry to a subsystem, Flyweight shares suitable immutable data, and Proxy controls use of a target. In the examples below, follow what each arrangement changes and what its contract preserves. A similar wrapper shape alone does not make two patterns interchangeable.

    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Adapter

    Our application asks a Sender to send a message and return an outcome such as accepted, declined, or uncertain, together with a reference when available. An SMS provider instead expects its own request format and returns its own status codes. An Adapter connects these different interfaces.

    The service calls adapter.send(message). The adapter encodes the message for sdk.submit(), invokes the provider, and maps the provider's response into the application's outcome. The service can then apply notification policy using its own vocabulary. SDK request objects and exceptions can stay inside the adapter rather than spreading through the service.

    The mapping must preserve meaning. If a timeout leaves it unclear whether the provider accepted the message, the adapter must not report a definite decline merely to fit a convenient branch. Check these mappings against the provider contract and its real integration behaviour. A Decorator usually retains an interface while adding behaviour around it; an Adapter's main purpose is to reconcile a mismatch in interface or representation.

    send(message):
    raw = sdk.submit(encode(message))
    return map_provider_outcome(raw)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Bridge

    Notifications vary in content: an alert and a receipt format different information. They also vary in transport: either might go by email or SMS. If we create a subclass for every combination, changes to content and transport become tangled across AlertEmail, AlertSms, ReceiptEmail, and ReceiptSms.

    A Bridge separates these dimensions through composition. A Receipt receives a transport object during construction. Its deliver(data) operation formats receipt content and calls transport.send(content). An Alert can use the same transport contract while formatting different content. We can add a transport implementation without rewriting every content class, provided it supports the agreed contract.

    The contract still needs to accommodate the actual transports, including their limits and outcomes. This separation earns its cost when both dimensions vary independently. One fixed sender may need far less structure. Adapter commonly reconciles an existing interface mismatch; Bridge deliberately arranges two kinds of variation so they can develop separately.

    class Receipt:
    constructor(transport): self.transport = transport
    deliver(data): return self.transport.send(format_receipt(data))
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Composite

    A notification audience may be one user, a department group, or a group containing other groups. The caller needs to obtain the recipients without writing separate traversal code for every shape. Composite gives an individual audience and a group a compatible operation.

    A leaf returns its authorised recipient. A group applies the same operation to its children and combines the results. Repeating this rule lets the caller traverse a nested audience. The example records visited node identifiers in seen so revisiting a node does not continue the same traversal indefinitely. The recipient contract must also say how repeated users from different groups are deduplicated.

    Real audience graphs need depth or size bounds and a policy for cycles and failures. A group send can reach some recipients before another send fails; the common interface does not make all deliveries atomic. Separate recipient selection from delivery where useful so the caller can inspect a bounded plan. When the domain has no meaningful nested structure, a simple collection and loop may be easier to understand.

    recipients(node, seen):
    if node.id in seen: return []
    seen.add(node.id)
    return node.users_or_recursive_children(seen)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Decorator

    We want to measure Sender.send() without placing timing code inside every provider adapter. A TimingSender receives another Sender, called inner. Its send(message) records a start time, calls inner.send(message), and records the elapsed time when that call finishes, including an error exit. It returns the original result or lets the original error continue.

    This is Decorator: an object adds behaviour around a collaborator while retaining its interface. Because TimingSender is also a Sender, the service can use it through the same contract. Startup code makes the added behaviour visible by assembling the wrapper around the selected adapter.

    Wrapper order matters. TimingSender(RetrySender(sender)) measures the whole logical call, including its attempts and waits. RetrySender(TimingSender(sender)) measures each attempt separately. A retry can also repeat an external effect, so it needs a contract for safe repetition and uncertain outcomes. Metrics alone cannot provide that contract. Keep essential notification decisions visible instead of scattering them through a long, difficult-to-inspect stack of wrappers.

    send(message):
    start = clock()
    try: return inner.send(message)
    finally: metrics.observe(clock() - start)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Facade

    A client that submits a notification should not have to coordinate every internal step itself. The subsystem may validate the command, select a template, build a delivery plan, and save a notification intent. A Facade offers a focused entry operation, such as submit(command), that carries out this coordination for its clients.

    In the example, submit first validates the command. It constructs the plan from the validated data and asks the intent store to persist it. The returned intent identifier tells the caller which accepted piece of work it can inspect later. Internal responsibilities can remain in separate collaborators even though the caller uses one entry point.

    The facade's response must state what has happened. Saving an intent is different from completing delivery to the recipient. Keep the facade focused on a coherent subsystem; adding every unrelated operation makes it difficult to change. A Proxy usually represents the same conceptual target while controlling its use. A Facade primarily simplifies how a caller works with several cooperating parts.

    submit(command):
    validated = validate(command)
    return intents.persist(render_plan(validated))
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Flyweight

    Suppose ten thousand notifications use the same version of a template. Parsing that template separately for every notification repeats data that does not change. Flyweight shares the reusable part while keeping each use's changing context separate.

    The application obtains one immutable parsed template for the selected version. To render notification A, it supplies A's recipient and variables; to render B, it supplies B's context to the same template. The template contains the common structure. The per-recipient context contains the information that must remain separate. This division reduces repeated storage without making recipients share their personal values.

    Putting recipient fields into the shared object could let one rendering affect another or disclose another user's data. Keep the shared part suitable for its allowed concurrent use. Measure memory pressure before adding complex pools: ordinary immutable reuse may be sufficient. Version selection, expiry, cache bounds, and lifetime still need their own rules. Flyweight identifies what can be shared; it does not supply a complete cache-management policy.

    template = parsed_templates.get(version)
output_a = render(template, context_a)
output_b = render(template, context_b)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Proxy

    A caller wants to read a document through read(document_id, actor). A Proxy presents that operation and controls access before forwarding it to the actual document reader. In the example, it checks the actor's current permission and calls target.read(document_id) only when the check permits it.

    The caller works through the target's interface while the proxy handles a particular aspect of its use. Other proxies can defer creating an expensive target until first use, or represent an object reached through a network. In each case, the proxy stands in for the same conceptual target, with additional rules around reaching it.

    Those rules remain part of the observable contract. A remote read may take time or fail with an uncertain result; a local-looking method name does not remove that behaviour. Avoid hiding unbounded retries or unlimited loading behind the interface. Facade usually offers a simpler entry to a cooperating subsystem, while Proxy controls access to a target that the caller conceptually already wants to use.

    read(document_id, actor):
    authorize(actor, document_id)
    return target.read(document_id)
    Think further · A notification job runs after both the creating request and the user session have ended. How should it obtain resources, and which authority should permit its action?

    Save durable job data and identifiers instead of capturing a request connection or session object. When execution begins, create a job scope, obtain current resources under a documented owner, load the required state, and release those resources when the job finishes or fails. The request and job now have separate ownership boundaries.

    The application must also choose an authorisation policy. Some jobs represent work validly accepted earlier; others must recheck current membership or permission before acting. Make that decision explicit and retain only the necessary context. A long-running job must not silently treat an expired user session as continuing authority.

    Remember: Identify a structural pattern by the relationship it changes. A wrapper can translate, extend, simplify, or guard, and each purpose carries a different behavioural contract.

    Try applying it: TimingSender(RetrySender(sender)) and RetrySender(TimingSender(sender)) both record durations. Which measures a logical call and which measures attempts, and what further contract makes the retries safe?

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.6

    Behavioral patterns

    Prerequisites: 6.5 · Structural patterns11 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A service chooses a pricing rule; a payment changes from pending to captured; a receipt command waits to be executed. Each case needs a different decision to be made explicit. We will follow ten behavioural patterns through their operations and compare the changes each makes easy.

    6.6.1 · Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Chain of Responsibility, Template Method, Iterator, Mediator, Memento, Visitor

    Choosing a pricing rule, reacting to a change, and advancing a payment's lifecycle are different kinds of behaviour. Behavioural patterns help place those decisions and interactions where they can be understood and changed.

    Strategy supplies a selected algorithm, Observer distributes reactions, Command represents a requested action, and State organises lifecycle-dependent behaviour. Chain of Responsibility arranges handlers, while Template Method fixes a process with selected extension points. Iterator controls traversal; Mediator coordinates collaborators; Memento supports local restoration; Visitor supplies operations over known node types. The individual examples explain these relationships. Use them where the actual source of variation warrants the structure; a direct function or small conditional may already express a stable case clearly.

    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Strategy

    A shop calculates an order price using either its ordinary pricing policy or an agreed partner policy. The order operation needs the resulting price, but it need not contain every formula. Strategy supplies the selected algorithm through a shared operation such as calculate(order).

    Assembly or policy-selection code chooses a strategy, and the caller invokes that strategy through the calculation contract. Adding another pricing policy then adds an implementation rather than another branch throughout the callers. The strategies must agree on what the result means: its amount and currency, permitted rounding, errors, and any effects. Matching a method name alone is insufficient.

    A function can serve as a strategy when that is the simplest expression of the algorithm. One stable formula may need no additional structure. Strategy varies a policy that can be selected for an operation. State, by comparison, varies behaviour according to an entity's valid lifecycle: a caller cannot choose a payment's captured state simply as a different calculation preference.

    price = pricing_strategy.calculate(order)
require(price.currency == order.currency)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Observer

    A local draft changes, and both a preview and a word-count display should update. The draft can keep a set of subscribed observers and notify them after a change. Each observer implements the agreed callback, so the draft does not have to know the concrete preview or counter. This is Observer, a one-to-many arrangement for reactions to change.

    First an observer subscribes. After the subject changes, it obtains the defined subscriber set and calls each observer according to the notification policy. The example takes a snapshot of the set for traversal, so subscription changes during a callback do not silently change that traversal's membership. The policy must still define ordering and whether callbacks run inline.

    If one callback is slow or throws, decide whether later observers continue and how the problem is reported. End subscriptions when their owners finish, or the subject may retain unwanted objects. These callbacks and subscriptions live in process memory. A reaction that must survive a crash needs durable publication and recovery rules in addition to local observation.

    for observer in snapshot(subscribers):
    notify_under_defined_failure_policy(observer, event)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Command

    Instead of immediately calling a receipt-sending function, the application can create SendReceipt(order_id, operation_id). This object represents a requested action as explicit data. A handler later reads the command, checks whether the action is currently allowed, and performs it. This is Command.

    Giving the intention its own representation lets the application pass it between components, record it for audit, or schedule it for later execution. The order identifier names the subject, while the operation identifier can help identify repeated attempts under a defined duplicate-handling policy. An event serves a different purpose: it records a fact already accepted, rather than asking a handler to act.

    If commands must survive restart, save versioned, serialisable domain data. A closure holding a request's open connection cannot provide that lifetime. At execution, the handler obtains valid resources and applies the chosen authorisation and current-state rules. Repeating a command can repeat an external effect unless the handler and provider protocol prevent it. Representing or storing the intention alone does not establish safe retry behaviour.

    command = SendReceipt(order_id, operation_id)
handler.handle(command)
# Handler checks current authorization and state
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    State

    A payment awaiting capture and a captured payment permit different actions. The captured payment may accept a refund request; the pending one must not behave as if money has already been captured. State organises these behaviour changes around the payment's lifecycle.

    When evidence arrives, the application checks whether the pair of current state and event is an allowed transition. It then computes the next state and saves the related changes atomically at the required persistence boundary. In the example, verified settlement moves a pending payment to captured. An event without the required evidence, or one that is invalid from the current state, must be handled explicitly.

    Separate state objects can hold the behaviour for each lifecycle stage, but a small transition table is often clearer. The central requirement is that lifecycle rules control the change. A pricing Strategy may be selected as an interchangeable policy; a payment state follows its history and evidence. The caller cannot bypass those rules by selecting whichever state would permit the action it wants.

    require((payment.state, event.kind) in allowed_transitions)
payment.state = next_state(payment.state, event)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Chain of Responsibility

    An incoming request must be authenticated, checked against its request budget, and parsed before the application handles it. We can connect handlers into a Chain of Responsibility. Each handler applies its part of the contract and either rejects, handles, transforms, or passes the request onward.

    In the example, authentication runs first. If it permits the request, rate limiting decides whether to admit the work. Parsing then produces the input for the application. The nested expression auth(rate_limit(parse(application))) assembles that order; it does not mean every request necessarily reaches the innermost handler. A rejecting handler ends its path according to the response contract.

    Continuation must be explicit. Forgetting to call the next handler can silently swallow work, while changing the order can change cost or policy. For example, expensive parsing before admission consumes resources even for work that will be rejected. This arrangement coordinates calls during execution. A multi-stage operation that must continue after a process crash also needs persisted progress and recovery; the chain alone provides neither.

    auth(rate_limit(parse(application)))(request)
# Each handler has explicit rejection and continuation rules
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Template Method

    Every supported import must validate its input, transform it into the application's representation, and commit the result in that order. CSV and another format may need different transformations, but neither should skip validation. Template Method keeps the shared sequence in one operation while exposing selected steps for customisation.

    In the example, run(input) calls validate(input), then transform(input), then commit(result). A specialised implementation supplies the format-specific transformation. Inheritance commonly expresses this arrangement: the base process defines run, and subclasses implement a permitted step. The fixed process must still arrange resource cleanup when any step fails.

    The extension contract determines which steps may vary and which ordering rules must hold. If a subclass can bypass validation or commit an incomplete transformation, the template no longer protects the intended process. When several steps need independent variation, composed strategies can be easier to combine than a growing subclass hierarchy. Use Template Method where one stable process has a small set of controlled extension points.

    run(input):
    validate(input)
    result = transform(input)
    return commit(result)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Iterator

    A caller wants to read records one at a time without knowing how they are stored. An Iterator maintains the current traversal position and supplies the next item until the sequence ends. The underlying collection can be an array, a tree, or a database query.

    This hides traversal mechanics while leaving their important behaviour in the contract. The caller needs to know the ordering, how end-of-stream is reported, and what happens if the underlying data changes during traversal. A lazy database iterator may fetch more rows only when the caller asks for them. It can therefore keep a cursor and connection open between iterations.

    In the example, the iterator is used inside a bounded cursor scope. Finishing the loop or exiting through an error must release the associated resources. A slow consumer can otherwise occupy a scarce connection for a long time, and closing the owner early can make the next read fail. For a small bounded result, fetching a list and releasing the connection before returning may offer a simpler lifetime contract.

    with open_bounded_cursor(query) as rows:
    for row in rows:
        consume(row)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Mediator

    Checkout needs to coordinate inventory and payment. If each collaborator directly calls the other whenever something happens, their knowledge of one another can grow difficult to follow. A Mediator receives their outcomes and decides the next action for this particular process.

    In the example, the coordinator asks inventory for a reservation and asks payments for authorisation under an operation identifier. It then interprets both outcomes and chooses the permitted next step. Inventory need not know the payment API, and the payment collaborator need not know the reservation implementation. The coordination rule has a clear home.

    The mediator still needs explicit treatment of failure and uncertain outcomes. Keep its responsibility focused so it does not become an object containing every application rule. If these calls cross systems and progress must survive restarts, a durable workflow orchestrator may implement the coordination with saved state and recovery. Mediator names the object relationship; it does not itself make the sequence persistent or make inventory and payment one atomic operation.

    reservation = inventory.reserve(command)
outcome = payments.authorize(command.operation_id)
coordinate_outcomes(reservation, outcome)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Memento

    Before changing a draft, the editor asks it for a snapshot of the values needed to restore its present local state. After an unwanted edit, the editor passes that snapshot back to restore(). Memento supports this capture and restoration without requiring every caller to read and rewrite the draft's internal fields.

    The draft defines what belongs in the snapshot. If editable paragraph data is copied appropriately, later edits do not change the saved version. If the snapshot merely stores a reference to the same mutable paragraph object, an edit can change both the current draft and the supposed snapshot. Ownership and copying rules are therefore part of making restoration meaningful.

    Restoration has a defined local scope. Returning the draft to earlier values cannot retract an email that was sent during the intervening operation or reverse a payment at a provider. Those effects require their own recovery or compensation arrangements. Use Memento when the supported state and restoration behaviour are clear; backups, event histories, and external compensation address broader and different recovery questions.

    before = draft.snapshot_owned_values()
draft.apply(edit)
draft.restore(before)
# No claim about undoing external effects
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Visitor

    A document tree has known node kinds, such as text and image. We want to add an export operation that handles each kind without placing all export logic inside the node classes. A Visitor groups the type-specific behaviour for that operation.

    During traversal, each node dispatches to the appropriate visitor operation, such as export_text or export_image. The example expresses the same decision with pattern matching on node.kind. Another visitor can perform validation over those same known kinds. This is useful when the structure is fairly stable and we expect to add operations over it.

    The trade-off appears when the structure changes. Adding a new node kind may require updating every visitor so each operation can handle it correctly. Define unknown-node handling: silently skipping an unfamiliar node could lose content during export. Some languages make pattern matching simpler than a separate visitor class hierarchy. Choose the representation that makes the known variants and each operation's coverage clear.

    visit(node):
    match node.kind:
        case "text": return export_text(node)
        case "image": return export_image(node)
        case _: raise UnsupportedNode
    Think further · A notification job runs after both the creating request and the user session have ended. How should it obtain resources, and which authority should permit its action?

    Save durable job data and identifiers instead of capturing a request connection or session object. When execution begins, create a job scope, obtain current resources under a documented owner, load the required state, and release those resources when the job finishes or fails. The request and job now have separate ownership boundaries.

    The application must also choose an authorisation policy. Some jobs represent work validly accepted earlier; others must recheck current membership or permission before acting. Make that decision explicit and retain only the necessary context. A long-running job must not silently treat an expired user session as continuing authority.

    Remember: Place each algorithm, reaction, intention, transition, or coordination rule where its changes belong. The object arrangement must also state ordering, failure, and resource behaviour where these affect the operation.

    Try applying it: A caller can choose a discount strategy, but cannot arbitrarily choose “captured” as a payment’s state. Which evidence and transition rules explain the difference?

    PART 2 / UNIT 06 / CHAPTER 6.7

    Enterprise patterns & boundaries

    Prerequisites: 6.6 · Behavioral patterns5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A reservation service must load a record, check a rule, and save related changes together. A screen may need a simpler view of the same data. We will separate these responsibilities using four enterprise patterns and identify the precise database boundary at which a commit takes effect.

    6.7.1 · Repository, Unit of Work, Specification, CQRS, and dependency boundaries

    A reservation operation must find data, decide whether a change is allowed, and save related changes. A Repository gives the application data operations. A Specification names a rule such as eligibility. A Unit of Work places related local changes under one commit decision. CQRS separates models for commands and queries when their needs differ.

    The following examples explain each boundary in more detail. These roles can all exist inside one process and database. A Unit of Work still needs rollback and cleanup, and its local commit cannot atomically commit an unrelated provider's remote effect. CQRS also does not require event sourcing or separately deployed services. Choose the boundaries from the behaviour and data guarantees the application actually needs.

    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Repository

    A reservation service needs to load a reservation, apply its confirmation rule, and save it. A Repository offers these data operations in the application's vocabulary while a concrete adapter performs SQL or other storage work. The service can use a repository contract without knowing table names and query syntax.

    In the example, get_for_update(reservation_id) obtains the reservation under the required update rules. The service calls confirm(payment_evidence), then asks the repository to save the changed record. The contract must state whether these calls share a transaction, who commits, and which outcomes represent missing data, conflict, or storage failure. Returning a record must also say whether it remains usable after a connection closes.

    The right boundary follows the data rule. A repository for each table can split values that need to change atomically as one aggregate. Also bound queries and expose relevant costs: a simple method name must not conceal an unlimited remote load or an unowned live cursor. A test substitute helps check service decisions, but real storage checks are needed to establish actual commit and recovery behaviour.

    reservation = repository.get_for_update(reservation_id)
reservation.confirm(payment_evidence)
repository.save(reservation)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Unit of Work

    To reserve a seat, the application changes inventory and inserts a reservation record. If both are in one transactional database, we want one commit decision: save both local changes or save neither. A Unit of Work groups the changes and owns the transaction resources for that operation.

    The application opens the unit, asks its inventory repository to reserve the seat, and asks its reservation repository to add the record. These repositories use the unit's transaction instead of committing independently. The explicit commit then makes the grouped changes durable according to the database's contract. If the operation fails before commit, the owning scope must roll back unfinished work and release resources.

    Keep this boundary short and precise. A remote payment provider is not a participant in the local database transaction merely because its call appears inside the same language scope. Rolling back the database cannot undo a provider charge. External effects need their own identity, outcome, and recovery protocol. The Unit of Work's atomicity follows the actual transaction boundary, rather than the indentation of the program.

    with unit_of_work() as uow:
    uow.inventory.reserve(seat)
    uow.reservations.add(record)
    uow.commit()
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    Specification

    A refund rule may ask whether a payment is captured, still within its refund period, and otherwise eligible. We can express that decision as a named predicate: RefundPolicy.satisfied_by(payment, now). A predicate returns whether the supplied values meet a condition. Specification gives a reusable rule such an explicit form and, where useful, lets rules be combined.

    The evaluation uses the payment state and time supplied to it. A successful result does not reserve that state. Another operation could refund the payment before this caller writes its change. In the example, refund_if_still_eligible(payment.version) performs the transition only if the relevant current conditions or version still permit it. The rule and the atomic update must agree.

    A specification may also be translated into a storage query for selection. That translation must preserve the same time, null-value, and access semantics as the in-memory decision. A plain function is often enough for one rule. Add a composable expression framework when shared rule composition or query translation gives a concrete benefit.

    eligible = RefundPolicy.satisfied_by(payment, now)
if eligible:
    repository.refund_if_still_eligible(payment.version)
    PATTERN / MECHANISM, USE, AND COST

    CQRS

    Capturing a payment needs a model that checks allowed transitions and records a valid change. Displaying an account statement needs a convenient arrangement of dates, descriptions, and amounts. Command Query Responsibility Segregation, or CQRS, separates the models used to change data and to answer queries when these needs differ enough to justify it.

    A command such as capture(payment_id, operation_id) goes through the write model's rules. A query such as account_statement(account_id) uses the read model's shape. A projection can update the read model from accepted changes. If that work runs later, a successful command may be followed by a statement that has not caught up yet. The query contract must explain that freshness, and the projection needs defined recovery and rebuilding behaviour.

    The models can live in one process and use one database. Event sourcing and separate services are additional decisions, rather than requirements of CQRS. With one simple model that already supports both operations, separate models may add more synchronisation and maintenance than they save. Choose the separation for actual differences in rules, access patterns, or query needs.

    commands.capture(payment_id, operation_id)
statement = queries.account_statement(account_id)
# Projection lag is part of the query contract

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · lifetime identities

    singleton = object()
def new_scope(): return {"scoped": object()}
a, b = new_scope(), new_scope()
assert a["scoped"] is a["scoped"]
assert a["scoped"] is not b["scoped"]
assert object() is not object()
assert singleton is singleton

    The code creates one singleton reference and two separate scope dictionaries, a and b. Each scope stores one object under "scoped". Looking up that key twice in a returns the same object; looking it up in b returns a different object. Calling object() twice models two transient creations, while reading singleton twice returns the one application-owned reference.

    The assertions compare identity, meaning whether two references point to the same object. They demonstrate reuse rules in one process. They do not implement a DI container, actual request handling, or disposal. A real scoped resource also needs cleanup at scope exit, and a long-lived service must not keep using it after that boundary.

    Download the executable mechanism collection ↓ · Follow the connected complete design →

    Think further · A notification job runs after both the creating request and the user session have ended. How should it obtain resources, and which authority should permit its action?

    Save durable job data and identifiers instead of capturing a request connection or session object. When execution begins, create a job scope, obtain current resources under a documented owner, load the required state, and release those resources when the job finishes or fails. The request and job now have separate ownership boundaries.

    The application must also choose an authorisation policy. Some jobs represent work validly accepted earlier; others must recheck current membership or permission before acting. Make that decision explicit and retain only the necessary context. A long-running job must not silently treat an expired user session as continuing authority.

    Remember: Repositories expose data operations, Specifications express rules, a Unit of Work owns a local commit decision, and CQRS separates command and query models. State each boundary’s actual guarantees.

    Try applying it: A Unit of Work updates inventory and inserts a reservation in one database, then calls an external payment provider. Which changes can its local commit cover, and what happens to that claim if the provider reply is lost?

    PART 2 / UNIT 07 / CHAPTER 7.1

    Layers, monoliths & ports

    Prerequisites: Object-Oriented and Modular Software Design, Design Patterns, Dependency Injection, and Object Lifecycles6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A shopping application can separate input, policy, and storage without putting them on different machines. Compare architecture styles by their dependency rules and the changes they help contain.

    7.1.1 · Layered/N-tier architecture

    A shopping request arrives through a controller, invokes an application operation, applies pricing rules, and stores the order. Layered architecture gives these different kinds of work clear places: presentation, application coordination, domain policy, and infrastructure.

    The layers can all run in one process. Deploying them as separate physical tiers is another choice. Use the division to protect useful rules: a controller should not bypass order validation simply because it can reach an SQL helper. Follow a change, such as a new pricing rule, to see whether the boundary helps. Classes that only forward every call add work without necessarily hiding any detail.

    7.1.2 · Modular monoliths

    Catalog, orders, and payments can be modules of one deployable application. Each exposes operations and owns its data, while calls between them remain local. This is a modular monolith.

    The word “modular” matters. If every module writes every table, changing a payment record can still break the whole program. Use agreed interfaces and enforce dependency rules through review or useful automated checks. This arrangement keeps deployment and local transactions relatively simple while giving business responsibilities separate homes. Later extraction remains possible, but it is an option supported by the boundaries, rather than a benefit obtained automatically by naming folders.

    7.1.3 · Monolith vs microservices

    Suppose inventory needs to scale independently and has a team ready to operate it. Making it a separate service may provide a useful deployment and ownership boundary. It also replaces some local calls with network calls that can time out or partially fail.

    Microservices aim for useful independent deployment and operation. A monolith can be well organised, while several services can remain tightly coupled. If five services must release together for each change, ask how much independence was gained. Compare the motivation for extraction with the added work in data coordination, compatibility, monitoring, and recovery. A process boundary should solve a demonstrated problem.

    7.1.4 · Clean Architecture

    An order rule should be testable without constructing an HTTP response or starting a web framework. Clean Architecture supports this by making framework and storage details depend on interfaces used by the application's policy.

    The inward arrows in its usual diagrams describe source dependencies. During execution, a use case can still call an outer storage adapter through an injected interface. Avoid making core rules depend on ORM-specific records or transport response objects. The separation costs mappings and contracts, so choose a proportionate version for a small application. The important question is whether policy can be understood and exercised without unrelated infrastructure details.

    7.1.5 · Hexagonal/Ports and Adapters

    An order can be created from a web request or a command-line tool. Both adapters can invoke the same application operation. Likewise, an SQL adapter and a test repository can satisfy the application's storage needs.

    Hexagonal architecture calls these application-facing contracts ports and their implementations adapters. An inbound port expresses an operation the application offers; an outbound port expresses work it needs from elsewhere. Design ports around those needs rather than copying an entire vendor API. The drawing does not imply separate machines. Test application decisions with controlled adapters, then separately check real encoding, transactions, and failure behaviour at the external boundaries.

    7.1.6 · Onion Architecture

    Onion Architecture arranges domain policy, application services, and infrastructure so that dependencies point toward the core rules. An order rule can then use an application-owned repository contract rather than import database-specific code.

    Its vocabulary overlaps with Clean and Hexagonal Architecture, and teams draw the layers differently. Compare the actual dependency and ownership rules instead of treating the shape as a guarantee. Can pricing run without a web server? Does a failed write remain visible to the caller? These questions reveal whether the separation helps. Extra layers are worthwhile when they protect such properties, rather than simply matching a diagram.

    Think further · What evidence would justify extracting payments into a separate service?

    Look for stable capability ownership, different scaling or isolation needs, and an operating team prepared for network and version failures. Compare those benefits with added data coordination and recovery. Preserve existing payment invariants and histories through migration. A separate deployment is useful only when the required independence can actually be exercised.

    Remember: Code boundaries and deployment boundaries solve related but different problems.

    Try applying it: What benefit would justify turning a well-separated module into a remote service?
