    PART 2 / UNIT 07 / CHAPTER 7.2

    Model a bounded context

    Prerequisites: 7.1 · Layers, monoliths & ports4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Catalog and fulfilment use different meanings for a product. Model those meanings with domain experts, then choose where rules need an atomic aggregate and which facts should become events.

    7.2.1 · Domain-Driven Design (DDD)

    Ask a shop's merchandising and warehouse staff what “available stock” means. Merchandising may mean stock that can be advertised. A reservation worker may mean units that can still be promised to a buyer. Treating both as one unexamined field can produce wrong decisions.

    Domain-Driven Design develops a model with the people who understand the business. The model names concepts and makes their rules explicit. Use this effort where business meaning is complex or disputed. A simple lookup table may need only straightforward data handling. DDD's value comes from clearer decisions and shared understanding, rather than assigning a class to every database row.

    7.2.2 · Bounded contexts and ubiquitous language

    Catalog's Product may describe a title, images, and marketing categories. Fulfilment's Item may describe a physical unit and its shelf location. Both models can be correct for their own work.

    A bounded context states where a model and its vocabulary apply. Within it, a ubiquitous language gives team members and code consistent names for the business concepts. Between contexts, translate deliberately and identify who owns each fact. One universal Product schema may obscure real differences. A context is a modelling boundary; deciding whether it becomes a separate service, repository, or team requires further reasons.

    7.2.3 · Aggregates, entities, value objects, domain services

    An order's line items and total must agree when it is committed. We can give an Order root responsibility for changing those related values together. An aggregate is this kind of consistency boundary, with a root controlling changes to its members.

    Entities have identity through change; value objects are distinguished by their values. A domain service can express a rule that does not belong to one entity. Keep an aggregate focused on invariants that need a common atomic change. Putting the entire shop into one aggregate creates contention and loading costs. Rules spanning aggregates need an explicit coordination design; an object reference alone does not create a distributed transaction.

    7.2.4 · Domain events

    After an order is accepted, other parts of the system may need to know. OrderPlaced records a business fact. Give it a stable identity, clear time meaning, and information that its intended consumers can interpret across versions.

    Creating an event object in memory is not the same as publishing it reliably. The process may commit the order and die before sending the event. An outbox records order state and publication intent in one local transaction, then relays the event. Consumers still need to handle repeated and delayed delivery. Define a fact's meaning before deciding how the broker will carry it.

    Think further · What evidence would justify extracting payments into a separate service?

    Look for stable capability ownership, different scaling or isolation needs, and an operating team prepared for network and version failures. Compare those benefits with added data coordination and recovery. Preserve existing payment invariants and histories through migration. A separate deployment is useful only when the required independence can actually be exercised.

    Remember: A model is useful within a context whose vocabulary, ownership, and invariants are understood.

    Try applying it: Which purchase-time facts should an order retain when the current catalog changes?

    PART 2 / UNIT 07 / CHAPTER 7.3

    Keep business policy inside

    Prerequisites: 7.2 · Model a bounded context5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    An order rule should not be rewritten in controllers, broker configuration, and provider adapters. Assign the business decision, its coordination, and its technical effects to clear owners.

    7.3.1 · Dependency rules and module boundaries

    Suppose the orders module updates a payment table directly. It now knows the payment representation and can bypass payment rules. A payment interface gives that interaction a controlled place.

    Dependency rules specify which modules may know about or call others. Enforce important boundaries with appropriate import checks, database permissions, or architecture tests. A cycle can reveal that coordination has no clear owner. Shared helpers also need scrutiny: one “common model” can accidentally force unrelated contexts to change together. Where meanings genuinely differ, use an explicit translation rather than sharing a type merely because its fields currently look similar.

    7.3.2 · Business logic vs orchestration vs infrastructure

    “A refunded order must not ship” is a business rule. Asking the payment service for a refund and then updating progress is orchestration. Encoding and sending a provider request is infrastructure work.

    These responsibilities may begin in one function, but distinguishing them helps assign tests and handle failures. Test the shipping rule as a decision. Test orchestration across success and partial failure. Test the provider adapter against its actual protocol. Moving a sequence onto a queue does not make its business rules belong to the broker. Keep the owner of each decision visible even when the execution arrangement changes.

    7.3.3 · Controllers, services, repositories, adapters

    A controller reads a request and builds a response. An application service coordinates an operation. A repository offers data operations, and an adapter connects a contract to a particular protocol or technology.

    These are roles, not required class-name endings. A service can be a function; a domain service is not necessarily a network service. Examine the work the code performs. If a controller calculates prices and retries transactions, creating an empty “services” directory has not moved those responsibilities. Choose names and boundaries that help readers follow one real operation from its input to its result.

    7.3.4 · Anti-corruption layers

    A legacy payment provider may use “settled” for an authorisation that our application still considers pending. Copying that label directly would import the provider's meaning into our own model.

    An anti-corruption layer translates the external model into the local one. It maps known states, retains useful provider references, and handles unknown meanings explicitly. This adds mapping and maintenance work, but keeps external quirks from spreading through business code. Never turn an unmapped result silently into success. Where the provider's state is uncertain or different from ours, preserve enough information to investigate and reconcile it.

    7.3.5 · Event-driven architecture

    An accepted order can trigger a receipt without making checkout wait for email delivery. Event-driven architecture allows components to react independently to recorded events. This can remove a synchronous dependency from the user's path.

    Decide which steps may actually be delayed. Inventory and payment requirements may require stronger coordination than receipts. Event processing also adds delivery, ordering, replay, and monitoring work. Name the owner of each event and state how it is persisted, recognised on redelivery, and recovered after a failure. A broker transports messages; the application must still arrange for the required business outcome.

    Think further · What evidence would justify extracting payments into a separate service?

    Look for stable capability ownership, different scaling or isolation needs, and an operating team prepared for network and version failures. Compare those benefits with added data coordination and recovery. Preserve existing payment invariants and histories through migration. A separate deployment is useful only when the required independence can actually be exercised.

    Remember: Preserve domain meaning while translating transport, storage, and external models at explicit boundaries.

    Try applying it: How would an anti-corruption layer handle a provider status whose name differs from your own model?

    PART 2 / UNIT 07 / CHAPTER 7.4

    Evolution without a distributed monolith

    Prerequisites: 7.3 · Keep business policy inside5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Five services always deploy together and share writable tables. Review whether the process split delivered independence, and use evidence to evolve toward a more manageable design.

    7.4.1 · Serverless and function-oriented architectures

    A cloud function can process an uploaded file when an event arrives. The platform manages invocation and some execution capacity, but the function still has deadlines, concurrency limits, credentials, and possible retries.

    Treat function-local memory as temporary unless the platform guarantees otherwise. Store required progress durably, and recognise repeated invocations before applying repeated effects. Small independently triggered tasks can fit this arrangement well. A long sequence with human review or remote uncertainty needs a durable owner for its state, often a workflow engine. “Serverless” changes operating responsibilities; it leaves application correctness and recovery decisions to be designed.

    7.4.2 · Evolutionary architecture

    The application must keep tenant data isolated while releases change its internals. A check that attempts a cross-tenant read can protect that property during development. Similar checks can protect module boundaries, migration compatibility, or a latency budget.

    Evolutionary architecture uses such feedback to change a system while preserving important qualities. A fitness check should express a useful property, rather than freeze an incidental class layout. Record why a choice exists and when evidence should prompt reconsideration. Evolution may involve removing an unnecessary service or simplifying a contract. It is a process of guided change, not an obligation to replace the architecture repeatedly.

    7.4.3 · Technical vs business boundaries

    Controllers and database adapters are technical groupings. Orders and fulfilment are business capabilities. The two kinds of division can coexist: each business module can have its own internal input, policy, and storage code.

    Making separate network services for “validation” and “SQL” may force every business operation to call both. Begin with ownership of decisions and facts, then choose the technical arrangement inside those boundaries. A bounded context describes a model's scope. It does not automatically dictate a deployment or team structure. Follow actual business changes to see which parts need to evolve together.

    7.4.4 · Distributed monolith antipattern

    Five services share writable tables and must be released together. Most requests synchronously pass through all five. Although deployed separately, they cannot change or fail independently. This is commonly called a distributed monolith.

    Network boundaries now add timeouts and debugging work without delivering the expected independence. Clarify data ownership and contracts before promising independent services. Sometimes consolidating unstable boundaries into a modular application is the easier improvement. In other cases, redesigning the interactions can justify the separation. Judge progress by independent behaviour and manageable failures, rather than the number of deployed processes.

    7.4.5 · When not to use microservices

    A small team is still discovering how orders and fulfilment should work. Splitting them into many services immediately would add contract and operating work while the boundaries are changing. A modular monolith can provide a simpler starting point.

    Consider extraction when a stable capability has distinct scaling, isolation, or ownership needs and the team can operate it. Include distributed transactions, version compatibility, telemetry, security, and incident response in the cost. Neither low traffic nor a service count settles the choice. Prefer the design that meets the actual requirements and can be changed and recovered by the people responsible for it.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Pseudocode · module contract

    place_order(command):
    priced = catalog.quote(command.items)
    reservation = inventory.reserve(command.items)
    payment = payments.authorize(command.operation_id, priced.total)
    return orders.record_outcomes(priced, reservation, payment)
# Modules expose contracts; they do not update each other's private tables.

    The modules communicate through their operations rather than writing each other's private tables. Their results let the caller record what actually happened.

    Calling three remote services in this order does not create one atomic transaction. Some local changes can share a deliberate transaction, while external effects need a workflow and recovery rules.

    Look for stable capability ownership, different scaling or isolation needs, and an operating team prepared for network and version failures. Compare those benefits with added data coordination and recovery. Preserve existing payment invariants and histories through migration. A separate deployment is useful only when the required independence can actually be exercised.

    Remember: Change architecture for demonstrated ownership, load, or failure needs while protecting existing properties.

    Try applying it: When might consolidating services make the system easier to change and recover?

    PART 2 / UNIT 08 / CHAPTER 8.1

    Model resources and messages

    Prerequisites: Introduction to System Design, Networking Foundations for System Design6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A client asks to create a payment. It needs a clear resource identity, valid amount representation, possible states, and bounded ways to read results. Build the contract before selecting request syntax.

    8.1.1 · API fundamentals and interface contracts

    A client calls create-payment. It needs to know the amount units, currency, permitted caller, returned states, and what to do if no reply arrives. A field schema alone cannot tell it whether retrying might charge twice.

    An API is an interface together with a communication contract. Describe inputs, results, effects, errors, timing, operation identity, and supported evolution. Begin with concrete histories: successful creation, invalid input, a repeated request, and a lost reply after submission. These expose decisions a transport framework cannot make for you. Keep a definite provider decline distinct from an operation whose outcome is still uncertain.

    8.1.2 · REST, GraphQL, gRPC, RPC

    The same payment capability can be exposed in several ways. REST emphasises resources and HTTP semantics. GraphQL lets clients query a typed graph. gRPC commonly supplies schema-defined remote calls and streaming. RPC more generally models operations called across a boundary.

    Choose by what clients need, how the API will evolve, and the cost of serving it. GraphQL can reduce unwanted data transfer but needs query-cost and field-access controls. An RPC name can make an action clear while leaving retries and compatibility to be specified. Compare complete operation histories and tooling, rather than assuming a request syntax establishes reliability or performance.

    8.1.3 · Resource modeling

    A payment and its refund are related, but they have different identities and lifecycles. A refund may be requested later, authorised separately, and succeed or fail independently.

    One resource model uses POST /payments, GET /payments/{id}, and POST /payments/{id}/refunds. The refund then has its own amount, status, and operation identifier. Resource modelling gives these continuing business objects clear identities. Avoid a generic /execute endpoint that hides every meaning, while also avoiding a forced CRUD model that makes domain actions unclear. Let ownership and allowed state transitions guide the interface.

    8.1.4 · Request/response schemas

    A request can contain valid JSON yet ask to charge a negative amount. Parsing establishes structural validity; application validation checks business meaning. Check both.

    Bound body size, collection length, and supported encodings before expensive work. Decide how unknown fields are handled so clients can evolve predictably. Return a stable machine-readable error code with a useful, safe message and a request identifier. Avoid exposing secrets or raw provider internals. Consider strict clients as well as tolerant ones: a new field can affect a client that rejects unknown input. The schema and its compatibility policy belong together.

    8.1.5 · Status codes and error models

    The server returns 201 after creating a payment resource whose status is pending. The resource exists; money has not necessarily been captured. Similarly, 202 indicates acceptance for processing rather than final approval.

    HTTP status describes the protocol response, while the body can describe the business operation's state. A timeout supplies neither a definitive approval nor a decline. Use application error codes to distinguish invalid input, conflicts, denied access, and uncertain submitted work. This lets clients choose an appropriate next action. Turning every provider problem into the same generic error can hide whether the caller should correct input, wait, or query an existing operation.

    8.1.6 · Pagination, filtering, sorting

    A request for every payment can return too much data and consume too much memory. Pagination divides the collection into bounded responses. Define maximum page size, permitted filters, ordering, and access checks.

    Sorting only by creation time can leave rows with equal timestamps in an unstable order. Add a unique tie-breaker such as the payment identifier. Decide what happens while the collection changes between page requests. Neither offset nor cursor pagination automatically gives the client one frozen snapshot. Enforce tenant access in the query itself, rather than retrieving a large shared collection and hoping the client filters it correctly.

    Think further · Can finite storage support a permanent promise to recognise every old idempotency key?

    Not for an unbounded set of arbitrary distinct operations unless another constraint supplies a bound or persistent evidence elsewhere. Define key retention, expiry, reuse, and client expectations. A permanent business identity may require a durable record rather than an expiring cache. Make the promise fit the information the system can retain.

    Remember: An API describes behaviour and meaning as well as message shape.

    Try applying it: Why can creating a payment resource succeed before the provider captures money?

    PART 2 / UNIT 08 / CHAPTER 8.2

    Compatibility & idempotency

    Prerequisites: 8.1 · Model resources and messages4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A collection changes between pages, and a payment reply disappears before the client receives it. Use stable continuation and operation identities to give repeated calls a defined meaning.

    8.2.1 · Cursor vs offset pagination

    Suppose a client reads the first ten rows, then asks to skip ten. A new row inserted near the beginning shifts positions, so the second page may repeat or omit an item. This is a difficulty with offset pagination on changing data.

    A keyset cursor instead records the last ordered key, such as (created_at,id), and continues after that key. It can reduce skipping cost and these shifting-position problems. Updates to existing rows still need a stated consistency policy. Validate opaque cursors or protect their integrity, and bind them to the applicable filters and tenant. A cursor must not become a way to escape the original query's access rules.

    8.2.2 · API versioning and compatibility

    A payment amount changes from cents to dollars while its JSON type remains numeric. Old clients can now submit a hundred times the intended amount. Compatibility concerns meaning as well as syntax.

    Adding an optional field is safer for tolerant clients than changing an existing field's meaning, but strict validators and enum handling may still break. Use an explicit version policy, an overlap period, and evidence about old consumers. Test representative clients. A versioned URL is one tool; it does not migrate callers or update stored events. Plan the transition for every reader that still relies on the earlier contract.

    8.2.3 · Idempotency and idempotency keys

    A client retries a payment after losing its reply. It sends the same idempotency key so the server can recognise the original logical operation. The server must bind that key to the authenticated owner, request content, progress, and result.

    Enforce uniqueness and the required atomic updates in storage. If the same key arrives with a different amount, return a conflict instead of replaying an unrelated result. Define how long the key is remembered. A provider timeout may require querying or reconciling that provider before another submission. Local key storage alone cannot promise one external charge if the provider does not support the necessary operation identity and recovery behaviour.

    Think further · Can finite storage support a permanent promise to recognise every old idempotency key?

    Not for an unbounded set of arbitrary distinct operations unless another constraint supplies a bound or persistent evidence elsewhere. Define key retention, expiry, reuse, and client expectations. A permanent business identity may require a durable record rather than an expiring cache. Make the promise fit the information the system can retain.

    Remember: Compatibility preserves meanings; cursors and idempotency keys need scope, validation, and recovery rules.

    Try applying it: What should happen when an old idempotency key is reused with a different amount?

    PART 2 / UNIT 08 / CHAPTER 8.3

    Control access, load & long operations

    Prerequisites: 8.2 · Compatibility & idempotency5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A signed-in client can still ask for another tenant's payment or overload an export. Combine access, resource limits, deadlines, and durable progress with clear acknowledgment boundaries.

    8.3.1 · Authentication vs authorization at API boundaries

    A user signs in successfully, then requests payment 42. The server still needs to check whether that user owns or may view payment 42. Knowing an identity and granting an action are separate decisions.

    Authentication establishes identity under the chosen trust mechanism. Authorisation checks permission for this action on this resource. Derive tenant context from validated membership rather than trusting an arbitrary tenant_id field. A gateway can perform coarse checks, but the service with ownership information must enforce the resource rule. Apply appropriate identity checks to internal service callers too. An obscure identifier reduces guessing; it is not an access-control mechanism.

    8.3.2 · Rate limits and quotas

    A client makes too many expensive validation requests at once. A rate limit controls that pace, often with a specified burst allowance. A daily export quota instead caps accumulated use over a longer period or resource dimension.

    State the identity being limited, window, cost unit, retry guidance, and behaviour if the limiter fails. Per-tenant controls can protect neighbours from one noisy client. Per-user limits alone may miss coordinated abuse. Across regions, a strict global limit needs shared coordination or safely allocated local budgets. If enforcement is approximate, specify the approximation rather than silently giving every region the full global allowance.

    8.3.3 · Retries and timeouts

    A payment request has an overall deadline. Connection acquisition, each attempt, and any backoff must fit inside it. Passing only a fresh full timeout to every downstream call can make the total wait exceed the client's intended limit.

    Retry transient work only where repetition is safe. Exponential backoff with jitter spreads attempts but does not add capacity. If four layers each allow three attempts, one intent can cause up to 3⁴ = 81 downstream attempts. Choose a shared retry budget and propagate remaining time. Side effects additionally need a stable operation identity and a way to resolve outcomes that may already have committed.

    8.3.4 · Streaming APIs and long-running operations

    A report takes minutes to generate. Instead of holding the initial request open, the server can return an operation resource that the client polls or subscribes to. Required progress must be stored beyond the request's memory.

    A streaming API returns a sequence of messages and needs framing, buffer limits, cancellation, and possibly a resume policy. Decide whether disconnecting cancels the business job or only the connection. A slow reader should not accidentally hold an unbounded database transaction. Use bounded pages or an explicitly owned streaming resource. The interface must explain how work is tracked after the initiating client has gone away.

    8.3.5 · Webhooks and delivery acknowledgments

    A payment service sends a webhook announcing a completed operation. The receiver commits its local effect, but the success reply is lost. The sender retries, so the same event arrives again.

    Give webhooks stable event identifiers and a documented signature and timestamp-verification policy. The receiver should persist the required inbox or effect before acknowledging, then recognise redelivery. The sender needs bounded retries and a recovery policy. A 2xx reply establishes only what the receiver's contract promises; it does not mean every later downstream action is complete. Treat the acknowledgment as a named step in the delivery protocol.

    Think further · Can finite storage support a permanent promise to recognise every old idempotency key?

    Not for an unbounded set of arbitrary distinct operations unless another constraint supplies a bound or persistent evidence elsewhere. Define key retention, expiry, reuse, and client expectations. A permanent business identity may require a durable record rather than an expiring cache. Make the promise fit the information the system can retain.

    Remember: Admission, permission, and completion answer different questions and need separate enforcement.

    Try applying it: What can a webhook receiver acknowledge safely if its effect must survive a crash?

    PART 2 / UNIT 08 / CHAPTER 8.4

    Evolve a public contract

    Prerequisites: 8.3 · Control access, load & long operations5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    An event saved today may be replayed a year later. Keep schemas, consumer expectations, gateway roles, and documentation usable across that lifetime.

    8.4.1 · Schema evolution

    A restored consumer replays last year's events. It encounters fields and status values no current request uses. Deleting the old decoder can therefore break recovery even if today's API traffic works.

    Schema evolution applies to events and stored records as well as live requests. Preserve field meanings, defaults, version identity, and handling of unknown values. Test historical samples and any transformations used to read them. An extra field can also affect signatures or uniqueness rules, so “additive” does not automatically mean harmless. Plan compatibility for the full life of the data, including replay, backup restoration, and delayed clients.

    8.4.2 · Consumer-driven contracts

    A consumer expects a payment status to be either pending or final. A provider test that checks only “status is a string” misses that assumption. Consumer-driven contracts record what actual clients need from their provider.

    Run relevant provider checks before releasing a change, including representative errors and state behaviour. Keep the contracts focused on meaningful obligations rather than incidental JSON formatting. Schema tests alone cannot establish retry safety, authorisation, or pagination correctness. Use concrete histories for these behaviours. The contract is useful when it protects a real dependency while still allowing the provider to change internal implementation details.

    8.4.3 · API gateways and BFF

    A mobile screen needs three small pieces of data from several services. A Backend for Frontend, or BFF, can assemble the response around that client's needs. A gateway usually handles shared edge concerns, such as routing and coarse admission.

    Both add operating work and can become bottlenecks. Keep ownership checks in services that know the resource rules, and give the aggregation layer a clear owner. A universal BFF that every product must edit can reduce independence. If results are cached, define the key, tenant scope, and freshness. Aggregating private results does not make them safe for a shared public cache.

    8.4.4 · Public vs internal APIs

    Two internal services may release at different times and communicate over a network. Their API therefore still has compatibility, trust, load, and failure concerns. “Internal” does not mean that every request is valid or authorised.

    A public API usually needs longer compatibility commitments, discoverability, abuse protection, and support processes. State the intended audience and lifetime of both kinds. Internal interfaces can become important dependencies whose accidental behaviour is difficult to change. Document their meaningful guarantees early, and apply proportionate authentication, validation, and resource limits instead of relying solely on location inside a network.

    8.4.5 · API documentation and discoverability

    A developer needs to create a payment and recover if the reply is lost. Documentation that shows only a successful request leaves the most consequential decision unexplained.

    Include complete examples for validation errors, access denial, pagination, operation keys, timeouts, and pending states. A machine-readable schema can generate client types, while prose explains the behaviour those types cannot express. Keep examples aligned with the implementation and test the important ones. A sandbox must clearly distinguish simulated effects from real charges. Good discoverability means a reader can find the operation, understand its scope, and choose a supported recovery action when the usual sequence is interrupted.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · keyset continuation

    from mechanisms import keyset_page
rows = [(1,1,"A"), (1,2,"B"), (2,3,"C")]
assert keyset_page(rows, after=(1,1)) == rows[1:]

    The ordered time/ID pair gives equal timestamps a stable tie-breaker. Continuing after (1,1) returns the later rows in this fixed fixture.

    A real cursor also needs validation, query and tenant scope, and a rule for changes between pages. Keyset continuation does not itself freeze a changing dataset.

    Download the executable mechanism collection ↓ · Follow the connected complete design →

    Think further · Can finite storage support a permanent promise to recognise every old idempotency key?

    Not for an unbounded set of arbitrary distinct operations unless another constraint supplies a bound or persistent evidence elsewhere. Define key retention, expiry, reuse, and client expectations. A permanent business identity may require a durable record rather than an expiring cache. Make the promise fit the information the system can retain.

    Remember: Supported consumers include delayed and recovering readers, not only today's newest client.

    Try applying it: Which historical samples would you retain to check that a new decoder still supports recovery?

    PART 3 / UNIT 09 / CHAPTER 9.1

    Storage promises & database families

    Prerequisites: Introduction to System Design9 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A ledger, profile, chat history, and search index do not make the same promises. Compare their reads, changes, and recovery needs before assigning a storage family.

    9.1.1 · What data storage must guarantee

    A chat history, a payment ledger, and a thumbnail cache all store data, but losing a copy has different consequences. Before choosing technology, state what is accepted, when it is committed, how callers read it, and which failures it must survive.

    Identify the authoritative record and the recovery procedure. A database category does not establish its configured isolation, durability, or backup behaviour. Begin with access patterns and invariants, then compare implementations against them. This prevents a familiar product name from standing in for decisions about the actual service being built.

    9.1.2 · Relational databases and SQL

    A ledger can represent accounts and entries as related tables. Keys identify rows, foreign keys protect appropriate relationships, and transactions can group changes. SQL expresses operations on this relational model.

    Joins let queries combine related facts. Their cost depends on indexes, row counts, data distribution, and the chosen execution plan; a join is not inherently a scaling mistake. Normalised facts often provide a clear starting point for ownership and consistency. If a measured read path needs a repeated or precomputed representation, add it deliberately and state how it stays correct. The relational model and the physical query cost are related but different questions.

    9.1.3 · Document databases

    A user profile and its preferences can be stored as one nested document. A document database gives that unit an identity and often allows flexible structures. This can suit data usually read or changed together.

    Decide which structure is valid and how it evolves. Flexibility moves some checking into application conventions; it does not remove the schema. Also ask how large the document can grow and whether changes across documents need a shared transaction. Placing every chat message in one ever-growing user document mixes different growth and ownership needs. Design the document boundary around actual operations rather than convenient JSON syntax.

    9.1.4 · Key-value databases

    A session lookup already knows its identifier. A key-value store can retrieve the corresponding value directly, making this a natural access pattern. A key such as tenant:42:session:7 also makes the intended identity scope visible.

    Other queries, such as finding values by an arbitrary field, may need separately maintained structures. Check the selected store's read, write, expiry, and durability contract; key-value products do not all behave alike. A session's expiry and revocation policy must also be explicit. Retaining an old value after permissions change can be a security problem even when the key lookup itself is correct.

    9.1.5 · Wide-column stores

    A conversation history is often read by conversation identifier and message order. A wide-column design can use the conversation as a partition key and a sequence as an ordering dimension, supporting bounded history reads.

    Work through the largest room as well as the typical one. One huge or popular partition can dominate traffic despite many storage nodes. Model the queries first, and duplicate representations for different queries only with a maintenance plan. State which joins or integrity rules the application must enforce. The common storage pattern is useful guidance; exact guarantees still depend on the implementation.

    9.1.6 · Graph databases

    A fraud investigator may follow transfers from an account to devices, other accounts, and further transfers. When variable-depth relationships are central to the query, graph storage can make traversals convenient.

    A relational model can also represent edges, so compare actual operations rather than assuming relationships require a graph database. Bound traversal depth and fan-out: one high-degree node can create enormous work. Apply access checks during expansion, not only after collecting results. A traversal that crosses tenant boundaries can expose data even if its starting node was authorised. Query usefulness, cost, and permission rules must be designed together.

    9.1.7 · Time-series databases

    A temperature measurement has a time, value, and dimensions such as device identity. Time-series storage can exploit nearby timestamps, compression, and time-based retention for these measurements.

    Choose dimensions carefully. A unique request identifier on every metric can create too many distinct series. Also decide how to handle late readings, clock errors, corrections, and downsampling. A device timestamp records what its clock reported; it does not automatically establish causal order. Preserve ingestion time or a sequence where investigation needs that distinction. Time-based organisation helps when it matches the measurements and queries, rather than simply because a row contains a date.

    9.1.8 · Search indexes

    A search query needs matching and ranking rather than a transaction over the original record. An inverted index maps terms to document references and supports this retrieval path. It is commonly built from another authoritative store.

    If indexing is asynchronous, a new document may appear late and deleted content may remain in the index temporarily. Permission enforcement must remain correct during that lag. Keep source identity and version information so updates can be ordered and the index rebuilt. A search result is a derived serving representation; treating it as the only recoverable copy creates different and usually much harder ownership obligations.

    9.1.9 · Vector indexes: introductory architecture only

    An embedding converts content into a numerical vector. A vector index finds nearby vectors, often approximately, to retrieve candidate documents with similar representations. Its architecture must balance recall, memory, updates, distance calculations, and filtering.

    Preserve the source document and version that produced each embedding. The index is derived and needs a rebuild path. Approximate search can miss relevant items, and a similarity score establishes neither factual truth nor access permission. Apply the required tenant and resource checks to candidates. Choose this structure for a demonstrated similarity-search need, rather than as a replacement for authoritative records or exact constraints.

    Think further · How should restoration from a historical backup respect later deletion decisions?

    Restore into a controlled path, apply relevant deletion decisions, and reconcile raw and derived copies before serving. Rebuild indexes from the permitted current state rather than blindly expose an older snapshot. Keep deletion evidence narrow and purpose-limited. The backup and live-data lifecycle need a combined recovery procedure.

    Remember: Choose storage from operations and invariants, then verify the selected implementation's guarantees.

    Try applying it: What would make a document model suitable for a profile but unsuitable for an unbounded chat history?

    PART 3 / UNIT 09 / CHAPTER 9.2

    Files, objects & analytical layouts

    Prerequisites: 9.1 · Storage promises & database families4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A PDF, a checkout row, and an analytical revenue scan read different shapes of data. Separate storage interfaces and physical layouts from the logical facts they represent.

    9.2.1 · Object storage vs block vs file storage

    Object storage offers named blobs and metadata. Block storage offers addressable blocks. File storage offers a filesystem namespace and operations on files. These interfaces suit different callers.

    A PDF upload often fits object storage with separate application metadata. A database engine may require a filesystem backed by suitable block storage. Check the actual protocol and implementation rather than assuming category-wide guarantees. An uploaded object and a database reference are also separate changes: either can exist without the other after a failure. Track incomplete uploads, orphaned objects, and deletion so the application knows when a file is actually usable.

    9.2.2 · OLTP vs OLAP

    Checkout performs short transactions over current orders. A revenue report may scan years of payments. OLTP describes the first kind of transactional workload; OLAP describes the second kind of analytical work.

    A large report on the checkout database can compete for memory and I/O. Copying or transforming data into an analytical store can reduce that interference, but adds lag, lineage, and reconciliation requirements. One engine may serve both uses adequately at a smaller scale. Measure their interaction before introducing another system, and decide how current analytical results need to be. The labels explain workload differences, not mandatory product assignments.

    9.2.3 · Row-oriented vs column-oriented storage

    To display one customer's full record, it is convenient to read fields stored together in a row. To sum revenue over millions of records, reading only an amount column can avoid unrelated fields and support compression.

    Row-oriented storage groups fields by record; column-oriented storage groups values by field. Each changes locality and the cost of reads and updates. Modern engines can combine techniques, so inspect the actual access path. Storage layout does not replace a sound logical model or useful indexes. Choose it according to which bytes the important queries need to read and how frequently those values change.

    9.2.4 · Normalization vs denormalization

    A customer's current address belongs in their profile. A completed order may also keep the address used for that shipment. This repetition preserves a historical fact; changing the profile should not rewrite the old order.

    Normalisation reduces duplicated facts and update anomalies. Denormalisation deliberately repeats or derives data for a purpose, often a faster read. State which meaning a copy has. A cached author name might be a historical snapshot or a value that should follow future edits. Without that distinction, developers cannot know whether a difference is correct history or stale data. Every maintained copy needs an update and recovery rule.

    Think further · How should restoration from a historical backup respect later deletion decisions?

    Restore into a controlled path, apply relevant deletion decisions, and reconcile raw and derived copies before serving. Rebuild indexes from the permitted current state rather than blindly expose an older snapshot. Keep deletion evidence narrow and purpose-limited. The backup and live-data lifecycle need a combined recovery procedure.

    Remember: Group bytes for the access pattern while preserving the meaning of current and historical facts.

    Try applying it: Why should changing a customer's address leave the shipping address of an old order unchanged?

    PART 3 / UNIT 09 / CHAPTER 9.3

    Model relationships and ownership

    Prerequisites: 9.2 · Files, objects & analytical layouts4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    An order line refers to an order and a product, but those records have different lifecycles. Model keys, cardinalities, and ownership so data stays meaningful as it changes.

    9.3.1 · ER diagrams and relational modeling

    An order has several lines. Each line belongs to one order, refers to a product identity, and retains the purchase-time values needed for its history. An entity-relationship model makes those identities and cardinalities explicit.

    Show keys, optional and required links, and the constraints that protect them. Also consider lifecycle: deleting a product must not remove the financial meaning of an old order. A diagram is more useful when it states these rules rather than merely joining table names. Translate the relevant constraints into the database or application so they are actually enforced.

    9.3.2 · Referential integrity

    An order line should not point to an order that does not exist. A suitable foreign key can enforce that relationship in a relational database. This is referential integrity.

    Decide deletion behaviour deliberately: automatically deleting dependent records may be wrong for historical payments. An application check before insertion can also race with deletion unless an atomic mechanism protects the relationship. Across separate services, one local foreign key cannot enforce a remote record's lifetime. Use stable identifiers, explicit ownership contracts, and reconciliation appropriate to the business rule. The integrity requirement stays important even when its enforcement crosses different storage boundaries.

    9.3.3 · Data ownership

    Payments records whether a charge was accepted. Analytics may keep a copy for reports, but should not rewrite that financial outcome. Data ownership identifies who may define and change each fact.

    If several services directly edit one table, they share transaction and release assumptions even if their source repositories are separate. Provide controlled read and change contracts, with only the permissions each consumer needs. Ownership also includes schema changes, incident response, retention, and recovery. Naming a table owner is a start; the design must give that owner a way to preserve its rules while others use the data.

    9.3.4 · Choosing storage based on access patterns

    List the operations before assigning an engine. Profiles need particular lookups and edits. Financial entries need transaction and audit rules. Chat history needs bounded conversation/time reads. PDFs need large-byte storage and lifecycle management.

    Several of these needs may be met by one system. A relational or document model could both serve a profile, depending on its actual constraints. Add another engine when its capability solves a demonstrated problem. Each additional store introduces backup, permissions, migration, monitoring, and expertise costs. Prefer a storage choice justified by the operations it supports over one chosen merely to include every database category in the diagram.

    Think further · How should restoration from a historical backup respect later deletion decisions?

    Restore into a controlled path, apply relevant deletion decisions, and reconcile raw and derived copies before serving. Rebuild indexes from the permitted current state rather than blindly expose an older snapshot. Keep deletion evidence narrow and purpose-limited. The backup and live-data lifecycle need a combined recovery procedure.

    Remember: Relationships need both an expressed rule and a mechanism that preserves it.

    Try applying it: What must happen to completed order history when a product is removed from sale?

    PART 3 / UNIT 09 / CHAPTER 9.4

    Access patterns, retention & operational cost

    Prerequisites: 9.3 · Model relationships and ownership4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Adding a search engine also adds another recovery and deletion path. Follow raw and derived copies through retention and operation before deciding that another store is worth maintaining.

    9.4.1 · Data retention and lifecycle

    A document's lifecycle includes its original bytes, extracted fields, indexes, archives, and recoverable copies. Deleting only the live row may leave other copies usable.

    Define purpose, retention, expiration, archival, and deletion behaviour from the start. Dropping time partitions can efficiently expire old data; deleting one user's records needs identity-aware propagation. A minimal deletion marker may be needed to prevent old events from recreating removed data, but that marker can itself retain personal information. Keep only what its purpose needs. Test restoration from an old backup so required deletion decisions are reapplied instead of silently reversed.

    9.4.2 · Polyglot persistence and its operational costs

    A shop adds a search engine because its current queries cannot meet a demonstrated relevance need. It now uses different stores for different workloads: polyglot persistence.

    The extra capability comes with indexing lag, rebuilds, permissions, schema changes, and another recovery procedure. A change across two stores is not automatically one transaction. Identify which record is authoritative and which representation can be rebuilt, then monitor progress between them. Compare the complete operating cost with the benefit of the new query path. Keeping fewer engines can be an advantage when one already meets the requirements.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Pseudocode · bytes and metadata

    upload = create_authorized_upload(tenant, expected_size)
object = store_and_verify_bytes(upload)
with transaction():
    insert_document(tenant, object.version, object.digest)
    insert_processing_intent(object.version)
# Orphan-byte cleanup handles incomplete metadata handoff.

    The metadata points to a verified immutable object version and records the processing obligation. If metadata commit fails, the object can remain orphaned and needs reconciliation or cleanup.

    The local transaction does not include the earlier separate object upload. Track that handoff explicitly instead of describing it as one cross-service commit.

Rebuild indexes from the permitted current state rather than blindly expose an older snapshot. Keep deletion evidence narrow and purpose-limited. The backup and live-data lifecycle need a combined recovery procedure.

    Remember: Additional engines earn their cost through a demonstrated capability and a complete lifecycle.

    PART 3 / UNIT 10 / CHAPTER 10.1

    Pages, indexes & query plans

    Prerequisites: Runtime, Processes, Threads, and Concurrency, Data Models and Storage Technologies6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A task lookup is quick for one identifier but slow for another. Both requests reach the same database, so adding another application server does not yet tell us how to help.

    We need to follow the work behind the query: how records are grouped into pages, how indexes locate candidates, and when storage must supply data that memory does not hold. The planner's choices connect these structures to the SQL we write.

    In this chapter, we will trace a lookup and a range scan, examine the later work caused by LSM writes, and use query plans to judge an index. The aim is to identify the physical work a proposed improvement actually avoids.

    10.1.1 · How databases store and retrieve records

    A lookup by task identifier looks simple to its caller. Inside the database, the engine must choose a way to find the task, obtain the stored data, and decide which row version the caller may see. Following these steps helps us explain where the time goes.

    An index is a separate search structure that helps locate records by selected values. For a lookup using an index, the engine searches its entries and follows the resulting record reference. It may need to bring parts of both the index and the table from storage into memory. Other queries may scan the table instead. The planner chooses an access path: the sequence of scans, searches, and other operations used to obtain the result.

    Two queries can therefore wait for different reasons. One needs storage reads; another spends CPU time filtering records; a third waits for a lock held by another transaction. Inspect the plan and resource behaviour before adding servers. The useful change is the one that addresses the expensive step.

    10.1.2 · Pages, records, indexes, and buffer pools

    Many database engines organise storage into pages. A page is a unit of storage the engine reads and manages together; it can contain several records or index entries. A buffer pool keeps useful pages in memory so later operations can reuse them.

    Suppose an index identifies the page containing a task. If that page is already in the buffer pool, the engine can use its memory copy. Otherwise, it must obtain the page from lower storage layers, which may require device I/O. Even a memory hit still involves work, such as finding the record and checking its visibility. The operating system may also cache data, so a database buffer miss need not mean a physical device read.

    The relevant memory question is which actively used pages fit. A query that visits a million scattered pages can put heavy demand on storage even when it returns few records. Extra web servers may only send more of those reads. Examine the pages touched and their locality: whether related accesses reuse nearby or already cached data. Page layout and replacement rules vary by engine.

    10.1.3 · B-tree/B+tree and hash indexing

    Suppose a query asks for keys 20 through 35. An ordered index can locate the beginning of that range and continue through its entries, rather than checking every record. B-tree-family structures organise keys into a tree of pages, with separators that direct a search toward a smaller range.

    In the figure, the root has separators 20 and 40. Key 25 belongs to the middle range, [20,40), so the search follows that branch to the leaf containing 20, 25, and 30. B+tree designs commonly keep records or record references in leaves, and allow a range scan to continue through neighbouring leaves. Larger trees add internal pages between the root and leaves; each step narrows the range.

    A hash index instead uses a hash calculated from a key to find equality candidates. It does not provide the same ordered walk from 20 to 35. Choose an index using the query's conditions, ordering, engine support, and update cost. A short tree path can still require page reads, and a range returning many rows still takes time to read and deliver.

    10.1.4 · LSM trees and write amplification

    An LSM tree, short for log-structured merge tree, organises updates by collecting them in memory and writing sorted groups to storage. Such a group is called a sorted run. Later, compaction merges runs and removes versions that the engine no longer needs.

    In the illustrated path, the engine first records the write in a recovery log under its durability policy, then updates the in-memory structure. When that structure is flushed, it becomes an immutable sorted run: later writes go elsewhere rather than editing that run in place. After several flushes, the same key may appear in several runs with different values. A read must find the relevant version; compaction combines this scattered history when permitted.

    Batching can turn many small changes into more sequential storage work. But compaction reads and writes existing data again. Write amplification is the physical bytes written divided by the bytes of logical changes. Its value depends on the layout and workload. Observe sustained ingestion and tail latency, because compaction can compete with requests for bandwidth or fall behind and cause stalls. A short burst that fits in memory conceals this later work.

    10.1.5 · Query planning and EXPLAIN

    A SQL query describes the desired result. The planner chooses how to obtain it, using statistics about the data and estimates of the work required. EXPLAIN shows that selected plan. An execution-analysis form can also report actual work; it may run the statement, including its side effects.

    Suppose the query asks for yesterday's orders. An index search may be useful if few orders match. If most of the table matches, a scan may be cheaper than many separate record fetches. The estimate of how many rows will match is called a cardinality estimate, and it influences later choices such as how to join the result to another table.

    Now suppose the planner expects ten rows and the operation actually produces a million. A join strategy chosen for the small estimate may perform much more work than expected. Compare estimated and actual row counts, filters, sorts, scans, and buffer activity. Updated statistics or a query rewrite may address the cause. Check the engine's command behaviour before analysing a statement that changes data.

    10.1.6 · Index selection and query optimization

    A tenant-scoped list query filters by tenant and sorts by time and identifier. An ordered index on (tenant_id,created_at,id) may support that access path, depending on the engine and query.

    The leading tenant field groups one tenant's entries. Within that group, the time and ID fields provide the requested order; the ID distinguishes records with the same time. A query that fixes the tenant can locate that group and walk a bounded matching range. If it filters or orders by different fields, the same index may fit less well. An index serves particular operations, rather than making every query on the table faster.

    Each index also consumes space and must be maintained when relevant data changes. A covering index contains the values needed for a query and may avoid some table-record fetches, subject to the engine's visibility rules. Its larger entries also use more memory and storage. Test representative values and distributions: a small uniform dataset can conceal a tenant holding most of the rows. Inspect both the resulting read plan and the additional write cost.

    Think further · What changes when one local transaction is divided across independent databases?

    The two changes no longer automatically share one commit decision. Suppose the seat update commits in one database but inserting the reservation fails in another. Each store can behave correctly locally while the combined booking is incomplete.

    First identify which invariant needs agreement. A distributed transaction may supply a suitable shared decision if the stores and operating requirements support it. Alternatively, a workflow can represent intermediate states explicitly and use retries, reconciliation, or compensation to reach an acceptable outcome. That choice must define what the caller sees while work is incomplete. Separate local commits alone do not preserve the former all-or-nothing business promise.

    Remember: Follow the query from its plan through index and data pages. Judge an index by the work it avoids and the write work it adds.

    Try applying it: An index makes a tenant list faster, but inserting tasks becomes slower. What additional work does each insert now require?

    PART 3 / UNIT 10 / CHAPTER 10.2

    Commit, logging & versions

    Prerequisites: 10.1 · Pages, indexes & query plans4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Our application transfers money between two accounts and reports that it has saved the result. A reader may still see an earlier row version while the writer commits a new one, and a crash may occur before every changed page has reached storage.

    These observations raise different questions. Which changes belong together? When has the database accepted them? What information allows recovery, and which version should each reader see?

    In this chapter, we will separate the ACID properties, follow commit and a lost reply, and connect the recovery log to delayed page writes. We will then use a version timeline to explain how readers can have different permitted views of the same row.

    10.2.1 · ACID properties

    Start with account A holding 100 and account B holding 50. A transfer of 10 should leave A=90 and B=60, preserving the total of 150. Saving only the debit would leave the two-account model short by 10. A transaction groups the related database changes into one unit.

    ACID names four properties of transactions. Atomicity means the related changes are accepted together or abandoned together. Consistency concerns preserving the required invariants: rules such as preserving this total. The application logic and database constraints must correctly express those rules. Isolation controls the observations and interactions allowed when transactions run concurrently. Durability concerns retaining committed changes under the configured guarantees and failure assumptions.

    These properties answer different questions. Atomicity can keep the debit and credit together, but it cannot recognise that the application calculated the wrong amount. Likewise, placing statements in a transaction does not tell us which isolation level they use. To judge the transfer, check its calculation, constraints, concurrency behaviour, and commit guarantee.

    10.2.2 · Transaction commit and rollback

    The application changes rows and asks the database to commit. Commit accepts the transaction under the engine's configured guarantees. If the application promises a saved result, it should report success only after the commit succeeds. A rollback abandons the transaction's uncommitted database changes.

    The database's decision and the client's receipt of that decision are separate events. Suppose the database commits, then the connection breaks before the reply reaches the application. The rows may already be saved even though the caller has no confirmation. A connection error at this point does not establish rollback. Recovery needs an operation identity stored with the change, or another reliable way to find its outcome before deciding whether to try again.

    The transaction boundary also limits what rollback can undo. If the application already charged a payment provider over HTTP, rolling back SQL does not reverse that charge. Replaying the operation without accounting for the earlier charge can repeat an external effect. Trace local changes, commit, and remote actions separately when designing recovery.

    10.2.3 · Write-ahead logging

    A database may commit while modified data pages are still in memory, awaiting their final storage writes. Write-ahead logging, or WAL, makes this possible by recording recovery information before the corresponding changed pages are written to persistent storage.

    Consider a logged change to a task. The engine creates the log records and modifies the page in memory. Under a commit policy that requires durable local WAL, it flushes the required records, including the commit record, before acknowledging success. It can write the data page later. If a crash happens first, recovery uses the persisted log to redo the required work and restore the appropriate database state. Commit therefore need not wait for every modified table and index page to reach its final location.

    The exact acknowledgement guarantee depends on synchronization and replication settings. A checkpoint advances the work already reflected in stored pages and limits later recovery work; it is not a backup. If the only device holding both data and log is destroyed, this recovery path is lost too. Independent recovery copies address that different failure.

    10.2.4 · MVCC

    Suppose a stored price changes from 10 to 12 while a reader is using it. Multiversion concurrency control, or MVCC, lets the engine retain multiple row versions and select the one the reader is allowed to see. A snapshot defines that reader's view according to the engine's visibility rules.

    In the figure, version one, containing 10, commits at logical time 10. A snapshot at 15 sees that version. Version two, containing 12, commits at 20, and a later snapshot at 25 sees it. The older snapshot can continue to use version one even after version two commits. These are illustrative logical times, rather than a requirement that an engine use wall-clock timestamps this way.

    Versions reduce some direct interference between readers and writers, but the isolation policy still decides when snapshots are taken and how conflicts are handled. Long readers can keep old versions needed and delay cleanup. Stable snapshots also do not by themselves prevent two transactions from making incompatible decisions about different rows. We examine that history in the next chapter.

    Think further · What changes when one local transaction is divided across independent databases?

    The two changes no longer automatically share one commit decision. Suppose the seat update commits in one database but inserting the reservation fails in another. Each store can behave correctly locally while the combined booking is incomplete.

    First identify which invariant needs agreement. A distributed transaction may supply a suitable shared decision if the stores and operating requirements support it. Alternatively, a workflow can represent intermediate states explicitly and use retries, reconciliation, or compensation to reach an acceptable outcome. That choice must define what the caller sees while work is incomplete. Separate local commits alone do not preserve the former all-or-nothing business promise.

    Remember: Keep related writes in one transaction, wait for the promised commit result, and distinguish recovery information from the versions readers may see.

    Try applying it: A price update commits while an older snapshot still reads the earlier price. Which visibility rule should you check before treating this as an error?

    PART 3 / UNIT 10 / CHAPTER 10.3

    Races, anomalies & isolation

    Prerequisites: 10.2 · Commit, logging & versions5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Two buyers both read that the last seat is available. Each then tries to reserve it. A transaction around each caller's work helps only if its concurrency rules prevent the conflicting decisions from both being accepted.

    A second example is less obvious: two doctors update different rows yet jointly leave nobody on call. Preventing one row from being overwritten does not necessarily protect a rule about several rows.

    In this chapter, we will write these histories in event order, compare locks with conditional updates, and distinguish read anomalies, lost updates, and write skew. We will use PostgreSQL 18 to make the isolation rules concrete and identify what must be repeated after a serialization failure.

    10.3.1 · Locking and optimistic concurrency control

    Two buyers read an available seat at version seven. Each proposes an update that changes the owner and advances the version, but only where version=7. One update succeeds and advances the version to eight. The other can no longer satisfy its version-seven condition.

    The condition and change must be one atomic database operation. Reading a version and then writing unconditionally in a separate step leaves time for another buyer to intervene. This guarded change is optimistic concurrency control: do the work on an expected state, then validate that expectation when applying it. For the illustrated competing claims, zero affected rows means the claim did not occur. The application must re-read and make a fresh business decision. Some isolation implementations may instead report a retryable conflict.

    Pessimistic locking coordinates access before conflicting work. A transaction might lock the seat, check availability, update it, and commit before releasing protection. Another claimant waits and then checks the resulting state. Locks can also deadlock: A holds row X while waiting for Y, and B holds Y while waiting for X. Consistent lock ordering helps avoid this cycle; the engine may abort a participant to resolve it. Choose the method for the complete invariant and expected contention.

    10.3.2 · Dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, phantom reads

    Different concurrent histories produce different read anomalies. For a dirty read, transaction A changes a value from 10 to 20 without committing; B reads 20; A then rolls back. B has used another transaction's uncommitted value, which never became committed state.

    For a nonrepeatable read, B first reads 10. A then changes the same row to 20 and commits. B reads it again and gets 20. Both values were committed when observed, but the repeated read did not stay stable.

    A phantom concerns the rows matching a condition. B asks for reservations for a flight and finds three. A inserts a fourth matching reservation and commits. B repeats the same query and finds four. A new matching row appeared, even though none of the original three had to change.

    These are histories to check against an isolation contract, rather than predictions for every database. For example, PostgreSQL 18 prevents dirty reads even when Read Uncommitted is requested, and its Repeatable Read also prevents phantoms. Other implementations can differ. Testing one repeated row read cannot establish all the guarantees needed for a query over a set of rows.

    10.3.3 · Lost updates, write skew, serialization anomalies

    A lost update can arise when two callers calculate from the same old value. Both read a counter at 10. A calculates 11 and writes it; B also calculates 11 and writes it later. If both writes commit, the final value is 11, although two increments were intended. B's stale replacement lost A's increment. This history depends on the statement form and conflict rules; an atomic increment or a checked version can change the outcome.

    Write skew has a different shape. Two doctors are on call. Transaction A sees doctor B on call and turns A off. Transaction B sees the earlier state with A on call and turns B off. If both commit, nobody remains on call. They changed different rows, so neither needed to overwrite the other's write. Each decision depended on a read that the other transaction made obsolete.

    The on-call rule spans both rows. With a correct check in serial execution, the second doctor would see that the first had left and would stay on call. The concurrent outcome has no equivalent serial ordering; it is a serialization anomaly. Protect the full rule with suitable serializable transactions, coordinated locking, or a shared conflict point. Protecting only each doctor's own row is insufficient.

    10.3.4 · Isolation levels and implementation differences

    An isolation level states which interactions concurrent transactions may have. Its implementation is part of the application's contract, so name the engine and version when relying on a particular behaviour.

    In PostgreSQL 18, ordinary Read Committed SELECT statements each use a new snapshot. Another transaction can commit between two SELECTs, and the second can see that change. Repeatable Read uses a snapshot established by the first non-transaction-control statement and excludes later concurrent commits from that view. It prevents nonrepeatable and phantom reads, but still permits serialization anomalies such as suitable write-skew histories. A stable view and a serially explainable outcome are different requirements.

    PostgreSQL Serializable adds checks for dependencies that could prevent a serial equivalent. The database may reject a transaction with a serialization failure; Repeatable Read can also require retries after concurrent updates. Restart the whole failed transaction, including its reads and decisions, with bounded attempts. Repeating only the last write retains assumptions from the failed attempt. Make external effects safe under replay before placing them inside retrying application code. Other engines and statement forms need their own documented analysis.

    10.3.5 · Serializable execution and serializability

    Serializable execution allows transactions to overlap while requiring their committed effects to match some execution of those transactions one at a time. It is a property of the permitted histories; it does not require the engine to run only one transaction at a time.

    Return to the doctors. If A runs first and leaves, B must see A off and stay. If B runs first, A must stay. An outcome with both off matches neither serial order. A serializable implementation must prevent that committed outcome, for example by rejecting a transaction that the application then restarts with fresh reads.

    Serializability alone does not add a real-time ordering requirement between separate callers. Linearizability describes operations as taking effect at a point between their invocation and reply, while respecting real-time precedence: an operation completed before another begins must come first. Strict serializability combines this real-time requirement with transaction serializability. State which property the application needs. Even a serial execution of a wrongly calculated transfer gives the wrong amount, and a local database guarantee does not automatically include an external payment call.

    Think further · What changes when one local transaction is divided across independent databases?

    The two changes no longer automatically share one commit decision. Suppose the seat update commits in one database but inserting the reservation fails in another. Each store can behave correctly locally while the combined booking is incomplete.

    First identify which invariant needs agreement. A distributed transaction may supply a suitable shared decision if the stores and operating requirements support it. Alternatively, a workflow can represent intermediate states explicitly and use retries, reconciliation, or compensation to reach an acceptable outcome. That choice must define what the caller sees while work is incomplete. Separate local commits alone do not preserve the former all-or-nothing business promise.

    Remember: Trace concurrent decisions in order and protect the complete invariant. A retry must repeat the reads and decisions of the failed transaction.

    Try applying it: Two transactions each lock only the doctor they will turn off. Why can that leave the shared on-call rule unprotected?
