    PART 3 / UNIT 10 / CHAPTER 10.4

    Pools, recovery & ticket correctness

    Prerequisites: 10.3 · Races, anomalies & isolation4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    The booking service becomes busy. Requests wait for a database connection, a seat claim must agree with its reservation record, and the backup job reports success. Each situation needs evidence about a different part of the operation.

    A pool limit tells us how many connections can be borrowed, but not how quickly they return. A save call tells us little about a shared transaction boundary. A completed backup job does not show that the application can use the restored data.

    In this chapter, we will calculate a simple pool bound, trace a multi-statement reservation transaction, and design a meaningful restore check. The conditional seat-claim example will show how an application distinguishes a successful local change from a claim that did not occur.

    10.4.1 · Database connection pooling

    A connection pool keeps a bounded set of database connections available for reuse. A request borrows one, performs its database work, and releases it. When all connections are held, later requests must wait, time out, or be rejected according to the pool's policy.

    Assume ten connections, each held for an average of 100 ms, or 0.1 seconds, per operation. In a simplified fully busy model, each connection completes 1/0.1 = 10 operations per second. Ten connections then give 10/0.1 = 100 operations per second before other constraints and variability. This is a modelled service bound, not a measured database capacity. Time waiting to borrow a connection adds to the caller's latency.

    Holding a connection while waiting for an unrelated HTTP service occupies capacity that another request could use. Shorten that interval where the transaction permits it. Measure acquisition time, connection hold time, lock waits, and transactions left open without work. Increasing the pool size may add database contention instead of throughput. Include pool acquisition in the request deadline so queued work cannot wait indefinitely before its query even starts.

    10.4.2 · Transactions across multiple operations

    Reserving a seat and inserting its local reservation record must agree. If the seat change commits but the record fails, the stored data no longer describes one valid outcome. Put both statements inside the same actual database transaction.

    Begin the transaction, conditionally claim the available seat or inventory, and check that the change succeeded. Then insert the matching reservation and commit. If insertion fails, roll back the seat change too. If the claim did not occur, the application must not insert a successful reservation. The shared commit boundary makes both local changes appear together or neither appear.

    Check how the database library manages that boundary. An object-relational mapper, or ORM, maps application objects to database records, but calling save on two objects does not establish that both calls share one transaction. They must use the same transaction owner and commit scope. Also release resources deliberately: a lazy result that reads records later may still need its connection. Across independent stores or remote services, local rollback cannot provide the same common boundary; choose an explicit coordination and recovery protocol.

    10.4.3 · Backup, recovery, and durability

    A backup job reports success. We still need to know whether its data can be decrypted, restored, and used by the application. A recovery procedure must include the compatible schema, keys, credentials, and any log history required to reach the desired state.

    Restore into a clean environment and open the recovered database through the application. For a booking service, find a committed reservation and check that its seat ownership agrees. Measure the full time until the service is usable, and identify how much recent history is missing. These checks give evidence about recovery time and recoverable data. A file in backup storage alone does not answer either question.

    Replication maintains live copies and may copy an accidental deletion to them. Backups retain recoverable history according to their retention policy. Point-in-time recovery can start from a suitable backup and replay the required logs to a selected point. State which acknowledged writes the procedure can recover after each failure, and keep suitable independent copies. Test that procedure, including the application checks, before relying on its recovery promise.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · conditional seat claim

    from mechanisms import open_demo_store, claim_seat
db = open_demo_store()
db.execute("INSERT INTO seats VALUES (1,NULL)")
db.commit()
assert claim_seat(db, 1, "A")
assert not claim_seat(db, 1, "B")
db.close()

    The store begins with seat 1 available: its owner is NULL. A's call executes an UPDATE guarded by owner IS NULL. It changes one row and commits, so claim_seat returns true. B's later call checks the same condition, now finds the seat owned by A, and changes zero rows. Its false result tells the application that B did not acquire the seat.

    This SQLite example checks availability directly; it does not use the version-seven column from the earlier optimistic-control example. Both place the check and change in one database operation. The executable mechanism collection also checks claims through two connections to the same file-backed store. These calls demonstrate the local ownership result; they are not a test of every overlapping schedule.

    The protected rule is that only an available seat can be claimed. A complete booking also needs deliberate rules for its reservation record, payment, hold expiry, and stale callbacks. This local transaction cannot atomically perform an external charge.

    Compare the two policies using the same order of steps. Does either caller learn that the seat has already been taken? This display replays a fixed example. The downloadable SQLite example separately tests the atomic conditional update.

    Think further · What changes when one local transaction is divided across independent databases?

    The two changes no longer automatically share one commit decision. Suppose the seat update commits in one database but inserting the reservation fails in another. Each store can behave correctly locally while the combined booking is incomplete.

    First identify which invariant needs agreement. A distributed transaction may supply a suitable shared decision if the stores and operating requirements support it. Alternatively, a workflow can represent intermediate states explicitly and use retries, reconciliation, or compensation to reach an acceptable outcome. That choice must define what the caller sees while work is incomplete. Separate local commits alone do not preserve the former all-or-nothing business promise.

    Remember: Keep connection ownership deliberate, give related local writes one commit boundary, and verify recovery by restoring and using the application.

    PART 3 / UNIT 11 / CHAPTER 11.1

    Locality and cache placement

    Prerequisites: Networking Foundations for System Design, Data Models and Storage Technologies4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A product is read repeatedly between edits. Work out which cost a cache can avoid, how much active data fits, and which layer should hold the reusable representation.

    11.1.1 · Why caching works

    A product description is read thousands of times between edits. Reusing a stored response can avoid repeating the database lookup or calculation. This reuse is why caching can help.

    Assume a cache hit takes 1 ms, a miss takes 50 ms, and 90% of requests hit. The simple average service time is 0.9×1 + 0.1×50 = 5.9 ms, excluding queueing and other work. Compare this saving with memory, lookup, and maintenance costs. A result used only once may be a poor cache candidate. Hit ratio also does not establish tail latency: slow misses and queues can still dominate some users' waits.

    11.1.2 · Cache locality and the working set

    A user repeatedly opens the same product: that is temporal locality. Reading neighbouring records together illustrates spatial locality. A working set is the data actively needed during a relevant interval.

    A cache much smaller than that set may continually evict entries just before they are reused. A large scan can also displace useful entries under some policies. Measure bytes and object sizes as well as key counts, and distinguish frequently used data from the full historical collection. Preloading every object can fill memory with cold content. Admission rules decide what deserves a place before eviction decides what must leave.

    11.1.3 · In-process vs distributed caches

    Two application instances each keep a price in memory. One has price 10 and another price 12. Their in-process caches provide fast access but create separate copies whose freshness needs coordination.

    A distributed cache provides a shared network-accessible layer, adding encoding, connection, and failure costs. Choose by reuse patterns, duplicated memory, and required behaviour when a copy is stale or unavailable. Ordinary cached stock counts should not become the sole authority for exclusive allocation. Placing the cache elsewhere changes its access and failure boundaries; it does not by itself resolve the application's consistency rule.

    11.1.4 · Browser, CDN, application, and database caches

    A page can be answered by a browser cache, a CDN, an application cache, or a database buffer pool. Each stores a different kind of copy. Database pages and a rendered account response also have different keys and update rules.

    Draw the layers actually used and specify freshness at each. Invalidating an application object does not clear a browser's response. A public edge cache with a poorly scoped key can expose personal data. When diagnosing a stale result, identify which layer answered and which version it held. “The cache was cleared” is incomplete unless it names the particular copy involved.

    Think further · When should a product stop serving rather than return a stale cached result?

    Stop when the operation requires current authority or the permitted stale interval has ended. An old description may be allowed, while allocating scarce stock or deciding current access may not be. State which actions degrade and which wait or reject, with visible status and a recovery path.

    Remember: Cache value comes from useful reuse under a valid freshness and access policy.

    Try applying it: Why can a high hit ratio coexist with slow or incorrect user responses?

    PART 3 / UNIT 11 / CHAPTER 11.2

    Copies, freshness & eviction

    Prerequisites: 11.1 · Locality and cache placement4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A delayed reader inserts yesterday's price after a writer invalidates it. Follow cache population, expiry, versioning, and eviction as separate decisions.

    11.2.1 · Cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind

    With cache-aside, application code loads from the source after a miss and populates the cache. Read-through places that loading behind the cache interface. Write-through includes backing-store work in the write path; write-behind delays it. Exact ordering varies by implementation.

    Trace failures explicitly. A volatile write-behind cache can lose acknowledged changes before backing persistence. Cache-aside also has a race: a reader fetches version one, a writer commits version two and invalidates, then the delayed reader inserts version one. Where freshness requires stronger behaviour, use an appropriate version or coordination protocol. A pattern name alone does not resolve these event sequences.

    11.2.2 · TTL and cache expiration

    A cache receives a value that was already five minutes old and gives it a one-minute TTL. The copy may then remain six minutes behind its source. TTL describes residence after insertion, rather than necessarily the age of the fact.

    Expiration also differs from eviction due to memory pressure. Choose lifetimes using tolerated staleness and refresh behaviour, and consider client-held copies. Adding jitter can spread expirations that would otherwise happen together. For a correctness-critical action, revalidate against the authority when required. A short display-cache TTL is useful only if it matches the promise made about that display.

    11.2.3 · Cache consistency and invalidation

    A writer updates the source and deletes a cache entry. A delayed reader can still repopulate it from an earlier read, leaving an old value after the invalidation. Simply deleting after writing does not prevent every race.

    Versioned entries, conditional population, or source-version checks can support a stronger protocol. Observe delayed or repeated invalidation events and their progress. Choose freshness per operation. Showing an older price may be acceptable if checkout verifies the actual price; allocating the last item from an old count can oversell it. Invalidation must serve the business rule, rather than merely keep copies approximately similar.

    11.2.4 · Eviction: LRU, LFU, FIFO, and alternatives

    At capacity three, access A,B,C,A,D. Ideal LRU treats the second access to A as recent and evicts B. FIFO preserves insertion order and evicts A. LFU favours frequently used entries but also needs a tie-breaking rule.

    Real cache policies may approximate these ideals. Test the actual policy with representative object sizes and request patterns. Eviction decides what leaves; admission decides what enters. Neither can make an arbitrarily large working set fit into memory. A policy that performs well on one tiny fixture may behave poorly during scans or changing popularity, so measure the workload it is meant to serve.

    Think further · When should a product stop serving rather than return a stale cached result?

    Stop when the operation requires current authority or the permitted stale interval has ended. An old description may be allowed, while allocating scarce stock or deciding current access may not be. State which actions degrade and which wait or reject, with visible status and a recovery path.

    Remember: Residence time and eviction policy do not by themselves establish current source data.

    Try applying it: How can a one-minute TTL serve a value that is more than one minute behind its source?

    PART 3 / UNIT 11 / CHAPTER 11.3

    Hot keys, stampedes & negative results

    Prerequisites: 11.2 · Copies, freshness & eviction5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A cache restarts just as a product becomes popular. Control duplicate loading, absent lookups, warming, and permitted stale results before the origin becomes overwhelmed.

    11.3.1 · Hot keys

    A single product becomes extremely popular. Even a large cache cluster can overload the one owner serving that key. Adding nodes mainly gives other keys more capacity unless the design also distributes this key's traffic.

    For reads, local copies, replicas, or coalescing repeated work may help, with an explicit freshness policy. For writes, determine whether the value can be split or combined safely. An aggregate counter may allow distributed increments; exclusive stock allocation needs a stronger rule. Identify whether the pressure is transfer volume, recomputation, object size, or serialised updates before selecting a remedy.

    11.3.2 · Cache stampedes, penetration, and avalanche

    Many requests miss the same key and all recompute it: a cache stampede. Repeated requests for nonexistent keys are often called penetration. Broad expiry or cache loss can cause an avalanche of origin traffic.

    Use controls suited to the cause. Single-flight loading combines concurrent work for one key. Negative caching can remember a genuine absence. TTL jitter spreads expiry, while bounded refresh and origin admission protect the source. A refresh lock needs its own failure and expiry behaviour. Test cache loss: allowing every application instance to rebuild everything at once can overload the database that remains responsible for the real data.

    11.3.3 · Negative caching

    A client repeatedly asks for a product that does not exist. A short-lived “not found” entry can prevent repeated source lookups. This is negative caching.

    Distinguish absence from failure. A temporarily unreachable database has not established that the product is missing. Likewise, one user's denied access must not poison another user's cache entry. Scope keys correctly and use deliberate lifetimes. If the product is created just after its absence is cached, it may stay invisible until expiry or invalidation. The policy should state whether that delay is acceptable and how newly created records become visible.

    11.3.4 · Stale-while-revalidate

    A cached product description expires while its source is slow. Stale-while-revalidate can return an allowed older copy and refresh it in the background. The user avoids the immediate wait, and combined refresh work can protect the origin.

    Define separate ages for fresh data, permitted stale data, and unusable data. Repeated refresh failures should not silently extend stale serving forever. A description may tolerate this arrangement; an old payment reply cannot authorise a new charge. Make degradation visible where appropriate and preserve authoritative checks for operations whose correctness depends on current state. Faster responses have value only within the agreed freshness rule.

    11.3.5 · Cache warming and prefetching

    New application instances start with empty caches. Warming loads likely useful entries before normal demand; prefetching predicts what will be needed soon. Both spend bandwidth and memory before a user actually asks.

    Load a measured working set gradually rather than scanning the entire database from every new instance. Check whether prefetched values are used and whether they evict more valuable entries. Staggering a rollout, sharing a cache, or limiting admission may solve a cold-start problem more simply. Stop obsolete speculative work. The useful question is how much future work was avoided, rather than how many entries were loaded.

    Think further · When should a product stop serving rather than return a stale cached result?

    Stop when the operation requires current authority or the permitted stale interval has ended. An old description may be allowed, while allocating scarce stock or deciding current access may not be. State which actions degrade and which wait or reject, with visible status and a recovery path.

    Remember: Bound refresh and fallback work while keeping the accepted stale and absent meanings explicit.

    Try applying it: What should happen if background refresh keeps failing past the allowed stale age?

    PART 3 / UNIT 11 / CHAPTER 11.4

    Edges, partitions & the price of a cache

    Prerequisites: 11.3 · Hot keys, stampedes & negative results4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A cache cluster and CDN add more copies and another failure path. Compare their operations with source correctness and recovery capacity, including whether the cache should exist at all.

    11.4.1 · Redis-like data structures

    A set can track identifiers, a sorted set can organise scores or timestamps, and a hash can group fields. Redis-like systems expose such structures with operations suited to particular tasks.

    Choose by the operations needed, then examine their atomic scope. One atomic command does not make an arbitrary sequence of commands atomic. A script or transaction may protect the local sequence, subject to the selected system's rules and key placement. Expiry, persistence, and replica behaviour remain separate decisions. A convenient list or stream is not automatically a durable queue with the required acknowledgment and recovery semantics.

    11.4.2 · CDN architecture and origin shielding

    An origin shield collects edge misses before they reach the source, reducing duplicate origin work. A CDN places permitted representations near users. Both depend on correct keys and sharing rules.

    Decide how query parameters, headers, identities, and content versions affect the representation. A signed URL is a capability with a scope and lifetime, not permission to ignore private-data policy. Purge propagation follows the provider contract and may not remove copies already kept by clients. Immutable versioned URLs can simplify public asset updates. Trace every remaining copy when immediate revocation matters; proximity and bandwidth savings do not establish access correctness.

    11.4.3 · Cache partitioning and replication

    Partitioning assigns different keys to different owners. Replication makes additional copies under a protocol. A distributed cache may use both, but failover can still lose, evict, or expose delayed entries.

    Specify whether the application falls back, serves permitted stale data, or rejects when the cache fails. Stable hashing can reduce key remapping during membership changes, while leaving hot-key traffic uneven. Keep source and cache recovery capacity explicit. The real peak may arrive when a cache cluster restarts and every missing value needs reconstruction. Test that scenario rather than sizing the origin only for a warm-cache hit ratio.

    11.4.4 · When caching is harmful

    A cache adds a lookup, encoding, memory use, and copy-maintenance work. If results are rarely reused, those costs can exceed the work saved. If its key omits authorisation scope, the cache can also serve the wrong user's result.

    Test with the cache empty and unavailable. A warm cache can hide insufficient source capacity until the day it disappears. Sometimes a better query or index removes the bottleneck with fewer freshness and recovery obligations. Keep caching where measured reuse and the agreed correctness policy justify it. Removing an unhelpful cache can simplify both performance and reasoning.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · ideal LRU

    from mechanisms import LRU
cache = LRU(3)
for key in "ABC": cache.put(key, key)
cache.get("A")
assert cache.put("D", "D") == ("B", "B")

    After A,B,C,A, ideal LRU considers B the least recently used. Adding D evicts B, as the assertion checks.

    The fixture models entry count and exact recency. Actual caches can approximate the policy and use byte or expiry limits. Eviction alone says nothing about whether a loaded value is current.

    Download the executable mechanism collection ↓ · Follow the connected complete design →

    THE WORKBENCH · TRY CHANGING THE INPUTS

    Follow which cache entry is used least recently

    The cache holds a fixed number of entries. Each access loads a missing key or moves an existing key to the most recently used end. Real caches may use approximate eviction, byte limits, and expiry. Choosing an entry to evict does not tell us whether its value is fresh.

    Think further · When should a product stop serving rather than return a stale cached result?

    Stop when the operation requires current authority or the permitted stale interval has ended. An old description may be allowed, while allocating scarce stock or deciding current access may not be. State which actions degrade and which wait or reject, with visible status and a recovery path.

    Remember: Evaluate each cache by saved work, maintained semantics, and the cost of losing it.

    Try applying it: Which workload would show that removing a cache improves the whole system?

    PART 3 / UNIT 12

    Scalability, Load Balancing, and Data Distribution

    READ NOW

    4 produced chapters, with original figures, worked mechanisms, and a complete eleven-question assessment with separate explained solutions.

    Before this unit: Unit 2, Unit 3, Unit 9, Unit 10, Unit 11

    Our URL shortener begins at 100 requests per second. We want to understand how it could grow towards 100,000 requests per second, adding components only when a demonstrated limit calls for them.     PART 3 / UNIT 12 / CHAPTER 12.1

    Scale compute & route requests

    Prerequisites: Requirements, Estimation, and Engineering Trade-offs, Networking Foundations for System Design, Data Models and Storage Technologies, Database Internals, Transactions, and Concurrency Control, Caching and Content Delivery6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Our URL shortener begins at 100 requests per second. We want to understand how it could grow towards 100,000 requests per second, adding components only when a demonstrated limit calls for them. The first tempting change is to run more application instances. But what happens when the next request reaches a different instance, or when all the new instances contact the same database?

    We will begin with the work performed by one request and decide which parts can be shared across machines. That requires knowing where sessions and accepted work live, how a destination is selected, and what makes an instance ready to receive traffic. We will then examine the delay between detecting demand and making new capacity available.

    By the end of the chapter, you should be able to explain when more compute helps, which conditions make an application instance replaceable, and which measurements can guide growth without overwhelming a shared dependency.

    12.1.1 · Vertical vs horizontal scaling

    Suppose our URL shortener receives 100 requests per second. Over time, the target rises to 100,000 requests per second. These numbers describe the work we want to support; they do not yet tell us how many machines to buy. We first need to find which resource limits the existing service while it meets its response-time and correctness requirements.

    One option is to give the current machine more CPU, memory, or other resources. This is vertical scaling. Another is to add machines and distribute suitable work among them. This is horizontal scaling. A machine or independently managed server in such an arrangement is often called a node.

    Consider a web application that spends most of its time performing independent calculations. More CPU on one node may let it perform more calculations at once. Several application nodes may also share that work, provided requests can reach them and each can obtain the state it needs. By contrast, if every request waits for the same database lock, adding application nodes mainly adds more callers waiting for that lock. A larger machine also cannot remove a rule that requires those updates to happen one at a time.

    Choose the change that addresses the measured limit, then measure completed useful work again. Include startup time, cost, and failure consequences in the comparison. A larger database machine can postpone the need to distribute data, while several application nodes can make replacement easier. Neither arrangement promises a proportional increase in throughput. After one limit is relieved, another resource may become the next constraint.

    12.1.2 · Stateless vs stateful services

    A user signs in through application instance A. The next request reaches instance B. To serve it correctly, B must establish the same identity, check the current permissions, and find the required application data. If the only record of the user's session exists in A's memory, B cannot simply continue where A stopped.

    A stateless service avoids keeping required per-client conversation state only in a particular application instance between requests. For example, a request can carry a session identifier, and either instance can use that identifier to retrieve the session from its designated store. The application still uses state. The useful property is that serving the next request does not require returning to the same application process.

    A stateful service keeps some continuing context that affects how later work must be handled. Local sessions are one example. A worker that has accepted a job into memory may also hold work that a replacement cannot reconstruct. Moving the session to a shared store does not, by itself, preserve that accepted job. Each kind of required state needs an owner and a recovery procedure.

    Before freely distributing requests, check that every eligible instance has compatible configuration, can access the required state, and follows the same contracts. Also preserve the handling of repeated operations: if a reply disappears, a retry reaching B must not accidentally repeat an effect already performed by A. The word stateless describes a useful arrangement of state; the replacement behaviour still has to be established.

    12.1.3 · Load distribution algorithms

    With several application instances available, someone must select the destination for each new unit of traffic. A load balancer performs this selection according to a policy. The policy should distribute work in a way that makes useful capacity available, rather than merely producing an even count of selections.

    Round-robin selects eligible backends in turn: A, then B, then C, then A again. It is simple and can work well when instances and requests have similar costs. Weighted selection gives a larger share to an instance expected to handle more work. For example, a higher-capacity instance can receive a greater proportion of new traffic. The weights need to reflect usable capacity under the actual workload.

    Least-connections uses the number of active connections as a clue to current load. This can help when some connections last much longer than others. It is less informative when connections carry very different amounts of work. Similarly, even request counts can hide a few expensive requests that keep one instance busy. Hash-based selection uses a key, such as a session identifier, to keep related traffic together; this can improve locality but can also concentrate a heavy user's traffic.

    The selection can happen in an intermediary, which is server-side balancing, or in a caller that knows the available destinations, which is client-side balancing. In either case, decide who discovers backends, excludes unhealthy targets, and performs retries. Observe per-instance queues and saturation to check whether the policy is working. Redistributing requests cannot increase the capacity of a database that all those instances already share.

    12.1.4 · Health checks and failover

    An application process answers a ping, yet every real request fails because it cannot initialise the state needed to serve users. A different process has lost an optional recommendation service but can still display the requested page. Both cases show why a health check must answer a particular operating question.

    A liveness check asks whether the process should be restarted. A readiness check asks whether the instance should receive traffic under the service's chosen policy. These decisions need different evidence. A process that is still starting may be alive but not ready. An instance that can give an acceptable reduced response may remain ready even when an optional dependency is unavailable.

    Suppose every instance checks the same optional dependency and declares itself unready whenever that dependency fails. One shared outage now removes the whole application from routing, including responses it could still provide. Choose checks that reflect the required response, give the checks bounded waiting times, and decide in advance which reduced behaviour is acceptable.

    Failover directs work to another eligible instance after the current one is removed or lost. A health check helps decide when to change routing, but the replacement must also have access to valid state and enough capacity. New traffic can be redirected while existing connections or in-flight requests still need handling. Work held only in the failed process's memory does not reappear because a routing table changed. Recovering that work requires its own state and retry rules.

    12.1.5 · Sticky sessions

    Suppose a load balancer selects instance A for a user's first request. Instead of selecting freely on later requests, it continues sending that user's traffic to A. This is a sticky session, also called session affinity. The routing arrangement may use a session identifier or another agreed way to recognise related traffic.

    Affinity can help when A holds local session state. It can also be an optimisation when A has already cached data likely to be needed by that user. These uses have different consequences. Losing a disposable cache entry may only make the next request slower; losing the only session record may force the user to sign in again or interrupt the operation.

    Now let A fail or leave service during maintenance. Sending the user to B changes the destination, but B still needs a way to recover the required context. Decide whether the session is recoverable elsewhere, whether the client must reconnect, and what happens to in-flight work. Keeping the user attached to A during normal operation does not answer these failure questions.

    Sticky routing also limits balancing. A few heavy users assigned to A can overload it while B remains lightly used. Externally owned sessions can remove this requirement for replaceable web instances. Where affinity remains useful, state whether it protects required state or merely improves reuse, and define how assignment changes when an instance fails or drains.

    12.1.6 · Autoscaling metrics

    A worker queue's oldest unfinished job is getting older, although CPU use remains moderate. The workers may be waiting for storage rather than computing. A rule that adds workers only when CPU is high will miss the growing delay that users experience.

    Autoscaling is a control process that changes the number or size of running instances in response to observed signals. Choose a signal that relates to the constrained work. CPU can be useful for computation. Queue age can expose delayed jobs. Connection use may reveal pressure in a workload that spends much of its time waiting. A request count is easier to interpret when requests require comparable work; a changing mix of cheap and expensive requests weakens that assumption.

    The controller cannot create ready capacity immediately. It observes the signal, requests new instances, waits for them to start, and may then wait for caches or other resources to warm. Traffic arriving during this interval still reaches the old capacity. Keep headroom and admission limits for that interval, rather than assuming that an instruction to scale has already increased throughput.

    Set minimum and maximum capacity and use stabilisation rules so short fluctuations do not repeatedly add and remove instances. The maximum should reflect cost and downstream limits as well as the application's own resources. Adding workers that all wait on one overloaded database can worsen the delay. After scaling, inspect completed jobs and their age to establish whether useful capacity actually increased.

    Think further · Every caller competes for one globally hot resource that can have only one exclusive owner. Can adding many partitions make these ownership decisions independent? Explain what a valid improvement would have to preserve.

    Extra partitions can distribute unrelated records, but they do not divide the decision about this one exclusive resource. Two partitions independently granting ownership could accept incompatible winners and break the rule. The hot decision still needs a protocol that establishes the permitted owner.

    Read copies or batching may reduce suitable surrounding work, and a different allocation model may be possible if the requirements permit it. For any proposal, explain which work it removes or distributes and how it prevents conflicting grants. Measure the hot owner's actual work instead of inferring progress from the number of partitions.

    Remember: Scale the measured limiting work. Freely replacing application instances requires accessible state, compatible behaviour, suitable routing, and bounded demand on shared dependencies.

    Try applying it: A signed-in user sends one request to A and the next to B. Which state and behavioural conditions must hold for B to serve correctly, and what changes if A fails after performing a write but before replying?

    PART 3 / UNIT 12 / CHAPTER 12.2

    Replicate and partition data

    Prerequisites: 12.1 · Scale compute & route requests6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Several application instances can now serve requests, but suppose the database is approaching a measured storage or write limit. We could copy its data to another database, or divide the data between owners. These changes look similar on a diagram, yet they solve different problems and create different obligations.

    In this chapter, we will distinguish replication from partitioning, then follow how a key selects its owner. We will compare ordered ranges with hash-based placement and examine what must happen when that placement changes. Moving data while users continue writing will let us see why calculating a destination is only one part of distribution.

    The aim is to choose placement from the actual queries and invariants, and to explain how a handover preserves accepted work. We will also examine a partition receiving 70% of writes, because evenly distributed storage does not establish evenly distributed traffic.

    12.2.1 · Replication

    Suppose a database primary accepts a new record and sends the change to a second database. Keeping additional copies of data under a defined protocol is replication. The primary is the current write authority in this example; the other copy is a replica. What the caller can rely on depends on which events must happen before the primary reports success.

    In asynchronous replication, the primary may reply before the replica receives the change. Consider the sequence: the primary commits, the caller receives success, and the primary becomes unavailable before the replica catches up. If that replica is made the new primary, the acknowledged record may be missing. The second copy exists, but its progress matters as much as its existence.

    A synchronous arrangement waits for a specified replica milestone before replying. That milestone might concern receipt or durable storage, according to the selected system's protocol; receiving a record and applying it for reads are different steps. State which copies must reach which milestone. Waiting for remote acknowledgment adds delay and may prevent completion when the required communication is unavailable.

    Replication can serve appropriate reads or help continue service after a failure. To assess those benefits, examine copy placement, lag, and the promotion procedure together. Two copies on one lost disk do little for a disk-loss requirement. Likewise, promoting a convenient but insufficiently current copy can violate the intended durability promise. The protocol and tolerated failures give meaning to the copy count.

    12.2.2 · Partitioning and sharding

    Suppose one database owns every short-link record. We can divide the records into portions, each containing some of the keys. Such a portion is a partition. When different storage owners manage those portions, the arrangement is commonly called sharding. Unlike replication, which makes additional copies, sharding divides responsibility for different data.

    A partition key determines the placement. If records are assigned by tenant identifier, a request for one tenant's links may reach just one owner. A query across all tenants may have to contact several owners and combine their results. The same key that simplifies one query can therefore make another query more expensive. Check the important reads and writes before selecting it.

    Ownership also determines where rules can be enforced. A shard may enforce uniqueness among its own records, but that alone does not establish uniqueness across all shards. A change involving several owners may require coordination that a local transaction previously supplied. Joins, transactions, and globally unique values need explicit treatment when their scope crosses the new boundaries.

    Keep a way to route requests to the current owner and a procedure for moving data when ownership changes. A large tenant can still dominate a tenant-based shard, and movement must preserve accepted updates. Introduce sharding when a measured storage or write limit justifies these obligations. A large user count, without a workload and resource diagnosis, does not identify either the need to shard or the correct key.

    12.2.3 · Range partitioning vs hash partitioning

    Suppose events have increasing time keys. Under range partitioning, each owner holds an interval of those keys. A query for a particular day's events can then visit the relevant intervals. Retiring an old interval can also fit time-based retention. The arrangement preserves useful order between the key and its location.

    That same order can concentrate writes. If all new events belong to today's interval, most incoming traffic reaches its owner, even while owners of older intervals are idle. Dividing historical data evenly does not divide current ingestion evenly. Splitting the range helps only if the new traffic can actually fall into different resulting ranges.

    Hash partitioning first transforms a key with a hash function and uses that result to choose a partition. Different keys can then spread across owners even when their original values are adjacent. The cost is reduced locality for ordered queries: retrieving one time interval may require visiting several partitions and combining their results. This extra set of requests is often called query fan-out.

    A design can combine a time bucket with a spread dimension, assigning today's events to several owners. This distributes suitable writes but makes a read of today's data combine several portions. Neither range nor hash partitioning automatically divides requests for one extremely popular key. Compare write distribution, read locality, retention, and the measured skew together; evenly placed keys are only one part of the problem.

    12.2.4 · Consistent hashing and rendezvous hashing

    A simple placement rule hashes a key and takes the remainder after division by the number of owners. This is modulo routing. It is easy to calculate, but changing the owner count changes the divisor. Many keys can then map to a different owner, creating a large movement task when capacity is added or removed.

    Consistent hashing uses a placement scheme designed to keep much of the old assignment when membership changes. In a common ring arrangement, both keys and owner positions are placed on a circular ordered space. A key is assigned to the next eligible owner position around the ring. Adding a position takes responsibility for part of an existing interval, so keys elsewhere can retain their owners. An owner can have several virtual positions rather than one, giving placement more opportunities to spread key ranges.

    Rendezvous hashing reaches a similar goal through scores. For a given key, calculate a stable score for each eligible owner and select the owner with the highest score. When an owner is added, a key moves to it only if the new score beats its previous winner. When an owner is removed, keys assigned to other winners can retain their assignment.

    These schemes calculate placement; they do not transfer records or preserve updates during a transfer. Callers also need agreement about membership and hash behaviour. Changing the hash function can change the mapping and therefore requires migration planning. Finally, spreading key assignments does not guarantee equal traffic: one frequently accessed key still has one selected owner unless another mechanism distributes its work.

    12.2.5 · Rebalancing

    A partition is being moved from owner A to owner B while users continue changing its records. Copying the records once is insufficient. An update accepted by A after its record was copied would be missing from B. Rebalancing must account for both the copied starting state and the changes made during the copy.

    Begin with a defined snapshot, which represents the source at a known point. Copy that snapshot to B and capture the subsequent changes. Apply those changes to the destination until it has reached the point required for handover. Check that the records and relevant invariants agree; a destination that merely contains some copied data is not ready to own new writes.

    Next establish the ownership transition. A routing epoch is a version of the placement information that lets participants distinguish the old assignment from the new one. The handover procedure must say when B may accept writes and how a request using the old assignment is rejected or redirected. Without such coordination, A and B could both accept incompatible changes, or a caller could continue writing to a copy scheduled for removal.

    Copying and applying changes consume the same resources that serve users, so throttle the move to leave serving capacity. Retain the old copy until validation and recovery conditions permit removal. Define rollback and reconciliation for an interrupted handover. Safe rebalancing is complete when data and request routing agree about the current owner, rather than when the initial copy finishes.

    12.2.6 · Hot partitions and skew

    A cluster's average load looks comfortable, yet one partition receives 70% of writes. That owner develops a queue while the other partitions remain mostly idle. This uneven distribution is skew. A partition carrying a disproportionate share of the work is a hot partition, and its delay can dominate the requests that depend on it.

    First identify what is uneven. One partition may contain more bytes, receive more requests, or perform more expensive operations per request. These require different remedies. Inspect traffic, bytes, resource use, and waiting by partition. A fleet average hides the relationship between the affected requests and their particular owner.

    If the hot partition contains many independently writable keys, splitting its range or changing placement may divide the work. If almost all requests change one entity, creating more cold partitions does not help that entity. Read copies may distribute allowed reads, and batching may reduce some write overhead. A write rule that needs one authoritative decision still needs a way to make that decision correctly.

    Spreading append operations with an extra key dimension can help when the records are independent, but later reads may have to combine several partitions. Before choosing that trade-off, ask whether the pressure comes from data volume, popularity, or a rule requiring updates to occur one at a time. The useful remedy changes the specific pressure that caused the hot partition.

    Think further · Every caller competes for one globally hot resource that can have only one exclusive owner. Can adding many partitions make these ownership decisions independent? Explain what a valid improvement would have to preserve.

    Extra partitions can distribute unrelated records, but they do not divide the decision about this one exclusive resource. Two partitions independently granting ownership could accept incompatible winners and break the rule. The hot decision still needs a protocol that establishes the permitted owner.

    Read copies or batching may reduce suitable surrounding work, and a different allocation model may be possible if the requirements permit it. For any proposal, explain which work it removes or distributes and how it prevents conflicting grants. Measure the hot owner's actual work instead of inferring progress from the number of partitions.

    Remember: Replication makes copies; partitioning divides ownership. Placement must support the important queries and invariants, while rebalancing must preserve updates and establish one current assignment.

    Try applying it: A new owner is added to a hash-based layout, but one key still dominates write traffic. Why might the new owner remain mostly idle, and what must a later ownership move preserve while writes continue?

    PART 3 / UNIT 12 / CHAPTER 12.3

    Lag, proxies & saturated pools

    Prerequisites: 12.2 · Replicate and partition data5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A user changes a profile, receives success, and then sees the old value on the next page. At the same time, another request waits for a database connection even though the web fleet's CPU looks comfortable. Adding more application instances could leave the stale read unchanged and increase connection pressure.

    To understand these outcomes, we will follow a write from the primary to a replica, distinguishing receipt from application. We will then follow a request through a database proxy and a connection pool, identifying which component owns its session state and where it waits.

    By the end of the chapter, you should be able to connect routing to a read's freshness requirement and distinguish a connection shortage from the work holding connections busy. That evidence will help us choose a change that affects the actual bottleneck.

    12.3.1 · Read replicas and read/write splitting

    A user changes a profile through the primary database and receives success. The next page reads a replica that has not yet applied the change. The old profile appears. Both requests may have completed as their databases allowed, yet the sequence fails the user's expectation of seeing their own update.

    Read replicas can distribute suitable queries. Read/write splitting sends writes to their authority and sends selected reads to other copies. To choose those reads, define the required freshness. A public report may permit delayed data, while the profile page may require read-your-writes: the next relevant read must include the user's completed update.

    One approach is to route the critical read to the primary under the database's required read semantics. Another, where supported, is to record the write's progress marker and use a replica only after it has applied at least that far. If no suitable replica is ready, the policy needs to say whether to wait, use another destination, or report that it cannot meet the requirement. The routing decision follows the observation the operation needs.

    SQL syntax alone cannot establish that requirement. A SELECT may acquire a lock or belong to a transaction whose decisions depend on current state. Splitting such a transaction across unrelated copies can change its meaning. Read replicas add capacity for appropriate reads; they do not make all reads interchangeable or remove the separate authority for writes.

    12.3.2 · Replication lag

    Replication usually has several stages. The source accepts a change, the change travels to a replica, and the replica applies it so reads can observe it. A replica can therefore have received a record without yet making its effect visible. Replication lag describes how far progress at one of these stages trails the source, and the stage being measured must be named.

    Suppose the source has accepted changes through position 100 in an ordered change history, while a replica has applied only through position 90. Its applied state is behind the source. Later it reaches position 95. In the trace, the source is still at 100 and the replica at 95, so a read there may miss the effects at positions 96–100. This is a comparison of progress markers, rather than proof that each position represents one second or one user request.

    Where the database supports them, examine source, receipt, and apply progress separately. A delayed transport and a replica that receives changes quickly but applies them slowly need different investigation. Time-based estimates also require interpretation: variable traffic means that a given position gap does not imply a fixed duration. An average across replicas can hide one that has stopped progressing.

    Use the relevant progress in operating decisions. A read-your-writes request needs a copy that includes its required change, not merely a reassuring fleet average. A promotion decision must honour the acknowledgment and possible-data-loss contract. Choosing a replacement quickly is useful only if its actual state is acceptable for the work it will take over.

    12.3.3 · Database proxying

    Several application instances need database connections, and database destinations may change during failover. A database proxy sits between clients and database servers. Depending on its features, it can choose a destination, manage backend connections, or let several client sessions share a smaller set of database connections.

    Sharing requires care because a connection can carry state as well as requests. A session variable, a temporary table, or an open transaction may belong to one particular backend session. If a later operation is sent to a different backend without preserving the required context, the application may observe different behaviour even though its SQL text is unchanged.

    A proxy may keep a client attached to one backend while that state is needed. This attachment is often called pinning. For example, the transaction must remain on the session that owns it until the transaction ends. Check which features the proxy can safely share and which require pinning, and define when the backend can be released for another caller.

    The proxy itself also needs capacity, identity handling, routing, and failure procedures. Reducing connection count does not remove transaction contention inside the database. Nor can a connection switch always repair a failed operation: a write may have committed before its reply was lost. Repeating that write requires the application's operation and retry contract, rather than an assumption that a fresh connection means nothing happened.

    12.3.4 · Connection pool saturation

    An application uses a pool of database connections so requests can borrow and reuse them. When every connection is in use, another request must wait or fail according to the pool's policy. Pool saturation means this borrowing capacity has been exhausted; it does not, by itself, explain why connections remain busy.

    Suppose ten application instances each permit twenty database connections. Together they can demand 10 × 20 = 200 connections. Add ten more application instances with the same configuration, and potential demand becomes 20 × 20 = 400 connections. The shared database has not gained capacity merely because more pools now point to it.

    There can be waiting at several boundaries. A request first waits to acquire a pool connection. After acquisition, its query may wait for a database lock while still holding that connection. CPU can remain modest throughout the lock wait, even as other callers queue for connections. Measure acquisition time, connection hold time, query time, and contention to locate the cause.

    Set an aggregate connection budget across the expected instance count, including capacity needed for recovery and administration. Include acquisition waiting in request deadlines and bound the number of waiting callers. Shorten unnecessary ownership of a connection where possible. Raising every pool limit can transfer a queue into an already constrained database; the useful goal is more timely completed work, rather than more simultaneous borrowers.

    12.3.5 · Bottleneck identification

    A request takes a long time to complete. Adding web instances seems plausible, but most of the delay may occur after the application has sent a database query. To choose an effective change, follow the request through the stages that determine when its response can be returned. This sequence of dependent work is its critical path.

    Separate execution from waiting at each stage. The request may wait for a worker, run application code, wait for a connection, execute a query, and wait for another service. The stage holding up the required outcome is the bottleneck for that workload and target. Its cause may be insufficient processing capacity, a slow access path, lock contention, or admission of more work than the stage can handle.

    Compare offered traffic with useful completions, queue growth, and resource evidence. Inspect CPU, memory, disk, network, connections, and locks where relevant. High utilisation helps form a hypothesis, but does not establish which change will improve the user's result. A busy resource serving unrelated background work may have a different effect from the query every user must await.

    If one query dominates the path, a justified index or query change may help more than extra web instances. If independent CPU work dominates, added compute may help. Change a material factor, then measure useful throughput and the slower end of the latency distribution again. This checks the proposed explanation and reveals whether the limit has moved to another stage.

    Think further · Every caller competes for one globally hot resource that can have only one exclusive owner. Can adding many partitions make these ownership decisions independent? Explain what a valid improvement would have to preserve.

    Extra partitions can distribute unrelated records, but they do not divide the decision about this one exclusive resource. Two partitions independently granting ownership could accept incompatible winners and break the rule. The hot decision still needs a protocol that establishes the permitted owner.

    Read copies or batching may reduce suitable surrounding work, and a different allocation model may be possible if the requirements permit it. For any proposal, explain which work it removes or distributes and how it prevents conflicting grants. Measure the hot owner's actual work instead of inferring progress from the number of partitions.

    Remember: Route reads according to their required progress, and trace connection acquisition and hold time before changing pool sizes or adding application instances.

    Try applying it: Ten instances each allow twenty database connections. Ten more instances are added while requests wait on database locks. How does potential connection demand change, and which measurements would help distinguish the cause from the resulting pool wait?

    PART 3 / UNIT 12 / CHAPTER 12.4

    Regions, write paths & scale economics

    Prerequisites: 12.3 · Lag, proxies & saturated pools5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A burst reaches the service while workers are already busy. The queue grows, and the team proposes both more nodes and a second region. Before accepting either proposal, we need to ask which work can finish in time, which failures must be tolerated, and who may authorise a write when regions cannot communicate.

    This chapter follows those questions from controlled waiting to regional ownership. We will compare a copied product description with a claim to the last seat, so the difference between read capacity and write coordination becomes concrete. We will also examine dependencies that can stop recovery even when several application replicas exist.

    Finally, we will compare the complete cost of designs that meet the same service requirements. The goal is to justify added capacity by useful outcomes, including behaviour during failure, rather than by the size of the topology.

    12.4.1 · Queueing and overload

    A queue holds work until a worker can process it. During a brief burst, requests may arrive faster than workers complete them. If arrivals later fall below completion capacity, the workers can drain the backlog. The queue has moved some work into a later interval; it has not increased the workers' processing rate.

    If arrivals remain above completions, the backlog continues to grow. Waiting consumes memory or storage and also consumes the caller's time. A request can become useless before the queue runs out of space. For example, a request with a two-second deadline cannot finish on time if it is silently accepted behind ten seconds of required work.

    Bound both the amount of waiting work and its age. Admission control decides whether to accept new work when capacity is limited. It can reject work that cannot meet its deadline, shed lower-priority work under the agreed policy, or reserve capacity for required operations. These decisions should happen before waiting callers consume the resources needed to complete existing work.

    Make the overload response clear enough for callers to react sensibly. Immediate repeated retries can add work to the very queue that caused the failure. Asynchronous acceptance is also a distinct contract: if the system promises to finish later, it needs to preserve and track that accepted work. A queue is useful for controlled waiting within a capacity and deadline policy; sustained excess demand still requires less admitted work or more useful completion capacity.

    12.4.2 · Single points of failure

    Two application containers run on one host. If one process crashes, the other may continue. If the host fails, both disappear. Counting two application boxes therefore answers a process-failure question, but does not establish that service survives a machine failure.

    A single point of failure is a dependency whose loss defeats the required service. It may be a machine, a router, a credential source, or a procedure that only one unavailable operator can perform. The requirement matters: a component can be dispensable for an already running request yet essential for replacing instances after an outage.

    A failure domain groups resources that can be lost together through a common cause. Place redundant capacity across the failure domains the service must tolerate, then inspect what remains shared. Two instances on different hosts can still depend on one unavailable state owner. Redundancy needs valid state, failure detection, a workable handover, and enough surviving capacity, as well as separated processes.

    Trace recovery as carefully as normal serving. Suppose existing instances can run with cached configuration, but every new instance must contact one configuration service during startup. Losing that service may leave present traffic working while preventing all replacement capacity. Include these startup and recovery dependencies when looking for single points of failure. The useful question is which required journey stops when a dependency disappears.

    12.4.3 · Multi-region strategies

    A service in one region is considering a second region to reduce distance to users or continue through a regional failure. Before choosing a topology, state the tolerated interruption, possible data loss, and location requirements. Then decide where each kind of write is authoritative and which copies can serve each kind of read.

    In an active-passive arrangement, one side normally owns the authoritative activity and another is prepared to take over. Promotion needs a rule for deciding when the old authority has stopped and whether the replacement has sufficiently current state. Recovery must also say how the former primary returns without resuming an incompatible role.

    In an active-active arrangement, more than one region handles normal activity. This still requires precise ownership. Some operations may have separate regional owners; others may coordinate before accepting an update or accept concurrent changes under a defined conflict policy. During a communication partition, the regions need a rule for which operations can continue and what each caller may observe.

    Waiting for a required remote acknowledgment adds propagation time to the write path. Asynchronous copying can avoid that immediate wait, but a promoted copy may lack recent acknowledged changes if the source is lost. Apply the chosen trade-off to actual operations: a delayed public page and an exclusive reservation need different contracts. A second region is useful when its authority, freshness, and recovery behaviour meet the requirement, rather than merely because another copy exists far away.

    12.4.4 · Scaling writes vs scaling reads

    Many users can read copies of a product description if the service permits a freshness delay. Two callers cannot both receive an exclusive claim to the last seat. Reads and writes place different demands on a design because a read observes a representation, while a write changes authoritative state under the application's rules.

    For suitable reads, replicas or caches let several owners serve reusable representations. The design still needs freshness, permission, and invalidation rules. Those copies can reduce pressure on the source, but serving more copies does not decide who wins a conflicting state change.

    To scale writes, first identify what must be coordinated. Independent tenants or records may be assigned to different owners. Batching can combine suitable work and reduce repeated overhead. Removing unnecessary coordination or maintaining fewer unnecessary indexes may also reduce the cost of each write. Each change must preserve the invariants the original operation enforced.

    One hot account or a global sequential allocator can remain a serial point even when thousands of unrelated keys are distributed. Some counter updates can be combined because their effects commute: applying them in different orders gives the same combined value. An exclusive seat claim has a different rule, because incompatible winners cannot both be accepted. The write design must distribute or reduce work without losing that rule; adding read replicas alone cannot supply it.

    12.4.5 · Scale-out economics

    Suppose two candidate designs meet the same workload target: one uses a larger node, and another uses ten smaller nodes. The smaller machine's individual price does not tell us which arrangement costs less. Compare the complete systems at equal response-time, correctness, and failure requirements.

    Each node can repeat baseline memory, connection pools, monitoring, and operating work. Distribution can add transfer and coordination. On the other hand, added nodes may let the service add capacity in smaller steps or keep useful capacity through a failure. Count both the added work and the benefit under the actual workload, rather than assuming that scale-out is automatically cheaper or more expensive.

    Include spare capacity for the same failures in both candidates. Also account for startup, cache warming, migration, and recovery. A design that meets the target only when every node is available is not equivalent to one sized to meet it after the required failure. Managed services can exchange provider charges for some operating work, while the application team still owns its correctness and recovery decisions.

    Finally, relate cost to useful outcomes. Cost per attempted request can look low when many attempts fail or repeat the same operation. Cost per successfully completed business outcome makes those retries and failures visible. Purchase capacity where evidence shows it can increase the required completions. Extra nodes beyond a shared bottleneck can raise the bill while leaving the service's useful throughput almost unchanged.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · stable rendezvous mapping

    from mechanisms import rendezvous
for key in range(1000):
    old = rendezvous(key, ["A","B","C"])
    new = rendezvous(key, ["A","B","C","D"])
    assert old == new or new == "D"

    The loop examines the 1,000 integer keys from 0 through 999. For each key, the first call selects its rendezvous owner among A, B, and C. The second call includes D as an additional candidate. The variables old and new hold those two selected owners.

    The assertion permits two outcomes: the key keeps its old owner, or its new owner is D. This follows from stable scores for each key-owner pair. A, B, and C retain their previous ordering, so their earlier winner cannot be displaced by another of those same owners merely because D joins. Only D can introduce a new winning score. The loop checks this property over the fixture; it does not assert that any particular fraction of keys moves.

    The code calculates assignments without moving stored data or synchronising clients' membership information. A real handover still needs those procedures. Also, every key has one selected owner in this model. If most requests use one key, they still reach that owner even when the counts of assigned keys look well spread.

    Download the executable mechanism collection ↓ · Follow the connected complete design →

    THE WORKBENCH · TRY CHANGING THE INPUTS

    Compare owners before and after adding D

    Change the key and compare its owner before and after D joins. The same key always receives the same scores in this example. Choosing a new owner does not copy data, agree on membership, or spread the traffic of a single popular key.

    Think further · Every caller competes for one globally hot resource that can have only one exclusive owner. Can adding many partitions make these ownership decisions independent? Explain what a valid improvement would have to preserve.

    Extra partitions can distribute unrelated records, but they do not divide the decision about this one exclusive resource. Two partitions independently granting ownership could accept incompatible winners and break the rule. The hot decision still needs a protocol that establishes the permitted owner.

    Read copies or batching may reduce suitable surrounding work, and a different allocation model may be possible if the requirements permit it. For any proposal, explain which work it removes or distributes and how it prevents conflicting grants. Measure the hot owner's actual work instead of inferring progress from the number of partitions.

    Remember: Queues, redundancy, regional authority, and cost must be judged against the same completion and recovery requirements. Added topology helps when it changes the actual limit without breaking the required behaviour.

    Try applying it: A team proposes more shards and a second region for an exclusive reservation service. Which part of the write rule still needs an authoritative decision, and how should the proposal define behaviour when the regions cannot communicate?
