    PART 4 / UNIT 15 / CHAPTER 15.1

    Choose a replication model

    Prerequisites: Distributed Systems Fundamentals6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Our task database now has copies on three machines. The primary reports that a task is saved, then stops before one copy has caught up. Can that copy take over without losing the task?

    We will compare who may accept writes, what a replica's acknowledgment means, and how several replicas combine evidence. These choices explain what replication protects and what still needs a protocol.

    15.1.1 · Primary/replica architectures

    Suppose our task database runs on machine A, with copies on B and C. A accepts a new task and sends the change to the other two machines. These copies can help us recover if A stops, and they may also serve reads. Keeping copies of a dataset on several participants is called replication. In a primary/replica architecture, the primary is the participant currently authorised to accept writes for that dataset.

    Now let A disappear just after telling the user “Saved.” If B has not received the task, promoting B may make a saved task disappear from the user's view. If A later returns and still accepts writes, there may be two competing histories. The arrangement of three machines has not, by itself, settled either problem.

    We need a contract for acknowledgment: what must happen before a write receives success? We also need rules for promotion, meaning the transfer of write authority to another replica. These rules must preserve the history the contract promises, restrict which replicas are eligible to become primary, and prevent the old primary from making unauthorised changes. A read from a lagging replica may return an earlier state even while the primary is healthy. Replica count is useful information, but persistence, ownership, and recovery rules determine what those copies let us promise.

    15.1.2 · Leader/follower replication

    Let the primary record “create task 7” followed by “complete task 7.” A follower must reproduce this order; applying completion before creation would not have the same meaning. In leader/follower replication, one leader sends an ordered stream of records to followers, which reproduce the changes.

    Follow one record through a follower. First, the follower receives its bytes into memory. Next, it writes them to the persistent storage required by the protocol. Later, it applies the record to its task collection. Receipt, durable storage, and application are different milestones. A crash after receipt can lose a memory-only record. A follower that has stored a record but has not applied it can still serve an older task list.

    Replication lag describes how far a follower trails the relevant leader position. The relevant position depends on the question: stored records matter for recovery, while applied records matter for what a local read can show. Some protocols also distinguish records that are present from records that have been committed, or accepted into the authoritative history. We will examine that distinction with Raft.

    When comparing implementations, ask which milestone a follower acknowledges, what reads it may serve, and which history it may continue after promotion. Saying that a follower “has the data” leaves these questions unanswered.

    15.1.3 · Multi-leader replication

    Imagine two regions, each with a writable copy of a task. Their connection fails. In region A, a user changes its title to “Read chapter.” In region B, another user changes the same title to “Review notes.” Neither region has seen the other change. When communication returns, both versions must be handled.

    Multi-leader replication allows more than one leader to accept writes for the same replicated data. It can make local writes possible during a regional disconnection, but the system must define the result of concurrent changes: changes made without either side having observed the other. One option keeps both versions for review. Another merges changes where the application's data model permits it.

    A last-writer-wins rule selects one version using an ordering such as a timestamp with a defined tie-breaker. This can make replicas converge, meaning they eventually agree, while still discarding a meaningful edit. A clock ahead of the others may make an earlier real-world edit appear later. The rule therefore needs a business justification as well as an unambiguous ordering.

    Also specify how deletions propagate and how a record already replicated through one leader is recognised, so it does not circulate as a new update indefinitely. Multiple writers are suitable when the conflict rules fit the application. Exclusive allocation, such as selling the final item, may still require coordination.

    15.1.4 · Leaderless replication

    Suppose a coordinator sends a task update to several replicas and waits for the responses required by its write rule. A later read asks several replicas for their versions. One may have an earlier value; others may report the update. The read protocol must interpret these versions and decide which result to return.

    Leaderless replication uses an arrangement of this kind instead of routing every write through one permanent leader. A coordinator handles a particular request, but that role need not give it permanent authority over the dataset. The absence of one permanent leader does not remove the need for rules about concurrent updates, membership, durable acknowledgments, or version comparison.

    Replicas also need ways to repair missing data. Read repair updates stale replicas discovered during a read. Hinted handoff temporarily keeps information intended for an unavailable replica and forwards it when possible. Background anti-entropy compares replicas and repairs differences outside individual requests. Each mechanism has its own scope; a stored hint is not automatically equivalent to acknowledgment by the original replica.

    Trace two concurrent writes and the return of a long-absent replica when evaluating such a system. Two responses out of three provide a count. Whether they establish a fresh, linearizable result depends on the full protocol, including how it handles versions and overlapping requests.

    15.1.5 · Synchronous vs asynchronous replication

    A primary stores a task and immediately reports success. Its replica will receive the update later. This is asynchronous replication: the caller's success does not wait for the specified replica work. If the primary is lost before another eligible replica durably stores the task, failover can lose an acknowledged write.

    Now change the order. The primary sends the record, waits for the required replica acknowledgment, and then reports success. This is synchronous replication. We still need to ask what that acknowledgment means. “Received in memory,” “stored durably,” and “applied to readable state” are distinct promises. Waiting for receipt alone does not provide the same protection against a replica process restart as waiting for durable storage.

    The required replicas matter too. Two durable copies on independent machines protect against a different set of failures from copies that share the same failed storage. A promotion rule must continue a history compatible with the acknowledgment contract; promoting any reachable replica can defeat the intended protection.

    Waiting for remote work adds latency. If a required replica cannot communicate, writes may have to wait or fail rather than receive success. Choose this boundary from the application's data-loss and availability requirements, then test the same boundary through failover. The words “synchronous” and “asynchronous” describe the waiting arrangement; the stated milestones determine its meaning.

    15.1.6 · Quorum-based systems

    In a fixed group of three voters A, B, and C, a majority contains two members. The group A+B overlaps B+C at B. Any two majorities in this group share at least one member. This intersection gives a later decision a possible witness to an earlier one.

    A quorum is a set of participants whose responses satisfy a protocol's decision rule. The shared participant is useful only if it remembers the required evidence and obeys rules that carry that evidence into later decisions. For example, a voter may need to persist a vote before replying, so restarting does not let it forget and vote incompatibly. A participant holding an accepted log record may have to reject a candidate whose history is too old.

    If B simply agrees with every request, intersection protects nothing: B can help two overlapping groups accept conflicting histories. The arithmetic establishes a shared member, while the protocol explains what that member must preserve and refuse.

    This reasoning assumes the same fixed voter group. Changing the group can change which quorums intersect, so membership transitions require their own rules. Use quorum counts to follow a specified protocol, together with its persistence, eligibility, and recovery rules. A majority count on its own is not an algorithm for consistent storage.

    Think further · A failed region has been repaired and can receive traffic. What evidence would you require before allowing authoritative writes there again?

    Reachability shows that communication is possible; it does not establish authority or a safe history. Require the current ownership and voter configuration, a history compatible with committed decisions, and the durable copies required by the acknowledgment policy. An old leader may need rebuilding and must remain fenced while obsolete authority could still act.

    Also verify that routing directs writes to the authorised participants and that the region has enough capacity to resume its assigned work. Apply the supported rejoin procedure and reconcile uncertain external effects. The evidence should cover safe failback under current state, rather than assuming that restoring the old machines restores the old permission to lead.

    Remember: To assess replication, trace a write from its authorised receiver through the required durable copies to the success reply. Then remove the primary and ask which replica may continue that history. The number of copies alone does not answer either question.

    Try applying it: A follower receives a record in memory and acknowledges it, but crashes before storing it durably. What would the acknowledgment need to establish for the primary to count it as a copy that survives this process loss?

    PART 4 / UNIT 15 / CHAPTER 15.2

    Raft and replicated state machines

    Prerequisites: 15.1 · Choose a replication model5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    The replicas agree through log index 8. A partition separates the leader from the other two machines, which must decide whether one of them can take over. Choosing a name is only the beginning: the new leader must continue the right history.

    We will follow command application, elections, log replication, and commitment. Raft and Paxos show why a later decision must carry evidence from earlier decisions, including while the voter group changes.

    15.2.1 · Consensus and replicated state machines

    Start with an empty task collection on A, B, and C. Suppose they agree that the first command is “create task 7” and the next is “complete task 7.” Each applies creation to the empty collection, then completion to the resulting task. Their task collections now agree.

    This is the replicated state-machine approach. A state machine applies a command to its current state to produce a new state and a result. Replication works when replicas begin from equivalent state and apply the same commands in the same order deterministically: the same state and command must produce equivalent results. Consensus lets participants agree on a choice; repeated decisions can establish the command sequence despite the failures allowed by the protocol.

    Agreement must preserve safety, so incompatible commands cannot both become the accepted command at one position. Progress also needs conditions, such as enough reachable participants and sufficiently favourable communication. Consensus does not promise continued decisions through every possible partition or endless delay.

    Suppose creation calls a random-number generator independently on each replica. The agreed command could then create different identifiers. Put the chosen identifier into the agreed command, or use another supported way to make the decision consistent. The same concern applies to reading the current time.

    Applying a command also differs from causing an external effect. If every replica applies “charge the customer” by calling a payment provider, the log alone does not prevent repeated charges. External work needs explicit ownership, stable operation identity, and recovery at the receiving boundary.

    15.2.2 · Raft: terms, elections, log replication, commit

    Return to three replicas A, B, and C. They share a committed history through index 8, where an index is a position in the log. A is leader, but a partition separates it from B and C. B stops receiving the expected leader messages. A timeout can make B a candidate: a participant seeking leadership. The timeout creates suspicion, rather than proving that A has stopped.

    Raft divides activity into numbered terms, or election generations. In the worked trace, B seeks leadership in term 5. A voter grants at most one vote in a term and checks the candidate's log. Raft compares the term of the last entry first; a higher last-entry term is more up to date. If those terms match, the longer log wins the comparison. Thus a candidate cannot obtain votes merely by being reachable. It must meet the log-eligibility rule as well. The current term, vote, and required log state are persisted before the replies specified by Raft, so a restart cannot erase the evidence on which safety depends.

    If eligible B obtains a majority, it becomes leader. It appends index 9 with term 5, sends it to C, and waits for the required durable replication. A follower checks that the preceding log position and term match before accepting the continuation. If its uncommitted suffix conflicts with the leader's history, Raft repairs that suffix under its log rules.

    B can use majority replication of index 9 to advance commitment because that entry belongs to B's current term. Commitment establishes the authoritative prefix through that position; the replicas can apply its commands in order. An entry inherited from an earlier term cannot be declared committed merely by counting its copies on a majority. Raft commits earlier entries indirectly when the required current-term entry commits. This restriction works with election eligibility to preserve history through later leadership changes.

    A remains unable to commit a new quorum-backed write alone. On learning a higher term, a participant returns to the follower role; the role diagram shows these transitions, rather than the entire algorithm. Reads need protection too. A leader can be isolated and unaware that a replacement exists. A supported linearizable-read path establishes current authority and the required committed position, then waits for local application before serving the result. Election, replication, commitment, reads, and membership must follow the implementation's complete Raft protocol.

    15.2.3 · Paxos: conceptual foundations

    Consider one decision, such as which command belongs at a particular log position. A proposer asks acceptors to choose a value. An acceptor is a participant that records promises and accepted proposals. Paxos gives each proposal a unique, ordered number, so an acceptor can distinguish an older attempt from a newer one.

    First comes preparation. A proposer chooses a higher proposal number and asks a majority for promises not to accept lower-numbered proposals. Each reply also reports the highest-numbered proposal the acceptor has already accepted, if there is one. If any such evidence is returned, the proposer must use the value from the highest-numbered accepted proposal among those replies. If none is returned, it may choose a new proposed value.

    Next comes acceptance. The proposer asks acceptors to accept that proposal number and value. An acceptor can accept if doing so does not break a promise it has made to a higher-numbered attempt. Acceptance by the required majority chooses the value. Promises and accepted evidence must survive the failures covered by the protocol.

    Why preserve an earlier value? A new preparation majority intersects any earlier choosing majority. Its replies carry evidence that prevents a later successful attempt from choosing a conflicting value. A new proposer is therefore not free to start the decision again with its favourite value. Competing proposers can still keep interrupting one another and delay progress.

    Multi-Paxos uses related decisions to build an ordered command sequence; a stable leader can reduce repeated preparation work. This is a conceptual introduction. Precise persistence, recovery, membership, and progress rules remain necessary in an implementation.

    15.2.4 · Log ordering and durability

    A replica's log can contain a command that the application is not yet entitled to treat as accepted. It can also contain a committed command that has not yet changed its local readable state. To follow recovery, keep four questions separate: where does the record sit in the order, is it durably stored, is it committed, and has it been applied?

    The figure shows a leader in term 5 with records 8:t4 and 9:t5. This notation means index 8 was created in term 4 and index 9 in term 5. One follower has durably stored both; another has only index 8. Under the fixed-membership Raft rules, the leader and the first follower supply the majority needed for the current-term entry 9. Its commitment also protects the preceding log prefix. The second follower can catch up later.

    Until commitment is established, the presence of index 9 on a particular machine does not by itself justify a success claim. After commitment, a replica still has to apply the entry before its local task state reflects it. A read requiring that position must wait for the appropriate application progress.

    Recovery preserves committed history while repairing incompatible uncommitted suffixes. A snapshot, which stores state representing an earlier applied prefix, must identify a history compatible with the remaining log. Monitor commit and apply positions as well as stored positions: each explains a different kind of delay.

    15.2.5 · Membership changes

    Suppose we replace a cluster's voters by editing a configuration file. The old group still believes that it may decide, while the new group begins deciding independently. If their decision majorities can be disjoint, neither group needs to consult a participant carrying the other's evidence. Both may accept incompatible histories.

    Membership is therefore part of the agreement protocol. It specifies which participants have voting authority. A safe change must preserve the required decision rules during the transition, including when messages are delayed or the leader fails halfway through it.

    Raft's joint-consensus approach introduces an intermediate configuration containing the old and new groups. Decisions in that stage need the required majority from each group. Only through the supported sequence does the new configuration become authoritative by itself. New servers can first receive the log as nonvoting participants, so catching them up does not immediately change who can decide.

    Use the reconfiguration procedure provided by the chosen implementation; some implementations expose a different supported procedure. Preserve persistent member identities and test interrupted transitions. Reusing an identity or replacing all members outside the protocol can invalidate assumptions about remembered votes and logs. Adding a server changes more than storage capacity if it also changes the decision group.

    Think further · A failed region has been repaired and can receive traffic. What evidence would you require before allowing authoritative writes there again?

    Reachability shows that communication is possible; it does not establish authority or a safe history. Require the current ownership and voter configuration, a history compatible with committed decisions, and the durable copies required by the acknowledgment policy. An old leader may need rebuilding and must remain fenced while obsolete authority could still act.

    Also verify that routing directs writes to the authorised participants and that the region has enough capacity to resume its assigned work. Apply the supported rejoin procedure and reconcile uncertain external effects. The evidence should cover safe failback under current state, rather than assuming that restoring the old machines restores the old permission to lead.

    Remember: An agreed log is useful because eligible leaders preserve its committed history and replicas apply its commands consistently. Raft and Paxos combine remembered evidence with restrictions on later decisions. Their election, commit, recovery, read, and membership rules must be followed together.

    Try applying it: A new Raft leader finds an earlier-term entry on a majority of replicas. Why is that observation alone insufficient for its usual copy-counting commit rule, and what current-term event can commit the preceding history?

    PART 4 / UNIT 15 / CHAPTER 15.3

    Fences, leases & failure detection

    Prerequisites: 15.2 · Raft and replicated state machines4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Worker A pauses while holding a lease. The lease expires, and worker B takes over. A then wakes and sends the write it had planned earlier. Both processes are alive, but only one should still have authority.

    We will separate detecting a possible failure, transferring permission, and checking that permission where an effect is accepted. This will help us see what locks, leases, metadata services, and fencing each contribute.

    15.3.1 · Split-brain prevention and fencing tokens

    Worker A is allowed to update a resource using token 7. It pauses for long enough that its lease expires. Worker B obtains token 8 and begins work. When A resumes, it still holds its old instructions and can send a write. Updating a coordinator's owner field has not stopped A's process or withdrawn messages it already sent.

    A fencing token is an ordered ownership generation carried with a protected request. The receiver checks the generation before accepting the effect. Suppose the resource records 8 as its highest accepted generation. An incoming request with 7 must be rejected. The comparison and the protected update must be atomic: another request must not slip between the authority check and the change.

    The point at which the receiver learns the new generation matters. Merely issuing token 8 at the coordinator does not make a receiver that has only seen 7 reject 7. The design must ensure that the newer generation is established where the effect is accepted, according to its ownership contract. The receiver must also retain the authority information across the failures covered by that contract.

    Fencing prevents later actions under obsolete authority once the relevant newer generation is established. It does not undo an effect already accepted, and it does not protect a separate external API that ignores the token. Trace every effect boundary when preventing split brain: the condition in which competing participants act as if each has current authority.

    15.3.2 · Failure detection

    A follower expects heartbeats from its leader. None arrives before its waiting limit. The leader may have crashed, but it may also be paused or separated by a congested network. From the follower's local observation, these situations can look the same.

    A failure detector turns observations such as missing messages into a suspicion that a participant has failed. Choosing a shorter timeout can start recovery sooner, but it can also produce more false suspicions. Choosing a longer one may avoid some unnecessary elections while making users wait longer after a real failure. These are choices about detection and recovery speed under assumptions about timing.

    The ownership protocol must remain safe when the suspicion is wrong. In Raft, a timeout starts an election subject to voting and log rules; it does not grant leadership immediately. For a worker operating on external storage, resource-side fencing may be needed to reject the old worker after authority changes.

    A heartbeat arriving successfully proves little about spare capacity or the latency of an unrelated request. Readiness and load checks answer additional questions. Keep these observations distinct: detection supplies evidence for taking action, while the authority protocol determines which decisions and effects may be accepted.

    15.3.3 · Strongly consistent metadata services

    A storage system needs to record which worker currently owns a partition. If two workers read incompatible owner records and both act on them, the payload can be damaged even when the payload store itself is healthy. Small records about ownership, configuration, or generations can therefore need stronger coordination than much larger application data.

    A strongly consistent metadata service maintains such control information under a specified consistency contract. For a linearizable ownership operation, a successful update must be observed by later operations that require current state, respecting their real-time order. Consensus can support this contract, but a cached read from any replica does not automatically provide it. Use the service's supported write and fresh-read paths.

    This service belongs to the control plane: the part that decides how work is assigned and managed. The data plane performs the ordinary reads, writes, or transfers using those decisions. Existing data-plane traffic may continue with safely usable cached state while the metadata service is unavailable. Acquiring a new lease or changing ownership may have to wait because it requires a fresh decision.

    State which cached decisions remain valid, for how long, and how stale authority is rejected. Consulting the metadata service on every payload request creates a capacity and availability dependency, so do so where the contract requires it. Its own storage, quorum, and recovery assumptions remain part of the system design.

    15.3.4 · Distributed locks and leases

    Suppose only one worker should update a shared file at a time. A lock grants permission to an identified owner. If the owner crashes while holding it, a lock with no recovery rule could block others indefinitely. A lease addresses this problem by granting permission only for a bounded period, with expiry and renewal defined by the lease service's timing rules.

    Now let the worker pause beyond that period. Another worker acquires the lease, but the first worker later resumes at the instruction following acquisition. Its old local variable may still say “I own the lease.” Acquisition and the protected action are separate events; time can pass and authority can change between them.

    Use fencing at the protected resource when this history threatens correctness. The receiver must reject the obsolete ownership generation under an atomic authority check. Releasing the lock also needs an ownership check: an old holder must not delete the newer holder's lock merely because the lock has the same name. Renewal needs the corresponding identity and validity rules.

    Leases rely on stated assumptions about expiry and time; a local clock comparison alone is not a complete distributed ownership protocol. When the entire invariant lies inside one database, a transaction or database-native coordination may protect it more directly. Choose the coordination boundary around the resource and the failures that can interrupt its use.

    Think further · A failed region has been repaired and can receive traffic. What evidence would you require before allowing authoritative writes there again?

    Reachability shows that communication is possible; it does not establish authority or a safe history. Require the current ownership and voter configuration, a history compatible with committed decisions, and the durable copies required by the acknowledgment policy. An old leader may need rebuilding and must remain fenced while obsolete authority could still act.

    Also verify that routing directs writes to the authorised participants and that the region has enough capacity to resume its assigned work. Apply the supported rejoin procedure and reconcile uncertain external effects. The evidence should cover safe failback under current state, rather than assuming that restoring the old machines restores the old permission to lead.

    Remember: A missing heartbeat can justify suspicion, and a lease can expire, while the old process remains able to send requests. Protect the effect by checking current authority at its receiver. A fencing token helps only where that receiver enforces it atomically with the protected operation.

    Try applying it: The coordinator has issued token 8, but the protected store has only seen token 7. What must the design establish at the store before relying on it to reject later requests carrying 7?

    PART 4 / UNIT 15 / CHAPTER 15.4

    Conflicts, CRDTs & regional trade-offs

    Prerequisites: 15.3 · Fences, leases & failure detection4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Two regions can keep serving local writes while disconnected, but their changes may disagree when communication returns. We need to decide whether to merge the changes, preserve a conflict, or require one authority to choose.

    We will build a simple convergent set, examine what its merge can guarantee, and then apply the same questions to regional replication and recovery. A merge must preserve the application's intended meaning, not merely make the copies equal.

    15.4.1 · Conflict resolution and CRDT introduction

    Two disconnected replicas begin with an empty set. Replica A adds X, while replica B adds Y. When they exchange state, each takes the union: the result contains X and Y. Merging again changes nothing. Reversing the exchange order produces the same result. A grow-only set, which permits additions but no removals, gives us a simple example of a conflict-free replicated data type, or CRDT.

    CRDTs define update and merge rules so that replicas can converge under stated delivery and state assumptions. For a state-based grow-only set, union is commutative, so merge order does not matter; associative, so grouping does not matter; and idempotent, so repeated receipt of the same state adds no new effect. With the required updates eventually exchanged, these properties make duplicate and differently ordered exchanges manageable. Other CRDT families use different update and delivery conditions.

    Removal needs more information. If one replica removes X while another concurrently adds X, simply choosing union cannot express the intended removal. An observed-remove set gives additions distinct identities and tracks which additions a removal actually observed. A concurrent addition that the removal did not observe can survive. Safe cleanup must preserve the information needed to distinguish these histories.

    Convergence says that replicas eventually agree according to the type's rules. It does not guarantee every application invariant. Two regions can each allocate the last item they see; merging both decrements can agree on negative stock. Exclusive allocation needs suitable coordination or a design that assigns separate spending rights. Some edits are better retained as conflicts for people to resolve. Choose the merge's meaning before choosing automatic convergence.

    15.4.2 · Multi-region replication trade-offs

    A user writes in one region while another region holds a recovery copy. If the local primary replies before that remote copy is durable, the request avoids waiting for that remote acknowledgment. It also leaves a period in which loss of the local history can lose an acknowledged write. Waiting for a required cross-region durable quorum changes that exposure, while adding remote communication and making some partitions block progress.

    Begin a regional design by stating where each dataset may be written and which locations must acknowledge success. A single-authority design needs safe promotion and stale-owner protection. A multi-leader design needs valid conflict semantics. The copies' geography matters: several replicas inside one region do not provide the same regional-loss protection as required durable copies elsewhere.

    During a partition, the chosen contract determines which side, if any, can accept authoritative writes. Some stale reads may remain acceptable even when new writes must fail. State this per operation rather than describing the whole application as simply available or unavailable.

    Recovery has a return journey too. A repaired old primary may carry a divergent uncommitted suffix or lack records committed elsewhere. Before it can write, it must rejoin under current authority and catch up, reconcile, or rebuild according to the protocol. Keep stale actions fenced and verify routing and capacity before returning traffic. Test failback, the return to a recovered region, as carefully as failover to the replacement.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Pseudocode · three replicas, one partition

    A,B,C contain committed index 8
partition isolates old leader A
B and C elect eligible B in term 5
B appends index 9, term 5
B and C durably replicate index 9
Raft commit rule establishes committed prefix
A cannot acknowledge a new quorum-committed write alone
rejoin: A follows term 5 and repairs uncommitted suffix

    The trace begins with three fixed voters A, B, and C, all containing committed history through index 8. Assume that participants follow the protocol rather than behaving maliciously, and that required protocol state is durable across the allowed crashes. A partition isolates the old leader A while B and C can still communicate.

    B becomes leader in term 5 only after satisfying Raft's election rules, including log eligibility and the required majority of persisted votes. B appends index 9 with term 5. B's durable copy and C's durable copy form a majority of the three voters. Because index 9 belongs to the current term, Raft's commit rule lets B establish commitment through index 9, including the preceding prefix. Replicas then apply committed commands in order; durable storage alone is a different milestone from application.

    A has only its isolated vote and cannot acknowledge a new quorum-committed write alone. It may remain alive and retain uncommitted work, which is why isolation must not be treated as proof that the old process stopped. On rejoining, A observes term 5, follows the current leader, and repairs an incompatible uncommitted suffix under Raft's rules. Committed history must be preserved.

    This pseudocode follows one history; it does not implement elections, log matching, recovery, membership changes, or fresh reads. Use the full supported protocol for those operations. In particular, an isolated node must not serve a supposedly current read merely because it still believes it is leader, and changing the three-voter configuration requires the implementation's membership procedure.

    Download the executable mechanism collection ↓ · Follow the connected complete design →

    Think further · A failed region has been repaired and can receive traffic. What evidence would you require before allowing authoritative writes there again?

    Reachability shows that communication is possible; it does not establish authority or a safe history. Require the current ownership and voter configuration, a history compatible with committed decisions, and the durable copies required by the acknowledgment policy. An old leader may need rebuilding and must remain fenced while obsolete authority could still act.

    Also verify that routing directs writes to the authorised participants and that the region has enough capacity to resume its assigned work. Apply the supported rejoin procedure and reconcile uncertain external effects. The evidence should cover safe failback under current state, rather than assuming that restoring the old machines restores the old permission to lead.

    Remember: Replicas can converge on an outcome that the application cannot accept. Choose update and merge semantics from the business rule, then state where regional writes may proceed, what success requires, and how a recovered region safely rejoins.

    Try applying it: Two regions each allocate the last item while disconnected, then merge both decrements consistently. What does their agreement establish, and which allocation rule still needs a different design?

    PART 4 / UNIT 16 / CHAPTER 16.1

    Queues, logs & delivery boundaries

    Prerequisites: API Design and Communication Contracts, Database Internals, Transactions, and Concurrency Control, Distributed Systems Fundamentals, Replication, Leader Election, and Consensus9 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    The order service saves a customer's order and asks a receipt worker to send an email. The worker sends it, but its acknowledgment is lost. When the same message arrives again, should the worker send another receipt? To answer, we need to distinguish the record being delivered from the effect it asks for.

    We will follow a message from producer to broker to consumer, comparing queues, retained logs, and publication to subscribers. Then we will use short crash histories to decide what acknowledgments and delivery guarantees actually establish. Partition order and transaction boundaries will help us state precisely which progress can be recovered and which effects still need protection.

    16.1.1 · Synchronous vs asynchronous communication

    A customer places an order. The order service can save the order and reply while receipt delivery continues later. If the request waits for the receipt result, that part of the communication is synchronous. If submission and observing completion happen separately, it is asynchronous.

    There are now two completion points. The first response may mean “your order and the obligation to send a receipt are saved.” It does not yet mean “the receipt was delivered.” The response should provide an order identifier and a way to check progress after the request ends.

    For the promise to survive a process crash, the receipt intent must become durable before the service reports that it has accepted this work. Keeping a background task only in request memory leaves nobody responsible after a restart. A queue lets workers handle a temporary burst later, but it does not create processing capacity: if arrivals continue faster than workers finish, the backlog keeps growing.

    16.1.2 · Queues vs logs vs pub/sub

    Suppose several receipt workers are available. A work queue can assign a receipt job to one worker, then assign another job to a different worker. This arrangement distributes work among consumers. A retained log instead keeps an append history that readers can revisit, each using a stored position to find its next record.

    Now suppose both a receipt service and an analytics service should learn about each order. Publication and subscription, or pub/sub, describes distributing publications to subscribers. Whether a subscriber can recover messages missed during an outage depends on the system's retention and acknowledgment policy. An ephemeral publication may retain nothing for an absent subscriber.

    A product can combine queue, log, and pub/sub behaviour. Choose by the work that recovery requires. A consumer returning after a long outage needs records retained for long enough and a way to recover its progress position. Calling a service a broker does not, by itself, establish that it provides this durable history.

    16.1.3 · Producers, consumers, brokers

    Follow one receipt event through the system. The order service submits the event; it is the producer. The broker stores or routes it. A receipt worker receives the event and performs the work; it is the consumer.

    Several replies can occur along this path. The broker might acknowledge receiving bytes in memory, or it might acknowledge persistence under specified storage and replication assumptions. Later, the consumer can acknowledge receipt or completion of a business effect. These statements establish different facts. A producer that has received a broker reply cannot assume that a customer already has a receipt.

    Name what each acknowledgment confirms. Give the message a stable identity, a schema version explaining its format, an owner, and correlation information linking it to the order. Then follow both its age and its business outcome. A broker can be healthy and accepting messages while every consumer rejects their payloads; broker uptime and enqueue rate alone would hide that failure.

    16.1.4 · Partitions, consumer groups, offsets

    A retained log may divide records into partitions. Think of each partition as an ordered lane. A key, such as an account identifier, selects a lane so related records can share its order. An offset identifies a position within that partition; a committed progress position tells a consumer where to resume.

    A consumer group distributes responsibility for partitions among its members. Suppose a consumer processes offset 42, then stops before saving its progress. After a membership change, another consumer may receive that partition and process the record again. This transfer of partition ownership is a rebalance. It does not erase effects the earlier consumer already performed.

    Each partition has its own order and progress. Reaching a particular offset in P0 says nothing about completion in P1. Choose keys from the ordering the application needs, and decide when progress may safely commit. One heavily used partition can limit the whole group while other consumers are idle. Adding consumers does not automatically divide that lane, and parallel work within a lane needs its own effect-ordering rules.

    16.1.5 · Delivery guarantees

    The broker delivers event E7 twice, but the application increments its local counter only once. These observations can both be correct. A delivery is an attempt to pass the record to the consumer. The counter change is the business effect produced while processing it.

    To obtain this result, the consumer recognises E7 and commits that recognition together with the counter change. On redelivery, it finds the saved identity and skips another increment. An external email sent during processing would be a further effect, with its own rules for repetition.

    A delivery guarantee therefore needs a stated boundary. Are we counting broker deliveries, execution starts, or committed effects? Follow acceptance at the source, retention and redelivery, effect commit, and progress acknowledgment. State what survives the failures under discussion at each step. A guarantee about one of these steps does not automatically describe the entire path from the original request to every business outcome.

    16.1.6 · At-most-once and at-least-once processing

    Consider two possible orders for processing a message. In the first, the consumer acknowledges the message and then updates its counter. If it crashes after acknowledgment but before the update, the broker may consider the work finished and never redeliver it. At this boundary, at-most-once handling allows a missing outcome: zero applications are possible.

    In the second order, the consumer updates the counter and then acknowledges. A crash between these events leaves the counter changed but the broker's progress unchanged. Redelivery can start processing again. Under the required retention and recovery assumptions, this supports at-least-once handling, so the application must make repetition safe.

    For one local database effect, an atomic inbox can record the processed event identifier and the effect in the same transaction. Either both commit or neither does. Saving them separately leaves another crash gap. We will examine this consumer pattern below. Neither acknowledgment order alone makes an unrelated email or payment call atomic with broker progress.

    16.1.7 · Exactly-once processing within defined boundaries

    Suppose a processor reads an input record, produces an output record, and saves where it has reached in the input. A supported stream-processing transaction can commit the output and consumed progress together. If it aborts, neither becomes committed; if it commits, both do. Recovery can then avoid skipping that input or exposing a second committed output for the same processing.

    This is a meaningful exactly-once claim within the records, transaction protocol, and fault model it covers. Now let the processing also call an external email server. The email may be sent before a crash even if the stream transaction does not commit. Recovery can execute the input again and send another email. The external call was outside the transaction.

    For an external provider, use the protocol that provider supports. A stable idempotency key may let several attempts produce one relevant outcome within its identity and retention rules, although execution still starts more than once. State which records and effects the guarantee covers, and which failures recovery can handle.

    16.1.8 · Ordering guarantees

    Two account events have sequence numbers 10 and 11. The log stores and delivers 10 first. Worker A starts processing 10 but waits for a provider. Worker B starts 11 and finishes first. Log order, delivery order, start order, and effect-completion order are different observations; the first two did not establish the last.

    If the account rule requires event 10 to take effect before 11, the consumer must preserve that dependency when applying changes. It can coordinate processing by account or use an equivalent sequencing boundary. A later record must not be reported as applied while an earlier required change remains unresolved.

    A permanently failing record makes this choice visible. Skipping event 10 may let processing continue, but can break the account's required sequence. Sequence numbers and gap detection help reveal the missing step. Decide the business ordering rule first, then choose partition keys, processing concurrency, and a deliberate policy for records that block progress.

    16.1.9 · Consumer acknowledgements

    A consumer commits its local update, sends an acknowledgment, and loses contact with the broker. If the broker did not record the acknowledgment, it can redeliver the message. The local update still happened. Moving the acknowledgment before the update would create the opposite risk: a crash could leave the broker finished and the update missing.

    An acknowledgment tells the broker that a specified responsibility has advanced. For example, “saved to a durable inbox” can allow later processing to recover from that inbox. “Business effect completed” claims that a later step has finished. In either case, the receiver needs durable evidence supporting the promise through the failures it covers.

    Choose the effect boundary before deciding when to acknowledge. Local transactions, inbox/outbox records, stable provider keys, and reconciliation each address particular gaps; acknowledgment alone cannot make a separate external system atomic. Set acknowledgment deadlines or extend processing leases to fit the expected work as well. Otherwise, a healthy but slow worker may repeatedly lose its assignment while it is still running.

    Think further · How could one broker transaction be exactly-once while two emails are sent?

    The broker can atomically commit consumed progress and produced records while email remains outside its transaction. A consumer can send an email, lose the completion reply, and send again during recovery. Use the provider's contract, stable identity where supported, and reconciliation. The broker's scoped guarantee does not automatically cover the email effect.

    Remember: Follow the accepted message, processing attempt, committed effect, and acknowledgment as separate events. State the failure assumptions and the boundary covered by each delivery or ordering guarantee.

    Try applying it: A consumer commits its counter update and crashes before acknowledgment. Explain why redelivery can be safe with an atomic inbox. What further problem appears if processing also sends an email?

    PART 4 / UNIT 16 / CHAPTER 16.2

    Retries, consumers & event history

    Prerequisites: 16.1 · Queues, logs & delivery boundaries4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Our consumer can recover a message after a crash, but recovery can deliver it more than once. Another record fails every time because its format is no longer understood. Repeating all work indefinitely would waste capacity, while dropping every failure would abandon valid obligations.

    We will separate temporary failures from records needing repair, then make a local effect safe under repeated delivery. Finally, we will examine a different use of events: preserving accepted business changes as authoritative history. The goal is to recover unfinished work without confusing transport attempts, completed effects, and the events used to reconstruct state.

    16.2.1 · Retries and dead-letter queues

    A receipt attempt fails because its provider is briefly unavailable. Waiting before retrying gives the provider time to recover and stops one failing job from immediately consuming another worker. An invalid address is different: sending the unchanged request a thousand times will not repair it. Classify failures and bound both attempts and waiting time.

    When the ordinary retry policy ends, a dead-letter queue can hold the unresolved work for repair or review. The job has moved to another recovery path; its business obligation has not thereby been completed. Important unresolved work still needs an owner and alerting.

    Keep the original event identity, source version, attempt history, and a safe error reason. After repair, replay should continue the same work under its duplicate and ordering rules. A replay tool that invents fresh identities could repeat established effects, while one that skips a required record could break a sequence. The repair path should restore valid progress.

    16.2.2 · Poison messages

    One record fails on every attempt while neighbouring records succeed. Its data may be malformed, its schema version unsupported, or its requested business action invalid. Such a record is often called a poison message because ordinary retries keep encountering the same obstacle.

    The response depends on the cause. If a corrected decoder can read a legitimate historical version, a controlled replay may recover the work. If the message requests an action the business rules forbid, retrying the unchanged payload will not make it valid. Before discarding records, inspect samples and failure patterns: a software bug can reject an entire valid version.

    Quarantine enough identity and error evidence to diagnose and repair the record, while avoiding unnecessary sensitive payloads. Decide whether records depending on it must wait. Bounded retries protect processing resources, and a review path protects the unresolved business work. During repair and replay, preserve the rules that prevent repeated effects and detect gaps in required ordering.

    16.2.3 · Idempotent consumers

    The consumer receives E1 and begins a database transaction. It inserts E1 into a table of processed event identifiers, then increments the orders counter. A uniqueness rule allows only one stored entry for E1. When this transaction commits, both the recognition and the counter change become durable.

    Suppose the acknowledgment is lost and E1 arrives again. The attempted insert finds the existing identity, so the consumer skips the increment. If the first transaction had rolled back, neither its identity nor its counter change would be committed, and another attempt could do the work. This is an idempotent consumer for the local effect: repeated deliveries leave the same relevant outcome.

    The two writes must share the transaction. Recording E1 first in a separate commit could cause recovery to skip a missing increment; incrementing first could cause recovery to repeat it. Keep the identity for the supported delivery and replay window, and retain it through restart. An external provider is outside this local transaction and needs its own stable key or reconciliation protocol.

    16.2.4 · Event sourcing

    An order can be represented by its latest state, or by a history of the accepted changes that produced it. With event sourcing, that accepted domain-event history is authoritative. For example, applying OrderPlaced and then later accepted changes under the order's rules reconstructs its current state.

    Reconstruction applies the events in order. A snapshot can save time by storing an intermediate state together with the event position it represents; replay then continues from the next event. A broker's transport log is not automatically this domain history. It may retain records for a different period and have different ownership and meanings.

    The history must remain interpretable as schemas change, so define how corrections, replay, privacy, and retention work. Rebuilding state or a read projection must not resend real charges or emails whenever an old event is read. Auditability also depends on the domain and its access rules: append-only storage alone does not establish a sufficient financial ledger. Choose event sourcing when preserving and interpreting this history serves a real need.

    Think further · How could one broker transaction be exactly-once while two emails are sent?

    The broker can atomically commit consumed progress and produced records while email remains outside its transaction. A consumer can send an email, lose the completion reply, and send again during recovery. Use the provider's contract, stable identity where supported, and reconciliation. The broker's scoped guarantee does not automatically cover the email effect.

    Remember: Classify failures before retrying. Preserve identity through repair, commit local duplicate recognition with its effect, and distinguish transport history from the domain history used to reconstruct state.

    Try applying it: A repaired decoder can now read a quarantined event, but that event may already have produced a local effect before failing later. Which identity and completion evidence should replay preserve, and how could skipping it affect dependent events?

    PART 4 / UNIT 16 / CHAPTER 16.3

    Read models, the outbox & sagas

    Prerequisites: 16.2 · Retries, consumers & event history4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    An order is saved successfully, but its event is never published because the service crashes. Later, payment succeeds and shipment fails. Both histories leave work owed to another part of checkout, even though a local database transaction has finished.

    We will first separate the authoritative command model from a convenient read view. Then we will record publication intent alongside the order and follow how a relay delivers it. Finally, we will coordinate several local outcomes with a saga, treating compensation as further tracked business work. These examples show what a local commit can settle and what requires continuing recovery across owners.

    16.3.1 · CQRS

    An order command checks whether a requested transition is legal before changing the authoritative order. A customer-history page has another task: show convenient rows of order summaries. Each can be simpler with a model suited to its work. Command Query Responsibility Segregation, or CQRS, separates these command and query responsibilities or models.

    A projection builds the read-friendly view from accepted changes. After an order command commits, the projection may still show the earlier state until it processes that change. Define what the customer should see during this interval. The application might read the current authoritative owner, show progress, or accept a stated delay. It also needs a way to rebuild the projection after failure.

    CQRS can use one database and one process. Event sourcing, separate databases, and separate services are additional choices. Introduce extra models and synchronisation where they simplify actual validation and query workloads enough to justify maintaining agreement between them.

    16.3.2 · Transactional outbox

    An order commits, but the process crashes before it publishes OrderPlaced. The database contains the order, while downstream services have no event to act on. A transactional outbox repairs this local gap: write the order change and an outbox row describing the event in the same database transaction. A commit establishes both the change and the obligation to publish; an abort establishes neither.

    A relay reads the pending outbox row and publishes its event. Suppose publication succeeds, then the relay crashes before marking the row sent. On recovery, the row still appears pending, so the relay can publish the same event again. The durable intent prevents forgotten publication, but it does not by itself prevent repetition.

    Keep a stable event identity so consumers can handle duplicates. Monitor the age of pending intents and retain enough history for the required recovery. The original transaction covers local state and publication intent; subscribers and their external effects keep their own transaction, identity, and recovery rules.

    16.3.3 · Sagas and compensating transactions

    Checkout reserves inventory, authorises payment, and requests shipment from separate owners. Each step can commit locally before the next begins. A saga records this sequence and the actions required when the overall operation cannot continue.

    Suppose inventory is reserved and payment authorised, but shipment creation fails. The workflow now owes compensating actions: release the stock reservation and cancel the authorisation or request the appropriate refund, according to the payment state. The reservation and payment step really occurred. Compensation is another business operation that moves the system toward an acceptable recovery outcome.

    Persist forward and compensating progress. If a refund attempt fails or its reply is lost, the saga remains unresolved until retry or reconciliation establishes the result. A refund may happen later, incur different costs, or leave user-visible consequences; compensation is not always a perfect inverse. When any step's reply is missing, check the relevant authority using its stable identity before assuming nothing happened or starting a fresh operation.

    Think further · How could one broker transaction be exactly-once while two emails are sent?

    The broker can atomically commit consumed progress and produced records while email remains outside its transaction. A consumer can send an email, lose the completion reply, and send again during recovery. Use the provider's contract, stable identity where supported, and reconciliation. The broker's scoped guarantee does not automatically cover the email effect.

    Remember: An outbox commits local state with the obligation to publish. A saga tracks outcomes and compensation across owners. Each mechanism settles a particular gap while later effects keep their own recovery rules.

    Try applying it: The outbox relay publishes OrderPlaced and crashes before marking it sent. What does recovery see, why can publication repeat, and which transaction should protect a subscriber’s local update?

    PART 4 / UNIT 16 / CHAPTER 16.4

    Coordinate durable workflows

    Prerequisites: 16.3 · Read models, the outbox & sagas6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Checkout may wait for approval long after the original request has ended. During that wait, a scheduler can restart, a worker can lose its lease, and a provider can finish an operation whose reply never arrives. Recovery needs to know which business intention still exists and which attempt currently has authority.

    We will compare participant-driven coordination with an explicit coordinator, then examine how engines and durable job records preserve progress. Stable identities will connect scheduled occurrences, worker attempts, and provider outcomes. We will also budget replay alongside live traffic and reconcile uncertain results, so restarting work advances the original operation safely.

    16.4.1 · Choreography vs orchestration

    After inventory is reserved, checkout needs to request payment. With choreography, a participant observes the InventoryReserved event and reacts by starting the next action. With orchestration, an explicit coordinator records “inventory reserved” and decides to issue the payment command. Both arrangements can implement the same business sequence.

    Follow where an operator would find the current progress and the next obligation. In choreography, that information is spread across participants and their events, which can make an entire stalled workflow harder to see. Orchestration gathers the decisions about retries and compensation into a coordinator, while adding that coordinator and a workflow definition that must evolve safely.

    Neither arrangement removes participant failure or the need for durable outcomes. Choose according to the sequence's complexity, audit needs, and teams changing it. Carry a shared correlation identity through either design so an operator can connect each participant's records to the same business operation and work out where it stopped.

    16.4.2 · Workflow engines

    A workflow requests human approval and waits. Its executor then restarts. If progress and the outstanding wait are durable, a replacement can continue waiting for the same approval instead of beginning checkout again. A workflow engine provides mechanisms for persisting progress, timers, and retry decisions under its supported programming model.

    External activities still have separate failure points. Suppose an activity sends a payment request, the provider accepts it, and the worker crashes before recording completion. The recovered workflow knows that it dispatched the activity, but may not know the provider's result. Running the activity again can repeat the call. A stable activity identity and effect key let recovery relate attempts to the original intention and reconcile with the provider.

    Understand the engine's replay, determinism, versioning, activity-identity, and cancellation rules. The application must still define legal transitions and safe external actions. Durable coordination makes long-running recovery easier within that model; it does not automatically establish one external effect for every activity.

    16.4.3 · Durable job execution

    A durable job record keeps the intended work's identity, input reference, progress, attempt history, and replaceable owner. The job is the business intention. An attempt is one worker's try at carrying it out.

    Suppose attempt seven stops responding, loses authority, and attempt eight begins. Attempt seven may later resume. Before accepting its result, storage must check that the attempt or fencing epoch is still current and that the result belongs to the expected input version. A conditional completion can then reject the obsolete worker's write. This check protects the result where it is enforced; external effect receivers need suitable protection too.

    Store large inputs separately and verify their version before processing. Bound retries and expose terminal or review states when automatic recovery cannot finish. Returning HTTP 202 does not itself give a process-local background task durable progress or a replacement owner. The accepted response must agree with the persisted job and with who will continue it after a crash.

    16.4.4 · Scheduling, leases, and worker coordination

    A report is due at noon. Two schedulers both observe that it is time to run. Give the occurrence a stable identity, such as (schedule_id, occurrence), and use an atomic claim or uniqueness rule to create one durable run for it. Later worker retries are attempts of that run; they are not new noon occurrences.

    A worker may hold a lease that grants authority for a limited period. If its lease expires while it is paused, another worker can take over, yet the old worker may resume too. Lease expiry does not stop its code. Protect accepted effects with the appropriate idempotency or fencing checks at the resource that receives them.

    Define what happens after missed periods, clock changes, overlapping runs, and scheduler failover. One scheduler process does not by itself make occurrences unique or recoverable across restarts. Deciding that an occurrence is due and safely executing its effects are separate stages, each needing durable identity and recovery rules.

    16.4.5 · Backpressure and replay

    A consumer returns after an outage and replays retained input. Its old records may call the same database or provider that is currently serving live requests. If replay uses all available capacity, current users can wait even though the recovery worker appears productive.

    For an illustrative capacity budget, suppose the dependency can handle 100 operations per second and live work needs 70. At most 30 operations per second remain for replay under those assumptions; allocating all 100 to replay leaves no room for the live work. These figures are teaching inputs, not measured capacity. Backpressure limits admission or slows producers when downstream work cannot keep up, while a separate replay budget limits catch-up work.

    Preserve source identities and suppress or separately control repeated external effects during replay. Retention must cover the required recovery interval. Monitor oldest unfinished age and blockage by key as well as queue length and throughput. Many completed records can hide one important operation that has remained stuck.

    16.4.6 · Reconciliation after partial failure

    The local payment record says pending, but the provider has charged the card. This can happen when the provider accepts the charge and its reply is lost before local completion is saved. A fresh charge would risk paying twice.

    Reconciliation compares the intended local operation with the observed external outcome. Use the original stable operation identity to query the provider. If evidence confirms the charge, apply the matching local transition under the usual uniqueness and state rules, and record the evidence. If the evidence is incomplete, keep a pending investigation state. Recovery is advancing the existing intention rather than inventing another payment to clear a pending row.

    The reconciler must be authorised, idempotent, and observable. Run reconciliation periodically and during recovery, and track unresolved discrepancies by age and owner. This is a normal part of handling partial failure. It still depends on correct persistence and validation on the main path: without the original identity and intent, there may be no safe basis for comparison.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · duplicate delivery, one local effect

    from mechanisms import open_demo_store, consume_local_event
db = open_demo_store()
assert consume_local_event(db, "E1", "orders")
assert not consume_local_event(db, "E1", "orders")
assert db.execute("SELECT value FROM counters").fetchone()[0] == 1
db.close()

    The first call receives E1 and returns True. Within its transaction, it inserts E1 into the processed-event table and increments the orders counter from zero to one. The second call uses the same E1, finds that identity already present, returns False, and leaves the counter at one. The assertion checks this committed local result.

    Event recognition and the counter update share one transaction. If that transaction rolls back, neither change is committed, so recovery can try again. If acknowledgment is lost after commit, repeated delivery can safely find E1. This example protects a local database effect. Replacing the increment with an external email or payment call would require another protocol because the provider is outside that transaction.

    Think further · How could one broker transaction be exactly-once while two emails are sent?

    The broker can atomically commit consumed progress and produced records while email remains outside its transaction. A consumer can send an email, lose the completion reply, and send again during recovery. Use the provider's contract, stable identity where supported, and reconciliation. The broker's scoped guarantee does not automatically cover the email effect.

    Remember: Keep a durable identity for the intention and a separate record of attempts and authority. Recovery can then reject stale completion, limit replay, and reconcile uncertain outcomes against the original operation.

    Try applying it: Attempt seven loses its lease and attempt eight starts. Meanwhile, the provider reports that the original payment succeeded although the workflow says pending. Which checks should govern worker completion, and how should recovery use the provider result?

    PART 4 / UNIT 17 / CHAPTER 17.1

    Failure domains & redundancy

    Prerequisites: Requirements, Estimation, and Engineering Trade-offs, Scalability, Load Balancing, and Data Distribution, Replication, Leader Election, and Consensus, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Two application replicas run on different processes, so we expect one to keep serving if the other stops. During an incident, both lose access to the same credential source and fail together. Later, a single surviving replica cannot carry the traffic that the pair had been serving.

    These histories raise different questions: which causes can remove several replicas at once, what information survives, and how much work the survivors can complete? In this chapter, we will map failure domains, separate availability from durability, and examine the state, capacity, and authority needed for active-active and active-passive operation.

    17.1.1 · Failure domains and fault isolation

    Two workers use the same disk and credential source. Their processes are separate, but one disk failure or credential change can stop both. A failure domain groups parts exposed to a common cause.

    List those shared causes as well as the separate processes. If both workers run on one host, losing that host removes both workers' CPU and disk access. Even on separate hosts, a credential rotation can deny both access to the same provider. A process boundary protects against some failures while leaving these others shared.

    Fault isolation limits how a failure spreads. For example, separating the resources used by payment and receipt delivery can keep a stalled email provider from occupying every payment worker. Map the shared hosts, zones, dependencies, and administrative controls before choosing a boundary. Separation costs capacity and operating work, so choose it according to the harm and recovery objective, then test the shared dependencies as well as individual processes.

    17.1.2 · Availability vs durability

    A database refuses requests during recovery but keeps all committed rows. Users cannot obtain service during this period, although their committed data remains recoverable. A web application can show the opposite problem: it keeps answering requests but loses writes that it had accepted into memory before a restart.

    Availability concerns whether users can obtain the required service when they need it. Durability concerns whether accepted, committed information remains recoverable through the stated failures. We need separate evidence for these promises. A successful response does not establish that a write will survive a restart; a recoverable database does not establish that it can serve requests now.

    Define which requests count and what a useful response means, then state the data-loss tolerance and failures covered. During a careful restore, stopping service may help preserve the correct history. Traffic failover may restore access, while backups may recover data. Neither measure alone establishes the whole reliability contract.

    17.1.3 · Redundancy

    Two instances each operate at 70% of their individual capacity. If one fails, the remaining instance cannot absorb both workloads at the same rate. Redundancy provides additional instances or copies, but it needs enough surviving capacity to carry the promised workload.

    For illustration, assume each instance can handle 100 requests per second while meeting the response-time target. Two running at 70% carry 140 requests per second together. After one fails, the survivor can complete only 100 at that assumed capacity. The remaining forty requests per second need a permitted reduced-service or rejection policy. A queue can absorb a short burst, but it will keep growing if this excess continues.

    The replacement also needs usable state, independent failure placement, failure detection, and traffic movement. Shared bad configuration can disable every replica at once. Test takeover and restoration under the expected load. Spare resources help when the system can find them, direct work to them, and preserve the required state during the transition.

    17.1.4 · Active-active vs active-passive

    In active-active operation, several locations or instances serve the selected function at the same time. Active-passive keeps a standby ready for takeover. The choice can differ by layer: application instances may all serve requests while one database leader owns writes.

    A standby may hold a data copy without accepting authoritative writes. To promote it, we must establish whether its history meets the data-loss policy and prevent the earlier owner from writing again. This prevention is called fencing. In an active-active arrangement, define which actions different participants may accept concurrently and how conflicting changes are prevented or resolved.

    A passive standby can have configuration drift or warmup problems that appear only during takeover. Multiple active instances need routing and suitable coordination. For either arrangement, define failure detection, surviving capacity, and the return after repair. Test that the replacement can reconstruct usable state and serve real requests. The operating model includes these transitions as well as the normal traffic arrangement.

    Think further · How can a disaster drill restore infrastructure yet fail the business recovery requirement?

    Machines can run while restored data is too old for the RPO, backups lack usable keys, accepted jobs are missing, or competing owners can still write. Validation and traffic return may also push useful service beyond the RTO even when machine startup is fast.

    Test the full business journey with its required state, identities, authority, credentials, and recovery objectives. Include unresolved effects and catch-up work. A successful drill provides evidence for the scenario it exercised, rather than every possible disaster.

    Remember: Redundancy protects the stated service only when survivors have independent failure placement, usable state, sufficient capacity, and a tested path to take over.

    Try applying it: Two instances each serve 70% of their measured capacity. After one fails, what must change for the survivor to preserve the required service?
