    PART 4 / UNIT 17 / CHAPTER 17.2

    Retries, circuit breakers & isolation

    Prerequisites: 17.1 · Failure domains & redundancy6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    During peak traffic, the payment provider slows down. Calls retain connections while they wait, new requests queue, and callers begin retrying. Soon the application has few resources left even for requests whose dependencies are healthy.

    Repeating the calls cannot restore the missing capacity. We need to decide how long work remains useful, which failures justify another attempt, and how much recovery traffic the service can afford. We will follow deadlines, retry budgets, circuit breakers, resource isolation, and rate limits to see where each can interrupt this sequence.

    17.2.1 · Timeouts

    A client permits two seconds for an operation. Spending three seconds waiting for a database connection would exceed that allowance before the query even starts. An overall deadline marks the time after which the request is no longer useful to its caller.

    Record the deadline when the request begins. Before each stage, calculate how much time remains. Waiting for a pooled connection, making remote attempts, backing off between attempts, and returning the reply all consume the same allowance. A stage timeout limits a particular wait; it should fit within the remaining overall time. Giving every stage a fresh full timeout can keep work running long after the caller has stopped waiting.

    Pass the remaining time downstream and cancel or clean up owned work when possible so it releases resources. Record which stage timed out to distinguish waiting for a connection from executing a query. A timeout does not prove that an external write failed: the provider may have completed it before its reply was lost. That uncertain effect needs recovery even though the caller's wait has ended.

    17.2.2 · Retries, exponential backoff, jitter

    A dropped connection during a safe lookup may justify another attempt. An invalid payment amount will not improve if the same request is repeated. Before retrying, decide whether the failure is likely to be temporary and whether repeating this operation is safe.

    Backoff increases the wait between attempts. With exponential backoff, the wait grows by a factor after each failure, usually up to a chosen maximum. Jitter varies these waits so callers are less likely to retry together. These techniques change timing; a maximum attempt count, an overall retry budget, and a deadline bound the extra work.

    If an effect may already have happened, retain a stable operation identity and use a repetition or lookup rule supported by the receiver. An identifier alone cannot make an arbitrary payment call safe to repeat. Respect relevant retry guidance and decide which layer owns retries. Several independent policies can multiply attempts around one request. Include retry traffic in capacity planning, because it competes with new work and recovery.

    17.2.3 · Retry storms

    Four nested layers each allow three attempts, including the initial attempt. One logical request can then create up to 3⁴ = 81 downstream attempts. During a dependency outage, this amplification can consume the capacity that might otherwise complete useful work.

    Draw a call tree. The outer layer can make three attempts. Each can cause three attempts at the next layer, giving nine. Repeating this through four layers gives 3×3×3×3 = 81 attempts at the bottom. This is a worst-case allowance: success, a deadline, or another limit may stop the tree sooner.

    Coordinate retry ownership and enforce a budget across the whole path. Jitter spreads attempts in time but does not reduce their configured total by itself. Bound admission and suppress redundant work where possible. Measure original user intents separately from attempts and useful completions; a rise in traffic during an outage may come from retries rather than new users. Leave capacity for successful work and recovery.

    17.2.4 · Circuit breakers

    A dependency repeatedly fails. A circuit breaker can temporarily reject new calls, preventing each caller from holding resources while waiting for another likely failure. Its common states are closed, open, and half-open.

    While closed, the breaker permits calls and observes their outcomes. When its configured failure rule is met, it opens and rejects selected calls promptly. After a wait, it becomes half-open and permits a limited number of recovery probes. Successful probes can close it again; failed probes can reopen it. Define the outcomes and thresholds that control these transitions.

    Bound probes across callers and avoid having all instances probe simultaneously after a shared timer. Otherwise, recovery can trigger another surge. The breaker controls resource expenditure; it does not repair the dependency or choose an acceptable business result. A failed authorisation call must not become a fabricated payment approval. The application still needs a deliberate failure, pending, or degraded response whose meaning fits the operation.

    17.2.5 · Bulkheads

    Receipt email stalls and occupies every worker. Payment authorisation now cannot obtain a worker even though its provider is healthy. Bulkheads reserve or separate resources so one kind of work cannot consume the entire allowance needed by another.

    Give receipt delivery its own bounded workers and connections, with a separate allocation for payment work. If email stalls, it can occupy only its allocation. Bound its waiting queue too, so a growing receipt backlog does not exhaust memory. Payment work can then continue within its reserved capacity, provided the resources it still shares remain available.

    Check those shared limits: two worker pools may still exhaust one database, network link, or host. Their combined limits must fit the shared capacity. Too much partitioning can leave resources idle in one pool while another rejects work, so choose boundaries according to workload and harm. Observe saturation and rejection in each pool. Isolation must cover the resource through which the failure would spread.

    17.2.6 · Rate limiting

    Suppose a caller may send occasional bursts, but we need to limit its continuing request rate. A token bucket records an allowance of tokens. Tokens accumulate at a configured refill rate up to the bucket's capacity, and each admitted request spends tokens.

    Start a bucket with ten tokens and a refill rate of two per second. Ten immediate unit-cost requests can use the initial burst. If no more requests are admitted, three seconds later the balance is six tokens; it can never exceed the bucket's capacity. Coordinate the balance update and spending decision so simultaneous callers cannot both spend the last token. Excess requests may be rejected. A shaper may instead delay work to control its pace, using bounded waiting.

    Define the caller identity, request cost, burst size, and total service budget. Per-tenant limits can support fairness, but their combined allowances must also protect shared capacity. If the limiter's remote state becomes unavailable, decide whether to reject, allow, or spend a previously allocated local budget. These choices have different availability and abuse consequences, so test that failure path.

    Think further · How can a disaster drill restore infrastructure yet fail the business recovery requirement?

    Machines can run while restored data is too old for the RPO, backups lack usable keys, accepted jobs are missing, or competing owners can still write. Validation and traffic return may also push useful service beyond the RTO even when machine startup is fast.

    Test the full business journey with its required state, identities, authority, credentials, and recovery objectives. Include unresolved effects and catch-up work. A successful drill provides evidence for the scenario it exercised, rather than every possible disaster.

    Remember: Deadlines bound useful lifetime; retry budgets bound repeated work; breakers, bulkheads, and rate limits protect the resources through which failures spread.

    Try applying it: Four nested layers each allow three attempts. Why can jitter spread those attempts without solving their total load, and where should the overall limit apply?

    PART 4 / UNIT 17 / CHAPTER 17.3

    Shed load and degrade deliberately

    Prerequisites: 17.2 · Retries, circuit breakers & isolation4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    The recommendation service is unavailable, but the catalog still works. We can show a useful product page without recommendations. If the ledger is unavailable, however, a convenient default balance cannot establish whether a payment is permitted.

    The challenge is to define useful reduced service while preserving the meaning of each operation. We will choose work to shed, examine graceful degradation and fallback paths, and distinguish health checks that control restarting from those that control incoming traffic. Each decision must account for the capacity and business rules that remain.

    17.3.1 · Load shedding

    Under overload, a service may stop generating recommendations while preserving order status and reconciliation. Load shedding rejects selected work early enough to leave resources for higher-priority outcomes.

    Rejecting before expensive parsing or remote calls can protect more capacity than rejecting after that work has already been done. Choose priorities from product and correctness requirements. Reconciliation may need reserved capacity to discover the outcomes of already accepted payments, even while optional recommendations are being refused. Return a clear overload result and bound subsequent retries so rejection does not simply create more work.

    Shedding can preserve useful completions while demand exceeds capacity; it cannot serve all of an indefinitely excessive workload. More capacity, less work per request, or a changed service target may still be needed. Measure useful accepted outcomes and fairness across callers. Raw throughput can fall while essential work improves, because the service has deliberately stopped spending resources on lower-priority work.

    17.3.2 · Graceful degradation

    A product page can remain useful without recommendations. A sale cannot safely proceed merely because an old cached count says stock exists. Graceful degradation preserves an agreed subset of useful behaviour while keeping the rules that still matter.

    Define that reduced result before the incident. If recommendations fail, the page can still show the product description and price. If the system cannot establish permission to allocate stock, it may need to pause purchase confirmation. Showing an optimistic confirmation would create a promise that the system cannot support.

    Specify which data may be stale, which actions pause, and what the user sees. Then test the reduced path, including its permissions and capacity. Such paths may be used rarely in ordinary operation and fail when first needed. Catching every error and returning a default does not establish safety; the alternative outcome needs a clear meaning of its own.

    17.3.3 · Fallbacks

    A cached help page may substitute for an unavailable content service. A default account balance cannot establish the state of an unavailable ledger. A fallback is an alternative behaviour whose meaning must be acceptable for this operation.

    The fallback is another path through the system, with its own data age, permissions, and load limit. If every failed cache request goes to one small database, the substitute can become the next outage. Check what all callers will do together, as well as whether one fallback request succeeds. Specify how long the alternative remains acceptable and make degraded operation visible where needed.

    Switching payment providers also requires care. If the first provider may already have charged the customer, sending the payment to another provider can create a second charge. The alternative must account for the first attempt's identity and uncertain outcome; changing providers does not settle that history. Evaluate a fallback as a business outcome and a recovery path, rather than treating any returned response as success.

    17.3.4 · Health checking

    A process keeps restarting because its liveness check calls an unavailable shared provider. Restarting cannot repair that provider. If every replica follows the same rule, they can all restart together and add warmup work during the outage.

    Keep each probe focused on the decision it controls. Liveness asks whether the process needs restarting, for example because it is stuck. Readiness asks whether traffic should be sent here now. Removing readiness can stop new traffic, while separately arranged draining lets ongoing work finish. A startup check or allowance gives initialisation time before ordinary checks apply.

    Bound probe work and avoid making every process restart depend on an external service it cannot repair. Readiness policy also needs care: marking every replica unready for one shared dependency may remove service that could still operate in a permitted reduced mode. A successful probe is evidence about that check, not proof that every critical operation meets its objective. Monitor real useful operations alongside these local signals.

    Think further · How can a disaster drill restore infrastructure yet fail the business recovery requirement?

    Machines can run while restored data is too old for the RPO, backups lack usable keys, accepted jobs are missing, or competing owners can still write. Validation and traffic return may also push useful service beyond the RTO even when machine startup is fast.

    Test the full business journey with its required state, identities, authority, credentials, and recovery objectives. Include unresolved effects and catch-up work. A successful drill provides evidence for the scenario it exercised, rather than every possible disaster.

    Remember: Choose reduced service by its business meaning, and check that its permissions, freshness, and capacity remain acceptable during the failure.

    Try applying it: Why can a cached help page remain useful during an outage while a default account balance cannot justify a payment?

    PART 4 / UNIT 17 / CHAPTER 17.4

    Recover, test & learn from failure

    Prerequisites: 17.3 · Shed load and degrade deliberately8 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    The replacement machines are running, yet checkout still cannot resume. A restored database is too old, an encryption key is missing, or a repaired primary attempts to write using its former authority. Infrastructure can return before the required business service does.

    We will set recovery time and data-loss objectives, follow a complete restore and authority handover, and test the failure scenarios that the design promises to cover. We will then use service objectives, controlled fault exercises, and incident evidence to choose changes that reduce the causes and consequences of future outages.

    17.4.1 · RTO and RPO

    An incident begins at noon. Service returns at 12:20, so the interruption lasted twenty minutes. If recovery restores data only through 11:55, there is five minutes of data-loss exposure relative to the incident point.

    The recovery time objective, or RTO, is the target time to restore the defined service. The recovery point objective, or RPO, specifies the acceptable gap between the incident and the recoverable data history, often expressed as time. In our example, twenty minutes and five minutes are observed results to compare with the targets. They do not tell us whether the business considers that recovery acceptable. The five-minute gap describes exposure; actual lost records depend on what was written in that interval.

    Set both objectives for the business function. Then measure detection, decision, restoration, validation, and traffic return. Timing only a file copy misses much of the interruption. A faster restore may use older data, so evaluate recovery time and data-loss exposure separately.

    17.4.2 · Backups and restore testing

    A backup survives the lost host, but its only decryption key was on that host. The bytes exist, yet the application cannot recover them. A useful backup needs the surrounding restoration resources too.

    A restore needs usable bytes, required keys and credentials, compatible software, configuration, and an environment in which the application can run. Document schema versions and any retained logs needed to reach the required recovery point. Keep these resources independent enough from the failed domain to remain usable. A rehearsal can find missing pieces while ordinary service still runs.

    Restore actual backups and check business invariants and reconciliation state, rather than relying only on a completed backup job or valid checksums. Live replication may repeat a mistaken deletion or corruption, while a retained historical backup may recover an earlier state. State which failure each copy protects against and test the corresponding procedure. A copy is useful recovery evidence only when the application can use it to restore the required service and history.

    17.4.3 · Failover and failback

    Failover moves service or write authority to a replacement. Failback returns it after repair. Both transitions need valid history, sufficient capacity, routing, and protection from conflicting owners.

    Before moving writes, establish which destination holds the required history under the data-loss policy and which owner may act next. Fence the old owner so that a delayed or restarted process cannot continue writing. After repair, the old primary must catch up or be rebuilt from the new history before regaining authority. Sending traffic back too soon can expose older data or allow two competing writers.

    A database promotion alone does not move every user request. Existing connections, cached addresses, and retries may continue using old paths. Test the full sequence: transfer authority, route traffic, validate useful service, and later return after repair. Include the old owner's attempted return in the test. Recovery is incomplete if that return can reintroduce incompatible writes.

    17.4.4 · Multi-zone and multi-region deployments

    Copies in separate zones can survive some local incidents. Copies in separate regions can cover other failures, but add propagation delay, transfer cost, data-placement concerns, and recovery work.

    Ask which failure each placement should survive. Separate zones can reduce shared local infrastructure risks. A remote region can protect against a regional incident while adding distance between data copies. Waiting for a distant copy can increase write latency; not waiting can leave recent writes unavailable there when failover is needed. The chosen replication and promotion rules must meet the stated recovery objective.

    Check dependencies that remain shared. A global credential change or configuration fault can still affect all regions. Plan capacity for surviving traffic and catch-up work, rather than only the normal traffic split. Geographic distance provides part of the independence. The authority protocol, usable data, and operational dependencies determine whether the remaining location can actually provide the promised service.

    17.4.5 · Chaos engineering

    Begin a fault exercise with a question: if a worker pauses past its lease, can its old completion overwrite a new result? A lease gives authority for a limited period; a pause can leave the worker acting on authority that has already expired.

    State the expected invariant, introduce a bounded fault, and check the result. Pause the first worker, let a replacement gain authority, then resume the first and attempt completion. The protected store should reject the stale result. Observing that both processes eventually run again would not establish that the invariant held.

    Chaos engineering tests such hypotheses by introducing controlled faults. Define the affected scope, stop conditions, observations, recovery owner, and environment appropriate to the risk. Random process killing without a hypothesis may cause harm without clarifying a mechanism. Increase scope when the evidence justifies it. A passing drill supports the tested scenario and configuration; it does not prove every future failure harmless.

    17.4.6 · SLO-based reliability decisions

    Suppose optional calls consume most of a request's deadline and cause most failures. Removing those calls from the critical path may improve the user experience more directly than adding another region.

    Use the service-level objective, or SLO, to identify the required useful outcome. Break down which eligible requests miss it and why. If an optional dependency dominates those failures, removing its wait may address the measured problem. Compare that change with the costs and new failure paths of another region. The error budget—the amount of failure allowed by the objective over its measurement period—helps show how quickly current failures are consuming the allowance.

    Keep important low-volume operations visible. Their failures can disappear inside a denominator dominated by cheap successful reads, so separate indicators where the harm differs. More redundancy has cost and complexity; choose it for a failure mechanism it can improve. An error budget helps prioritise work, but a small event count does not make a severe payment or data-loss incident harmless.

    17.4.7 · Cascading failures

    A slow provider holds connections. Waiting requests accumulate, callers retry, and the extra work overloads previously healthy components. This feedback creates a cascading failure: an initial problem spreads through the resources and dependencies that connect the system.

    The first slowdown reduces useful completions. Waiting work retains resources for longer, so fewer resources remain for new requests. Callers then retry, adding demand to the same reduced capacity. A healthy component can become overloaded even though it had no original fault. Interrupting this loop requires reducing admitted or repeated work and releasing scarce resources, while preserving an explicit outcome for obligations already accepted.

    Use deadlines, bounded admission, retry budgets, isolation, and permitted degradation at the resource boundaries involved. Leave capacity for reconciliation and recovery. A breaker that sends every failed request to one fallback can start another cascade. Trace the original and recovery paths under a shared failure; testing dependencies one at a time can miss the interaction that turns a modest slowdown into a widespread outage.

    17.4.8 · Incident analysis and prevention

    After an incident, reconstruct what happened, which conditions allowed it, how it was detected, and what helped or delayed recovery. Stopping at “human error” leaves unanswered why one action could affect every replica.

    A timeline separates the initiating event from the conditions that let harm spread. A mistaken command may be the trigger; broad permissions and shared placement may explain its reach. Connect corrective work to those observed mechanisms. Scoped credentials can reduce exposure, a tested restore can improve recovery, and bounded retries can limit amplification. The incident evidence should explain why each action is useful.

    Give each action an owner and a way to verify completion. Replaying the relevant failure sequence can show whether the changed system now limits the harm. An added alert helps only when it leads to a useful response. The aim is to reduce recurrence or impact by changing the system and its operating conditions, with evidence that the change addresses what happened.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · retry amplification

    attempts_per_layer = 3
independent_retry_layers = 4
assert attempts_per_layer ** independent_retry_layers == 81

    The assertion calculates 3⁴ = 81 permitted downstream attempts in the nested worst case. The first layer can make three attempts; each can cause three at the next layer, giving nine, then twenty-seven, then eighty-one. Each layer's three attempts include its initial attempt. Actual execution can stop earlier after success or when another limit is reached.

    The code checks the arithmetic, not an outage policy. Use an overall retry budget and deadline to bound the whole path, protect capacity for useful work and recovery, and retain operation identity under a supported repetition rule. Jitter changes when attempts occur; it does not reduce the configured total by itself.

    Think further · How can a disaster drill restore infrastructure yet fail the business recovery requirement?

    Machines can run while restored data is too old for the RPO, backups lack usable keys, accepted jobs are missing, or competing owners can still write. Validation and traffic return may also push useful service beyond the RTO even when machine startup is fast.

    Test the full business journey with its required state, identities, authority, credentials, and recovery objectives. Include unresolved effects and catch-up work. A successful drill provides evidence for the scenario it exercised, rather than every possible disaster.

    Remember: Recovery restores useful service, required history, and valid authority. Measure the whole journey, then use drills and incident evidence to test specific improvements.

    Try applying it: A drill brings machines back quickly but restores only old data. Which recovery objective may still be missed, and what else must be checked before declaring recovery?

    PART 5 / UNIT 18 / CHAPTER 18.1

    Threats, identity & authorization

    Prerequisites: Networking Foundations for System Design, Application Architecture and Domain-Driven Design, API Design and Communication Contracts, Data Models and Storage Technologies7 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A document service serves two organisations. An administrator from tenant A signs in successfully and changes a document identifier in the request to one belonging to tenant B. The service recognises the administrator, yet must still reject the read.

    We will follow this request from the browser through identity validation and the resource permission check. Along the way, we will distinguish login from delegated access, connect roles to their tenant scope, and decide how much authority a worker needs. The aim is to explain which evidence permits a particular action, rather than assuming a successful login permits every later request.

    18.1.1 · Threat modeling

    Begin with a document service's valuable assets: private files, credentials, processing capacity, and trustworthy audit records. The organisations using this shared service are its tenants. Each tenant's administrators should manage that organisation's documents without gaining access to another's.

    Take one asset, a private PDF. An unauthorised reader might guess its identifier, reuse an old download link, or find its contents in a worker's logs. An attacker might also submit files that exhaust the extraction workers. These paths cause different harms and need different controls.

    Threat modelling connects a possible misuse to the asset at risk, the actor's actual privileges, a control, and a way to check that control. Draw how the document travels through the service and where the assumptions about its caller or contents change. For the guessed-identifier path, require a resource ownership check and test a request from another tenant. Prioritise plausible harmful paths; the drawing is useful when it helps explain how a particular harm is prevented.

    18.1.2 · Trust boundaries

    A browser submits a document, a worker reads it from storage, and an operator changes production settings. Each crosses a boundary with different expectations about identity, data, and authority. A trust boundary marks where those expectations change.

    At the browser boundary, a submitted tenant identifier is a claim made by the caller. The application must establish the caller's identity and permitted tenant before using that claim to select private data. If a trusted gateway forwards identity headers, configure which gateway may supply them and prevent a direct caller from impersonating it.

    The worker boundary raises another question. A file may have been uploaded by an authenticated user, but its contents remain untrusted. Parsing it may require restricted execution, limited storage access, and limits on time or memory. An internal job message also needs a trustworthy job identity and scope. State what evidence each receiver relies on and what it must validate before performing its sensitive operation.

    18.1.3 · Authentication vs authorization

    An administrator of tenant A signs in and asks for tenant B's document. The identity can be genuine while the requested action is forbidden. Authentication establishes who the actor is. Authorisation checks whether that actor may perform a particular action on a particular resource.

    Follow the request in order. Validate the credential, resolve the actor's permitted tenant from trusted membership information, and load the document within that scope. Then check whether the actor may perform the requested action. An “administrator” label is incomplete unless we know which organisation it applies to. A tenant value supplied in the request cannot grant membership by itself.

    Deny access unless the policy permits it. Apply the relevant resource and action check to reads, edits, exports, and background work. Difficult-to-guess identifiers can reduce enumeration, but someone who learns an identifier must still be denied another tenant's data. Test both allowed and forbidden operations with two tenants, including documents that share the same local identifier.

    18.1.4 · Sessions, cookies, tokens

    After a successful login, the application needs a way to recognise later requests. One design creates a random session identifier and stores the associated identity and expiry on the server. The browser sends that identifier in a cookie, and the server looks up the session on each request.

    Another design uses a token carrying claims that the receiver validates, such as who issued it, its intended recipient, and its expiry. A cookie describes browser storage and transport; a token describes a credential or its representation. These are different dimensions: a signed token can also be carried in a cookie. A valid signature alone does not establish that the token is current, intended for this service, or sufficient for this action.

    Protect credentials in transit and use suitable cookie attributes and cross-site request forgery (CSRF) controls. CSRF occurs when another site causes the browser to send an unwanted request using credentials it attaches automatically. Decide how logout and revocation take effect: removing a server session and waiting for an independently validated token to expire have different behaviour. Use reviewed libraries and document the chosen lifetime.

    18.1.5 · OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect

    Suppose the document application wants permission to read a user's files from another service. OAuth 2.0 supports delegated access: the application receives authority to call a resource API within an allowed scope. Establishing which user signed in is a related but different task. OpenID Connect adds an identity layer to OAuth, including an ID token intended for the client application.

    In an OpenID Connect authorisation-code journey, the browser goes to the identity provider, where the user authenticates. The provider returns a code to the registered redirect location. The application exchanges that code for the intended tokens, following the protocol. Proof Key for Code Exchange, or PKCE, binds the exchange to a verifier held by the client, helping prevent misuse of an intercepted or injected code.

    The client validates the ID token for its identity purpose. The API validates its own access token for API access; an arbitrary access token is not a login assertion, and an ID token is not a substitute API credential. Use maintained libraries and current OAuth security guidance. The checks include who issued the token (issuer), whom it is intended for (audience), its expiry, and the permitted redirect location. Where the flow requires state or nonce checks, a state value links the returned response to the initiating browser request; a nonce links the ID token to that login attempt. Follow the checks specified for the chosen flow and role.

    18.1.6 · Role-based and attribute-based access control

    A tenant administrator may export documents while an ordinary member may only read them. Role-based access control assigns permissions through roles such as administrator or member. Attribute-based access control evaluates facts about the actor, resource, and request, such as tenant membership, document owner, or classification.

    The service can combine them. First require a role that permits export. Then require that the document belongs to a tenant in which the actor currently holds that role. “Administrator” without the tenant condition would grant much broader authority. Both the role assignment and the document's tenant must come from trusted state, rather than fields the caller can freely choose.

    Broad roles are easy to describe but can grant too much. Detailed attribute rules can express narrower permissions but need understandable inputs and tests. A central policy engine evaluates rules; enforcement points are the places that act on its answer. Every relevant API and worker path must enforce the decision, including the chosen policy for membership changes while work waits in a queue.

    18.1.7 · Least privilege

    An extraction worker needs to read one input and write its output. It does not ordinarily need to list every tenant's files or alter deployment settings. Least privilege gives an identity the operations and scope required for its work.

    For one job, give the worker a narrowly scoped credential or capability. A capability is authority carried by possession of something such as an object access link: whoever can use it may obtain the access it grants. Limit the objects, operations, and lifetime to the job's needs. If that worker is compromised, the reduced authority limits what the attacker can reach.

    Review actual inherited permissions as well as the role's description. A narrow application API is insufficient if the same identity can read all objects directly from storage. Separate runtime, deployment, and administrative identities where appropriate. Short-lived credentials need workable refresh and failure behaviour; emergency access needs its own limits and audit. Check what the identity can actually do, then remove authority it no longer requires.

    Think further · What should revocation mean for an issued object capability and a queued export?

    Define when each form of authority stops working. A queued export can check current membership before the later actions required by policy. An already issued object capability may remain usable until expiry unless the delivery mechanism supports earlier revocation. If immediate download denial is required, choose a delivery design that can enforce it rather than relying on expiry alone. Test revocation before execution, before publication, and after link issuance, and describe the resulting lifetime accurately to users.

    Remember: Validate identity first, then decide whether that actor may perform this action on this resource within the permitted tenant. Preserve that distinction in roles, protocol tokens, and worker permissions.

    Try applying it: A tenant A administrator has a valid session and knows tenant B document 7. Which identity, tenant, resource, and action checks should the request pass through, and where should it be denied?

    PART 5 / UNIT 18 / CHAPTER 18.2

    Secrets, encryption & trust boundaries

    Prerequisites: 18.1 · Threats, identity & authorization7 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A private file is encrypted, but its processing worker can read every file and obtain every decryption key. If the worker is compromised, the encryption may offer little protection against the actions that identity can already perform.

    We will trace the real access paths, then examine complementary controls: limited credentials, protected transport and storage, suitable password hashing, key custody, and network boundaries. We will also rotate a credential and consider restoring old encrypted data. The goal is to identify what each control protects and what must remain available for legitimate recovery.

    18.2.1 · Defense in depth

    A private document can be protected by tenant-scoped queries, storage permissions, limited object capabilities, worker isolation, and audit records. Defense in depth uses complementary controls so that one failure is less likely to cause the full harm.

    Suppose an application query accidentally omits its tenant filter. Independently scoped storage access may still prevent the worker from reading another tenant's object. An audit event can help detect an unexpected attempt, although recording the attempt does not prevent the read. State the role of each control rather than counting them as equivalent barriers.

    Check whether the protections can fail together. If every layer accepts the same client-supplied tenant field without validating it, repeating the check offers little independence. Also decide what happens when a policy dependency fails: an error should not silently turn a private operation into an unrestricted one. Trace a misuse path, identify which controls can interrupt it, and verify that their results actually govern the sensitive effect.

    18.2.2 · Secrets management

    A secret has a lifecycle: creation, distribution, use, rotation, and revocation. For example, a storage credential must reach the intended workers without appearing in source, logs, client bundles, or command history. Assign an owner and control who may read or replace it.

    Rotation introduces a new credential and moves legitimate users of the old credential to it. A planned change may briefly allow both versions while running instances refresh. Observe that the new version works, retire the old one, and verify that the old credential is rejected. Revocation is the step that makes earlier authority unusable under the system's enforcement rules. A suspected compromise may require faster retirement than an ordinary planned change.

    Managed identities or short-lived credentials can reduce stored secrets, but the service still needs a way to obtain initial authority and handle renewal failures. A secret-management service provides facilities; the application owns the operating plan. Encrypting a secret file adds little separation if every reader can also obtain its decryption key.

    18.2.3 · Encryption in transit and at rest

    Trace a private download. Encrypted storage is read by an authorised service, decrypted for processing, and sent to the browser over a protected connection. Plaintext exists at the processing endpoint because the endpoint needs to use it.

    Encryption in transit protects bytes while they travel between the endpoints of the protected connection. TLS supplies this protection under its protocol and configuration. If TLS ends at a gateway, examine the gateway-to-service hop separately. Encryption at rest protects stored bytes under particular assumptions about key custody and access. Neither protection makes a service with legitimate decryption rights unable to read the data.

    Now follow the copies: backups, extracted text, logs, and exported CSV files may have different storage and delivery paths. Encrypting the original PDF does not automatically protect those copies. Identify where each protection begins and ends, who can obtain plaintext there, and whether the resource policy permits that use. Use reviewed cryptographic protocols and libraries rather than constructing a new scheme for the application.

    18.2.4 · Password hashing

    If a password database is stolen, an attacker can test candidate passwords without using the login endpoint. Fast general-purpose hashes make these offline guesses inexpensive. Purpose-built password hashing deliberately requires more computation and, for suitable algorithms, memory.

    At registration, a maintained library generates a random salt and derives the stored hash using the chosen algorithm and parameters. The salt is stored with the hash; it need not be secret. Different salts prevent one precomputed result from being reused across many users. At login, verification uses the stored settings to check the supplied password without recovering the original password.

    Follow current OWASP guidance and select supported parameters after measuring their cost on the deployment's hardware and expected demand. Store the algorithm and parameters so successful verification can trigger an upgrade when needed. Do not invent one universal work setting. Reversible encryption exposes passwords to anyone who obtains the decryption key. Online login and account recovery still need separate abuse controls.

    18.2.5 · Key management and rotation

    Data encrypted with key version one may still be needed after version two becomes active. Key rotation therefore needs a mapping from encrypted data to the key version that can decrypt it. Changing the active key does not re-encrypt earlier data.

    New writes can use version two while version one remains available for required old data. Record the key reference with the ciphertext. In envelope encryption, a data key encrypts the content and a separate key-encryption key protects that data key. Recovery must obtain the protected data key and the authority needed to unwrap it.

    Key management covers generation, custody, permitted use, rotation, recovery, and destruction. Restore an older backup with its required key versions and credentials before retiring them. Otherwise, a backup can remain intact but unreadable. Map keys to live data, retained copies, and recovery requirements; then decide when older data must be re-encrypted or a key can be destroyed. Keeping every old key indefinitely can conflict with deletion goals, so recovery and retirement need one consistent lifecycle plan.

    18.2.6 · Network segmentation

    An upload worker may need storage access but no route to the production administration interface. Network segmentation divides reachable paths so a compromised component has fewer opportunities to move into unrelated systems. This further movement is often called lateral movement.

    Draw the worker's actual communication needs. Permit the required storage and coordination routes, then test that unnecessary administration paths are blocked. An allowed connection still needs authentication and permission for the requested operation. Network reachability establishes that a request can arrive; it does not establish that the caller may read a document.

    Outbound paths matter too. A service that fetches a user-supplied URL might be induced to contact a private internal endpoint. Restrict and validate destinations, including what happens after name resolution or a redirect, rather than accepting a superficially acceptable URL. Test real reachability and return paths under the deployed configuration. A firewall-rule description alone cannot show whether the intended boundary is effective.

    18.2.7 · Zero-trust principles

    A worker sends a request from an internal address. The destination recognises the address, but the worker may be compromised or may be asking for data outside its job. Network location alone cannot settle either question.

    Zero-trust principles make the actor, resource, action, and relevant context explicit instead of granting broad implicit access from location. Authenticate the workload identity, then authorise its requested resource operation. A mesh or VPN may help protect communication and establish identity; the application still needs to decide whether this worker may read this document.

    Turn the principle into operating rules. Define credential lifetimes, limited privileges, and how policy changes take effect. Cached credentials or decisions may remain usable for a stated interval, so revocation behaviour must account for that interval. The approach is not a single product and does not imply a new central lookup for every packet. Review the evidence used at each sensitive boundary and test the lifetime of the authority it grants.

    Think further · What should revocation mean for an issued object capability and a queued export?

    Define when each form of authority stops working. A queued export can check current membership before the later actions required by policy. An already issued object capability may remain usable until expiry unless the delivery mechanism supports earlier revocation. If immediate download denial is required, choose a delivery design that can enforce it rather than relying on expiry alone. Test revocation before execution, before publication, and after link issuance, and describe the resulting lifetime accurately to users.

    Remember: Trace credentials, plaintext, and decryption authority through their real lifecycles. Rotation must retire old authority without accidentally destroying the keys and access needed for required recovery.

    Try applying it: New files use key version two. Which key references, permissions, and older versions must a restore test exercise before version one can be retired?

    PART 5 / UNIT 18 / CHAPTER 18.3

    Tenant isolation, audit & deletion

    Prerequisites: 18.2 · Secrets, encryption & trust boundaries5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Tenant-scoped database queries work correctly, but a cache mixes two documents numbered 7. Later, a deletion removes the database row while an old extraction job recreates its text. Both failures occur outside the original query.

    We will carry trusted tenant context through caches, jobs, objects, and exports, then follow private data through diagnostics, audit, retention, and deletion. The goal is to account for the copies and delayed work that can expose or recreate data after the main request has ended.

    18.3.1 · API security and common vulnerabilities

    A document endpoint uses a parameterised SQL query. Submitted values remain values rather than becoming SQL instructions, which addresses injection through those values. Yet the same safe query can return another tenant's document if it lacks the required ownership condition. Input safety and object authorisation answer different questions.

    Follow an accepted request beyond parsing. Check whether the caller may use the selected object, change each submitted property, and receive the fields in the response. A valid JSON request that changes a protected tenant field can still be harmful. An export can also consume excessive CPU, storage, or delivery bandwidth even when its contents are permitted, so bound expensive operations and apply the intended quotas.

    Review file paths, callback destinations, and fetched URLs at the point where they are used. Safe syntax does not establish that a destination or operation is allowed. Test cross-tenant identifiers, protected-property changes, injection attempts, privileged operations, and resource limits. Different failure paths require different controls.

    18.3.2 · Multi-tenant isolation

    Tenant A and tenant B each have a document numbered 7. The database query includes the tenant, but a shared cache uses only document_id as its key. A result cached for A under key 7 can now be returned on B's path. Isolation failed after the correct query.

    Include trusted tenant scope in the cache identity, such as (tenant, document_id), and preserve the same distinction through search indexes, queues, workers, and exports. A worker should resolve the job's actual resource relationships; an unchecked tenant field in a message must not let it select another organisation's input or output. Database policies can add enforcement when correctly configured, but the other stores and paths still need their own checks.

    Follow the resulting object to download. A correctly scoped export is exposed if its output is public or its access capability grants too much. Include telemetry and administrative tools in the review. Test two tenants through every route by which their data travels, including overlapping local identifiers and direct object access.

    18.3.3 · Data minimization

    A conversion fails, and an operator needs to find out why. An operation identifier and error class may be enough to connect the failure to its processing stage. Copying the whole private document or an access token into the log adds exposure without necessarily helping the diagnosis.

    Data minimisation asks which information is necessary for a defined purpose. Make that decision when designing messages, logs, database fields, and derived records. A job message might contain a scoped object reference instead of another full copy of the document, provided the worker can obtain it through the required access checks.

    For each retained field, identify its intended use, permitted readers, and retention period. Collecting less sensitive content reduces both disclosure risk and the work needed to remove copies later. Keep enough evidence to operate the service, but do not store a field merely because someone might find it interesting in the future.

    18.3.4 · Audit trails

    An administrator requests a private export. A useful audit trail connects a trusted actor to the tenant, target, action, and outcome, with time or sequence information. Give the operation an identifier so its request, authorisation decision, and eventual result can be related.

    “Request received” proves only that a request reached that recording point. It does not prove that the worker produced an export or that the output was published. Record events whose meanings match those boundaries. If a worker stops after producing the object but before recording completion, recovery should reconcile the operation's durable state and object rather than leave an unexplained success or repeat the action blindly.

    Protect the trail against inappropriate alteration, including by people whose actions it records. Restrict its readers and retention too: an audit store can become another source of private data. Necessary identifiers and outcome classes are often more useful than full sensitive payloads. Trustworthy evidence needs clear event meanings as well as protected storage.

    18.3.5 · Privacy, retention, and deletion

    A tenant deletes a document. Removing its main database row may leave the object, extracted text, search entries, cached results, and earlier exports. Begin with a map of the copies and the retention rules that apply to each.

    Record a durable deletion request before reporting that work has been accepted. Track its progress through the required stores so a restart can resume unfinished removal. Distinguish acceptance from completion in the API. Workers must also check whether an input is still permitted: an extraction job queued before deletion must not recreate the removed text afterward. Coordinate deletion and publication so a late worker cannot publish a new copy after the deletion process has passed that store.

    Treat recovery as another path that can bring data back. When restoring an older snapshot or replaying history, apply the current deletion decisions before serving the recovered data. Document retained copies and any applicable exceptions under the approved policy. Make the promised collection, access, retention, and deletion behaviour match these actual operating steps.

    Think further · What should revocation mean for an issued object capability and a queued export?

    Define when each form of authority stops working. A queued export can check current membership before the later actions required by policy. An already issued object capability may remain usable until expiry unless the delivery mechanism supports earlier revocation. If immediate download denial is required, choose a delivery design that can enforce it rather than relying on expiry alone. Test revocation before execution, before publication, and after link issuance, and describe the resulting lifetime accurately to users.

    Remember: Tenant isolation follows data through every store and worker. Deletion must account for those copies, delayed publication, and restore paths, while audit records describe the outcomes actually reached.

    Try applying it: A document is deleted while an extraction job waits. Which copies and worker transitions must the deletion process account for so that the document does not reappear?

    PART 5 / UNIT 18 / CHAPTER 18.4

    Supply chains and security reviews

    Prerequisites: 18.3 · Tenant isolation, audit & deletion4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A reviewed change becomes a running release through dependencies, builds, stored artifacts, and deployment credentials. Each step can change what reaches production. Users also need recovery paths that are practical without granting authority to the wrong organisation.

    We will examine the release path and the user journey, then bring the unit's controls together in a private export review. We will change membership, cancellation, and deletion state while the job waits. The aim is to state what should happen at each later boundary and identify evidence that it actually happens.

    18.4.1 · Supply-chain security

    A source change passes review, but the deployed executable contains a different dependency or was replaced after the build. Reviewing application source alone does not cover this path. Build tools, dependencies, artifacts, deployment credentials, and update mechanisms form the software supply chain.

    Follow one release from its source commit and selected inputs to the built artifact. Record the artifact's identity, such as its digest, and verify that the same artifact is deployed. Provenance is evidence about where and how the artifact was produced; it helps connect a running release to the inputs and process that were checked.

    Control dependency resolution and limit who or what can publish artifacts and deploy them. Untrusted contribution builds should not inherit deployment secrets merely because trusted branch builds use them. A valid signature establishes a signing relationship and integrity under the scheme's assumptions; the signed code or build inputs can still be harmful. Keep a way to identify affected releases and replace or withdraw compromised ones.

    18.4.2 · Security vs usability trade-offs

    A user loses access to an account and needs recovery. A process that is too difficult may lead legitimate users to share accounts or seek unsupported workarounds. A shortcut that lets any administrator reset any tenant's account creates a different failure: it grants authority across organisation boundaries.

    Walk through the same journey as the legitimate user and as someone attempting account takeover. Ask what evidence each can provide, who may approve recovery, and what authority the completed process restores. A fallback should not quietly bypass the identity and tenant restrictions required during normal login.

    Safe defaults, scoped support tools, understandable recovery, and proportionate extra verification can improve both protection and usability. Test successful legitimate recovery as well as denial of the abusive path. Mandatory constraints remain explicit: a convenient recovery cannot justify cross-tenant access. The useful trade-off concerns ways to meet those constraints while making the supported path practical for the people who need it.

    18.4.3 · Secure-by-design reviews

    Follow a sensitive export from request to download. Validate the caller, resolve permitted tenant membership, and select only authorised resources. Record the export operation with trusted scope before placing it in the queue. The worker obtains that operation, checks the policy required at execution, and uses limited authority to read inputs and write a private output.

    Before publication, check the operation's current state and the policy required there. A retry after cancellation or deletion must not publish an obsolete export. When a user downloads it, authorise delivery or issue a deliberately scoped, time-limited capability. Record the relevant result in the audit trail. If a capability can be forwarded and used without another identity check, account for that property in its permissions and lifetime.

    Now revoke membership after enqueue. Specify whether later execution, publication, and download must stop, and how already issued capabilities are handled. Test those transitions, including deletion racing with publication. Assign an owner to each control and retain evidence that the deployed path enforces it. A checklist helps coverage; the review's conclusion depends on the actual permissions, configurations, and observed outcomes.

    Try the mechanism in code

    Python · synthetic tenant policy

    from mechanisms import permit_demo
actor = {"tenant":"A", "active":True, "actions":["read"]}
assert permit_demo(actor, {"tenant":"A"}, "read")
assert not permit_demo(actor, {"tenant":"B"}, "read")

    The first assertion returns True: the active actor belongs to tenant A, the resource belongs to A, and read is in the actor's allowed actions. The second returns False because the resource belongs to B. The predicate also requires active to be exactly True and the action to appear in actions.

    The example assumes that actor and resource attributes have already been supplied by a trustworthy source. It does not authenticate credentials, load current membership, or validate malformed identity records. In a real path, establish those facts before evaluating permission, and ensure that a denial stops the effect. Trace the same tenant scope through cache keys, queued jobs, object access, exports, and search; the two assertions alone do not verify those paths.

    Download the executable mechanism collection ↓ · Follow the connected complete design →

    Think further · What should revocation mean for an issued object capability and a queued export?

    Define when each form of authority stops working. A queued export can check current membership before the later actions required by policy. An already issued object capability may remain usable until expiry unless the delivery mechanism supports earlier revocation. If immediate download denial is required, choose a delivery design that can enforce it rather than relying on expiry alone. Test revocation before execution, before publication, and after link issuance, and describe the resulting lifetime accurately to users.

    Remember: Connect the reviewed source to the deployed artifact, provide workable bounded recovery, and test sensitive journeys as authority and data state change.

    Try applying it: Membership is revoked after an export is queued. What should happen at execution, publication, and download, including a capability issued before revocation?

    PART 5 / UNIT 19 / CHAPTER 19.1

    Observe behavior with three signals

    Prerequisites: Requirements, Estimation, and Engineering Trade-offs, Networking Foundations for System Design, Runtime, Processes, Threads, and Concurrency, Database Internals, Transactions, and Concurrency Control6 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A user waits five seconds for a payment request. The CPU dashboard looks ordinary, so adding processor capacity has no clear justification yet. We need to find where the time went and whether this request represents a wider problem.

    We will combine population measurements, individual request timelines, and structured event records. We will then follow tracing context across calls and messages and relate the user's symptom to traffic, errors, and resource pressure. The aim is to ask a precise question of each signal and connect the answers into an explanation we can test.

    19.1.1 · Monitoring vs observability

    A user waits five seconds for a payment request while the CPU dashboard looks normal. The dashboard answers one question: how much processor capacity is in use? It does not tell us where the request spent those five seconds. The application could be waiting for a database connection while the processor has little work to do.

    Monitoring tracks selected conditions, such as CPU use or a known failure rate. Observability concerns our ability to investigate internal behaviour using the evidence the system produces. These are useful emphases rather than universal boundaries between products.

    Begin with the user's operation and follow its work, waits, dependencies, and state changes. We need evidence that can distinguish a slow query from a wait before the query starts. Collecting more unrelated measurements does not necessarily help us make that distinction. The useful question is which observation would support or weaken the explanation we are considering.

    19.1.2 · Logs, metrics, and traces

    A latency histogram groups request durations into ranges. It can show that slow requests have become more common, but it cannot tell us where a particular request waited. For that, we can inspect a trace: a record connecting related intervals of work along one execution path. A log records an event, such as a payment attempt ending with a timeout, together with its context.

    These signals answer different parts of an investigation. Metrics summarise measurements across a population. A trace lets us follow an individual path. Logs can supply the event details needed to understand what happened on that path. A stable operation identity helps connect the relevant records.

    One slow trace does not establish the cause of every slow request. Compare individual histories with population measurements. Sampling, dropped records, clock differences, and privacy limits also affect the evidence available. A missing record may be a gap in collection rather than proof that an event never happened.

    19.1.3 · Structured logging

    Suppose one instance writes “payment failed” while another writes “provider unavailable.” Finding every timeout now depends on knowing which phrases the code uses. Structured logging records named fields with consistent meanings, such as event_type=payment_attempt, operation_id, outcome_class=provider_timeout, and duration.

    We can query the outcome class across instances without interpreting each sentence. The fields still need precise definitions. A payment attempt starting, a provider reply arriving, and a local outcome committing are different events; recording one does not establish the others.

    If a finish event is missing, the process may have stopped or the record may have been lost. We still need to recover the provider's result through the payment's supported status or reconciliation path. Keep credentials and raw private documents out of routine logs. Bound record sizes and volume so an error burst does not overwhelm logging resources, and retain records for a defined investigative purpose.

    19.1.4 · Distributed tracing

    Consider the constructed five-second request in the figure. It spends 4,600 ms acquiring a database connection, 100 ms executing a query, and 300 ms elsewhere. Most of its elapsed time passes before the query can begin. Faster query execution alone would leave that long wait largely intact.

    A span records an interval such as handling a request, acquiring a connection, or executing a query. Parent and child relationships connect spans into a trace. Recording acquisition separately from execution makes the wait visible; without that boundary, it may appear as unexplained application time. Distributed tracing carries these relationships across components.

    For later asynchronous work, a span link can preserve the causal connection even when processing continues after the original request ends. A trace remains evidence about one execution and may be sampled. Compare slow paths with normal paths and latency distributions before extending this example's explanation to the service as a whole.

    19.1.5 · Trace IDs, span IDs, context propagation

    A trace identifier groups related spans, while a span identifier names one interval within that trace. To connect work across a network call, the sender must carry the relevant identifiers and relationship information to the receiver. This is context propagation.

    Suppose a request starts trace T7. The service records its database work and publishes a message with tracing context. The worker can use that context to relate its later processing to the request. If the context is lost at the queue boundary, both sides may produce valid spans that the investigator cannot follow as one connected history.

    Check each transport rather than assuming a standard format instruments every library automatically. Preserve a durable business operation identity as well: progress must remain recoverable even when traces are not retained. Incoming tracing context may be untrusted, so validate or replace it according to policy. A trace ID supplies diagnostic correlation, not identity or permission, and context fields should not become a way to pass unnecessary private data.

    19.1.6 · Golden signals

    Traffic rises, the connection queue grows, and responses slow down while errors initially remain low. Looking only at failure counts would miss this developing problem. Four commonly used golden signals bring together latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.

    Latency describes how long the selected operations take. Traffic describes the amount of work arriving or completing. Errors describe failed outcomes. Saturation describes pressure on a constrained resource, such as requests waiting behind an occupied connection pool. Together, these signals connect demand, resource pressure, and what users receive.

    Define the outcomes being counted. An HTTP 200 does not necessarily establish that a payment completed, and many successful cheap reads can hide failures in a less frequent critical operation. Examine important operations separately where needed. For work continuing after a request ends, add domain measures such as the age of the oldest unresolved payment; request-serving signals alone may miss that harm.

    Think further · What evidence would support a latency explanation beyond correlation with a release?

    Locate the extra wait or execution on affected paths and compare them with normal paths and population measurements. If the hypothesis is that a release holds connections longer, inspect changed request behaviour, connection hold times, occupancy, and acquisition waits in the timeline. Consider competing explanations and test a focused intervention under comparable conditions. Support is stronger when the mechanism predicts the symptom and changing that mechanism changes the observed behaviour; a release marker alone establishes timing.

    Remember: Use metrics to establish the population symptom, traces to locate work and waits, and logs to explain relevant events. Correlate their evidence without treating one history as the whole population.

    Try applying it: A latency histogram shows a worsening p99 and one trace shows a long connection wait. What does each establish, and what further evidence would support applying that explanation to the wider slowdown?

    PART 5 / UNIT 19 / CHAPTER 19.2

    Choose indicators, budgets & alerts

    Prerequisites: 19.1 · Observe behavior with three signals5 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    The connection pool is full and request durations rise, but the on-call engineer is already receiving pages about harmless CPU fluctuations. Collecting and alerting on every available measurement has made it harder to recognise the condition that needs action.

    We will connect request measurements to resource measurements, define eligible outcomes and a service objective, and calculate how quickly failures consume its allowance. We will then choose alerts, sampling policies, and dashboard views for the decisions they must support. By the end, we should be able to explain both what an urgent signal means and which useful response should follow it.

    19.2.1 · RED and USE methods

    For the payment API, we can ask how many requests arrive, which fail, and how long they take. This is the RED view: rate, errors, and duration. For its database connection pool, we ask how much capacity is in use, how much work waits, and which resource errors occur. This is the USE view: utilisation, saturation, and errors.

    The two views help connect a symptom to a possible explanation. RED may show rising request duration. USE may show that all connections are occupied and more requests are waiting. CPU can remain low because those waiting requests are not executing processor work.

    The pool measurement narrows the investigation; it does not explain why connections remain occupied. Inspect their holders and compare the timing with affected requests. Use enough time detail and per-owner views to expose bursts or hot shards hidden by averages. Keep domain indicators too: uncertain charges can still require attention after ordinary request durations recover.

    19.2.2 · SLIs, SLOs, error budgets

    First define what counts as a good event and which events are eligible. For example, a success fraction divides good eligible outcomes by all eligible outcomes. This measured behaviour is a service-level indicator, or SLI. A service-level objective, or SLO, sets a target for that indicator over a stated window. Its error budget is the allowed shortfall.

    For a 99.9% success target, the allowed bad fraction is 100% − 99.9% = 0.1%, or 0.001. Suppose 1% of eligible events are bad during an observed interval. The burn rate is 0.01 / 0.001 = 10: the observed bad fraction is ten times the allowance's fraction. Sustained behaviour like this uses the budget rapidly.

    Keep the eligible population and windows explicit. This ratio alone does not tell us the remaining budget or how long it will last; event volume and earlier consumption also matter. A large denominator can hide harm to critical operations, while a few events can make a low-volume indicator fluctuate sharply. The objective describes the stated population and window, rather than guaranteeing every request's outcome.

    19.2.3 · Alert design and alert fatigue

    A brief CPU spike pages the on-call engineer, who finds that useful service never degraded. Repeated pages like this consume attention needed when users are actually affected. An alert should connect a meaningful condition to a useful response.

    For an urgent page, state which outcome is threatened, who owns the response, and where investigation should begin. Sustained rapid error-budget burn may justify immediate attention; a condition needing planned capacity work may belong in a ticket. Match the urgency to how soon someone must act and what that action can achieve.

    Choose thresholds and windows for the objective and response time. Include context and a runbook, meaning a procedure for investigation, action, and verification. Group related alerts where they would otherwise demand the same action during one incident. Review unnecessary pages and incidents that were missed. The aim is a paging channel that helps responders recognise harm and begin mitigation promptly.

    19.2.4 · Sampling and telemetry cost

    Keeping every trace may exceed the available storage and processing budget. Sampling retains a selected subset. Head sampling makes the selection early, before the whole trace is known. It cannot choose an initially discarded trace because that request later fails. Tail sampling waits for later observations and can select traces by duration or error, but needs capacity to buffer and process the arriving data.

    The selection policy changes what the retained evidence represents. A collection favouring errors is useful for diagnosis, but its error fraction cannot be read as the failure rate of all requests. Late or dropped spans can also leave an incomplete history.

    Metrics have a related cost boundary. Each combination of label values identifies a time series. Giving every request its own label can create a growing number of series. Use bounded dimensions for population metrics and keep detailed identities in suitable logs or traces. Choose sampling, retention, privacy limits, and ingestion capacity together, including behaviour during failure bursts when telemetry volume may rise.

    19.2.5 · Dashboards

    Begin a dashboard with the decision it should support. For “Are payments completing?”, show accepted operations, required completions, failure classes, and the age of unresolved work. These measurements establish the service outcome before the responder examines resources that might explain a change.

    A useful path then leads from a changed outcome to the relevant workload, deployment, dependency, or resource. For rising request latency, that might mean opening a duration distribution and then examining connection-pool wait. This arrangement reduces the number of unrelated graphs the responder must interpret before forming a hypothesis.

    Include units, denominators, measurement windows, deployment markers, and visible data gaps. A flat line caused by missing telemetry has a different meaning from a measured zero. Provide drill-downs and ownership, and check the dashboard against known examples or earlier incidents. Its value comes from helping someone make a supported decision, rather than from the number of panels it contains.

    Think further · What evidence would support a latency explanation beyond correlation with a release?

    Locate the extra wait or execution on affected paths and compare them with normal paths and population measurements. If the hypothesis is that a release holds connections longer, inspect changed request behaviour, connection hold times, occupancy, and acquisition waits in the timeline. Consider competing explanations and test a focused intervention under comparable conditions. Support is stronger when the mechanism predicts the symptom and changing that mechanism changes the observed behaviour; a release marker alone establishes timing.

    Remember: Define eligible outcomes and the objective before calculating budget burn. Choose bounded telemetry, dashboards, and alerts that support a clear decision and a useful response.

    Try applying it: A 99.9% success objective has an observed 1% bad-event fraction. How do you calculate burn rate, and what population, window, and response information would you need before turning it into a page?
