    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.2

    Rate Limiter

    Prerequisites: Requirements, Estimation, and Engineering Trade-offs, Runtime, Processes, Threads, and Concurrency, Scalability, Load Balancing, and Data Distribution, Reliability, Fault Tolerance, and Disaster Recovery4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Suppose three application instances each start with ten tokens for the same customer. Each instance follows its local arithmetic correctly, yet together they may admit thirty requests at once.

    Before building a rate limiter, we must decide what the allowance covers. We will begin with one bucket, trace its refill and spending, and then examine what changes when several processes or regions share the policy.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.2.1 · Functional requirements

    A request asks to perform work with a known cost. The limiter checks whether the caller's policy permits that work now, then allows it or supplies useful waiting or rejection guidance.

    Separate three requirements. A continuing rate limits sustained work; a burst allowance permits some work to arrive together; a cumulative quota limits a total over a longer period. Also state the enforcement scope. An exact global allowance and a bounded regional approximation are different policies. Giving every region a full copy of the global bucket multiplies the permitted work.

    22.2.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Admission should add little delay while protecting downstream resources and preserving tenant fairness. Specify what happens when the limiter cannot reach its authoritative state.

    During a partition, an exact global cap may require waiting or rejection because a region cannot safely know what others have spent. Continuing to allow all requests, often called failing open, cannot preserve that cap unless previously allocated safe budgets cover the work. Choose latency, availability, and precision together, with the protocol and assumptions needed to support them.

    22.2.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume 100,000 checks/s and one million active keys. Our sample bucket holds at most ten tokens and refills at two tokens/s. A token represents an amount of admitted work.

    At an assumed 64 bytes per key, raw state is 1,000,000 × 64 = 64 MB. Engine allocations, expiry metadata, replicas, and network work add to this. These are teaching assumptions rather than benchmarks. A small state record can still be expensive if many requests contend to update it.

    22.2.4 · Naive initial architecture

    Begin with a dictionary in one process. A suitable lock protects the entire refill-and-spend transition for one bucket, so two callers cannot spend its last token together.

    This protects only callers sharing that owner. An unrelated second process starts another allowance, and restarting may reset the first. The local design is suitable when that scope and reset behaviour meet the requirement. To enforce a shared cap across instances, we must add a shared authority or an explicit allocation protocol.

    22.2.5 · Core API contracts

    check(key,cost,policy_version) returns the decision, remaining allowance, and a meaningful retry delay. Derive the key from trusted caller and resource identity so callers cannot escape a limit by inventing new keys. Require a positive, bounded cost.

    Authorise policy changes and define when a new version takes effect. Distinguish overload from invalid input, and specify whether rejected attempts consume a separate abuse allowance. These meanings let callers decide whether to wait, correct the request, or stop retrying.

    22.2.6 · Data model and schema

    A bucket record contains scope_key, policy_version, tokens, last_refill, and expiry. Refill and spending belong to one atomic update. A daily cumulative quota may need separate state because it has a different lifecycle.

    Use integer or fixed-point units where useful to avoid numeric drift. Define how policy changes treat existing tokens and capacity. Trust the server's time basis rather than client timestamps. Expiring a record may recreate a full bucket, so expiry must be chosen as part of the protection contract.

    22.2.7 · Low-level component organization

    KeyResolver establishes trusted scope, PolicyResolver loads a validated policy, and Clock provides the time basis. BucketStore owns the coordinated state transition. AdmissionService turns its result into the caller-facing decision.

    These boundaries make deterministic tests easier: a test can supply time and policy directly. They do not create concurrency safety by themselves. Two correct calculations can both start from one old token count. Keep load, refill, comparison, and debit under one owner or supported transaction so only one decision can spend the final token.

    22.2.8 · High-level system architecture

    Use coarse admission near ingress and more specific checks before expensive resources. Independent keys can have different storage owners. A strict shared bucket still needs one atomic authority or a reviewed distributed protocol.

    Regions can receive bounded portions of an allowance in advance and spend locally. This reduces remote checks but introduces allocation and replenishment rules. State the outstanding-budget or overshoot bound. Protect the limiter's own capacity too: otherwise, the service intended to absorb excessive traffic may become the first overloaded dependency.

    22.2.9 · Data and control flows

    First derive trusted scope and the current policy. Under coordinated access, load the bucket and calculate elapsed time, never allowing a negative interval to add tokens. Refill by elapsed time × refill rate, capped at capacity. Compare the available tokens with cost, then debit only an allowed request.

    If a meaningful wait can be computed, divide the token deficit by refill rate. Record bounded metrics and return the decision. The code keeps the whole transition atomic; unprotected reads followed by writes would let two requests spend the same token.

    22.2.10 · Capacity estimates

    One million 64-byte records need 64 MB of raw state. If every incoming request makes a remote check, the assumed workload also creates 100,000 limiter requests/s before retries and replica work.

    Measure update rate, active state, contention, and replication cost separately. Evenly distributed records do not help a single key receiving most requests: its transitions still need coordination. Batching and local budgets can reduce remote traffic, but may change decision timing or precision. Include those changes when comparing capacity.

    22.2.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Suppose the application has a 100 ms response target and assigns 5 ms to admission. That allocation is a proposed budget to validate under contention and failover.

    A strict cross-region check adds network propagation and queueing and may exceed it. Preallocated local budgets can shorten the request path, while adding replenishment work. Measure the complete path, including policy lookup and store replacement, against the required protection rule. A faster design that grants a different allowance needs to be described as a changed contract.

    22.2.12 · Failure scenarios

    Imagine two requests reading one remaining token. Each sees enough allowance, and both approve the work. Combining refill, comparison, and debit atomically repairs this race because the second request then observes the first debit.

    Also test backward time, record expiry, forged keys, and conflicting policy versions. These can create extra allowance even when the refill formula is correct. During owner loss, apply the documented rejection, safe local budget, or bounded fail-open rule. Protection depends on identity, time, and deployment scope as well as arithmetic.

    22.2.13 · Scalability improvements

    Partition independent keys while keeping each bucket's decisions coordinated. Versioned policy definitions can be cached where suitable, but token spending still needs the required authority.

    A strict hot bucket cannot be divided into unrelated full buckets without changing its cap. Hierarchical limits or allocated local allowances can distribute some work when their semantics fit the resource. Give expensive operations appropriate costs. Expand the part that limits protected work or coordinated checks; adding space for more cold keys will not relieve a hot decision.

    22.2.14 · Consistency requirements

    A strict token bucket preserves its refill-and-debit rule under the chosen time model. A distributed approximation needs an explicit bound, such as the total allowance independently outstanding in regions.

    The algorithm also defines the policy: token buckets permit bursts, fixed windows have boundary effects, and sliding windows describe recent traffic differently. Usage counters that agree later cannot undo excessive work already admitted. State the invariant required when a decision is made, then choose a mechanism that preserves it.

    22.2.15 · Security model

    Bind scope keys to authenticated tenant or service identity. Authorise policy administration and limit creation of new keys, since unlimited keys could exhaust state memory. Validate tenant headers, policy names, and time inputs.

    Limit what remaining-allowance responses reveal about other callers. Admission and permission answer different questions: having enough tokens does not permit reading another tenant's document. The protected operation must still enforce its resource access rule.

    22.2.16 · Deployment approach

    Deploy policy and bucket owners with stated state-loss and failover behaviour. If replacement grants every caller a new full bucket, the system may admit another burst that the contract did not allow.

    Roll out policy versions compatibly and test older callers, clock behaviour, and owner failure. A fallback must have an acceptable bound. Preserve state or allocate safe replacement allowance according to the design, even though each individual bucket record is small.

    22.2.17 · Observability design

    Measure allowed and rejected cost, check latency, owner errors, active keys, hot-key pressure, and policy-version disagreement. Compare these signals with the load and health of the protected resource.

    Many rejections can mean successful protection or a mistaken policy denying legitimate work. Few rejections can hide fail-open behaviour during state-store failure. Observe both unsafe admission and unnecessary denial. Keep metric dimensions bounded so one label per arbitrary key does not overwhelm monitoring.

    22.2.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Cost includes state memory, check requests, replicated updates, transfer, and operating work. A remote strict check on every inexpensive business operation can cost more than the work it protects.

    Compare strict and local-budget designs with their guarantees stated, using symbolic or explicitly fictional rates for teaching. If a cheaper design allows more overshoot or behaves differently during failure, include that consequence. A smaller infrastructure bill alone does not establish equal protection.

    22.2.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    A token bucket admits bounded bursts. A leaky-bucket shaper smooths output by making work wait. Fixed-window counters are simple, but traffic can cluster on both sides of a window boundary. Sliding approaches track recent traffic at additional state or computation cost.

    Regional budgets add allocation work in exchange for shorter local decisions and some independence during failure. Choose using the protected resource's needs. Include the rejection response and expected retry behaviour, because callers can otherwise recreate the same burst immediately.

    22.2.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    First build a deterministic local bucket with one atomic owner. Introduce shared state when multiple processes need one cap. Partition keys when measured load requires it.

    Add regional allocation for a specific latency or failure requirement and state its bound. At every step, preserve the original policy meaning or explicitly version the changed contract. Increasing the number of enforcement instances should not silently increase the customer's allowance.

    22.2.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Review whether the advertised scope matches actual enforcement. Ask what a policy update does to existing tokens and how the hottest key behaves. These questions cannot be answered by the refill formula alone.

    Test simultaneous spending of the last token, backward time, expiry, policy replacement, owner loss, and regional reconnection. Full independent buckets do not support an exact-global claim. Record unresolved evidence about the real protocol rather than assuming that a shared storage product automatically establishes every required behaviour.

    22.2.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Build the sample bucket with an injected monotonic clock. Spend its ten initial tokens, reject an immediate eleventh one-token spend, then advance three seconds. At two tokens/s, six tokens should return, within capacity ten.

    Reject invalid costs and check that backward time adds no allowance. Reproduce the race in which two unprotected readers spend one token, then coordinate the transition and confirm that only one wins. Keep both histories so the test explains why the repair works.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    def spend(bucket, now, cost):
    require(cost > 0)
    elapsed = max(0, now - bucket.last)
    available = min(bucket.capacity,
                    bucket.tokens + elapsed * bucket.rate)
    allowed = available >= cost
    bucket.tokens = available - cost if allowed else available
    bucket.last = max(bucket.last, now)
    return allowed
# Entire transition executes atomically for this bucket.

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.

    THE WORKBENCH · TRY CHANGING THE INPUTS

    Use a burst of tokens, then let the bucket refill

    The bucket holds at most ten tokens and gains two per second. Spend tokens, then advance the simulated clock. One browser owns this bucket. A shared implementation must update the balance atomically; several independent owners need a protocol to enforce a global limit.

    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.3

    Chat Application

    Prerequisites: Networking Foundations for System Design, Data Models and Storage Technologies, Distributed Systems Fundamentals, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A chat message appears on the sender's screen. The recipient's phone has just disconnected. What should “sent” mean while that phone is unreachable?

    We will store the conversation before relying on live delivery, then let a returning device recover what it missed. Following those two paths will help us distinguish saved history, device delivery, human reading, and approximate presence.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.3.1 · Functional requirements

    Two people exchange messages in an authorised conversation. Online devices receive updates; disconnected devices later fetch missing history. Support bounded groups and a defined retention policy as well.

    A message moves through several stages: the service accepts it, storage persists it, a device receives it, and a person may read it. Give each receipt the meaning its evidence supports. Presence is an approximate indication of connectivity. A WebSocket supplies a live communication path, but opening it proves neither durable history nor human reading.

    22.3.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Retain acknowledged messages under the selected storage-failure contract and protect conversation privacy. Define ordering within each conversation, or state a deliberately weaker rule. For the supported workload, target online delivery below one second.

    An offline device has a different delivery timeline and catches up later. Approximate presence expiry need not satisfy the strict rules used for exclusive allocation. Specify retention and visibility for moderation, deletion, and returning devices so recovery does not reveal history they may no longer access.

    22.3.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume 100,000 concurrent connections and 10,000 accepted messages/s. Each stored message averages 500 bytes and produces five recipient deliveries in this simplified workload.

    Ingestion is 10,000 × 500 = 5 MB/s. Over 86,400 seconds, that is 432 GB/day. Five deliveries multiply body traffic to about 25 MB/s before framing and overhead. Model multiple devices, large groups, connection memory, and reconnect bursts separately. These assumptions describe work to test; they do not establish gateway or database capacity.

    22.3.4 · Naive initial architecture

    Begin with one connection server and a transactional history store. Commit the message before returning a persistence receipt, then try to deliver it to online devices.

    If the gateway crashes, clients lose their connections, but committed history can survive under the storage contract. They reconnect and fetch missing messages. This separates the server's availability limit from message persistence. A database commit says the message was retained; only later evidence can establish delivery to a particular device.

    22.3.5 · Core API contracts

    A send includes conversation_id, client_message_id, and bounded content. Fetch history after a sequence with an operation such as GET /conversations/{id}/messages?after=sequence. Check membership on both reads and writes.

    Delivered and read receipts identify the relevant device or user and the highest sequence covered by the product's policy. A repeated client_message_id in the sender's uniqueness scope returns the original message. A client can therefore recover from a lost send reply without adding another logical message.

    22.3.6 · Data model and schema

    Store conversations and membership separately from messages. Each message contains conversation_id, sequence, sender, client_message_id, body, and version. Receipt records hold delivered and read progress for the appropriate user or device; heartbeat records provide expiring presence.

    Enforce the intended client-identity uniqueness scope. A sequence authority, or a supported conflict model, must establish conversation order. Client-clock timestamps alone cannot supply a stable total order. Keep the identity used for retries valid across reconnects.

    22.3.7 · Low-level component organization

    ConnectionGateway owns live connections. MembershipPolicy checks access. MessageService coordinates identity and persistence, SequenceOwner assigns conversation order, and HistoryRepository reads bounded pages. DeliveryWorker distributes committed messages.

    ReceiptAggregator combines progress without moving backward under the chosen device policy. Large groups need bounded fan-out work rather than one long loop inside the message transaction. These components can initially run together, but their contracts should distinguish durable history from routing information that may disappear during a gateway restart.

    22.3.8 · High-level system architecture

    Use replaceable connection gateways and route durable message work by conversation. Commit delivery intent through a log or outbox, then let workers find currently connected recipient devices. An outbox is a durable record of work to publish, saved with the message so a crash cannot lose the obligation between the two writes.

    Connection routes may be stale. A missed frame is therefore repaired from history. If the broker is unavailable, committed intent can wait while acknowledged history remains retained. The gateway is a route to the device, rather than the only record of its messages.

    22.3.9 · Data and control flows

    The client sends a stable message identity. The service checks membership, assigns a sequence, and commits both message and delivery intent before returning the persistence result. The code illustrates this durable boundary; device delivery and read receipts follow later.

    Workers send frames and apply valid receipts. On reconnect, a device supplies its last observed sequence, fetches bounded missing pages, and detects gaps. It recognises repeated frames by identity. This lets the retained conversation and the device's current display recover independently after an interrupted live connection.

    22.3.10 · Capacity estimates

    The assumptions give 5 MB/s of raw storage growth, or 432 GB/day. Five recipients per message produce 50,000 deliveries/s and 25 MB/s of message bodies.

    Measure connection memory separately. At an illustrative 20 kB each, 100,000 connections need 2 GB before other process memory or queued content. Bound outbound buffers. A slow device may receive less than a sender produces, allowing its queue to grow until the gateway runs out of memory even though storage remains healthy.

    22.3.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Suppose ingress takes 20 ms, commit coordination 30 ms, delivery queues 20 ms, and the recipient path 80 ms. The budget totals 150 ms before rendering.

    This does not establish online p99. Test hot conversations, congestion, failover, and slow-device buffers. Measure persistence-receipt delay, device-delivery delay, and human-read delay separately. Offline delivery follows a different timeline, and a successful transport reply cannot establish every later stage.

    22.3.12 · Failure scenarios

    If the send reply disappears after commit, the repeated client identity recovers the saved message. If a gateway stops, devices reconnect and catch up from history. If a device consumes messages too slowly, disconnect or reduce its service before its buffer exhausts the gateway.

    Membership removal can race with cached access state, so enforce the documented visibility rule on live delivery and history. Reconnect storms need admission controls and staggered retries. Test these event sequences directly; two permanently connected clients do not exercise them.

    22.3.13 · Scalability improvements

    Distribute independent gateway connections and partition history and ordering by conversation where useful. Let bounded workers perform group fan-out.

    One popular conversation can still concentrate ordering and delivery work. It may require explicitly different large-channel semantics instead of including every recipient in a low-latency acknowledgment chain. Preserve sequences and deduplication identities when ownership moves. Include history catch-up in capacity tests, because many devices returning after a gateway failure produce a different workload from ordinary message averages.

    22.3.14 · Consistency requirements

    Define a per-conversation order, and make the sender's confirmation agree with the saved message. A history cursor must resume without silently skipping required records. Cross-conversation total order is unnecessary unless the product requires it.

    Live frames may repeat, so devices deduplicate by identity. Presence and receipts may propagate later, while delivered and read progress follow the chosen monotonic model: old updates must not move progress backward. These are separate guarantees; using WebSockets does not by itself provide exactly-once messaging.

    22.3.15 · Security model

    Enforce membership on sends, history, fan-out, search, and media access. Limit abusive sending, payload size, and group size. Keep message bodies out of routine telemetry.

    If end-to-end encryption is required, specify device keys, recovery, membership changes, and the resulting limits on server features. TLS protects a connection but does not supply that full product guarantee. Attachments also need access and retention rules. An authorised chat page does not automatically protect every derived content URL.

    22.3.16 · Deployment approach

    Drain gateways during rollouts and support reconnects from older clients. Evolve message and receipt formats compatibly. Preserve history through the chosen replication and promotion rules.

    Test reconnect and catch-up alongside ordinary sending. Restarting every gateway together may create a much larger burst than normal traffic. A new region needs explicit ordering and membership behaviour. Retain client identities and progress during replacement so uncertain sends do not become duplicated history records.

    22.3.17 · Observability design

    Measure persistence delay, live-delivery lag, sequence-gap recovery, reconnect rates, fan-out backlog, and hot conversations. Observe slow-device limits and membership denials too.

    Correlate client and server identities in suitable detailed records without adding one unbounded metric label per message. Synthetic clients can send, disconnect, reconnect, and check both history and forbidden access. This follows the user's journey. A healthy connection count alone cannot establish that accepted messages are retained or revoked devices are blocked.

    22.3.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Separate costs for connections, retained history, fan-out transfer, indexes, replicas, media, and telemetry. Thirty days of the assumed raw history need 432 GB/day × 30 = 12.96 TB before indexes and copies.

    Media can dominate storage and transfer, so give it a separate quota and lifecycle. Use explicit or symbolic rates rather than assumed provider prices. Cost per retained message describes a different burden from cost per delivered body, especially when recipients and devices multiply the delivery path.

    22.3.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    WebSockets support bidirectional communication with low live delay, while requiring connection management. Server-Sent Events (SSE) can carry server updates alongside HTTP sends for suitable clients. Polling is simpler but creates requests during idle periods.

    A single conversation sequence authority simplifies order and creates a hot-key boundary. Concurrent regional writing needs an explicit merge and ordering model and changes the contract. Compare alternatives using offline recovery, receipts, and privacy; transport features alone do not decide the architecture.

    22.3.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    First make durable history and reconnect recovery correct. Add gateway replicas with explicit connection routing. Introduce durable fan-out for growing volume or groups, then partition conversation ownership when measured storage or ordering work requires it.

    Regional placement introduces another authority and failure decision. Throughout these changes, retain message identity: a retry after a shard move or gateway replacement should still name the same logical send. Increasing connection capacity while losing that identity can create duplicate messages.

    22.3.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Review the meanings of “sent” and “delivered,” the hottest conversation, slow-device memory, and membership revocation. For each, describe an event sequence and its required result.

    Test a commit followed by a lost reply, a dropped frame, gateway loss, stale routing, and a history request after membership removal. Check both the resulting list and receipts. These checks examine recovery and privacy, which a demonstration with two always-online clients cannot establish.

    22.3.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Build a client model that recognises message identities and detects sequence gaps. Save a message but suppress its live frame. Reconnect from an earlier sequence and confirm that history adds the message once to the visible list.

    Then repeat its client_message_id and verify that storage creates no second logical message. Deduplicating displayed frames and deduplicating history creation protect different boundaries. Test both so a neat display does not hide duplicated durable records.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    with transaction():
    existing = find_by_client_id(sender, client_message_id)
    if existing: return existing
    require_member(sender, conversation)
    seq = allocate_conversation_sequence(conversation)
    msg = insert_message(conversation, seq, body)
    insert_outbox(msg.id, "deliver")
return persisted_receipt(msg)
# Device delivery and read receipt happen later.

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.

    Notification Platform

    Prerequisites: Design Patterns, Dependency Injection, and Object Lifecycles, API Design and Communication Contracts, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows, Reliability, Fault Tolerance, and Disaster Recovery4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A password-reset message reaches a user hours after it was requested. The sender may have completed its work, yet the notification has missed its purpose.

    We will follow a durable notification intent through channel selection, provider submission, and later evidence. The design must keep accepted work recoverable while recognising that provider acceptance, device delivery, and human viewing are different outcomes.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.4.1 · Functional requirements

    An application records an intent to notify someone. The platform chooses permitted email, SMS, or push channels, renders a versioned template, submits the message, and tracks the outcome. Some intents may be scheduled or cancelled within a defined window.

    Keep message purpose in the policy: operational and product messages may follow different preference rules. A channel adapter handles delivery mechanics; it should not silently decide which messages the user may receive. Provider acceptance, device delivery, and human viewing need distinct states and evidence.

    22.4.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Preserve accepted intents and make delay, expiry, and permanent failure visible. Give each message a business expiry. A password-reset message delivered hours late may be useless or harmful even if submission eventually succeeds.

    Reserve resources for critical work so a marketing batch cannot occupy every worker. Avoid duplicate external effects where the provider contract supports it and expose uncertainty where it does not. The promised outcome must match what the service can establish.

    22.4.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume ten million intents/day. Dividing by 86,400 seconds gives about 115.7 intents/s; a tenfold peak gives about 1,157/s. At 1 kB of initial intent and attempt metadata each, raw growth is 10 GB/day.

    Retries, retained content, indexes, and copies add work. Treat channel quotas as separate configured inputs to check with the actual provider. The daily service average does not establish how quickly one SMS or email route can submit its share.

    22.4.4 · Naive initial architecture

    A first version calls a provider directly after a user action. The user waits for it, and a crash after the business commit but before sending can lose the notification obligation.

    Save required intent in the business transaction or its outbox, then let a worker submit it. This closes that local loss window and lets a provider outage delay delivery without erasing accepted work. The repair introduces queued state, attempts, and recovery ownership; an untracked background function would not supply these guarantees.

    22.4.5 · Core API contracts

    POST /notifications accepts recipient, template version, variables, channel policy, expiry, and idempotency key. GET /notifications/{id} reports pending, submitted, delivered, expired, failed, or cancelled according to defined transitions.

    Cancellation cannot recall a message already accepted by a provider. Callback endpoints verify the sender and recognise repeated events. A delivered state requires the relevant provider evidence, rather than simply an exception-free worker call. State which later outcomes remain outside the platform's knowledge.

    22.4.6 · Data model and schema

    Store the intent, template version, relevant preference information, channel/recipient tasks, attempts, and a provider-event inbox. Stable identities and uniqueness rules bind each intended effect to its task. Retain provider references, including uncertain outcomes.

    Separate sensitive content from minimal progress and audit records. Decide whether a preference change affects already queued work. Where the policy requires current consent or cancellation checks, a submission-time snapshot alone is insufficient.

    22.4.7 · Low-level component organization

    NotificationService records intent, PreferencePolicy selects allowed channels, and TemplateRenderer creates content. SenderStrategy selects channel behaviour; ProviderAdapter translates that provider's protocol and outcomes. DeliveryRepository owns attempts and durable progress.

    Factories can construct genuine channel variations, and decorators can measure calls, provided their lifetimes and result meanings stay clear. A retry wrapper must preserve operation identity and handle an uncertain prior submission. Sharing a method signature does not make two providers' recovery contracts interchangeable.

    22.4.8 · High-level system architecture

    Use durable ingress, preference and template access, channel queues, bounded workers, callback inboxes, and an outcome store. Separate critical and bulk capacity where their priorities require it.

    Limit how much capacity one failing provider can occupy. For recovery, intent, attempt state, queue acknowledgment, and progress must agree about ownership. Draw those durable boundaries with the normal send path so a worker or broker restart has a clear starting point.

    22.4.9 · Data and control flows

    Deduplicate and save the intent, choose permitted content and channel, then persist a delivery task. Before submitting, the worker checks current attempt authority, expiry, and the required current-preference policy.

    Use a stable provider operation identity where supported. Save either the submission evidence or an uncertain outcome before acknowledging according to the task protocol. Verified callbacks may arrive before or after the attempt reply. Apply them by identity and allowed transition, so an old event cannot incorrectly reverse later progress.

    22.4.10 · Capacity estimates

    The overall average is about 115.7 intents/s, but channels have separate limits. Suppose SMS tasks arrive at 100/s while the route submits 40/s. The queue gains 100 − 40 = 60 tasks/s. If both rates persist for ten minutes, 60 × 600 = 36,000 submissions accumulate.

    Include retries, recipient fan-out, and expiry. Some waiting messages may become useless before the queue drains. Admission, priority, or a supported alternate route must respond to that channel limit, regardless of the service-wide average.

    22.4.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Suppose durable API acceptance takes 50 ms, queue wait takes 2 seconds, and provider submission takes 500 ms. Provider acceptance then occurs around 2.55 seconds after the API request.

    These are illustrative budgets, not measured percentiles. Device delivery and human viewing require further events and evidence. Measure the end event that matters for the message's purpose as well as API latency. A quick acknowledgment only establishes quick acceptance of the obligation.

    22.4.12 · Failure scenarios

    A worker submits a message and dies before recording the reply. The provider may already have accepted it. Recover using a supported status query or provider idempotency; if neither resolves the outcome, retain the duplicate risk explicitly.

    Switching providers can create a second message while the first is still in flight. Also handle malformed templates, bounded outage retries, expiry, and forged callbacks. Reconcile old submitted or uncertain tasks rather than leaving their outcome permanently implied by an empty worker queue.

    22.4.13 · Scalability improvements

    Distribute independent recipients and channel tasks, preserving any required per-recipient order and concurrency bounds. More workers help only while the downstream route has capacity.

    Add providers with explicit selection, quota, and uncertainty rules. An alternate route may improve some outages, but timeout followed by switching can submit twice. Keep critical capacity and business expiry visible. Useful, permitted progress is a better scaling objective than the largest possible number of parallel submissions.

    22.4.14 · Consistency requirements

    Commit accepted intent and its deduplication result atomically. Task delivery may repeat, so local transitions recognise stable identities. Provider acceptance and final delivery each require their own evidence.

    Retain the template version so a retry does not change content under an old identity, and apply current preferences at the boundary the policy requires. Email, SMS, and push contracts differ. Name the local record or external effect protected by each mechanism instead of assigning a general exactly-once guarantee.

    22.4.15 · Security model

    Authorise which actors may send particular templates to particular recipients. Validate variables and encode or escape them for their channel, including safe header and content construction. Protect recipient data, credentials, and callback authenticity.

    Bound intent creation to prevent abuse. Keep message bodies and tokens out of routine logs. Links inside messages need an appropriate audience and lifetime; rendering or delivery must not accidentally broaden the access they grant.

    22.4.16 · Deployment approach

    Deploy workers with durable attempt state and graceful draining so scale-down does not abandon unrecorded work. Template changes create new versions rather than altering content behind an existing retry identity.

    Evolve task schemas compatibly and plan credential rotation. Test replacement during an outage and recovery: accumulated work must not flood a returning provider. Verify that acceptance and critical delivery still work when another channel is saturated.

    22.4.17 · Observability design

    Track accepted intents, queue age by channel, expiry, submission delay, uncertain outcomes, callbacks, and duplicate recognition. Separate critical and bulk outcomes so a good aggregate does not hide delayed important messages.

    Alert on old unresolved tasks and rapid error-budget consumption. A queue can age into an incident without any worker exception. Correlate task, attempt, and provider evidence without exposing private content. Enqueue success is one observable stage of the journey.

    22.4.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Include intent and attempt storage, provider-submitted units, workers, callbacks, transfer, and operating effort. A retry can be billable even when it produces no useful delivery. Model channel_unit_price × submitted_units using explicit inputs.

    Content length and character encoding may affect SMS billing under the selected provider's contract, which must be checked. Cost per accepted intent and cost per relevant successful delivery describe different work; keep their denominators separate.

    22.4.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    Direct synchronous sending uses little infrastructure and ties the user's request to the provider. Queued delivery adds durable state, recovery, and delay. An orchestrator can make escalation across channels explicit, while independent event reactions can make overall progress harder to inspect.

    A backup provider adds both a recovery option and an uncertainty boundary. Compare alternatives using expiry, criticality, permissions, and available evidence. Eventually submitting something may fail the original notification purpose.

    22.4.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    Start with one sender behind a clear contract. Add durable intent and a worker when required work must survive failure or leave the user's request path. Introduce channel strategies and factories for real variation.

    Separate critical and bulk resources as volume and harm justify it. Add failover and escalation after defining uncertain-outcome recovery. Preserve task, template, and attempt identities through these changes so scaling does not accidentally create fresh effects for the same intent.

    22.4.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Review whether “delivered” matches the evidence, whether expiry and current preferences are checked, and whether failover can duplicate a message. These questions involve product meaning as well as implementation.

    Test send-then-crash, forged and repeated callbacks, preference revocation after enqueue, template changes, and channel saturation. Late events must not incorrectly reverse terminal progress. Successful submission requests alone cannot establish timely delivery to the intended people.

    22.4.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Build a recording sender that stores a submission but returns uncertainty. Process the task again and inspect its attempt identities and local state. It must not invent delivery evidence.

    Add expiry and current-preference checks. Then switch providers after the uncertain submission and demonstrate how a second external effect can result. Implement only the recovery your mock provider supports, and make the remaining duplicate risk visible.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    def deliver(task, now):
    require_current_attempt(task)
    if now >= task.expires_at: return mark_expired(task)
    if not permitted_now(task): return mark_cancelled(task)
    sender = sender_factory.for_channel(task.channel)
    result = sender.send(task.stable_provider_key, render(task))
    if result.uncertain:
        return persist_uncertain(task, result.reference)
    return persist_submission_result(task, result)
# A provider acknowledgment is not a human-read receipt.

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.

    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.5

    Social Media Feed

    Prerequisites: Data Models and Storage Technologies, Caching and Content Delivery, Scalability, Load Balancing, and Data Distribution, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A popular author publishes a post. Preparing a copy for every follower can make later reads quick, but many followers may never open their feeds. Waiting until each read avoids that unused work and makes the read more expensive.

    We will compare both journeys and build a hybrid where it helps. Throughout, finding and ranking candidates must preserve the viewer's permission to see the underlying posts.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.5.1 · Functional requirements

    Users publish posts, follow accounts, and read a ranked home feed. Provide bounded continuation while enforcing privacy, blocking, moderation, and deletion.

    Ranking chooses among permitted posts. A high score cannot grant visibility. Candidate lists and engagement totals can lag their source, but the product must define their acceptable freshness. Separate finding interesting posts from deciding which posts the viewer may receive.

    22.5.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Assume a feed p99 target of 300 ms at the supported workload. Retain accepted posts, define how promptly access changes take effect, and give pagination understandable duplicate and omission behaviour.

    Ranking may change between refreshes. State whether a refresh begins a new generation and what its continuation cursor preserves. Because candidate caches can be old, specify which source and permission properties are rechecked on every served page.

    22.5.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume ten million daily readers make twenty feed reads each. That is 200 million reads/day, or about 2,315/s. Assume one million posts/day.

    For ordinary authors, use a simplified average of one hundred followers and a 32-byte candidate reference. Preparing all those references creates 100 million/day, or 3.2 GB raw. A celebrity with millions of followers belongs to a different workload class: this average hides both the publication burst and work spent for inactive followers.

    22.5.4 · Naive initial architecture

    Start with indexed posts and follow relationships. When a reader requests a feed, retrieve posts by followed authors and rank the candidates. This avoids maintaining a prepared copy for every follower.

    As follow sets grow, retrieval and ranking can make each read expensive. Measure that work and the follower distribution before materialising feeds. Materialisation means storing a derived result in advance; it saves repeated reads while adding publication work, storage, and refresh responsibilities.

    22.5.5 · Core API contracts

    POST /posts creates a versioned post. POST /follows changes a relationship. GET /feed returns a bounded page, continuation cursor, and relevant ranking generation. DELETE /posts/{id} records authoritative removal.

    Bind cursors to the viewer and applicable filters, validate them, and define their snapshot or continuation meaning. A cursor locates a page; it does not preserve permission after access changes. Reapply the required visibility policy whenever another page is served.

    22.5.6 · Data model and schema

    Posts contain identity, author, version, visibility, state, and creation time. Follows connect reader and author. Optional candidate records connect reader to post and source version, with ranking information. Retain model version or generation where reproducibility needs it.

    Posts and access relationships are authoritative; candidates are derived references. Stable source identity supports deduplication, removal, and rebuilds. State whether copied features are snapshots or are expected to follow later updates.

    22.5.7 · Low-level component organization

    PostService owns publication and FollowService owns relationship changes. CandidateGenerator finds or prepares references, FeatureFetcher obtains bounded ranking inputs, and Ranker scores them. VisibilityFilter enforces access; FeedAssembler merges, deduplicates, and pages results.

    Keep visibility independent of desirability. Missing features may change ranking, but must not broaden permission. These boundaries let us improve candidate or feature performance without moving access rules into a model score.

    22.5.8 · High-level system architecture

    Commit publications durably with outbox intent. Workers prepare candidates for ordinary authors, while high-fan-out authors can be retrieved at read time. Candidate storage, ranking compute, and permitted caches support serving.

    This hybrid avoids immediately writing every celebrity post into every follower's feed. It introduces a rule for choosing and changing strategies, plus reconciliation work. Keep model deployment decisions distinct from the data path, and preserve source state and access checks whenever derived copies lag.

    22.5.9 · Data and control flows

    Publication commits the post and fan-out intent. Workers insert candidate references under stable identity. A read combines prepared candidates with posts pulled from high-fan-out authors, checks required current access and post state, fetches bounded features, ranks, deduplicates, and returns a continuation.

    Track the generation. A deleted reference may remain physically stored while serving rejects it, if the deletion contract permits that delay. Permission to expose a post and eventual storage cleanup have separate completion boundaries.

    22.5.10 · Capacity estimates

    The assumed 200 million daily reads average about 2,315/s; a fivefold peak is about 11,574/s. One million posts × one hundred followers creates 100 million candidate writes/day.

    A post reaching ten million followers creates its own burst, regardless of the average. Also estimate candidates ranked per request and feature lookups per candidate. A modest API rate can multiply into much larger storage and compute demand through these internal fan-outs.

    22.5.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Suppose the path spends 20 ms at the edge, 50 ms retrieving candidates, 80 ms fetching features, 70 ms ranking, and 30 ms preparing a response. The proposed total is 250 ms before further tail and queue allowance.

    Measure end-to-end p99 against the 300 ms objective. One required slow feature can dominate completion, so define safe missing-feature behaviour. Measure publication freshness separately: a fast page can still contain old or empty candidates.

    22.5.12 · Failure scenarios

    A worker may repeat fan-out after a crash. Stable candidate identity prevents the repeat from adding duplicate effects. A celebrity burst needs its selected pull or bounded distribution path to avoid unrestricted queue growth.

    Privacy changes can precede candidate cleanup, so current serving checks remain essential. If ranking fails, a permitted chronological feed may be an acceptable fallback. Test access on that fallback too; its simpler ordering does not remove deletion or visibility obligations.

    22.5.13 · Scalability improvements

    Partition candidate work by a measured ownership key, batch feature reads, and cache within the allowed freshness scope. Bound candidates retrieved and ranked per read. Give rebuilds separate budgets so they cannot consume all live-serving resources.

    Choose the push/pull threshold from write amplification, reader activity, and read cost. Moving an author across that threshold needs a transition that prevents missing and duplicate candidates. More workers help only while the stores they update have remaining capacity.

    22.5.14 · Consistency requirements

    Post identity, updates, and deletion need a suitable transactional authority. Candidate projections and engagement totals may propagate later. An author who expects an immediate view of their own post may need a direct-source overlay or another supported read path.

    Access still follows its own freshness rule even when candidates are stale. Specify which page properties belong to a ranking snapshot and which are revalidated. The feed contains several observable consistency requirements.

    22.5.15 · Security model

    Enforce author permissions, viewer visibility, blocking, and moderation on every relevant path. Validate cursors and bound scraping and feature-query amplification. Client scores must never grant access.

    Ranking records may expose private behaviour. Limit retention and access, and propagate required deletion into features and analytical copies. Apply tenant and content-scope rules to model inputs and outputs as well as the final page.

    22.5.16 · Deployment approach

    Version rankers, use representative canary cohorts, and check rollback compatibility with stored features. Mixed-version readers must understand fan-out formats during rollout.

    Separate rebuild capacity from live reads and publication. A region-local feed needs a defined route for source and access-policy updates before promising privacy and local reads together. Observe model releases alongside code and schema releases because each can change the served result.

    22.5.17 · Observability design

    Track publication-to-candidate delay, candidate counts, visibility denials, read latency, feature tails, model versions, duplicates, and hot-author backlog. Measure relevance and useful content separately from infrastructure timing.

    Low p99 does not establish correct, varied, current pages. Pair operational measures with content and privacy checks. Detailed evidence can retain source versions and generations without adding unbounded per-user or per-post labels to metrics.

    22.5.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Include candidate writes, feature storage and reads, ranking CPU, response transfer, and rebuilds. The simplified 3.2 GB/day of raw references excludes indexes and other metadata.

    Compare push and pull using the fraction of followers who actually read. Preparing feeds for inactive readers can spend work never used. Use explicit fictional rates or verified current quotes, and compare designs with equal visibility, retention, freshness, and recovery requirements.

    22.5.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    Fan-out-on-write performs work when a post arrives to make later reads cheaper. Fan-out-on-read avoids unused preparation and adds work to each active read. A hybrid assigns different traffic classes to each and adds transition complexity.

    Precomputed ranking can save serving CPU while adding freshness delay. Compare these choices with active-reader ratios and author skew. Include deletion and privacy requirements in the comparison, since a faster page with weaker visibility is a different service contract.

    22.5.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    Begin with indexed pull reads, then add bounded ranking and useful caching. Prepare ordinary-author candidates when repeated read work becomes limiting. Introduce a distinct high-fan-out path after measuring author skew.

    Regional copies need source-version and privacy-update rules. Revisit thresholds as reading, posting, and follow distributions change. Preserve stable candidate identity and explicit generations so each stage retains the intended continuation and duplicate behaviour.

    22.5.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Review inactive-reader assumptions, high-degree authors, and access revocation. Put a post into cached candidate pages, then delete it or make it private. Verify that later pages obey the visibility rule.

    Replay fan-out, pause a worker, and disable a feature dependency. Check candidate identities, source versions, and fallback access. An empty queue establishes progress through a worker, but does not prove that each intended reader obtained one usable, authorised reference.

    22.5.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Build push and pull generation over a small follow graph containing one very high-degree author. Count work for explicit user journeys so inactive-reader costs remain visible.

    Delete a materialised post and test the serving filter. Replay a fan-out event and check for visible duplicates. Explain which strategy spends work before anyone reads and which moves work into active reads, while enforcing the same privacy rules in both.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    def feed(reader, cursor):
    candidates = materialized(reader) + pull_hot_authors(reader)
    unique = deduplicate_by_post_id(candidates)
    permitted = [p for p in unique if visible_now(reader, p)]
    features = fetch_bounded_features(permitted)
    ranked = rank(permitted, features, model_version)
    return page(ranked, validated_cursor(cursor, reader))

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.

    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.6

    Video Streaming Platform

    Prerequisites: Networking Foundations for System Design, Caching and Content Delivery, File Systems, Search Infrastructure, and Data Pipelines, Deployment, Cloud Infrastructure, and Platform Architecture4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    An encoder has written two of the three segments required for a video. If the service now displays “Ready,” a viewer may start playback and encounter a missing piece.

    We will follow uploaded bytes through validation, conversion, and publication. A playable generation must name a verified set of outputs, and the delivery path must enforce the video's access and deletion rules.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.6.1 · Functional requirements

    An owner uploads a video, the service validates and converts it, and an authorised viewer receives a playback manifest and media segments. Support resumable upload, processing progress, and deletion.

    Adaptive playback lets a client switch among available renditions as conditions change. A rendition is an encoded version suitable for a particular playback profile. Switching cannot repair missing media. We need both a transformation workflow and a deliberate decision that a complete generation is ready to play.

    22.6.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Preserve sources and required derived media under stated durability and retention rules. Choose playback-start and smoothness objectives for supported clients and measure the delivery journey.

    Asynchronous processing must expose failed and review states. Protect manifests, segments, thumbnails, and download links as well as the player page. A private metadata row cannot protect media bytes that remain publicly fetchable.

    22.6.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume 1,000 uploads/day averaging 1 GB and thirty minutes each. That is 1 TB/day of source bytes and 500 source-hours/day. If selected renditions total five output GB per source GB, they add 5 TB/day.

    Assume 10,000 simultaneous viewers average 3 Mb/s each. Delivery is 30 Gb/s; dividing by eight gives 3.75 GB/s before overhead. Encoding, retention, and playback impose different work. These teaching ratios are not codec or infrastructure benchmarks.

    22.6.4 · Naive initial architecture

    A prototype accepts an upload and lets one worker create one playback file. This is easy to trace, but large transfers and computation depend on fragile local execution, and one file adapts poorly to varying networks.

    Direct upload to storage keeps large bytes out of application workers. Durable encoding tasks retain required progress. Start with a small supported rendition set; producing many unused formats adds compute and storage without necessarily improving the intended viewers' experience.

    22.6.5 · Core API contracts

    POST /videos creates an upload intent. Scoped multipart authorisation permits transfer; completion validates the stored input. A status endpoint reports progress, and playback returns an authorised manifest reference. Deletion tracks required cleanup.

    Distinguish upload complete, processing, playable, and failed. Define playback-capability scope, lifetime, and cache behaviour so an old URL does not grant indefinite access. Accepted bytes are input to processing, rather than proof of usable media.

    22.6.6 · Data model and schema

    Store video identity, owner, source version, and state. Upload sessions track unfinished transfers. Encoding jobs reference input digest, profile version, and attempt epoch. Renditions identify profile, version, object key, and checksum. A manifest generation names its required artifacts.

    Publish only after verifying that set. Keep published references immutable, introducing a new version when bytes change. Source and owner relationships let deletion, repair, and inventory reconciliation find every derived object.

    22.6.7 · Low-level component organization

    UploadService grants upload permission, MediaValidator checks supported bounded input, and EncodingPlanner chooses profiles. WorkerLease manages attempts; TranscoderAdapter performs isolated conversion. ArtifactPublisher advances published metadata only after required outputs are verified.

    PlaybackService checks access and issues scoped references. Separate writing artifacts from publishing a generation: finishing one file says nothing about the remaining required files. Publication needs evidence about the whole set.

    22.6.8 · High-level system architecture

    Use object storage for immutable sources and segments, durable workflow state and a task queue, isolated transcoders, metadata storage, and edge delivery. The application handles control and access while bytes flow through storage and CDN facilities.

    Give untrusted parsers limited resources, permissions, and egress. Keep source and derived retention explicit. The queue schedules work; source storage, workflow state, and published metadata still have distinct recovery responsibilities.

    22.6.9 · Data and control flows

    Validate the completed upload's identity and choose a versioned plan. An attempt produces artifacts, then verifies the required segments and manifest. Atomically publish the playable metadata generation only when that set is valid.

    Failed attempts may leave unpublished objects for cleanup or safe reuse. Viewers obtain authorised references and fetch supported renditions. Publishing after only the first output is valid only under an explicitly supported progressive-publication contract. Otherwise, it exposes an incomplete generation as ready.

    22.6.10 · Capacity estimates

    Thirty days of the assumed input need 30 TB of originals and 150 TB of renditions before copies and overhead. Viewer transfer at 30 Gb/s is much larger than metadata traffic.

    Encoding capacity depends on measured content and profile costs. For illustration, two compute-hours per source-hour would turn 500 source-hours/day into 1,000 compute-hours/day. Measure that ratio with representative media before sizing workers; the calculation provides a workload assumption, not a performance result.

    22.6.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Suppose playback authorisation takes 50 ms, manifest delivery 30 ms, and initial buffering 800 ms. The example path totals 880 ms.

    A cache miss or constrained client changes this path. Measure startup, rebuffering, rendition switches, and failures separately from metadata API p99. Segment delivery and player behaviour are part of the experience. A quick permission check provides little evidence about a missing or slowly arriving first segment.

    22.6.12 · Failure scenarios

    An interrupted upload, corrupt source, partial encoding, and missing published object are different failures. Give each an explicit state and repair path. Keep partial generations unpublished and verify the final set.

    If edge delivery fails, fallback can send enormous traffic to the origin, so protect it. Revocation and deletion must affect playable references and copies under the selected capability and cache rules. Test through actual media requests rather than checking only metadata state.

    22.6.13 · Scalability improvements

    Scale upload transfer, encoding, and playback separately. Bound encoding concurrency and prioritise jobs by deadlines. Cache immutable segments where access policy permits reuse.

    A viral video creates hot-object delivery pressure, which may leave metadata storage mostly unaffected. Plan origin protection and regional-copy cost during cache loss. More profiles and transcoders also create backfill and storage work. Expand the measured limiting path rather than increasing every component together.

    22.6.14 · Consistency requirements

    A published generation must name a usable artifact set. Attempts may repeat, but stable output identities and conditional completion prevent an old worker from replacing a newer generation. An epoch is an attempt-authority number; publication rechecks it at the authoritative transition, as the code illustrates.

    Declare cache reuse intervals and separate privacy and deletion requirements. A recovery region must possess the objects required by its publication metadata. Copying only some bytes does not make a complete failover source.

    22.6.15 · Security model

    Authorise upload and playback, bound sizes and supported formats, isolate parsers and encoders, and give workers narrow storage permissions. Protect signed capabilities and keep them out of routine logs.

    Check manifests, segments, and thumbnails directly. Test capability expiry, cache keys, membership removal, and deletion end to end. Privacy must cover every route to content, including objects fetched without reopening the player page.

    22.6.16 · Deployment approach

    Version encoding profiles and retain usable older outputs until a validated transition permits removal. Workers need durable claims and graceful shutdown. Give expensive backfills budgets that preserve live processing and playback.

    Test restoring metadata to an older point while source bytes survive. Source identities and artifact inventories must let the application reconcile what exists. Preserving running containers alone cannot repair a lost relationship between media and metadata.

    22.6.17 · Observability design

    Observe upload completion, oldest jobs, failed profiles, compute-to-media ratios, and ready-generation integrity. Track edge hits, origin transfer, startup, rebuffering, and access outcomes for playback.

    Correlate source, profile, and generation in detailed evidence. Alert on missing segments and stuck videos even when workers report few exceptions. A synthetic private-video journey should include successful playback followed by revocation, covering both delivery and access changes.

    22.6.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Include originals, renditions, repeated encoding, compute, delivery requests, transfer, metadata, and telemetry. Sustaining 3.75 GB/s for one hour transfers 3.75 × 3,600 = 13,500 GB, or 13.5 TB, before overhead.

    Viewer-demand duration matters alongside peak concurrency. Compare profile count and retention with quality needs, using labelled fictional rates or verified quotes. A smaller rendition set saves work while changing the client's playback choices.

    22.6.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    A single file is simple to manage and offers little adaptation. Segmented adaptive delivery adds manifests and a larger artifact lifecycle. Pre-encoding makes outputs ready early while spending resources on profiles some viewers never use.

    On-demand encoding reduces unused work and adds startup or burst risk. Managed conversion delegates selected operations, while publication, access, and reconciliation remain design decisions. Compare alternatives under equal client, privacy, and recovery requirements.

    22.6.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    Start with resumable upload and durable processing identity. Add a small tested adaptive set with versioned publication. Introduce suitable edge delivery and grow encoding independently from playback.

    Add regional objects or profiles for demonstrated locality, recovery, or quality needs. Retain exact source and profile identities so each result remains explainable and reproducible. Increased capacity must preserve what playable, private, and deleted mean for existing videos.

    22.6.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Review three claims separately: every ready generation is playable, private artifacts remain protected, and origin survives edge failure. Each needs its own evidence.

    Test corrupt input, interruption between output and publication, repeated completion, missing segments, expired access, and deletion after caching. One successful warm-cache playback leaves these partial-processing and private-recovery paths unexamined.

    22.6.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Build a publisher that requires three segments. Write two and stop. The manifest must stay unpublished. Resume with the same job identity, write the third, validate checksums, and atomically advance one metadata generation.

    Next remove a published segment deliberately and run an integrity check. It should identify the broken set. Explain the difference between the boundary that established readiness and the later failure that damaged an already published generation.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    def publish(job):
    require_current_epoch(job)
    artifacts = expected_artifacts(job.source, job.profile)
    require(all(exists_and_valid(a) for a in artifacts))
    with transaction():
        assert_current_epoch(job)
        generation = record_complete_manifest(artifacts)
        mark_playable(job.video, generation)
# Partial worker output is never silently declared ready.

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.
