    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.7

    Ride-Hailing System

    Prerequisites: Data Models and Storage Technologies, Scalability, Load Balancing, and Data Distribution, Distributed Systems Fundamentals, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Two riders request a trip, and both matchers choose the same nearby driver. The search may be accurate, yet it has not decided who receives the assignment.

    We will separate recent-location search from the authoritative claim on a driver. That distinction lets us improve matching and distribute location traffic while preserving one valid active assignment.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.7.1 · Functional requirements

    A driver reports location and availability. A rider requests a trip; the service finds candidates, offers work, records an accepted assignment, and tracks progress or cancellation.

    A nearby driver is a candidate. Receiving an offer also does not establish assignment. Define offer expiry and what the rider sees while matching is unresolved. Two matchers observing the same old availability must not create incompatible active trips for one driver.

    22.7.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Set a bounded machine-side dispatch target for the assumed region and preserve exclusive active assignments. Treat position age and accuracy as uncertainty rather than ground truth, and protect precise location information.

    Trip transitions must survive retries and temporary disconnection. A missing heartbeat does not prove a trip has ended. Human offer acceptance and payment-provider outcomes follow different timelines. Keep those states visible so every delay does not become an unsupported failed-trip result.

    22.7.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume 100,000 online drivers report every five seconds. This produces 100,000 / 5 = 20,000 updates/s. At 100 raw bytes each, the stream is 2 MB/s, or 172.8 GB/day if every update is retained.

    Assume 100 new trip requests/s. Estimate map requests, candidate evaluation, regional skew, and retention separately. The high-volume location projection and lower-volume assignment authority have different jobs and need not use the same storage or coordination mechanism.

    22.7.4 · Naive initial architecture

    Begin with a service holding recent positions and selecting a nearby available driver. Sequential requests are easy to follow. With concurrent requests, two matchers may select the same driver before either changes availability.

    Keep search positions as a derived projection and perform the exclusive claim against authoritative assignment state. Improve spatial lookup after this boundary is correct. Faster nearest-neighbour search can produce better candidates, but cannot decide between simultaneous claims. Stale locations can still harm match quality without violating exclusive assignment.

    22.7.5 · Core API contracts

    Location updates include position, source sequence, and observed time. POST /trips creates a stable rider request. POST /offers/{id}/accept attempts a valid claim; status and cancellation expose explicit trip transitions.

    Derive driver identity from authentication and validate plausible updates. Expired or superseded offers return a documented conflict. Repeated acceptance recovers the existing result. A caller-supplied driver identifier must not bypass ownership checks or replace another assignment.

    22.7.6 · Data model and schema

    driver_state holds availability, assignment_id, and version. A trip holds rider, state, driver, and version. An offer identifies trip, driver, expiry, and status. Latest-position records include driver sequence, spatial cell, and observation time; retained location history has a separate restricted lifecycle.

    Protect active assignment through conditional transitions or suitable uniqueness constraints. A spatial index helps find candidates; it must not independently decide whether a driver is free.

    22.7.7 · Low-level component organization

    LocationIngestor validates update order. SpatialIndex finds candidates, Matcher ranks a bounded set, and OfferService checks offer validity. AssignmentRepository owns the claim; TripStateMachine controls later transitions.

    Map and ETA adapters have separate deadlines so provider failure cannot corrupt assignment. Stable trip and acceptance identities make retries recover the same work. Many matchers may choose candidates, while the final availability decision stays at its atomic owner.

    22.7.8 · High-level system architecture

    Use a regional location stream and spatial projection, durable trip and assignment storage, matching workers, offer delivery, and trip events. Geographic partitioning can keep searches local, provided driver movement has a defined handoff.

    Configuration may arrive from a control plane, but two regions with stale availability copies must not both assign one driver. Assignment requires one valid authority or a transfer protocol. Draw local search and exclusive ownership as distinct paths.

    22.7.9 · Data and control flows

    Commit the rider request identity. Search sufficiently fresh candidates, recheck authoritative availability, and create a bounded-lifetime offer. On acceptance, verify that the offer is still pending, unexpired, and compatible with current ownership.

    Atomically bind driver and trip under the chosen transaction model. Repeated acceptance recovers its result; stale acceptance conflicts. If the reply disappears, trip status resolves uncertainty. The conditional acceptance, rather than delivery of the offer, prevents incompatible winners.

    22.7.10 · Capacity estimates

    The workload produces 20,000 position updates/s and 100 dispatches/s. Evaluating twenty candidates per dispatch adds 100 × 20 = 2,000 candidate evaluations/s before retries and ETA requests.

    Do not automatically call a routing service for every position update. Estimate hot cells, city-centre peaks, and boundary crossings. Candidate pruning can lower map cost while leaving the exclusive claim unchanged. Global averages can hide the one area where most work is concentrated.

    22.7.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Suppose ingress takes 30 ms, candidate lookup 40 ms, bounded ETA evaluation 80 ms, and assignment work 30 ms. The machine-side planning budget totals 180 ms.

    Human acceptance is a separate interval. Missing candidates, communication delays, expiry, and retries extend the whole matching journey. Measure time in those states and validate the budget against representative cities, traffic, and providers. An optimistic machine sum does not establish the rider's total wait.

    22.7.12 · Failure scenarios

    An older position must not move the serving projection backward under its source-sequence rule. If two requests choose one driver, only one authoritative claim may win. A paused worker must not accept an offer superseded while it was stopped.

    Recover lost offers or replies through status. A map outage may allow a justified simpler ranking or require paused matching, but cannot bypass exclusive ownership. Exercise each failure at its state boundary so a search problem cannot become conflicting trip commitments.

    22.7.13 · Scalability improvements

    Scale location ingestion and spatial serving separately from assignment transactions. Prune or batch ETA calls. When splitting regions or cells, transfer the driver's authority explicitly.

    Candidate caches need age information. Extra matchers cannot automatically divide a hot claim owner whose decisions remain serialised. Finer cells add boundary queries and movement coordination, so choose them from measured concentrated work while retaining one active-assignment rule.

    22.7.14 · Consistency requirements

    Location can propagate through a delayed projection with a declared age policy. Assignment requires a coordinated conditional change linking driver and trip. Crossing a regional boundary requires authority transfer, rather than independent acceptance on each side.

    Give status reads the required read-after-accept behaviour. Observation time helps judge position age; sequence rules reject old updates, and fencing rules reject old owners. These mechanisms protect different kinds of state and should be explained separately.

    22.7.15 · Security model

    Authenticate driver updates and limit rider and driver views to the relevant trip. Restrict precise history, including support and administrator paths, retain only justified data, and audit privileged use.

    Bound geographic scraping and costly map requests. Choosing an arbitrary driver identifier does not confer claim authority. Keep raw coordinates out of broad telemetry where unnecessary. Apply privacy rules to streams, caches, exports, and logs as well as the displayed map.

    22.7.16 · Deployment approach

    Use regional placement with a stated failure model and durable assignment state. Keep releases compatible with older clients and in-progress offers. Drain new work while retaining existing trips and offers.

    Recovery must reconcile active assignments and uncertain provider outcomes. An old snapshot must not reoffer a driver still assigned elsewhere. Establish valid history and fencing before replacement authority acts. Test recovery with active trips, since an empty-system restart cannot reveal conflicting ownership.

    22.7.17 · Observability design

    Track location age, stale-update rejection, cell skew, candidate counts, claim conflicts, offer expiry, matching outcomes, and time in each dispatch state. Observe map-provider errors separately.

    Correlate stable trip-creation and acceptance identities. Alert on unresolved assignments and invariant violations as well as HTTP failures. Simulated drivers can cross cells, disconnect, and accept near expiry while riders compete, testing fresh search and exclusive outcomes together.

    22.7.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Include ingestion, recent-location state, map and ETA calls, assignments, offer attempts, history, transfer, and operations. Route calls for every update could dominate cost despite efficient position storage.

    Model calls per candidate and dispatch, then compare pruning and batching using explicit fictional rates or verified terms. Keep the accuracy and latency effects of cheaper ranking visible. The model makes no claim about a real company's internal architecture or bill.

    22.7.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    Straight-line distance is inexpensive and may ignore road travel. Route-based ETA can improve ranking while adding delay and a provider dependency. Sequential offers reduce simultaneous acceptance opportunities; multiple offers require a controlled single winner.

    Fine spatial cells can improve locality and add handoffs and boundary queries. Compare fairness, rider wait, candidate quality, and machine cost. Each choice must preserve exclusive assignment.

    22.7.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    Start with a correct regional claim and basic proximity search. Add streamed positions and spatial indexes when lookup work requires them, then distribute matching with bounded ETA evaluation.

    Split geographic ownership after measuring hot areas and defining a safe transfer procedure. Regional expansion adds a failure and partition policy for active trips. Preserve request identities and claims throughout: replicating matcher processes does not replicate the authority on which they depend.

    22.7.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Review what nearby, recently observed, available, offered, and assigned each mean. A spatial index answers proximity and age questions, but cannot alone establish current ownership.

    Test competing riders, out-of-order positions, acceptance after expiry, paused workers, and handoff. One claim should win, and losers should receive meaningful state. Confirm that search projections never become independent writers of authoritative availability. A fast matching demonstration can otherwise conceal the decisive race.

    22.7.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Build an optimistic driver claim with an expected version and offer expiry. Start two requests from the same version. Verify that one local claim wins and the other conflicts.

    Deliver an older position and a delayed acceptance after the winner commits. Neither may overwrite the active assignment. Explain the boundary demonstrated: a local transaction establishes one local owner, while external trip or payment effects still require their own contracts and recovery evidence.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    def accept_offer(offer, driver, now):
    with transaction():
        current = lock_offer(offer.id)
        require(current.pending and now < current.expires_at)
        won = claim_driver_if_available(driver, current.expected_version)
        if not won: raise AssignmentConflict
        bind_trip_and_offer(offer.trip, driver, offer.id)
    return current_trip_state(offer.trip)

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.

    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.8

    Online Ticket Booking

    Prerequisites: API Design and Communication Contracts, Database Internals, Transactions, and Concurrency Control, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows, Security Architecture and Privacy4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A buyer holds a seat and starts payment. The hold expires, another buyer reserves the seat, and the first payment finally succeeds. A paid flag alone cannot tell us which ticket may safely be issued.

    We will trace seat ownership, versioned holds, and provider evidence through that sequence. The same rules must also handle repeated requests and delayed expiry tasks without selling one seat twice.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.8.1 · Functional requirements

    A buyer browses an event, holds selected seats, pays, and receives tickets. Holds last a defined period; cancellation and refunds follow explicit policies.

    The displayed seat map is advisory. The authoritative reservation decides who owns the opportunity to buy. Retries, expiry tasks, and payment callbacks can overlap, but must never confirm one seat for two buyers. Establish that invariant before improving the map or adding a waiting room.

    22.8.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Prevent duplicate confirmed ownership and retain accepted payment and ticket records under the selected failure contract. Pending holds must resolve through supported confirmation, expiry, or recovery.

    Set launch admission and waiting objectives, including fairness. Fixed inventory cannot satisfy every simultaneous request. Queue or reject excess demand clearly. Distinguish an admitted transaction's delay from the buyer's total time waiting for admission and payment.

    22.8.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume 50,000 seats and a short peak of 100,000 reservation attempts/s. At 200 raw bytes each, seat records occupy about 10 MB before indexes.

    The small inventory size hides heavy contention: many callers want the same ownership changes. Assume two-minute holds and a bounded seat count per user. Estimate retries, conflicts, and expiry work separately. This launch scenario is a teaching workload rather than a database benchmark.

    22.8.4 · Naive initial architecture

    Start with a transactional seat table. Change available to reserved conditionally and insert the reservation in the same transaction. Check whether the claim actually affected the seat.

    With a naive read and unconditional write, two buyers can both read available and both report success. The conditional transition makes one winner visible to the other. Once this boundary is correct, address flash demand, payment uncertainty, and expiry races. A faster interface alone would only accelerate the incorrect history.

    22.8.5 · Core API contracts

    POST /reservations includes event, seat identities, and idempotency key. The returned resource gives status and expiry. A payment operation belongs to that reservation; authorised ticket reads expose committed issuance.

    Bind repeat keys to trusted actor and content so a retry returns the earlier result. Distinguish provider authorisation, capture, decline, and uncertainty under its contract. An expired hold and an uncertain payment require different next actions and should remain distinct states.

    22.8.6 · Data model and schema

    A seat stores event and seat identity, state, reservation owner, and version. A reservation stores owner, state, expiry, version, and its seat relationships. Payments and tickets have separate identities.

    Enforce one relevant confirmed active ticket per seat. Expiry and confirmation check current reservation identity and state/version. A delayed expiry task for an old hold must not release a seat acquired by a newer reservation. Use actual constraints or atomic checks to preserve these relationships.

    22.8.7 · Low-level component organization

    SeatRepository owns conditional claims or locks. ReservationService applies selection and hold rules. PaymentWorkflow coordinates external effects, TicketIssuer commits valid issuance, and ExpiryWorker conditionally releases old holds.

    Represent prices and refunds with explicit amounts and units. Put ownership checks at the shared authoritative boundary, where callbacks and workers also pass them. Return enough state to distinguish conflict, expiry, confirmed success, and provider uncertainty.

    22.8.8 · High-level system architecture

    Put bounded admission or a waiting room before the ownership store. Keep durable reservations, a payment adapter, workflow or outbox progress, and ticket reads. Cache event descriptions and advisory seat maps separately.

    Partitioning by event can keep its transactions local, but a popular event can remain hot. Admission and contention controls still matter. The cache suggests what may be available; the transaction establishes what this buyer reserved. They must not become competing allocation authorities.

    22.8.9 · Data and control flows

    Atomically claim seats and create the hold, then return its expiry after commit. Submit payment with a stable provider identity. Confirmation verifies a still-valid transition and commits the required reservation, seat, and ticket changes.

    If payment succeeds after expiry, apply the defined recovery: safely reacquire if current ownership permits, or refund or follow another supported resolution. Never issue against another buyer's seat. Expiry checks current identity and version before release so delayed work cannot undo a later valid state.

    22.8.10 · Capacity estimates

    Suppose launch admission permits 2,000 attempts/s from an offered 100,000/s. The rest wait or are rejected under policy. The 2,000 limit is a configured input to validate, not demonstrated capacity.

    Seat inventory bounds concurrent holds, but does not bound attempts or retries during a two-minute hold. Estimate writes per attempt, duplicate-key checks, conflicts, and expiry scans. Web concurrency may grow rapidly while the same small seat set remains contested.

    22.8.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Suppose the admitted path takes 20 ms at the edge, 30 ms acquiring transaction resources, 40 ms for conditional seat and reservation work, and 20 ms returning the reply. The budget totals 110 ms.

    Contention may exceed it, so bound waiting and stop work that is no longer useful. Measure waiting-room time separately. Payment has another expiry-sensitive timeline. Quick admitted transactions do not establish a quick booking journey for buyers still queued outside allocation.

    22.8.12 · Failure scenarios

    Only one buyer may win after both read available. If reservation commit succeeds but its reply disappears, the repeat key recovers the hold. Repeated payment evidence must not issue another ticket.

    Test late payment and stale expiry after confirmation or reassignment. Conditional transitions and reconciliation handle their overlapping histories. If ticket email fails after issuance commits, the ticket still exists and needs another delivery route. A communication failure must not undo accepted ownership.

    22.8.13 · Scalability improvements

    Cache advisory data, bound admission, and keep the correct seat transaction short. Partition independent events when measured work justifies it.

    Multi-seat claims need an explicit all-or-nothing rule and consistent lock order. Splitting one event across shards complicates group booking, and extra shards do not divide contention for one seat. Scale surrounding work while preserving the atomic owner. Adopt a more complex allocation protocol only for a demonstrated benefit.

    22.8.14 · Consistency requirements

    Seat ownership and ticket issuance need an atomic authoritative rule. Displays may lag if buyers understand their advisory status. Payment and email remain external effects with stable identities and tracked progress.

    A serializable local transaction can protect local concurrency; it does not include a provider automatically. Retry serialization failures through bounded whole-transaction retries with safe external-effect placement. State which records change together and which outcomes are reconciled later.

    22.8.15 · Security model

    Authorise holds, payments, tickets, transfers, and refunds. Calculate prices server-side, verify provider callbacks, protect credentials, and limit automated abuse under a defined identity policy.

    Scope idempotency keys so one actor cannot recover another's result. Give ticket capabilities appropriate scope and lifetime, and audit important changes. A waiting room controls capacity; identity, permissions, and fairness require their own enforcement and tests.

    22.8.16 · Deployment approach

    Keep states and expiry meanings compatible during rollouts. Durable expiry survives worker replacement, and database promotion must respect the acknowledged-data rule.

    After recovery, reconcile provider evidence before declaring bookings resolved. If write authority is uncertain, pausing allocation may preserve exclusivity while descriptions remain readable. Test with live holds and callbacks. An old restored snapshot cannot establish permission to sell seats confirmed after that snapshot.

    22.8.17 · Observability design

    Track admitted attempts, claim conflicts, transaction waits, hold age, expiry backlog, payment uncertainty, late successes, and ticket uniqueness. Follow each logical booking through retries and callbacks.

    Check invariants across seats, holds, and tickets and compare them with payment evidence. Empty error logs cannot prove that the relationships agree. Measure user-visible waiting and completion separately from raw API latency.

    22.8.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Include burst admission, transactions, abandoned holds, payment calls, ticket delivery, retention, telemetry, and recovery capacity. Use the launch's duration rather than applying its peak for the entire month.

    More web workers cannot remove contention on one seat. Compare designs under equal no-double-ticket and recovery requirements using explicit fictional rates or verified prices. Include retry and expiry work even for buyers who abandon purchase.

    22.8.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    Pessimistic locking serialises early and may cause waiting or deadlocks. Optimistic conditional claims produce conflicts that callers must handle clearly. One event owner simplifies order while imposing a capacity boundary.

    Distributed allocation can reduce some central work and complicate group-seat atomicity or fairness. First explain why one buyer wins under the chosen mechanism, then integrate that winner with payment and expiry. Acquiring a lock alone does not finish the booking workflow.

    22.8.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    First implement the seat transaction and repeat-key result. Add durable expiry and payment reconciliation, then launch admission and advisory caching.

    Partition independent events after measurement. Change one-event allocation only when demonstrated limits justify the added protocol. Recheck no-double-ticket behaviour at every stage, including old expiry and retry paths. Additional throughput must preserve the earlier safe ownership decisions.

    22.8.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Check that expiry and confirmation refer to the same current reservation identity and state. Review successful payment after the hold is gone, and verify that displayed availability never grants ownership.

    Test competing buyers, repeated callbacks, commit-then-crash, stale expiry after reassignment, and late payment. A correct happy-path seat update covers only one boundary. The review must explain money and tickets still unresolved after a request ends.

    22.8.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Reproduce the last-seat race using two connections or an explicit interleaving. Let both buyers read available, then demonstrate the incorrect unconditional writes. Replace them with a conditional claim and reservation transaction, checking affected rows.

    Add versioned expiry. Confirm or reassign the seat, then deliver the old expiry task. It must leave the current owner's seat unchanged. Identify the checked identity and version that make this safe, independently of usual task timing.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    with transaction():
    insert_reservation(reservation_id, owner, expires_at)
    updated = reserve_if_available(event, seat, reservation_id)
    if updated != 1: raise SeatUnavailable
# Expiry later releases only the same current reservation version.
# Provider payment is coordinated outside this local transaction.

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.

    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.9

    Payment System

    Prerequisites: API Design and Communication Contracts, Database Internals, Transactions, and Concurrency Control, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows, Reliability, Fault Tolerance, and Disaster Recovery, Security Architecture and Privacy4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A provider charges successfully, but the payment service stops before recording the reply. The client sees a timeout and tries again. How can the service recover the existing charge instead of requesting another logical payment?

    We will give the operation a durable identity, preserve uncertain outcomes, and reconcile provider evidence. We will also connect that evidence to balanced local postings, because a provider result, an order status, and an accounting record describe different parts of the journey.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.9.1 · Functional requirements

    A client creates a payment intent. The service requests authorisation or capture, reports supported outcomes, records balanced accounting entries, and reconciles provider evidence. Refunds have separate operation identities and progress.

    Represent money with currency, integer minor units, and an explicit rounding policy. An order's status, a provider operation, and the ledger are related records, but cannot be replaced by one paid flag. The design must explain their sequence, uncertainty, and accounting consequences.

    22.9.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Preserve financial invariants and auditable state. Prevent duplicate relevant provider effects where its contract permits that guarantee, and resolve uncertainty from evidence rather than inventing success or decline.

    Measure intent acceptance separately from completion. Under the chosen accounting model, each settled amount needs unique balanced postings and authorised corrections. During a provider outage, a durable pending state can be the correct result. Fast unsupported finality would leave an outcome the system cannot explain later.

    22.9.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume one million intents/day, about 11.6/s, and an illustrative 200/s peak. Suppose each initially produces six operational or audit records of 1 kB. That is six million kB, or 6 GB/day raw.

    Ledger details, callbacks, indexes, copies, and retention add storage. Provider concurrency and reconciliation traffic need separate estimates, especially during long waits or recovery. These synthetic assumptions make no claim about actual provider fees or institutional architecture.

    22.9.4 · Naive initial architecture

    A simple service calls a provider, sets an order flag, and replies. If charging succeeds and the process dies before saving the result, a retry may charge again.

    Add a durable operation identity and explicit uncertainty before scaling. Local transactions protect related local changes. Provider keys, status queries, and reconciliation address the gap outside that transaction. Each protects a different part of the history. More instances cannot recover an ambiguous effect for which no stable identity was kept.

    22.9.5 · Core API contracts

    POST /payment-intents accepts amount_minor, currency, business reference, and idempotency key. Status exposes supported states such as pending, authorised, captured, declined, or uncertain. A refund endpoint creates a separately keyed refund.

    Bind keys to actor and financial payload; changed content under an existing key conflicts. Verify provider webhooks instead of trusting client approval fields. Define how clients wait or query uncertainty so a missing reply does not automatically start another financial operation.

    22.9.6 · Data model and schema

    payment_intent and operation records retain actor, key, fingerprint, progress, and result. Provider attempts keep stable keys, references, and outcomes. A verified-event inbox deduplicates evidence.

    Ledger transactions own entries with account, currency, and signed amount. Within each required currency and accounting scope, the signed entries sum to zero: the amount debited is matched by the amount credited. Enforce operation linkage and correction identity. An authorised correction adds a new accounting event rather than rewriting past evidence, keeping the financial history reviewable.

    22.9.7 · Low-level component organization

    PaymentService controls transitions; Money and policy values validate amounts. ProviderAdapter maps explicit outcomes, OperationRepository recognises duplicates, and LedgerService validates and commits postings. Reconciler compares provider evidence; RefundWorkflow tracks refunds.

    These roles can begin inside one application. Map a timeout to uncertainty, not definite decline. Hide protocol details at the adapter while retaining evidence needed for recovery. A useful boundary clarifies meaning and ownership without requiring a network service for every responsibility.

    22.9.8 · High-level system architecture

    Use an authenticated API, durable intent and operation storage, bounded provider workers, verified callbacks, a ledger boundary, and scheduled reconciliation. Commit any required downstream publication intent with the relevant local change.

    Reserve reconciliation capacity so it can repair uncertainty during incidents. Regional serving must preserve provider-operation and ledger authority. Draw provider calls outside the local transaction boundary: this makes the external gap and its recovery path visible.

    22.9.9 · Data and control flows

    Commit intent and logical operation identity, then submit its stable provider key. Record supported evidence or uncertainty. Capture or settlement evidence drives an idempotent transition that creates the required balanced postings once.

    Callbacks can precede the synchronous reply, so valid transitions must handle either order without regressing. Reconciliation queries the stable reference and repairs discrepancies. A local pending row is not permission to resend blindly. Trace each evidence and commit boundary to identify what a crash can leave unresolved.

    22.9.10 · Capacity estimates

    At a stable 200 provider calls/s and an assumed average 500 ms wait, Little's Law gives 200 × 0.5 = 100 in-flight calls within that boundary.

    This estimates average occupancy, not a safe pool size. Account for variance, deadlines, provider limits, and failures. Initial records add 6 GB/day raw. Callbacks and reconciliation continue after request traffic subsides, so they need their own capacity instead of only the daily-average allowance.

    22.9.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Suppose ingress takes 20 ms, intent commit 20 ms, provider work 500 ms, and final local update 20 ms. The successful synchronous budget totals 560 ms.

    Returning durable pending after about 40 ms is a different contract with later completion. Neither sum establishes p99. A timeout calls for status recovery or reconciliation; it does not establish that no payment occurred. Measure acceptance and final resolution separately.

    22.9.12 · Failure scenarios

    Test lost replies after local commit, provider execution followed by process loss, reordered or repeated callbacks, uncertain refunds, and posting-commit failure.

    Keep unknown outcomes and repeat only through a supported safe identity or established evidence. If the ledger is unavailable, setting paid bypasses a required boundary rather than repairing it. Recovery must account for provider state and required postings before declaring the operation resolved. A restarted healthy API does not establish agreement between those histories.

    22.9.13 · Scalability improvements

    Scale independent acceptance and workers while bounding provider concurrency and preserving per-payment and relevant per-account invariants. Isolate enough reconciliation capacity to repair uncertain operations during trouble.

    Read projections can expose status under a stated freshness rule. Ledger partitioning requires an explicit balancing and transaction scope; a hot account may remain concentrated. Partition only for a demonstrated bottleneck, since additional ownership boundaries also add recovery work.

    22.9.14 · Consistency requirements

    Local deduplication, payment transitions, and required postings need suitable atomic boundaries. The provider remains outside them and requires its own identity and recovery contract.

    Uniqueness and transactions can establish one local posting set without proving one provider execution. Refunds have independent state and may not reverse timing, fees, or downstream consequences perfectly. Define the evidence for each accepted result and retain uncertainty until a valid final transition is supported.

    22.9.15 · Security model

    Authorise payments and refunds, validate amounts server-side, verify callbacks, and protect credentials. Avoid retaining unnecessary sensitive data through an appropriately reviewed provider integration or tokenisation arrangement.

    Restrict and audit privileged corrections. Operators need explicit authority and must not silently rewrite accounting history. Scope effects and queries to tenant and account. Preserve useful identity and outcomes in logs without secrets. These controls do not by themselves assert any financial or legal compliance status.

    22.9.16 · Deployment approach

    Evolve states and event formats compatibly, retain operation identities during releases and recovery, and control provider configuration and key changes.

    An old restore may forget keys for effects already executed externally. Establish replay protection and reconcile before resubmission. Test delayed callbacks from earlier releases and recovery after outages. Restored pending rows must be compared with provider evidence before being treated as untouched work.

    22.9.17 · Observability design

    Separate acceptance and completion delay. Track age of pending and uncertain work, attempts, duplicate events, callback verification, imbalances, unmatched settlements, refunds, and reconciliation outcomes.

    Alert on invariant violations and old unresolved money movement even when HTTP success is high. Evidence must distinguish attempted, provider-accepted, and locally posted states. Stable identities let an investigator reconstruct those stages without treating one response or log line as proof of the entire journey.

    22.9.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Include provider attempts, secure storage, ledger work, retained audit evidence, telemetry, reconciliation, and operations. Use symbolic fees or labelled hypothetical inputs unless prices are verified.

    Compare cost per reconciled successful business payment as well as per HTTP attempt. Retries can increase attempts while useful outcomes decline. Designs must preserve the same financial invariants; an inexpensive system that cannot explain uncertain charges fails a required part of the service.

    22.9.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    Synchronous completion may suit clients expecting immediate results and exposes provider waits. Asynchronous intents make pending progress explicit while adding workflow state.

    A local transactional application simplifies related invariants. Separating provider and ledger services may improve ownership or isolation and adds coordination. Append-only accounting history can coexist with mutable status projections. Compare boundaries by the work and recovery they clarify instead of forcing one paid record to serve every purpose.

    22.9.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    Start with explicit states, currency-aware integer amounts, local transactions, and stable provider identity. Add durable callbacks and reconciliation before multiplying traffic paths.

    Then introduce projections and bounded workers for measured needs. Partition only where a demonstrated limit justifies a preserved invariant boundary. Earlier payments must remain explainable through evidence and postings after topology changes. Increased capacity must retain that historical meaning.

    22.9.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Ask what evidence establishes financial success, who commits the postings, and how recovery handles an older deduplication snapshot beside newer external effects.

    Test charge-then-crash, callback-before-reply, duplicate evidence, partial refunds, and earlier-state restore. Check for one valid local posting set and explicit unresolved state where evidence is missing. A timeout cannot be turned into decline merely to make the request path appear complete.

    22.9.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Build a synthetic provider that remembers stable keys and a local ledger accepting only balanced entries. Stop after provider execution and before recording the local result.

    Reconcile by key and verify that one logical operation produces one balanced posting set. Replay its event and reject changed financial content under the old key. Explain that the test demonstrates this synthetic provider contract and local boundary, rather than a guarantee about arbitrary real providers.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    def apply_settlement(event):
    with transaction():
        if inbox_contains(event.id): return prior_outcome(event.id)
        payment = lock_payment(event.payment_id)
        validate_transition_and_amount(payment, event)
        entries = [debit_entry(event), credit_entry(event)]
        require_balanced_by_currency(entries)
        insert_unique_posting_set(event.operation_id, entries)
        update_payment_and_insert_inbox(payment, event)
# Provider execution is reconciled separately from this transaction.

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.

    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.10

    Distributed Job Scheduler

    Prerequisites: Runtime, Processes, Threads, and Concurrency, Replication, Leader Election, and Consensus, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows, Reliability, Fault Tolerance, and Disaster Recovery4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A worker pauses while running a scheduled job. Its lease expires, so a replacement begins. When the first worker resumes, both may be capable of doing work even though only one currently owns the attempt.

    We will give the schedule, occurrence, attempt, and effect separate identities. This lets recovery recognise what it is resuming and shows why rejecting an old local completion is only one part of protecting an external effect.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.10.1 · Functional requirements

    A user creates a schedule, the service identifies due occurrences, and workers execute jobs. Users inspect history, configure retries, and cancel supported future work.

    Define fixed times versus intervals, timezone handling, missed runs, and overlap. One schedule can produce many occurrences; retrying an occurrence must not invent another logical run for the same due time. Establish this timing meaning before choosing a timer or queue.

    22.10.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Keep accepted schedules and required runs recoverable under supported failures. Bound scheduling delay and prevent superseded attempts from overwriting newer results. Execution may start repeatedly around failure, so effects need suitable identity or enforced fencing.

    Define cancellation's boundary. Stopping future dispatch, cancelling pending work, and attempting to interrupt a running effect are different promises. A local cancellation flag does not establish that a remote effect was undone. Run status must preserve this distinction.

    22.10.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume one million schedules produce 100,000 occurrences/hour. Dividing by 3,600 gives about 27.8 runs/s. At an initial 2 kB of state per run, raw growth is 200 MB/hour.

    With ten-second average execution at a stable rate, average active work is 27.8 × 10, or about 278 runs. Top-of-hour bursts, long jobs, retries, and retention add requirements. Saved-schedule count alone does not describe the concentration of due work.

    22.10.4 · Naive initial architecture

    One process scans due schedules and launches local functions. If it saves a run and advances the schedule in separate commits, a crash between them can repeat or miss an occurrence.

    Create a stable occurrence record and advance due state in one transaction. A leader can simplify scanning, but leadership alone does not make worker effects occur once. First establish durable identity and atomic progress. Adding another process to the unsafe loop merely creates more opportunities for the same failure.

    22.10.5 · Core API contracts

    POST /schedules accepts timing, timezone, payload reference, retry rules, and overlap policy. Cancellation changes documented future behaviour. GET /runs/{id} reports attempts and outcome. A run-once operation has its own idempotency identity.

    Bound timing-expression and payload complexity. Return durable acceptance separately from execution completion. If an external effect is unresolved, report uncertainty. A worker's missing reply does not prove that its effect never happened.

    22.10.6 · Data model and schema

    A schedule stores id, version, next_due, timing policy, and state. A run binds unique (schedule_id,occurrence) to input version and progress. Attempts contain epoch, lease deadline, worker, and result. Retain original due time separately from dispatch time.

    An epoch numbers successive owners so completion can reject an old attempt. Another attempt still belongs to the same logical run. Outbox and effect records retain durable dispatch and external identities where needed.

    22.10.7 · Low-level component organization

    ScheduleParser and TimePolicy calculate occurrences. DueScanner locates candidates. RunRepository saves the run and next_due atomically. Dispatcher routes work, LeaseManager grants attempts, and WorkerAdapter executes them. Reconciler finds stuck or uncertain outcomes.

    The scheduler decides when work is due; a worker acts under a current bounded claim. Each effect adapter needs explicit repetition or fencing semantics. This separation lets tests examine time calculations without accidentally performing an irreversible external operation.

    22.10.8 · High-level system architecture

    Keep durable schedules, coordinated scanners or partition owners, dispatch records, bounded workers, attempt state, and reconciliation. Store large versioned payloads separately rather than copying them into each retry message.

    Timing control and execution have different capacity and failure paths. A control-plane outage may delay new dispatch while existing jobs continue. Worker loss must leave a recoverable run. A queue attached to a cron loop does not supply these behaviours without durable state and ownership rules.

    22.10.9 · Data and control flows

    A scanner claims due state, creates the unique occurrence and dispatch intent, advances next_due, and commits. A worker then claims an attempt epoch and executes under the stable run identity. It renews its lease where supported and completes only while current.

    After expiry, a replacement may take over. The old worker may still resume, so effect-side identity or fencing must limit harmful stale actions. Reconcile runs without an acceptable terminal state. Starting a callback is an intermediate event, rather than the end of the durable history.

    22.10.10 · Capacity estimates

    At about 27.8 runs/s with ten-second average execution, average concurrency is roughly 278. If each worker sustains four independent I/O jobs, 278 / 4 is about 69.5: roughly seventy workers before headroom and other limits.

    CPU-heavy jobs require measured compute capacity instead. Estimate burst concentration, retries, and outage catch-up. A steady-state average cannot establish that the same worker count meets start-time objectives during a large due-time burst.

    22.10.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Scheduling delay runs from due time to dispatch or start. Runtime begins after execution starts. As an illustrative target, require 95% of eligible runs to start within five seconds under supported load.

    Scan intervals, claims, queues, cold starts, and concurrency limits consume that budget. A ten-minute task can meet a five-second start target. Give completion deadlines a separate rule and measure both when required, rather than combining all durations into an ambiguous job-latency figure.

    22.10.12 · Failure scenarios

    Test interruption between occurrence creation and schedule advancement; the transaction must leave both committed or neither. Then pause a worker past its lease so it overlaps a replacement. The current-epoch check must reject the resumed worker's local completion.

    This does not undo external effects already accepted. Those require effect-side protection and reconciliation. Also define clock changes, timezone transitions, malformed input, and poison-job handling. Correct due-time arithmetic alone does not establish safe repeated execution.

    22.10.13 · Scalability improvements

    Index due time, claim bounded batches, and partition schedules with stable ownership when scanning is limiting. Scale workers according to measured CPU, memory, and I/O demands.

    Separate long, priority, and CPU-heavy work where necessary. Bound catch-up so overdue runs do not starve current critical work. Removing a global lock must preserve atomic occurrence creation through another valid mechanism. Lower contention is useful only if it retains the logical-run invariant.

    22.10.14 · Consistency requirements

    Creating an occurrence and advancing the schedule require uniqueness and atomicity. Worker delivery can repeat. Current-epoch completion protects local progress, while effect identity or resource-enforced fencing protects the relevant external effect.

    A lease is permission valid for an interval; it does not stop a paused process from resuming. It therefore cannot alone guarantee one execution. With fencing, the protected resource recognises current authority and rejects requests carrying stale epochs; the receiver must actually enforce that rule. Define missed-run and overlap policies so incidental timing does not decide which logical runs exist. Schedule, occurrence, attempt, and effect are distinct scopes.

    22.10.15 · Security model

    Authorise schedule ownership, payload references, run views, and cancellation. Support validated work types rather than arbitrary code or unrestricted URLs supplied through the API.

    Bind each run to tenant and immutable input. Give workers only required capabilities and audit administration. A broad administrator credential in every worker makes one compromised job unnecessarily powerful. Follow permission from schedule through task to the actual resource used by execution.

    22.10.16 · Deployment approach

    Keep schedule and run formats compatible during rollout, including epoch and lease meanings. Drain new claims and save progress before shutdown. During recovery, compare queues with authoritative runs.

    An older restored schedule table may lag effects already executed externally. Recover stable occurrence identity and evidence before replaying. Test control-plane loss separately from worker loss. Restarting scans must restore the meaning of due work and prior outcomes, rather than merely resume timer activity.

    22.10.17 · Observability design

    Measure due-to-dispatch and due-to-start delay, oldest eligible work, repeated attempts, lease expiry, stale-completion rejection, retries, duration, and tenant fairness. Verify that one occurrence maps to one logical run.

    CPU may remain low when a broken scanner creates no work. Monitor generation and progress directly, alerting on accepted jobs that stop advancing. Detailed histories must distinguish runs from attempts so operational repetition is not confused with new scheduled demand.

    22.10.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Include scanning, indexes, history, dispatch, execution, spare capacity, external calls, and recovery. At 2 kB/run and 100,000 runs/hour, raw daily history is 200 MB/hour × 24 = 4.8 GB before attempts and indexes.

    Compare scan frequency and batching against the start-delay requirement. Use explicit rates and include catch-up and idle headroom. A lower cost obtained by silently missing occurrences does not satisfy the same service contract.

    22.10.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    Polling an indexed due-time field is simple and recoverable. Timer wheels and delayed-message facilities may improve some timing workloads, provided they can be durably reconstructed. Central scanning simplifies authority; partitioned scanning adds coordination while dividing work.

    Long-lived workers reduce startup cost. Managed invocation may fit bursts under different limits. Compare timing precision, duration, recovery, and effects. A fast timer data structure solves due lookup, leaving occurrence and attempt semantics to the rest of the design.

    22.10.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    Begin with deterministic time policy and atomic occurrence creation. Add durable dispatch and bounded execution. Introduce leases and epochs together with safe effect identity before claiming supported worker takeover.

    Partition whichever scan or execution path measurements identify. Regional ownership needs transfer and partition rules for due work. Preserve identities throughout, so replacements do not reinterpret retries as new occurrences or lose the evidence needed to resolve older runs.

    22.10.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Review occurrence identity, next_due atomicity, stale workers, cancellation, and recovery from older state. Each can leave a different gap.

    Run competing scanners at commit boundaries, pause a worker past expiry, cancel during execution, cross a timezone transition, and recover after a long outage. Check which runs should exist and which effects remain uncertain. One on-time callback demonstrates timing for one run, rather than the scheduler's full recovery contract.

    22.10.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Use an injected clock and transactional run table. Start two scanners for the same due occurrence and verify that they establish one logical run.

    Pause an epoch-7 attempt, replace it with epoch 8, and submit the old completion. The local store must reject it. Identify the stable key or receiver-enforced fencing still needed for an external effect. The exercise demonstrates local progress protection without claiming that the job physically executes only once.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    with transaction():
    schedule = claim_due_schedule(now)
    run = insert_unique_run(schedule.id, schedule.next_due)
    insert_dispatch_outbox(run.id)
    advance_next_due(schedule)
# Worker completion compares the current attempt epoch atomically.
# A stale worker's external effects need resource-side protection.

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.

    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.11

    Collaborative Document Editor

    Prerequisites: Networking Foundations for System Design, Distributed Systems Fundamentals, Replication, Leader Election, and Consensus, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    Two collaborators insert text at the same place. One replica receives X and then Y; the other receives Y and then X. If each simply applies arrival order, their documents may differ.

    We will define what an edit means and how its identity and context survive repeated delivery and reconnects. We will then examine the separate questions of durable acceptance, safe history cleanup, and permission to keep editing.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.11.1 · Functional requirements

    Collaborators create a document, edit together, reconnect after disconnection, recover required history, and export or delete under access rules.

    First choose the document model. Plain text, structured rich text, and embedded objects have different valid operations and conflicts. Define those operations before selecting their transport. Cursor positions and presence are temporary hints, separate from durable content and its history.

    22.11.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Preserve acknowledged operations and enforce a defined access-revocation policy. Online editing should respond locally and meet a supported synchronization-delay objective.

    The protocol must converge under its assumptions, but equal final strings alone do not establish intended edits, Unicode correctness, or structural validity. A returning offline user may have lost access. Decide how unaccepted edits are rejected or presented, and distinguish them from accepted history. Optimistic local display is not a durable acknowledgment.

    22.11.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume 100,000 active documents, with 10,000 edited simultaneously by three users each. At two operations/s per user, ingestion is 10,000 × 3 × 2 = 60,000 operations/s.

    At 200 retained bytes each, this is 12 MB/s, or 1.0368 TB/day if sustained throughout the day. Actual activity duration, batching, snapshots, metadata, fan-out, and retention change the estimate. Peak concurrency must not silently become a full-day assumption in a real storage plan.

    22.11.4 · Naive initial architecture

    Start with whole-document updates carrying an expected version. If two writers replace the same version, one succeeds and the other conflicts. This is a clear simple contract, but awkward for continuous collaboration.

    An operation-based protocol handles smaller edits and their concurrency. Use a reviewed operational transformation (OT) or conflict-free replicated data type (CRDT) model suited to the document structure. Arbitrary patches applied by arrival order are insufficient: operation meaning, context, identity, and reconnect rules must work together.

    22.11.5 · Core API contracts

    Creation returns document identity. Sync messages carry document and replica identities, stable operation IDs, known progress, and protocol version. Snapshots return a versioned base and specify the history they already cover.

    Authorise exports and membership changes separately. Prevent clients from impersonating another replica. Define acknowledgments and reconnect so each edit is recognisably accepted, pending, or rejected. A successful connection handshake does not authorise every later edit or export.

    22.11.6 · Data model and schema

    Store owner, protocol version, membership, accepted operation IDs, ordering or causal context, and snapshots with covered positions. Compaction metadata records what can safely be retired.

    Sequence CRDTs need stable element IDs and ordering rules. OT needs transformation context for its supported offline interval. A snapshot must identify already included operations; otherwise, a receiver may omit or repeat work even when snapshot and log files are each intact.

    22.11.7 · Low-level component organization

    DocumentService owns identity and membership. SyncCoordinator validates protocol use, EditModel applies its rules, and OperationLog persists acceptance. SnapshotBuilder produces recovery bases; Compactor retires only permitted history. Presence uses a temporary path.

    Keep the deterministic edit core apart from rendering and transport. Tests can then deliver the same operations in controlled orders. Expose durable progress explicitly, so a gateway reply is not mistaken for a committed edit.

    22.11.8 · High-level system architecture

    Use authenticated gateways, client replicas, durable operation storage, snapshots, and the ordering or merge arrangement required by the selected algorithm.

    OT commonly uses ordered server context and transformation. CRDT approaches rely on their defined identities and merge rules. These families cannot be substituted as labels on an otherwise undefined box. Select a supported protocol per document version and plan transitions. Gateway replacement must preserve its required history and context.

    22.11.9 · Data and control flows

    A client applies an allowed edit locally and assigns a stable identity. The server checks access and protocol context, saves accepted work, then distributes and acknowledges it according to the contract.

    Reconnect exchanges missing operations or a compatible snapshot and continuation. Recognise repeats by identity and surface rejected offline changes explicitly. This sequence preserves local responsiveness while giving durable acceptance and access decisions their own boundaries. It also tells users which visible work still needs synchronization.

    22.11.10 · Capacity estimates

    The assumed 60,000 operations/s at 200 bytes produces 12 MB/s raw history. Fan-out and extra copies multiply the work. One popular document may concentrate transformation, merge metadata, and gateway traffic despite many cold documents elsewhere.

    Snapshots reduce replay work in exchange for storage and background compute. Measure batching, document size, offline duration, and tombstone growth. Tombstones retain information about deleted elements where the protocol still needs their identities. Size the hot editor separately from the average.

    22.11.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Local optimistic editing can update the screen before a round trip while indicating unsynchronised work. Suppose ingress takes 30 ms, durable acceptance 20 ms, and peer delivery 50 ms. The proposed sync path totals 100 ms before additional waiting.

    Measure p99 separately. Distance, disconnection, and large documents alter the path. Track pending duration as well as frame responsiveness: a smooth local screen does not prove an edit survives loss of that client.

    22.11.12 · Failure scenarios

    Concurrent inserts need a deterministic interpretation, and repeated delivery must not add a character twice. Missing context, unsafe compaction, and incompatible snapshots can break reconnect even after ordinary online editing works.

    Test stale membership and expensive malformed operations too. Keep enough privacy-safe failing-history context to reproduce interleavings. A brief convergence demonstration does not cover long partitions or retired metadata. Recovery assumptions must match the offline behaviour advertised to users.

    22.11.13 · Scalability improvements

    Distribute independent documents, batch suitable operations, bound gateway buffers, and use snapshots to shorten replay. A single hot document may need its own coordination and fan-out design rather than another ordinary hash partition.

    Compaction must retain context for the supported offline and merge horizon. An apparently unused old identifier can still anchor a returning operation. Scale cursor updates separately from durable edits, since their retention and correctness requirements differ even over one connection.

    22.11.14 · Consistency requirements

    OT transforms an operation against relevant concurrent operations. For example, an insertion before a later edit can shift that edit's position; the transform must use the correct ordered context. A sequence CRDT can instead name stable elements and define a shared order for concurrent insertions after the same element.

    If X and Y are inserted after one element, replicas need compatible identities and tie-breaking rules to produce the same sequence despite opposite arrival orders. Neither family automatically specifies rich text, undo, or user intent. Access and durable acknowledgment are additional properties. Select and test an actual algorithm with explicit assumptions.

    22.11.15 · Security model

    Authorise sync sessions and individual operations under the revocation policy. Long-lived connections and returning offline clients require checks at later boundaries. Protect exports and snapshots too.

    Validate protocol inputs and avoid content leaks through presence or logs. End-to-end encryption changes server search, validation, retention, and revocation possibilities; design those consequences when required. TLS protects transport, but does not itself provide that document-level guarantee.

    22.11.16 · Deployment approach

    Negotiate protocol versions and keep accepted history interpretable. Never reuse an operation identity with silently changed meaning. Gateway replacement must rely on durable recovery, rather than one client's memory.

    Validate snapshots before retiring source history and test restoration from saved artifacts. Protocol migration and rollback affect stored documents and offline context as well as code. An older executable that misinterprets accepted operations can damage content that remains durably stored.

    22.11.17 · Observability design

    Measure pending and accepted edits, sync delay, duplicate recognition, reconnect gaps, snapshot age, replay time, compaction growth, protocol rejection, and access denial.

    Keep reproducible histories for failing interleavings and test convergence alongside permission and structural validity. User pending duration can reveal harm hidden by gateway latency. Use limited diagnostic artifacts and privacy-safe identities instead of copying private documents into routine traces.

    22.11.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Include history, snapshots, connections, fan-out, protocol compute, compaction, and telemetry. Replace sustained-rate arithmetic with measured activity durations when estimating expenditure.

    Longer offline support can require more context and metadata. Compare designs at an equal recovery horizon. Deleting information still needed by returning clients changes the contract. Storage savings therefore need a valid compaction rule, rather than an arbitrary age threshold.

    22.11.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    Whole-document versions suit limited collaboration with explicit conflicts. OT supports particular transformation and ordering models. CRDTs provide specified merges with identity, metadata, and cleanup costs.

    A tested editing library may be preferable to a custom algorithm. Evaluate Unicode graphemes, selections, undo, rich-text structure, and offline context as well as final convergence. Choose a complete model the team can verify and maintain; no family supplies every editing behaviour automatically.

    22.11.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    Begin with versioned documents and clear conflicts. Add a tested operation model, durable log, and reconnect. Introduce snapshots and justified compaction, then distribute independent documents.

    Isolate hot workloads and add regional or offline merging only under supported protocol assumptions. Preserve identities, access rules, and deterministic regression histories. Each stage must retain the meaning of accepted edits and the context older supported clients need for recovery.

    22.11.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Review convergence, supported offline duration, history retirement, and revocation. Deliver concurrent inserts in opposite orders, repeat a delete, lose an acknowledgment, and reconnect using an old snapshot plus later operations.

    Reconnect a revoked user and check document structure separately. Equal strings may conceal forbidden edits or invalid structure. Name the protocol and assumptions supporting each claim, rather than treating the final string comparison as complete validation.

    22.11.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Implement a miniature merge of two insertions with stable IDs and an explicit tie-break rule. Deliver both orders and repeat each operation. Verify equal final sequences with no duplicate insertion.

    State the exercise's limit: it is not a complete rich-text CRDT. Add snapshot-context and revoked-client checks to expose distinct recovery and access boundaries. The example demonstrates identity and deterministic ordering without claiming production-editor correctness from two operations.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    def receive(operation, document):
    with transaction():
        current = lock_document(document.id)
        require_authorized(operation.actor, current)
        require_protocol_version(operation, current)
        if log.contains(operation.id): return prior_ack(operation.id)
        next_state = edit_model.apply(current.state, operation)
        append_unique_operation(operation)
        commit_state_and_progress(current, next_state)
    return durable_ack(operation.id)
# The edit model must implement a specified, tested algorithm.

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.
