    PART 6 / UNIT 22 / CHAPTER 22.12

    Large-Scale Document Processing Platform

    Prerequisites: File Systems, Search Infrastructure, and Data Pipelines, Message Queues, Events, and Distributed Workflows, Reliability, Fault Tolerance, and Disaster Recovery, Security Architecture and Privacy, Observability, Monitoring, and Incident Engineering, Deployment, Cloud Infrastructure, and Platform Architecture4 original figures
    Blue: normal flowGreen: healthyAmber: cautionRed: failurePurple: control / shared infrastructureGray: external / inactiveSolid arrow: labeled action · dashed: dependency or boundary · dotted: acknowledgment where labeled. Snapshot cards compare stated observations; they do not imply network calls.

    A document has finished extraction, but some fields are uncertain and need review. Meanwhile, its owner requests deletion. A worker's finished flag cannot explain what may now be published.

    We will trace immutable input through extraction, validation, human decisions, and publication. The workflow must keep those stages recoverable, preserve the source of every result, and reject stale work after its authority or document has been withdrawn.

    The workload, timing, and prices in this design are teaching assumptions. They are not measured benchmarks or a description of a particular company.

    22.12.1 · Functional requirements

    A tenant uploads a document. The platform classifies it, extracts fields, sends uncertain results to review, and publishes validated output for authorised search or export. Users inspect progress, correct results, reprocess versions, and request deletion.

    Upload success establishes accepted bytes under the upload contract. Extraction, review, and publication remain separate work. Give each stage a visible state so users can tell which output is usable and what remains unresolved.

    22.12.2 · Nonfunctional requirements

    Preserve accepted inputs and required workflow progress under selected failures. Results identify exact source and pipeline versions. Protect tenant data and set processing-age objectives for supported inputs.

    Uncertain extraction must not silently become verified fact. Human decisions need durable actor and rationale information. Search has its own publication delay and permissions. Complete therefore means usable, traceable, permitted output, rather than merely a worker finishing without an exception.

    22.12.3 · Explicit assumptions and workload numbers

    Assume one million files/day averaging 2 MB, giving 2 TB/day raw input. Average arrival is about 11.6 files/s; a tenfold peak is about 116/s.

    At an illustrative five CPU-seconds/file, extraction consumes five million CPU-seconds/day. Dividing by 3,600 gives about 1,389 CPU-hours. Classification, I/O, retries, and review add work or delay. Measure actual files and model behaviour; these are accounting assumptions rather than extraction throughput or accuracy results.

    22.12.4 · Naive initial architecture

    A prototype saves a file and extracts it within the upload request. Difficult files lengthen the request, process loss can erase progress, and human review has no natural durable waiting point.

    Separate resumable byte ingestion from durable stages. Keep immutable source versions and identified outputs so retries and corrections retain evidence about earlier results. This fixes a concrete lifecycle and recovery problem before more workers are introduced for capacity.

    22.12.5 · Core API contracts

    POST /documents creates an upload intent; completion verifies stored bytes. Status exposes stages, while field reads return versioned values and provenance. Review decisions, reprocessing, and tracked deletion have separate operations.

    Search and export expose only authorised published output. Distinguish deletion acceptance from full cleanup. Define which version reprocessing creates: a new pipeline must not silently reinterpret old output under the same identity.

    22.12.6 · Data model and schema

    A document binds tenant, source version, digest, and state. Upload sessions track bytes. Workflows name input and pipeline versions; attempts carry epochs. Artifacts carry kind, version, and object reference. Fields retain value, confidence, source region, and extractor identity.

    Review records identify decision, actor, and version. Track publication and deletion progress, preserving tenant and version scope in keys. Retain sufficient provenance under an explicit lifecycle rather than keeping every raw intermediate forever.

    22.12.7 · Low-level component organization

    UploadService and ContentValidator check ingestion. WorkflowCoordinator owns stages. Versioned Classifier and Extractor adapters generate results; ProvenanceRecorder links evidence. ReviewPolicy selects review, ReviewService records decisions, and Publisher creates permitted projections. Reconciler repairs stuck or orphaned work.

    Workers receive limited capabilities and cannot change tenant because a message supplies another tenant field. Keep generation of model output separate from deciding whether it is valid, reviewed, and ready to publish.

    22.12.8 · High-level system architecture

    Use immutable object storage, durable relational workflow metadata, task delivery, bounded isolated compute or model workers, review interfaces, and a search projection. Scoped storage carries bulk bytes; metadata controls progress.

    A document waiting hours for review must release its compute slot and database transaction. Durable workflow state survives without an attached process. Link sources, artifacts, decisions, and publication generations so a failure can be investigated and repaired across those components.

    22.12.9 · Data and control flows

    Verify upload identity and digest, create a stable workflow, classify and extract, then validate structure and meaning. Save evidence and either publish or request review. A review decision creates a new validated version and publication intent.

    Each stage completes conditionally under its current epoch. Reprocessing creates a new run over identified input while retaining earlier provenance. Deletion blocks inappropriate later publication. These persisted conditions protect local progress even when attempts repeat or an old worker resumes.

    22.12.10 · Capacity estimates

    Thirty days at 2 TB/day requires 60 TB of input before copies. Five million CPU-seconds/day divided by 86,400 gives about 57.9 continuously busy cores. At 60% target utilisation, 57.9 / 0.6 gives about 96.5 cores before other work and failure margin.

    A tenfold arrival peak exceeds the average arrival rate. Its duration, queue age, scaling delay, and admission determine whether objectives hold. Include large-file and model-memory distributions rather than treating every document as average-sized.

    22.12.11 · End-to-end latency estimates

    Upload transfer and durable acceptance have one timeline. Automated work adds queueing, classification, extraction, validation, and publication; human review creates a separate wait.

    Suppose queueing takes two seconds, classification one, extraction five, and validation/publication one. The automated path totals nine seconds in this model. These are assumptions to test. Report current stage and age so users can distinguish computation from a pending human decision.

    22.12.12 · Failure scenarios

    Incomplete uploads, hostile or corrupt files, and crashes after artifact write need different repairs. Repeated tasks, stale attempts, invalid output, concurrent reviews, and missing provenance can each damage another boundary.

    Use stable artifact identity and conditional transitions. Quarantine unsupported output with a reason, and test deletion during processing. A finished label with missing, forbidden, or unexplained output still fails the business requirement even when workers report no exception.

    22.12.13 · Scalability improvements

    Transfer bulk bytes directly through storage and scale independent extraction with bounded workers. Partition metadata by a justified tenant or workflow key, accounting for hot tenants and large files.

    Test batching and model-memory limits explicitly. More workers can saturate storage or an external model. Reserve separate replay and backfill capacity so upgrades do not starve live inputs or deletion. Expand the stage limiting useful output rather than multiplying every worker equally.

    22.12.14 · Consistency requirements

    Source versions are immutable. Related workflow and review changes need suitable atomic transitions. Artifacts identify their input and transform; repeats use stable output identity and current-epoch completion.

    Search may lag publication while preserving access rules. External model calls can be uncertain or nondeterministic. Retain relevant requests and version information, validate results, and state the actual reproducibility boundary. A recorded model name alone does not establish that a later run produces the same answer.

    22.12.15 · Security model

    Enforce tenant scope on objects, tasks, review, search, export, and audit. Bound worker resources and egress, validate supported files, and keep private data and credentials out of routine telemetry.

    Treat extracted text as untrusted content rather than infrastructure instructions. Reviewers need scoped access and traceable decisions. Deletion covers sensitive derived output as well as input bytes. Follow permission through every stage that reads, transforms, or republishes the document.

    22.12.16 · Deployment approach

    Version pipelines and schemas compatibly. Evaluate models on authorised samples or controlled cohorts before replacing output, and retain a usable earlier generation until the transition is verified. Drain workers through durable attempts.

    Restore exercises must reconnect objects, workflow state, decisions, and deletion history. Metadata-only restoration can leave missing artifacts or revive obsolete publication. Test the recovered journey before treating the platform as usable again.

    22.12.17 · Observability design

    Measure accepted bytes, stage waits, compute, retries, stale-completion rejection, invalid output, review age, provenance completeness, publication lag, tenant denial, and deletion progress.

    Confidence is not measured accuracy. Use an appropriate labelled evaluation for quality claims. Link source, run, attempt, model, artifact, and reviewer through privacy-safe evidence. This reveals whether a particular result is usable and where it stopped, beyond showing that workers are busy.

    22.12.18 · Infrastructure cost considerations

    Include source and derived storage, compute or model calls, retries, review labour, search, transfer, telemetry, and recovery. Five million CPU-seconds/day describes compute; review may dominate operating cost.

    Use explicit unit rates and a stated review fraction. Avoid invented accuracy or throughput figures. Compare equal provenance, access, quality, and recovery requirements, since removing review or history may lower cost while changing the output users require.

    22.12.19 · Alternative architectures and trade-offs

    Synchronous extraction fits a tiny demonstration while coupling upload to model delay and failure. Durable stages add metadata and operations but support recovery and human waits. Batching may improve resource use while adding delay and memory demand.

    Managed models or workflows delegate selected duties without automatically providing validation, provenance, tenant isolation, or review policy. Compare the complete output and recovery contract. Choose the smallest arrangement that supports those needs for the intended workload.

    22.12.20 · Architecture evolution from small scale to large scale

    Start with immutable upload and explicit status. Add durable stages and stable artifacts before increasing concurrency. Give provenance and human decisions identities from the beginning.

    Then grow storage and workers independently and introduce authorised search and versioned reprocessing. Regional placement needs a named locality or recovery requirement and compatible lifecycle rules. Earlier results must stay explainable, and old work must continue to respect current access and deletion decisions.

    22.12.21 · Design review identifying weaknesses and improvements

    Check whether a stage can silently change its input version, whether a superseded attempt can publish after deletion, and how reprocessing preserves human decisions.

    Test task repeats, artifact-write interruption, invalid output, concurrent reviews, stale completion, missing objects, index lag, and full restoration. A few correct extracted fields cannot establish recoverable progress and provenance. Review the connected lifecycle, including rejection, review, and deletion outcomes.

    22.12.22 · A short implementation exercise

    Implement three stages with immutable input identity, result version, and attempt epoch. Stop after writing an artifact but before recording completion. Replay it without duplicating the established output.

    Add a review state that releases compute while waiting. Pause an old worker, delete the document, then submit its completion. Publication must stay blocked by the authoritative current-state condition. Explain how that persisted check prevents stale work from reversing deletion, independently of whether cancellation reached the worker.

    A small implementation of the key rule

    PSEUDOCODE · ONE PART OF THE DESIGN

    def complete_stage(run, epoch, artifact):
    require(artifact.input_version == run.input_version)
    validate_output_schema_and_provenance(artifact)
    with transaction():
        current = lock_workflow(run.id)
        require(current.epoch == epoch and not current.deleted)
        insert_artifact_once(run.id, artifact.version, artifact)
        advance_or_request_review(current, artifact)
        insert_next_stage_outbox_if_needed(current)
# Retry reuses identities; old attempts cannot publish new state.

    Use the implementation exercise to test the rule and the failure described above. You can also run local examples of seat claims, duplicate handling, ledger balance, and workflow epochs in the mechanism collection.

    Unit 1 · Introduction to System Design

    UNIT 01 / C1

    A program adds a task to a dictionary and displays “Saved.” What can it do while running, and what happens when it starts with a new dictionary?

    While the program runs, it can list and update the task in that dictionary. After restart, a new empty dictionary contains none of the previous tasks. To keep the task across a restart, the program must save it in persistent storage and wait for the save to finish before reporting success.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 01 / C2

    What does the signature create(title) tell a caller? What must the contract explain?

    The signature names the operation and its input; a typed signature can also describe the result type. The contract explains the behaviour: which titles are valid, what changes when the call succeeds, and which errors may occur. In our persistent application, it also says that creation returns successfully only after commit. Callers need these rules to use the operation correctly.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 01 / C3

    The task service depends on a repository. Does this dependency necessarily make the design difficult to change?

    No. The service needs a way to save tasks. A repository contract lets it request that work without knowing the SQL or file layout. A column rename can then be handled in the repository. The useful question is how much one module must know about another and whether a change to those details spreads through the application.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 01 / C4

    How do a high-level view, a low-level view, and a deployment view help explain the task application?

    The high-level view shows the main parts, such as the application and database. The low-level view explains the service methods, task records, and repository interface inside the application. The deployment view places the running application and database file on machines. These views describe the same system, so their decisions must agree. A separate repository box in a module diagram does not imply a separate server.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 01 / C5

    A service stops accepting requests during recovery but keeps every committed task. Which observation concerns availability, and which concerns durability?

    The period when users cannot perform task operations concerns availability. The fact that committed tasks remain concerns durability under that recovery scenario. A system can preserve data while being temporarily unavailable. Conversely, it can keep replying while losing tasks that were stored only in memory.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 01 / S1

    Task 7 is committed, but its success reply is lost. The client waits, then retries. Can it conclude that the first attempt failed?

    No. In this sequence, task 7 exists even though the client has not received the reply. A fresh create request may add task 8. To recognise the retry, the client needs to reuse an operation identifier, and the server must keep that identifier with the committed result. The design must also specify how it checks that the repeated request matches and how long it remembers the result. Chapter 8.2 develops these rules.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 01 / S2

    The web adapter and command-line adapter each enforce an 80-character title limit. Only the web adapter is changed to allow 200 characters. How would you prevent this disagreement?

    Move the shared title rule into the task service and make both adapters call it. Each adapter still checks its own input format, such as whether a web request contains valid JSON. Check that the database can store the longer title and update any matching storage constraint. Editing both copied rules fixes today’s mismatch but leaves the same risk for the next change.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 01 / S3

    The team runs two application machines, each with its own unrelated local task database. A user sees a task on one request and cannot find it on the next. What could explain this?

    The two requests may have reached different machines. A task saved in one local database is absent from the other. The design now needs a way for the applications to use shared or coordinated data. Adding a load balancer distributes requests; it does not copy or merge the task databases.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 01 / D1

    A handler adds a task to memory and replies “Saved.” A background writer saves it later. Trace a crash that loses the task, then propose a change that meets the restart requirement.

    The failing sequence is: add to memory, reply “Saved,” crash before the background write commits. After restart, memory is empty and there is no saved task to reload. Change the order so that success follows a durable commit, and report a write error if the save fails. A local database is enough for our stated single-machine example. A background queue would need its own durable-save and acknowledgment rules before it could support the same promise.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 01 / I1

    Run examples/todo.py. Make a test repository raise a storage error. Then use the real repository to save a task, close it, and read the task through a new connection. What should each check show?

    When insert raises a storage error, create must pass that error to its caller rather than return a successful Task. With the real SQLite repository, the task should still be present after closing and reopening the same database. Also submit an invalid title and check that no row is added. The first check covers error handling, the second persistence across reopen, and the third validation. An in-memory substitute cannot establish the persistence result.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 01 / T1

    The team now requires saved tasks to survive destruction of the only disk. Why is ADR 001 insufficient, and what must the next design address?

    ADR 001 assumes that committed storage remains intact. Destroying its only disk removes the copy it relies on. The new design needs recoverable data on independent storage and a rule for when it may report success. If copying happens only later, a task reported as saved can be lost before the copy is made. Specify which failures the copies must survive, how much loss is acceptable, and how recovery will work. Then test those cases. Simply counting replicas does not answer these questions.

    ← Return to question

    Unit 2 · Requirements, Estimation, and Engineering Trade-offs

    UNIT 02 / C1

    Opening a feed appears to be one action. Why might it create many requests and writes?

    The browser may fetch a list of posts, request each image, and send analytics. A publish action may save the post once and then write references into many follower feeds. These are separate operations even though the person performed one action.

    Count user intentions separately from requests, stored bytes, and physical writes. Otherwise an estimate based only on feed openings or published posts will miss much of the work at the storage and delivery boundaries.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 02 / C2

    Requests keep arriving faster, but successful completions stay at the same rate. What happens next?

    Once a limiting resource cannot complete work faster, excess arrivals must wait, be rejected, or leave before completion. At 200 arrivals/s and 180 completions/s, twenty unfinished requests accumulate each second if none are rejected or abandoned.

    Compare offered traffic, useful completions, errors, and queue growth. A steady completion rate can coexist with a rapidly worsening user wait; it does not establish that increasing demand is being handled.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 02 / C3

    How can a 19.9 ms mean hide a request that took one second?

    The 99 fast requests contribute 99 × 10 = 990 ms, and the slow request contributes 1,000 ms. Their total is 1,990 ms, so the mean is 1,990/100 = 19.9 ms. The arithmetic is correct, but the mean compresses very different experiences into one number.

    Inspect the slow observations and the distribution. In this particular 100-request set, nearest-rank p99 is the 99th sorted value, which is still 10 ms. Reporting a percentile alone can also miss an extreme observation.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 02 / C4

    Which requests belong in an event-based error budget?

    The requests specified by the objective's eligible population belong in its denominator, and each must be classified using the stated good-outcome rule. Define both before measuring.

    At 99.9% success over one million eligible requests, the allowed bad fraction is 0.1% = 0.001. The budget is therefore 1,000,000 × 0.001 = 1,000 failed requests. Excluding the failures the objective was meant to track would make the result misleading. A time-based objective uses time, rather than request count, as its denominator.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 02 / C5

    When is L = λW useful for estimating work in progress?

    Use stable long-run averages measured within the same boundary and in matching units. Here L is the average number present, λ is the arrival rate, and W is mean residence time, including relevant waiting. At 500 operations/s and 40 ms = 0.04 seconds, L = 500 × 0.04 = twenty operations.

    The result describes average work in progress, not an exact count at every instant or p99 latency. It does not show that a queue with sustained excess arrivals will become stable.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 02 / S1

    A traffic spike ends before new instances can start. What protects the service?

    Existing spare capacity can serve some excess work before new instances are ready. A bounded queue can hold a temporary excess if the wait is acceptable, while admission limits reject or defer work before downstream resources become overwhelmed.

    Measure the spike's height and duration and include retries. An excess of 1,000 requests/s for 30 seconds adds 30,000 queued requests if none are rejected or completed by additional capacity. Starting instances later cannot undo the waits already experienced; the remaining backlog still needs to drain.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 02 / S2

    Only 80% of a job can run in parallel. What ideal speedup can four workers give?

    Imagine a 100-second job: twenty seconds must run sequentially, while eighty can be divided perfectly. Four workers reduce the shareable part to 80/4 = 20 seconds, giving 20 + 20 = 40 seconds overall. The ideal speedup is 100/40 = 2.5 times.

    Equivalently, the new duration is 0.2 + 0.8/4 = 0.4 of the original. Coordination can reduce the actual gain further. The unchanged sequential part also limits ideal speedup to five times even with arbitrarily many workers.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 02 / S3

    Why can requiring fifty parallel calls increase tail latency?

    The request waits for its slowest required result. If each call independently has a 1% chance of exceeding a threshold, its chance of staying within the threshold is 0.99. All fifty are fast with probability 0.99⁵⁰ ≈ 0.605. Thus at least one is slow with probability 1 − 0.605 ≈ 0.395, or about 39.5%.

    Independence is an assumption; shared dependencies can correlate delays. Parallel initiation removes the need to start calls one after another, but it does not remove the wait for the last required result.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 02 / D1

    A team sizes servers from daily average RPS alone. Identify the missing evidence and propose a safer estimation process.

    Begin with the user journeys, required outcomes, and operation mix. Estimate the requests, physical writes, stored bytes, and transfer each journey causes. Calculate an average with explicit units, then add separate peak and growth assumptions, including peak duration and the delay before scaling takes effect.

    Measure per-instance capacity using a representative workload and the required latency and error targets. Choose operating headroom and check whether the remaining instances can handle traffic during the failures the design must tolerate. Size the database and image path separately.

    Treat the worksheet as a workload to test. Verify user latency, rejection, queue growth, and recovery under normal, peak, and degraded conditions. A calculated instance count alone cannot establish that the complete design meets its requirements.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 02 / I1

    Implement a capacity worksheet with explicit user activity, peak, and per-instance inputs.

    Make daily users, requests per user per day, peak multiplier, tested RPS per instance, and target utilisation explicit inputs. Validate positive workload and capacity values and require a utilisation fraction strictly between zero and one. Calculate daily requests, divide by 86,400 seconds/day, and multiply by the peak factor.

    The defaults give about 5,787.04 average requests/s and 28,935.19 peak requests/s. At an assumed 600 requests/s per instance and a 60% operating target, each contributes 600 × 0.6 = 360 requests/s of planned capacity. Dividing peak demand by 360 gives about 80.38; rounding upward gives 81 active instances. Providing 82 leaves 81 after one instance is lost.

    Keep the inputs and intermediate results in the output so changes can be checked. The arithmetic covers this request-serving resource and one-instance loss; database capacity, image delivery, routing, and failures that remove several instances still need their own evidence.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 02 / T1

    How would simultaneous retries change an estimate based on average user sessions?

    Retries add attempts without adding new user intentions. A daily session estimate therefore undercounts offered work when failed requests are repeated. If many callers retry at once, those attempts can arrive while the same dependency is still overloaded, creating another concentrated burst.

    Model the timing and maximum number of attempts separately from normal sessions. Bound retries and admission, and test useful completions, queue growth, and recovery under that burst. A peak factor based only on ordinary user arrivals may not cover the retry wave.

    ← Return to question

    Unit 3 · Networking Foundations for System Design

    UNIT 03 / C1

    A web service listens on port 443. Why might a browser on another machine still fail to reach it?

    The listener may be attached only to the local loopback address. Or the request or reply may have no usable route, or a firewall may block it. Check the server address, listening address, and both directions of the path. Reaching the program still leaves the application’s permission checks to perform.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 03 / C2

    A sender writes HELLO and then WORLD through TCP. Why might the receiver not get two separate reads?

    TCP carries an ordered byte stream, not the sender’s write boundaries. One read could contain HELLOWO and the next RLD. The application needs a framing rule to recover its messages, such as a length before each one. UDP instead preserves datagram boundaries; QUIC provides its own ordered streams over UDP.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 03 / C3

    The DNS address changes. Why do some clients still use the old server?

    A resolver or client can still have a usable cached answer. An already open connection may also continue without another lookup. Updating the published record does not replace every saved answer or close existing connections. Their lifetimes affect when traffic moves.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 03 / C4

    The gateway recognises the signed-in user. Why must the task application still check ownership of task 42?

    Knowing who the caller is does not establish which tasks the caller may read. The task application can compare the recognised user with task 42’s owner and enforce the permission rule. The gateway can perform common sign-in and allowance checks, while the application uses its resource information.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 03 / C5

    What work can SSE or WebSockets save, and what work do they add?

    They can avoid repeated empty polls by keeping a path open for messages. The system then maintains connections and buffers and must handle slow or disconnected clients. If updates occur during disconnection, it needs retained events or a fresh snapshot. A new connection alone cannot recover the missing history.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 03 / S1

    The server saves task 7, but the reply is lost. What does the client learn from its timeout?

    It learns only that a reply did not arrive in time. The task can already exist. If the request carried op-9 and the server saved that identity with its result, the client can look up or resend op-9 to recover task 7. Sending a new operation would risk a duplicate.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 03 / S2

    Our cold request takes 155 ms. Why can the next request take 55 ms with the same server work?

    The assumed cold stages are DNS 20 ms, TCP setup 40 ms, TLS setup 40 ms, and request plus work 55 ms. They add to 155 ms. A usable warm connection and lookup remove the first three stages in this model. The 55 ms stage already includes its request and reply travel. These durations are assumed, not measured.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 03 / S3

    All twenty pool connections are borrowed, but CPU has free time. Why can the next request still wait?

    The request needs an available connection, not just CPU time. Existing borrowers may be waiting on storage, locks, or another operation. Find why they still hold their connections and whether every exit returns them. Adding connections helps only if the database can use the extra work effectively.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 03 / D1

    “Read” appears twice after a create request times out and is sent again. How would you change the request flow?

    Give the original request a stable operation identifier. Save the new task and that operation’s result together. An identical retry uses the same identifier and receives the saved result; a changed request must not reuse that identity as if it were identical. This repairs task creation within the stored-operation rules. A remote provider would need its own repetition and recovery rules.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 03 / I1

    Write a cold/warm request calculator. How will you check it?

    Store each stage’s time in milliseconds and add the stages actually needed. Check that 20, 40, 40, and 55 total 155, and that reusing setup leaves 55. Reject negative and non-finite times rather than producing a misleading total. Also check zero-duration stages and a request that reuses only some setup.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 03 / T1

    Our application used to call a local function. Now it calls a service in another region. What new events can affect the result?

    The request must travel to another machine and the reply must travel back. Setup and travel add time. The server can finish while the reply is lost, leaving the caller uncertain. The interface now needs a waiting limit and a way to recognise or find the original operation when repeating it could cause another effect.

    ← Return to question

    Unit 4 · Runtime, Processes, Threads, and Concurrency

    UNIT 04 / C1

    How are a program, a process, a thread, and a source-code module different?

    A program is saved instructions; a process is one running instance. Threads execute within a process and can share its data. A module organises source code. Several modules can run in the same process and stop together when it crashes, so separate modules do not automatically create separate failure boundaries.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 04 / C2

    An upload handler is marked async. Why might other work on its event loop still wait?

    The handler may call a blocking library function or keep calculating without yielding. That occupies the loop’s thread. Other tasks can become ready but cannot run there until the current work gives up the thread. Async describes how the operation presents completion; it does not change every library call underneath.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 04 / C3

    Can one core make progress on two uploads without running them at the same instant?

    Yes. A can start, wait for storage, and resume after the core has run B. Their progress overlaps, so they are concurrent. Running instructions for both at the same instant would require parallel execution resources. Taking turns can still cause a race if both use a shared old value.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 04 / C4

    A transfer changes balances from 100,100 through 90,100 to 90,110. Why are separate atomic writes insufficient?

    Each write can be indivisible while the pair still passes through an incomplete state. A reader could see 90,100. Protect both changes as one operation and make readers of the pair follow the same rule, such as taking the same lock. A database transaction can supply a different appropriate boundary for stored balances.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 04 / C5

    A log says A set the title before B read it. Why do we still need safe publication?

    Clock order alone does not supply the language’s memory-visibility guarantee. Use a defined synchronisation relationship. For example, A sets and shares the record while holding a mutex, releases it, and B later acquires the same mutex before reading. Under the required memory-model rules, A’s writes happen before B’s read.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 04 / S1

    A and B read count zero, then both write one. Which steps must the shared lock protect?

    Protect the read, addition, and write together. If A completes those steps first, B reads one and writes two. Protecting only the assignments still allows both to calculate from zero. Separate private locks also fail because neither makes one caller wait for the other.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 04 / S2

    An upload read completes while a callback uses the only event-loop thread for two seconds. When can the upload task continue?

    Its result is ready, but its continuation still needs a turn on the thread. It waits until the callback yields or finishes. The distinction is between a completed I/O operation and execution of the code that uses its result. More queued tasks do not let that one thread run both pieces at once.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 04 / S3

    150 jobs arrive and 100 finish each second. If all are accepted, how much extra work remains after ten seconds?

    Each second adds 150 − 100 = 50 unfinished jobs. Ten seconds add 500, assuming none are rejected or abandoned. More queue space stores the excess without changing its growth. A bounded queue can reject or wait when full, and the producer must react to that feedback for arrivals to slow.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 04 / D1

    Every upload starts another background task. How would you limit the work and keep accepted jobs through a restart?

    Use a worker limit for active conversions and a queue limit for waiting jobs. Store large file bytes separately and queue small references. Give each accepted job a saved identity, input reference, and progress record. Replacement workers can then find unfinished jobs after restart. Return acceptance only after the required record is saved; define a clear busy or waiting result when capacity is unavailable.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 04 / I1

    Build a lost-update demonstration and a bounded upload queue. What should each show?

    Arrange for A and B to read zero before either writes, producing one. Then protect the complete update with a shared lock and show two. For uploads, set limits on both workers and waiting identifiers. Fill the queue and show the busy response. Also make conversion fail and check that its files and other resources are released. An in-memory demonstration needs saved job records before it can promise restart recovery.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 04 / T1

    The client disconnects after an upload job is accepted. Should processing stop?

    First decide what acceptance promised. If the job must continue, its saved record and a worker outside the request scope own the remaining work. Request-owned children can stop and release their resources. If cancellation of the job is allowed, record that decision so later workers can obey it. Closing the connection alone neither deletes the saved job nor reverses work already completed.

    ← Return to question

    Unit 5 · Object-Oriented and Modular Software Design

    UNIT 05 / C1

    When can composition avoid many subclasses?

    A payment service may vary both its gateway and its fraud policy. Combining those choices through inheritance can require a subclass for each combination. With composition, the service receives a policy and gateway and calls each for its own work. Either can be replaced while keeping the other.

    This needs clear collaborator contracts and wiring. Inheritance remains appropriate when specialisation preserves the behaviour callers are promised. Similar fields alone do not establish that relationship.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 05 / C2

    What must a payment gateway contract explain beyond charge(amount)?

    State the currency and amount units, the operation identity, repeated-operation behaviour, and the meanings of results and errors. For example, 100 USD minor units means one dollar, while “accepted” may mean only that processing has begun.

    A timeout after submission can leave a charge uncertain because the provider may have performed it before the reply was lost. The contract should preserve this distinction and explain a supported recovery path. A Boolean cannot express approval, definite decline, and uncertainty separately. Merely including an operation identifier does not make duplicate handling work.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 05 / C3

    Why does applying SOLID not require an interface for every class?

    Each principle asks about a design property: focused responsibilities, useful extension points, valid substitution, caller-specific interfaces, or the direction of dependencies. An interface is useful when it protects meaningful variation or hides details callers need not know. An application-owned gateway contract can do this for provider communication.

    An interface that only forwards every call may add navigation and maintenance without helping a real change. Evaluate a concrete change or test need rather than maximising interface count. A contract also needs behavioural meaning; matching method signatures alone does not make implementations substitutable.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 05 / C4

    How is Payment 42 different from Money(USD,100)?

    Payment 42 retains its identity as its status changes, so it is an entity. A second payment for the same amount has a different identity and history. Equal Money values can represent the same amount and currency without separate identities, making Money a value object.

    Identity and mutability are separate questions. Money is often represented immutably, and a payment can also have successive immutable snapshots sharing its identifier. Both still need valid rules; adding different currencies requires an explicit conversion policy rather than arbitrary arithmetic.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 05 / C5

    How can pure functions and external payment effects work together?

    A pure decision function takes explicit state and command data and returns a decision, new state, or requested action. A separate coordinator performs storage and provider calls and supplies their observed outcomes to later decisions. We can check the decision using inputs and outputs without making a real charge.

    The effect path still needs durability, authorisation, duplicate handling, and reconciliation of uncertain outcomes. Replaying a pure calculation does not authorise blindly repeating its requested charge. Pure local calculation does not make a remote effect atomic with a local database write.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 05 / S1

    Why ask an account to reserve an amount rather than overwrite its balance from outside?

    The account owner can keep the reservation rule and its update together. For example, it can reject a reservation that would make reserved money exceed the balance. External read/compare/write logic spreads the policy across callers. Reading a balance for reporting remains a valid query.

    The method boundary does not itself coordinate writers. If two processes both see 1,000 available and each reserve 600, both can pass a separate check. The actual shared storage boundary must make the check and update atomic so that one operation sees the effect of the other and rejects the conflicting reservation.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 05 / S2

    A mock confirms every expected method call. What could still be wrong?

    The order may still end in the wrong state, shipment may start after a decline, or an uncertain result may be recorded as paid. Checking the requested private calls does not necessarily check the business outcome. Assert the required state and effects for approved, declined, and uncertain results.

    Real transaction rollback, request encoding, resource cleanup, and provider retry behaviour also need evidence at their actual boundaries. A mock makes a path controllable but cannot prove how the component it replaced behaves. A harmless internal rearrangement should not break a test unless it changes a required interaction or outcome.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 05 / S3

    A refactor changes provider timeout into decline. Has it preserved behaviour?

    No. A definite decline says the operation was rejected. A timeout after submission can mean the effect happened but its reply was lost. Reporting that as decline can cause callers to start a new payment and risk a second charge.

    Keep the outcome uncertain until supported evidence resolves it, retaining the operation identity needed for recovery. A structural refactor should preserve these meanings. Include a timeout test alongside approval, decline, and storage-failure tests, and check that the timeout leaves the payment pending for investigation rather than definitely declined.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 05 / D1

    A payment class mixes fee rules, HTTP parsing, provider calls, and storage. Plan a behaviour-preserving refactor.

    First record the required outcomes for approval, decline, timeout, and storage failure, including amount units and the order of visible effects. Extract fee calculation and check its results on the same inputs. Then move HTTP parsing, provider translation, and persistence into focused collaborators in small steps, rerunning the behavioural checks after each move.

    Give the gateway an explicit outcome contract and supply its implementation from outside the service. Keep storage ownership clear. Preserve operation identity and uncertainty: a failed local write after a remote charge does not prove that no charge occurred. Judge the change by preserved behaviour and clearer responsibilities, rather than by the number of classes.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 05 / I1

    Replace hardcoded payment-provider construction with an injected recording gateway.

    Pass the gateway as an argument or constructor dependency. Its charge method should record the supplied command and return a controlled result. Use it to exercise approved, declined, and uncertain outcomes without real charges, and check that currency and minor-unit amounts cross the boundary unchanged.

    The small worked example records a command and returns “uncertain”; it isolates the dependency rather than implementing a complete payment service. Extend the surrounding service checks to its resulting business state as appropriate. Real request encoding, persistence, and provider recovery need separate evidence. Preserve uncertainty rather than treating a canned timeout as decline.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 05 / T1

    Which payment rules should remain the same when objects are replaced by pure functions?

    Currency, units, allowed state transitions, operation identity, and the meaning of uncertainty remain requirements regardless of representation. For the same inputs and observed provider outcomes, the new design should make the same business decisions. Tests can check these decisions through explicit function inputs and outputs.

    The separate effect coordinator still needs authorisation, durable progress, transactions for local changes, provider identity, duplicate handling, and reconciliation. Replay should recompute decisions without blindly repeating external effects. Moving methods into functions changes the representation, not the obligations of a payment system.

    ← Return to question

    Unit 6 · Design Patterns, Dependency Injection, and Object Lifecycles

    UNIT 06 / C1

    A notification service receives an SMS SDK through its constructor. Has it necessarily achieved dependency inversion?

    It has used dependency injection because another part of the program supplied the SDK. But suppose the service still builds the SDK's request objects and interprets its exceptions. Its policy still depends on those provider details.

    Dependency inversion requires a suitable contract for the application's needs. Define Sender in application terms and let an adapter translate that contract to the SDK. Injection can supply the adapter, while the service relies on Sender's message and outcome meanings. The argument's presence alone cannot establish this separation.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 06 / C2

    Two application processes each register a singleton sender. Must they receive the same object, and is either sender automatically safe for concurrent calls?

    Each process can have its own sender. A singleton lifetime promises reuse within the stated container or application boundary, not one object across every host. Even inside one process, the framework's exact boundary matters.

    Reuse also says nothing about safe concurrent access. If requests share mutable state in that sender, its implementation must coordinate the permitted calls. State who owns it, when it is released, and what concurrent use its contract supports.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 06 / C3

    A factory returns a connection. Why does the caller need more than the connection object to use it correctly?

    It needs the ownership rule. The connection might be newly created and transferred to the caller, borrowed from a scope, or shared under another owner. The first case requires the caller to release it; the other cases require the caller to respect the owner's boundary.

    Closing a shared connection can interrupt other users. Failing to return a connection the caller owns can remove capacity from a pool. The contract must therefore say who releases it and how long it may be retained.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 06 / C4

    A service receives a DI container, then calls resolve() throughout its methods. Why are its dependencies still difficult to see?

    The constructor names only the container. To discover whether the service needs a sender, repository, or formatter, we must inspect the runtime lookups in its methods. A missing registration may remain unnoticed until the relevant branch executes. This is service-locator behaviour even though the container itself was injected.

    Resolve collaborators at a deliberate composition or integration boundary, then pass the focused contracts the service needs. Its inputs make those dependencies and their ownership easier to review.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 06 / C5

    Each notification chooses email or SMS at runtime. How can dependency injection and a factory work together?

    Create a narrow SenderFactory and inject it into NotificationService. When a command arrives, the service reads its channel and asks the factory for the corresponding Sender. Injection supplied the collaborator; the factory performs the later selection or construction.

    Specify whether the returned sender is caller-owned, scope-owned, or shared by the application. That tells the service whether it must close it, may retain it, or only borrows it for the operation.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 06 / S1

    A singleton stores the unit of work obtained during request one. That request finishes. What can go wrong on request two, and how should the relationship change?

    Request one's scope can dispose the unit of work while the singleton still holds its reference. Request two then tries to use expired resources and may also encounter context retained from the wrong user or tenant. This is a captive dependency.

    Supply a valid unit of work for each operation, or supply a narrow factory that creates the appropriate scope and defines its cleanup. Every use must fit that scope. Looking up the same expired object globally, or extending all connections indefinitely, does not repair the ownership relationship.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 06 / S2

    A report generator is constructed lazily. Two first requests arrive together. What must the initialisation contract define?

    Both callers can observe that the generator is absent before either finishes constructing it. Coordinate the check, construction, and publication so the application does not create unintended duplicates or expose a partially constructed object. Use a supported lazy primitive or the runtime's appropriate locking and publication rules.

    Also decide how construction failure reaches the waiting callers and whether a later request retries. If the generator is essential to ordinary service, constructing it before readiness may make failures easier to handle.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 06 / S3

    A pool starts with ten connections. Each failed request keeps one connection instead of returning it. Why can later healthy requests stop making progress?

    Every leak reduces available capacity: after one such failure, nine connections remain; after enough failures, none may be available. The later request's own operation could succeed, but it cannot begin its database work without a connection.

    Release belongs in a structured scope or finally-style path that covers failure and cancellation as well as success. Roll back unfinished work as required before returning the resource. Memory garbage collection is not a guarantee that the pool will regain capacity in time.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 06 / D1

    A singleton notification service resolves a request connection from a global container and stores it. Identify both design problems and propose an assembly and ownership arrangement.

    The lookup hides the connection dependency from the service's visible inputs. Retaining it also captures a request-owned resource in a longer-lived object. After the request closes its scope, the singleton can keep using an invalid connection.

    Keep the singleton's lasting collaborators safe for that lifetime. For database work, pass a currently valid per-operation unit of work or inject a narrow scope factory. Create the request or job scope at its explicit boundary, obtain its connection, perform the operation, and release resources on exit. Preserve the right user and tenant context. Making every connection live indefinitely would replace the original lifetime rule with uncontrolled sharing.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 06 / I1

    Demonstrate transient, scoped, and singleton identities across two request scopes. Then add an owned disposable resource and show what happens when it is retained beyond its scope.

    Record two resolutions of each lifetime inside scope one and again inside scope two. Expected scoped identities are A,A followed by B,B. Transient resolutions should produce distinct instances, while resolutions of the application-owned singleton should return S within its stated boundary. Compare object identity rather than equal field values.

    Give the scoped resource an observable closed flag or cleanup record. Exit its scope through both a normal operation and a failure, and confirm that cleanup occurs. Keep a reference in the longer-lived object and demonstrate that a later use is rejected after closure. This shows why a surviving reference does not extend validity. Finally, obtain a fresh resource for each operation and verify its own cleanup boundary.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 06 / T1

    A notification job runs after both the creating request and the user session have ended. How should it obtain resources, and which authority should permit its action?

    Save durable job data and identifiers instead of capturing a request connection or session object. When execution begins, create a job scope, obtain current resources under a documented owner, load the required state, and release those resources when the job finishes or fails. The request and job now have separate ownership boundaries.

    The application must also choose an authorisation policy. Some jobs represent work validly accepted earlier; others must recheck current membership or permission before acting. Make that decision explicit and retain only the necessary context. A long-running job must not silently treat an expired user session as continuing authority.

    Unit 7 · Application Architecture and Domain-Driven Design

    UNIT 07 / C1

    What makes a monolith modular if it has one deployment?

    Its modules have clear responsibilities, controlled interfaces, and data ownership. Orders should use a payment contract rather than alter private payment tables. One deployment keeps calls local but does not prevent useful boundaries. Enforce important dependencies through review or appropriate checks.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 07 / C2

    Why can dependency arrows point differently from runtime calls?

    A service can depend on an application-owned repository interface, while a database adapter implements it. At runtime, calls execute the supplied adapter. The source arrow describes knowledge or implementation relationships, not necessarily the physical direction of a message or a separate network service.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 07 / C3

    Why can catalog Product and fulfilment Item be different valid models?

    They describe different business work. Catalog may care about descriptions and categories, while fulfilment tracks units and locations. A bounded context identifies where each meaning applies. Translate between them deliberately rather than forcing both into one schema that obscures their rules.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 07 / C4

    How should an aggregate boundary follow the rule it protects?

    Group state that must change atomically under a root controlling those changes. An order's line values and total may need one consistency boundary. Making the entire shop one aggregate adds contention. Cross-aggregate work needs explicit coordination rather than an assumption that object references create a shared transaction.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 07 / C5

    What should an architecture fitness check preserve?

    A meaningful required property, such as allowed dependencies, migration compatibility, or tenant isolation. It should detect erosion of that reasoned boundary without freezing incidental class names. Update the check when the architecture decision legitimately changes, and keep evidence within the check's actual scope.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 07 / S1

    An order commits, then the process dies before publishing its event. What is missing?

    Publication intent existed only in memory or a separate unsafe step. An outbox can commit that intent with the order so a relay can resume later. The relay may publish again after losing its own progress record, so consumers still need stable event identity and duplicate handling.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 07 / S2

    Five services share writable tables and always release together. What independence is missing?

    They cannot change their contracts or stored representation independently and can remain tightly coupled operationally. The network split adds failure and diagnosis work without delivering much independent deployment. Clarify ownership and boundaries, or consider a modular consolidation where appropriate.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 07 / S3

    When would extracting a module into a service be justified?

    Look for a stable capability with a concrete scaling, fault-isolation, or team-ownership need, plus the ability to operate it. Compare the benefit with network failures, versioning, data coordination, security, and on-call costs. A rapidly changing model alone is not evidence that more process boundaries will help.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 07 / D1

    Several services share tables and require simultaneous releases. Review whether the deployment split is useful.

    Map who owns decisions and data, what changes together, and what fails together. A modular consolidation may be simpler, or revised contracts and ownership may justify separation. Compare independent operation with the actual network, migration, and incident costs.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 07 / I1

    Implement shopping modules and one meaningful dependency-boundary check.

    Let orders use a payment contract without importing private payment storage or writing its tables. Check that boundary, then replace the provider adapter while preserving the order rule. Avoid a test tied to every internal class name; protect the dependency whose violation would spread provider details or bypass ownership.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 07 / T1

    What evidence would justify extracting payments into a separate service?

    Look for stable capability ownership, different scaling or isolation needs, and an operating team prepared for network and version failures. Compare those benefits with added data coordination and recovery. Preserve existing payment invariants and histories through migration. A separate deployment is useful only when the required independence can actually be exercised.

    Unit 8 · API Design and Communication Contracts

    UNIT 08 / C1

    Why give a refund its own identity and status?

    A refund can be requested later, authorised separately, and complete or fail independently of the original payment. Its own identity supports amount checks, retries, and investigation. Treating it as an untracked toggle on paid loses the history and uncertainty needed for recovery.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 08 / C2

    What does a keyset cursor improve, and what does it leave unresolved?

    It continues after a stable ordered key rather than skipping a shifting row count, avoiding some duplicates and omissions from insertions before an offset. It also needs validation and query/tenant scope. Changing records can still affect results; the cursor does not automatically provide one consistent snapshot.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 08 / C3

    What makes an idempotency key more than a string in a request?

    Durable state binds owner, key, payload fingerprint, progress, and result with suitable uniqueness and atomicity. Identical retries recover the same operation; different content conflicts. Retention and provider recovery rules matter too. A separate unprotected lookup and insert can race or forget an external effect.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 08 / C4

    Why does signing in not grant access to GET /payments/42?

    Authentication identifies the caller. Authorisation must still check this caller's permitted action on payment 42 using trusted membership and resource scope. Guess-resistant IDs and gateway authentication do not establish ownership. Apply the rule on every relevant query and effect path.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 08 / C5

    How can removing an old event decoder break recovery after a successful release?

    Historical logs and backups can still contain that version. A restoring or delayed consumer needs to interpret it even when current traffic uses only the newest shape. Keep supported historical samples and transformations, including meanings, defaults, and unknown values, for the required replay horizon.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 08 / S1

    Does 201 Created for a pending payment mean money was captured?

    No. It can mean the payment resource was created successfully while its financial operation remains pending. The body and operation contract describe that later state. HTTP response semantics do not make a provider effect part of the local resource transaction.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 08 / S2

    Four layers each allow three attempts. How much downstream work can one request cause?

    Up to 3⁴ = 81 attempts in the nested worst case. Early success can reduce actual work, but failure can trigger amplification precisely when capacity is scarce. Use an overall retry budget and deadline, and safe operation identity for effects.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 08 / S3

    A webhook effect commits but its reply is lost. What should redelivery do?

    Recognise the stable event identity and avoid repeating the established local effect. Persist recognition and effect together when that is the protected boundary. An unrelated external call needs its own protocol. The sender may legitimately retry because it did not observe acknowledgment.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 08 / D1

    A payment API returns a Boolean and provides no operation status. Redesign it for an uncertain provider reply.

    Create a stable intent identity, explicit pending/approved/declined/uncertain semantics, validated money units, and scoped repeat-key handling. Offer status recovery. Define compatibility and permission as well as field shape so clients know what repeating the request means.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 08 / I1

    Implement keyset continuation and a durable operation-key model for synthetic payments.

    Use a stable ordered pair for continuation and test an insertion before a page boundary. Bind actor, key, fingerprint, progress, and result under appropriate atomicity. Identical retries return the old operation; changed payloads conflict. A dictionary lookup followed by an unrelated insert does not protect concurrent or restarted callers.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 08 / T1

    Can finite storage support a permanent promise to recognise every old idempotency key?

    Not for an unbounded set of arbitrary distinct operations unless another constraint supplies a bound or persistent evidence elsewhere. Define key retention, expiry, reuse, and client expectations. A permanent business identity may require a durable record rather than an expiring cache. Make the promise fit the information the system can retain.

    ← Return to question

    Unit 9 · Data Models and Storage Technologies

    UNIT 09 / C1

    What must be decided before choosing a storage family?

    State the important reads and changes, accepted-result boundary, invariants, retention, and supported failures. Identify the authoritative copy and recovery procedure. A product category does not establish configured isolation, durable acknowledgment, or usable backups, so verify the selected implementation against those needs.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 09 / C2

    Why is a similar embedding result not proof of truth or permission?

    An embedding is a derived numerical representation used to find candidates. Approximate similarity can miss items or retrieve imperfect matches. Preserve source versions, verify required evidence, and enforce access. A vector score describes its retrieval relationship, not factual correctness or authorisation.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 09 / C3

    When is storing an address twice correct?

    A profile can hold the current address while a completed order retains the address actually used at purchase. Those records represent different facts. A maintained cache of the current address has another meaning and needs an update policy. State whether repetition preserves history or tracks a changing source.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 09 / C4

    Why is data ownership broader than creating a table?

    The owner defines allowed changes and access contracts and is responsible for schema evolution, retention, incidents, and recovery. If every service writes the table directly, they share release and transaction assumptions despite separate repositories. Ownership needs an enforcement mechanism and operating responsibility.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 09 / C5

    What work appears when a second storage engine is added?

    Backup and restoration, access policy, schema changes, monitoring, expertise, and reconciliation now cross another boundary. If it is a derived search store, also manage lag and rebuilding. Compare the new capability with that ownership cost rather than assuming a specialised engine is automatically a net improvement.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 09 / S1

    Why do more cold partitions not solve one very busy conversation partition?

    The hot conversation's requests still reach its owner. Extra unrelated capacity does not divide that key's work. Measure whether the pressure comes from size, reads, writes, or ordering, then choose supported splitting, read distribution, or a changed data model that preserves the required semantics.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 09 / S2

    Search still holds a deleted private document. What must the system do?

    Enforce the required access and deletion policy when serving, even while asynchronous cleanup catches up. Carry source identity and version so old updates cannot recreate an invalid visible record. Track physical cleanup and derived-copy lifecycle rather than treating a successful delete in the source as completion everywhere.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 09 / S3

    What prevents an older backup from restoring deleted content into live service?

    Recovery must apply the relevant deletion history and lifecycle rules before exposing restored copies. Track raw and derived data, including indexes and replay paths. A narrowly retained marker can help prevent resurrection, but has its own minimisation and retention needs.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 09 / D1

    A search engine holds the only copy of private document text. Review ownership, recovery, and deletion.

    Keep a recoverable source and exact identity/version relationships for derived entries. Enforce access while indexing lags, and track deletion across copies and restores. If search truly owns the authoritative data, it needs the corresponding complete durability and recovery contract rather than assumptions borrowed from a projection.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 09 / I1

    Model profiles, financial entries, chat history, events, and PDFs from their required operations.

    List access patterns, rules, identity, retention, and recoverability before choosing stores. Several needs may share an engine. Keep immutable bytes distinguishable from metadata and derived search results. Explain how each copy is rebuilt or recovered, rather than assigning one product family per data type without a reason.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 09 / T1

    How should restoration from a historical backup respect later deletion decisions?

    Restore into a controlled path, apply relevant deletion decisions, and reconcile raw and derived copies before serving. Rebuild indexes from the permitted current state rather than blindly expose an older snapshot. Keep deletion evidence narrow and purpose-limited. The backup and live-data lifecycle need a combined recovery procedure.
