    Unit 10 · Database Internals, Transactions, and Concurrency Control

    UNIT 10 / C1

    Why might range and equality queries need different indexes?

    An ordered tree can locate the first key in a range and continue through neighbouring entries. A hash index locates equality candidates using a hash and does not provide that ordered walk. An ordered tree can also serve equality queries, so equality alone does not require a hash index.

    Compare the query conditions, ordering, output size, storage locality, update cost, and indexes supported by the engine. The useful choice is the structure that reduces the actual work for the required operations.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 10 / C2

    Why does an ACID transaction not automatically preserve every business rule?

    The application and constraints must express the rule correctly. In our transfer, both account changes can commit atomically even if the application calculates the wrong amount. Atomicity groups the changes; it does not validate the business calculation.

    Check the invariant, the code and constraints that enforce it, the selected isolation level, and the durability configuration. Each answers a different question about whether the transaction provides the promised result.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 10 / C3

    Why is MVCC alone insufficient to claim serializability?

    MVCC retains versions and chooses which version a reader can see. That mechanism can give both doctors a stable view in which the other is still on call. Each can then update a different row, leaving nobody on call if both changes commit.

    No correct serial execution of those checks permits that result: the second doctor would see the first off and stay. Check the isolation and conflict rules that prevent this history, rather than inferring serializability from the existence of row versions.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 10 / C4

    Why state the engine and statement behaviour when discussing isolation?

    The same isolation name can have different implementations. A plain read and a locking or updating statement can also have different conflict behaviour. In PostgreSQL 18, ordinary Read Committed SELECTs take statement snapshots; Repeatable Read holds a transaction snapshot and prevents phantoms, but can still allow serialization anomalies.

    Use the documented engine, version, level, and statement form when analysing a history. When a transaction fails with a retryable serialization conflict, restart its reads and decisions as part of the whole transaction, using fresh state and bounded attempts.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 10 / C5

    How do serializability and linearizability differ?

    Serializability requires committed transactions to have an effect equivalent to some serial transaction order. It permits their instructions to overlap and does not by itself add a real-time ordering condition.

    Linearizability treats each operation as taking effect between its invocation and reply and respects real-time precedence between operations. Strict serializability combines transaction serialization with real-time order. None of these properties automatically brings a provider call outside the database into its local transaction boundary.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 10 / S1

    Two doctors each see the other on call and both go off duty. What rule was missed?

    At least one doctor must remain on call. That invariant covers both rows. Each transaction relied on an earlier read of the other doctor, so the updates can be individually plausible while their combination is invalid. This is write skew, rather than one transaction overwriting the other's row.

    Protect the full decision with suitable serializable transactions, coordinated locking, or a shared conflict point. If serialization rejects an attempt, repeat the whole transaction with fresh reads; the remaining doctor must then stay on call.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 10 / S2

    A conditional seat update changes zero rows. What does that mean?

    No row satisfied the condition when the database applied the update, so the seat claim did not occur. In the competing-buyer example, the earlier winner changed the availability or version. More generally, the seat might also be missing; the guarded update alone does not distinguish those causes.

    Re-read the relevant state and decide whether to report unavailability, a missing seat, or another supported outcome. Do not report a reservation merely because the SQL statement completed without an error. Success requires the guarded transition and its commit to succeed.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 10 / S3

    A backup job succeeded. What recovery evidence is still needed?

    Restore the backup in a usable environment with the required decryption keys, schema, credentials, and recovery logs. Open it through a compatible application and check meaningful relationships, such as a reservation agreeing with its seat owner.

    Measure how long full recovery takes and identify how much acknowledged history can be recovered. File creation and checksums are useful checks, but do not establish that the service can restore the required state and serve correctly.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 10 / D1

    Two doctors can each go off call after seeing the other available. Propose a transaction design preserving at least one on call.

    One design runs every operation that changes this on-call rule in a serializable transaction. Read the relevant doctors, check that another doctor will remain on call, and only then mark the requesting doctor off. Commit before reporting success. If a serialization failure occurs, retry the complete transaction with fresh reads and bounded attempts. Once one doctor has left, the other's new attempt must refuse to leave.

    An alternative uses a shared coordination row for the rota with Read Committed isolation. Every participating transaction locks that row before issuing the reads that check the doctors and making its change. A waiting transaction performs those reads after acquiring the lock, so its new statement snapshot includes the preceding transaction's committed decision. All writers must follow the same protocol. Locking only the doctor being changed leaves the original write-skew history possible. Keep external notifications safe under retries and release them only under a deliberate completion policy.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 10 / I1

    Run the conditional last-seat claim with two connections to one store.

    Open two connections to the same database file and create one available seat. Call claim_seat for A through one connection, then for B through the other. Assert that A returns true, B returns false, and a fresh read shows A as the owner. Two separate in-memory databases would not test competing claims on one seat.

    Inspect the guarded UPDATE and its transaction: owner changes only where the seat exists and owner IS NULL, and success is based on one affected row. Test rollback of an equivalent guarded update before commit and confirm that another connection can still claim the seat afterward. These checks establish the local ownership rule. Payment, expiry, and a genuinely overlapping concurrency stress test require their own checks.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 10 / T1

    What changes when one local transaction is divided across independent databases?

    The two changes no longer automatically share one commit decision. Suppose the seat update commits in one database but inserting the reservation fails in another. Each store can behave correctly locally while the combined booking is incomplete.

    First identify which invariant needs agreement. A distributed transaction may supply a suitable shared decision if the stores and operating requirements support it. Alternatively, a workflow can represent intermediate states explicitly and use retries, reconciliation, or compensation to reach an acceptable outcome. That choice must define what the caller sees while work is incomplete. Separate local commits alone do not preserve the former all-or-nothing business promise.

    ← Return to question

    Unit 11 · Caching and Content Delivery

    UNIT 11 / C1

    Why does a working set matter more than the full history size for caching?

    Reuse concerns the data active in the chosen interval. A small cache can serve a much larger history if most requests reuse a small portion. If the active set exceeds it, eviction and reload can churn. Include bytes, object size, scan traffic, and admission behaviour as well as entry count.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 11 / C2

    How can cache-aside reinsert an old value after invalidation?

    A reader fetches version one, then pauses. A writer commits version two and invalidates the key. The reader resumes and inserts its old value. Ordering a source write before cache deletion alone does not prevent this history; stronger freshness needs suitable version or coordination rules.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 11 / C3

    Why can a one-minute TTL serve data older than one minute?

    TTL starts when the cache inserts the value. If that value already lagged the source by five minutes, another minute of residence can make it six minutes old. Expiry and source freshness are different measurements. Choose the policy according to the operation's tolerated staleness.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 11 / C4

    For A,B,C,A,D at capacity three, what do ideal LRU and FIFO evict?

    Ideal LRU refreshes A's recency, leaving B oldest when D arrives, so it evicts B. FIFO preserves insertion order and evicts A. This fixture explains their difference; real engines can approximate policies and use byte limits or separate expiration rules.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 11 / C5

    When might removing a cache improve the design?

    When reuse saves less than lookup, encoding, memory, and maintenance cost, or when a simpler source improvement meets the requirement with fewer freshness risks. Test the empty and unavailable paths. A warm cache can hide an origin-capacity problem, while a wrongly scoped cache can create a data leak.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 11 / S1

    A cache restart sends misses to the origin. How can that load be controlled?

    Combine same-key loading where useful, bound refresh workers, apply origin admission, and rebuild gradually. Negative caching and expiry jitter address particular patterns. Do not let every new instance independently scan the whole source. Protect recovery capacity as well as normal cache-hit traffic.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 11 / S2

    A product is created just after “not found” is cached. What should the policy explain?

    How long the negative entry may hide the new product and whether creation invalidates it. Distinguish genuine absence from temporary source failure and authorisation denial. Keys and lifetimes must prevent one tenant's response from misleading another.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 11 / S3

    Refresh keeps failing while stale data is served. What limit is needed?

    Define fresh, stale-permitted, and unusable ages or another explicit degradation bound. Serving must stop or change once the allowed stale condition ends. Some descriptions tolerate old values, but correctness-critical operations need their authoritative checks. Do not silently extend stale use forever.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 11 / D1

    A cache-aside reader repopulates old data after the writer invalidates it. Define and repair the actual freshness requirement.

    Trace old read, new commit, invalidation, delayed old insertion. If that stale result is forbidden, use a supported version or coordination protocol. If bounded staleness is allowed, state its limit and validate authoritative state for critical actions. TTL is not a universal repair.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 11 / I1

    Run ideal LRU, then reproduce stale cache-aside population after invalidation.

    A,B,C,A,D at capacity three evicts B. Next pause a reader with version one, commit version two and invalidate, then resume old population. Show the stale result. Apply a justified version or coordination rule if the freshness requirement forbids it; shortening TTL alone does not remove the race.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 11 / T1

    When should a product stop serving rather than return a stale cached result?

    Stop when the operation requires current authority or the permitted stale interval has ended. An old description may be allowed, while allocating scarce stock or deciding current access may not be. State which actions degrade and which wait or reject, with visible status and a recovery path.

    ← Return to question

    Unit 12 · Scalability, Load Balancing, and Data Distribution

    UNIT 12 / C1

    The application becomes slow, so the team adds web servers. Under which conditions would you expect more useful completions, and when might the extra servers mainly create more waiting?

    More web servers help when they can share the limiting work. If requests spend their time performing independent CPU calculations, additional compute may increase completions while other required resources still have capacity.

    If every request instead waits on one saturated database, disk, lock, or provider, extra web servers can send more work to that same constraint. Trace where requests execute and wait, then compare the useful completion rate before and after a change. The intervention should address the stage that limits the required outcome.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 12 / C2

    A dataset is divided among several storage owners. Explain what changes for routing, queries, and rules that previously fitted inside one database.

    The application must now find the owner of each key and account for ownership changes. A query confined to one shard can remain local, while a query spanning shards must contact several owners and combine results. Uniqueness and transactions that cross those owners need more than one shard's local check.

    The partition key changes which operations stay together. A tenant key can keep a tenant's records local, but one large tenant can still overload its owner. Choose placement and recovery from the important operations and invariants, rather than assuming that division by itself removes the limit.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 12 / C3

    In the rendezvous example, owner D is added to A, B, and C. Explain which assignments can change, and why this does not establish balanced request traffic.

    For each key, A, B, and C keep the scores they had before. Their previous winner therefore remains the best of those three. Adding D either leaves that winner in place or gives the key to D if D has the winning score. In this model, a changed assignment cannot jump from A to B merely because D was added.

    This property concerns key placement. It neither transfers records nor makes clients agree about membership. It also says nothing about popularity: many keys can be evenly placed while one frequently requested key sends most traffic to a single owner. Measure key distribution and request traffic separately.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 12 / C4

    A dashboard says that a replica has received an update. Why is that insufficient evidence that a read can observe it, or that it will survive the required failure?

    Receiving a change, preserving it durably, and applying it to served state are different milestones. A replica may have received newer log records while its read state still reflects an earlier applied position. A read there can therefore miss the update.

    Durability depends on the protocol's required persistence milestone and failure assumptions. Identify the source, receipt, persistence, and apply progress relevant to the decision. A freshness decision needs evidence about visibility; a promotion decision must also honour the acknowledgment and possible-loss contract. The phrase “has the update” leaves these distinctions unresolved.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 12 / C5

    Why should the cost comparison between one larger node and several smaller nodes use the same failure and recovery requirements?

    A design that is cheap while every node works may have too little surviving capacity after a required failure. Another may recover quickly but lose more acknowledged data than the requirement permits. Those designs are providing different service, so their healthy-state prices alone are not comparable.

    First require each candidate to meet the same workload, response-time, data-loss, and interruption objectives. Then include surviving capacity, copies, coordination, transfer, monitoring, and operating work. Compare cost against successful outcomes, including the retries and recovery work needed to obtain them.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 12 / S1

    One partition receives 70% of writes while the other partitions are mostly idle. Which evidence would help you choose between splitting it, changing placement, and redesigning the hot operation?

    Inspect which keys produce the writes, how large the records are, and where the owner spends time. Many independent hot keys may be divisible between owners. One huge record may create a different cost from many small writes. One entity whose rule requires exclusive updates can remain serial even after unrelated data moves away.

    A range split helps when incoming work actually divides across the resulting ranges. More cold partitions do not automatically divide one hot key. Choose a change that reduces the observed pressure while preserving the required query results and ownership rule, and measure the hot owner's queue again.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 12 / S2

    During a database slowdown, an autoscaler adds application replicas. Explain how this can increase timeouts even though the application now has more machines.

    Each application replica may create another connection pool. More instances can therefore produce more simultaneous database borrowers and more competing queries without adding database capacity. If slow queries or lock waits keep connections busy, new callers accumulate both at pools and inside the database. Retries may add further attempts.

    Bound aggregate admission across the instances and include acquisition waiting in request deadlines. Inspect connection hold time, query work, and contention before raising limits. Extra application capacity helps only if it increases useful completions rather than increasing the pressure on the same constrained owner.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 12 / S3

    Two application replicas run on one host. What protection do they provide, and which additional evidence would you need before claiming that they survive a host failure?

    One process may continue when the other process alone fails, but losing the host can remove both. The host is a shared failure domain. Process count therefore does not establish machine-failure tolerance.

    To survive the required host failure, place suitable serving capacity elsewhere and check its state, routing, and takeover procedure. Inspect other shared dependencies, such as storage, power, configuration, and credentials. Also establish that the survivor has enough capacity. Separated processes provide useful protection only for the failures that do not defeat their remaining common dependencies.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 12 / D1

    After the team doubles application replicas, database timeouts increase. Describe an investigation and a correction that would preserve service while testing the cause.

    Start with the request path. Measure offered work, useful completions, connection acquisition time, connection hold time, query execution, and lock waiting. Count the pools across all instances and compare their aggregate demand with the database's connection budget. This can distinguish an application compute limit from pressure created by the new callers.

    Bound admission and retain capacity needed for recovery while investigating. If a particular query or contention pattern is responsible, change that access path or resource use where the evidence supports it.     A payment provider commits a charge, but its reply never reaches the order service. Why is this a partial failure, and how should the order service proceed?

    The provider completed its part while the order service failed to learn the result. The local order may remain pending even though the charge exists. Keep that uncertainty in a durable operation record and query the provider using the stable reference where supported. Then reconcile the local order with the observed outcome. Rolling back local data cannot erase the charge, and blindly submitting another charge can repeat the effect.

    UNIT 14 / C2

    A Lamport event has value 5 and another has value 9. What can you conclude from those numbers alone? What extra information can a vector comparison provide?

    The numbers alone do not prove that event 5 happened before event 9. Lamport's guarantee works in the other direction: if one event happens before another, the later event receives a larger value under the algorithm. Independent events can also receive different values. With correctly maintained vector clocks for the same participant set, componentwise comparison can distinguish a recorded dependency from concurrency. Neither clock decides how conflicting business updates should be merged.

    UNIT 14 / C3

    The later read must return 2 because the completed write must precede it in the allowed order. If the operations overlap, the read may return 1 or 2, provided its result fits a legal common history. We can place the read before or after the write within their invocation-to-response intervals. A write whose reply times out is different from a confirmed failed write: its effect may still need to be included.

    UNIT 14 / C4

    A later read on the other side cannot learn the new value while communication is cut off. Returning its old value can violate atomic consistency; waiting indefinitely or refusing the operation sacrifices the formal availability requirement. CAP concerns these defined properties for the shared object under the partition model. It does not classify an entire product permanently or determine normal-operation latency. Specify which operations wait, reject, or return an explicitly weaker result.

    UNIT 14 / C5

    Can a booking service prevent double sales while failing to provide useful service? Explain why the progress requirement must be stated carefully.

    Yes. It can leave accepted bookings pending forever without ever assigning one seat twice. This preserves the safety rule but violates a promise that accepted bookings eventually resolve. Rejecting every request also avoids double sales, and leaves no accepted booking to violate that particular promise. To rule out this second behaviour, require useful progress for valid requests under stated healthy and reachable conditions. Safety, completion of accepted work, and admission of useful work are distinct requirements.

A replica below that position can wait to catch up, route to a sufficiently current owner, or report unavailability for that promised read. The progress information also needs a defined path through failover and device changes; ordinary sticky routing alone does not cover those transitions.

The protocol must still explain what acknowledgments persist, how versions and concurrent writers are ordered, how reads treat unfinished writes, and how recovery and membership changes preserve that evidence. For example, a read must not expose a pending write and then allow a later read to forget it without an intervening write. Set overlap does not establish those rules.

Once epoch 8 is established there, A's epoch-7 request is rejected. The takeover must establish the needed fence before relying on exclusive new-owner effects, and the authority record must survive the failures covered by the contract. A timer in A's process cannot provide this enforcement. Test delayed messages and resumed processes as well as clean crashes.

B and C can potentially establish the required decision; A alone cannot issue a new exclusive allocation. Before the new owner's effects are relied on, establish the authority fence so a delayed or resumed older owner cannot also succeed. Requests without valid authority wait or receive an explicit failure. Operations explicitly permitted to use stale information may continue separately. On recovery, discover and retain the authoritative allocation, reconcile pending requests, and bring the old participant up to date before allowing it to act. For the direct majority-replication rule, the entry being used to advance commitment must belong to the leader's current term. Its commitment also commits the preceding prefix.

Raft's joint-consensus transition temporarily requires the relevant majority of each configuration before moving to the new configuration alone.     Why are two replicas not necessarily enough surviving capacity?

Losing one leaves capacity for only 100, so the service needs more headroom or a permitted way to reduce or reject work. Continuing to queue the excess will not solve a sustained gap.

    Also check independence, usable state, and traffic movement. A second replica cannot take over if the same storage or configuration failure disables it too.

Calculate the remaining time before each stage and release owned resources when work ends.

    A timeout still leaves a remote effect uncertain if the request may have reached the provider. Stopping the wait does not establish that the write never happened.

    An open breaker rejects selected calls promptly, reducing repeated waits and resource use while a dependency is failing. Half-open probes admit limited work to test recovery before ordinary calls resume. The policy must define which outcomes open or close the breaker and bound the probes.

    The combined limits must fit shared capacity. Partitioning also has a cost: one pool can be idle while another rejects work.

    UNIT 17 / C5

    How do RTO and RPO differ?

    RTO is the target time to restore the defined service. RPO specifies the acceptable gap in recoverable data history relative to the incident. A noon incident followed by service return at 12:20 gives twenty minutes of interruption. Recovering data only through 11:55 gives five minutes of data-loss exposure.

    Compare these separate measurements with the agreed targets. Count detection, restoration, validation, and traffic return in the recovery journey; measure actual lost records separately from the time-based exposure.

    Bound admission and resource use, keep a stable identity where the receiver supports safe repetition, and track useful intents and completions separately from attempts. Reserve capacity for recovery and for resolving effects whose outcomes remain unknown.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 17 / D1

    A provider slowdown holds every connection and triggers layered retries. Break the cascade without inventing business success.

    Start with the resource history: slow calls retain connections, queues grow, and retries add work to the reduced capacity. Apply an overall deadline and release owned resources; bound admission, queues, and retries; isolate optional workloads; and use a breaker with limited recovery probes.

    Return failure or a valid pending or degraded outcome according to the operation's contract. Preserve identities and track uncertain external effects so they can be reconciled. Reserve recovery capacity and test the fallback under the combined failed traffic, since it can become another bottleneck.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 17 / I1

    Calculate nested retry amplification and design a bounded provider-outage policy.

    With three attempts at each of four nested layers, the worst-case downstream allowance is 3×3×3×3 = 81 attempts for one logical request. This includes the initial attempt at each layer; deadlines or earlier success may stop execution sooner.

    Give the operation an overall retry budget and deadline, bound admission, and isolate the resources at risk. Use backoff and jitter for retry timing and limited probes for recovery. Return a permitted pending or failure result rather than fabricated payment approval. After the provider returns, reconcile uncertain operations using their retained identities.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 17 / T1

    How can a disaster drill restore infrastructure yet fail the business recovery requirement?

    Machines can run while restored data is too old for the RPO, backups lack usable keys, accepted jobs are missing, or competing owners can still write. Validation and traffic return may also push useful service beyond the RTO even when machine startup is fast.

    Test the full business journey with its required state, identities, authority, credentials, and recovery objectives. Include unresolved effects and catch-up work. A successful drill provides evidence for the scenario it exercised, rather than every possible disaster.

    ← Return to question

    Unit 18 · Security Architecture and Privacy

    UNIT 18 / C1

    Why is an internal network address not proof of a caller's identity?

    An internal address tells us something about the route, but does not by itself identify the requesting workload or grant resource permission. A compromised internal worker can use that same route. Validate the caller's credential at the receiving boundary and check the requested action against the actual resource. If identity arrives in forwarded headers, accept those headers only from the configured trusted source.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 18 / C2

    How do OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect differ in purpose?

    OAuth 2.0 supports delegated permission to access resources. OpenID Connect adds a defined identity layer, including an ID token for the client. In a login journey, the client validates the intended identity result; the API separately validates its access credential. Issuer, audience, expiry, and required flow context matter. An arbitrary access token cannot be substituted for a login assertion.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 18 / C3

    Why use purpose-built password hashing rather than a fast hash?

    An attacker with the database can test guesses offline. A fast hash permits many cheap guesses; password hashing deliberately adds work, with salts preventing reuse of the same precomputed result across users. Use a maintained implementation and current deployment-appropriate settings. Store the settings for later upgrades and protect the separate online login and recovery paths.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 18 / C4

    Which paths need tenant isolation beyond the database query?

    Follow a document through cache keys, job messages, worker inputs and outputs, search, export objects, download capabilities, telemetry, and administration. Each path needs trustworthy tenant and resource context. If A and B both have document 7, a shared cache key of 7 merges distinct records even when the database query was correct. Include the tenant in the identity and enforce permission on delivery.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 18 / C5

    Does an artifact's valid signature prove its code is safe?

    A checked signature can establish the expected signing relationship and that the signed content has not changed, under the scheme's assumptions. It does not establish that the signer, dependency, or build was safe. Connect reviewed inputs to the artifact actually deployed, control build and release privileges, and retain a way to identify and replace affected releases.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 18 / S1

    A tenant A administrator guesses a tenant B document ID. What denies access?

    Validate the actor, resolve A's permitted tenant context, and load or select the document under that scope. B's document must fail the resource and action policy: the administrator role applies to A. Apply the same rule to direct download, cache, export, and worker paths so another route cannot bypass the denial. Knowing the identifier and possessing a valid session do not grant the missing permission.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 18 / S2

    A backup survives but its only decryption key is destroyed. What went wrong?

    The recovery plan preserved ciphertext but lost a required dependency. The backup needs the key version that encrypted its data, any protected data key, and the credentials or authority needed to use those keys. Test an actual restore with those dependencies before retiring an old version. Keeping the backup bytes alone does not make the data recoverable.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 18 / S3

    Membership is revoked after an export is queued. Where must that policy be enforced?

    State the revocation contract first. If revoked members must receive no newly published exports, check current membership at execution and publication as required, coordinate those checks with publication, and durably record denial or cancellation. Protect download according to its own contract. A capability already issued may remain usable until expiry unless the delivery mechanism can revoke it; do not assume the queue-time decision covers these later stages.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 18 / D1

    A private export is authorised at submission but its worker trusts the old tenant field forever. Review the complete journey.

    Resolve the requester and permitted tenant from trusted state, select scoped resources, and durably record the export operation. Queue a reference to that operation; let the worker resolve its scope and enforce the chosen current permission policy. Limit its input and output authority, keep the result private, and control publication and download. Track cancellation and deletion so retries cannot publish obsolete output. Record meaningful audit outcomes. Test membership removal between submission, execution, publication, and download, including the behaviour of any capability already issued.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 18 / I1

    Test the synthetic tenant predicate, then trace all data paths using that decision.

    The shown assertions permit active actor A to read an A resource and reject reading a B resource. Also test an inactive actor and an action absent from its permissions: both should be denied. These checks test the predicate with supplied attributes, not credential validation or completeness of the attributes. Then trace trusted tenant scope through cache keys, job resolution, object access, export, and search. A correct predicate cannot protect a path that bypasses it.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 18 / T1

    What should revocation mean for an issued object capability and a queued export?

    Define when each form of authority stops working. A queued export can check current membership before the later actions required by policy. An already issued object capability may remain usable until expiry unless the delivery mechanism supports earlier revocation. If immediate download denial is required, choose a delivery design that can enforce it rather than relying on expiry alone. Test revocation before execution, before publication, and after link issuance, and describe the resulting lifetime accurately to users.

    ← Return to question

    Unit 19 · Observability, Monitoring, and Incident Engineering

    UNIT 19 / C1

    How do logs, metrics, and traces complement one another?

    Metrics summarise a population, so a latency distribution can establish how widespread a slowdown is. A trace connects one execution's work and waits, helping locate its delay. Logs record particular events and context, such as an attempt's outcome class. Stable operation identities help relate the appropriate records. Compare individual histories with the population, allowing for sampling, dropped records, and collection limits; one trace or missing log does not establish every user's outcome.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 19 / C2

    Why is a trace ID not an access credential?

    A trace ID labels diagnostic context. A caller may supply it without proving who they are or whether they may access a resource. Validate or replace incoming context according to policy, then use the intended authentication and authorisation evidence for the action. Propagating tracing context connects evidence about the operation; it grants no resource permission.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 19 / C3

    Why can low CPU coexist with severe request delay?

    A request waiting for a connection, lock, storage response, or remote call may use little processor time. RED can show rising request duration while USE exposes pressure on the resource holding up progress. For a full pool, inspect waiting requests and the work occupying its connections. Extra CPU will not by itself release those connections, so locate the delay before choosing capacity to add.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 19 / C4

    What is tenfold budget burn for a 99.9% success target?

    The allowed bad fraction is 100% − 99.9% = 0.1%, or 0.001. An observed 1% bad fraction is 0.01, so burn rate is 0.01 / 0.001 = 10. The observed fraction is ten times the allowed fraction for the defined eligible events. State the windows and denominator. Remaining budget and event volume are also needed to judge how long the allowance will last; the ratio alone does not supply that duration.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 19 / C5

    Why avoid unique request IDs as ordinary metric labels?

    Each combination of label values identifies a time series. A new request ID can therefore create another series, making the number of series and its storage and processing cost grow with requests. Use bounded metric dimensions for population measurements. Keep detailed operation identities in appropriate logs or traces, with retention and sampling chosen for the investigation they support.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 19 / S1

    A five-second request waits 4.6 seconds for a connection. Where should investigation focus?

    Acquisition takes 4.6 / 5 = 0.92, or 92%, of this request's elapsed time. Examine pool occupancy, queueing, connection hold times, and the work holding connections, including relevant transactions or lock waits. Compare normal and slow paths and population measurements before extending the explanation. The trace locates a wait; it does not establish why the pool is full. Faster execution of this path's 100 ms query would remove little of its five-second duration.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 19 / S2

    Serving recovers but charges remain uncertain. Why is recovery incomplete?

    A responsive API establishes that new serving work can proceed, but it does not resolve previously accepted payment outcomes. Some operations may still need provider-status reconciliation or required local postings. Follow their durable identities through the supported recovery path to safe final states. Verify those outcomes and assign any remaining recovery work; an infrastructure alert clearing supplies no proof that every accepted charge is resolved.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 19 / S3

    HTTP 202 is fast while jobs wait for hours. Which indicators are missing?

    Measure acceptance-to-start delay, stage waits and processing durations, useful completions, and acceptance-to-required-outcome duration. Also track the age of unfinished work, especially the oldest unfinished operation: completed-job durations exclude jobs that never finish. Follow stable operation identity across attempts and stage commits to locate stuck work. HTTP acceptance measures the beginning of this journey and can remain fast while later progress stops.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 19 / D1

    HTTP acceptance stays fast while background jobs stop finishing. Redesign the service indicators and alert.

    Define which accepted jobs are eligible, which terminal outcomes satisfy the service, and the relevant age limits. Preserve operation identity across delivery, attempts, stage commits, retries, and final outcomes. Track queue delay separately from processing duration, useful completions, and current age of unfinished work. Break down the stage or owner where progress stops. Alert on actionable completion harm or oldest unfinished age, with an owner and a procedure for locating and recovering the work. Keep detailed operation IDs out of ordinary metric labels; use drill-down records to investigate individual jobs.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 19 / I1

    Build the five-second trace model and an asynchronous completion indicator.

    Use the fixture's sequential stages: 300 ms elsewhere + 4,600 ms pool acquisition + 100 ms query = 5,000 ms. Check that pool acquisition accounts for 4,600 / 5,000 = 92%. These assertions check the constructed accounting, not a measured cause of saturation. For jobs, record accepted_at and the required outcome under a durable operation identity. For an unfinished job compute now − accepted_at; for a completed job compute outcome_at − accepted_at. Track useful completions and oldest unfinished age alongside stage wait and processing times. Store detailed identities in suitable records and aggregate with bounded metric dimensions.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 19 / T1

    What evidence would support a latency explanation beyond correlation with a release?

    Locate the extra wait or execution on affected paths and compare them with normal paths and population measurements. If the hypothesis is that a release holds connections longer, inspect changed request behaviour, connection hold times, occupancy, and acquisition waits in the timeline. Consider competing explanations and test a focused intervention under comparable conditions. Support is stronger when the mechanism predicts the symptom and changing that mechanism changes the observed behaviour; a release marker alone establishes timing.

    ← Return to question

    Unit 20 · Deployment, Cloud Infrastructure, and Platform Architecture

    UNIT 20 / C1

    What important boundary differs between a VM and a typical container?

    A VM supplies a guest operating system on virtualised hardware; containers commonly share a host kernel while isolating processes. Both need resource, identity, network, storage, and image management. Check actual isolation and shared failure domains rather than treating packaging as a complete security or reliability guarantee.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 20 / C2

    How can a control-plane outage differ from a serving outage?

    Existing workloads may keep serving while new placement or configuration changes cannot proceed. Replacement may need a dependency that current requests do not use. Draw control and data paths separately and define cached-configuration validity. Avoid unnecessary fresh control decisions in each request.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 20 / C3

    Why must a canary receive representative traffic?

    A candidate exposed only to cheap reads can appear healthy while failing the expensive checkout path. Select cohorts and indicators that exercise the release risks, with stop conditions and sufficient observations. A small exposure is useful only when it tests behaviour relevant to the broader rollout.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 20 / C4

    Why can an old executable fail as a rollback?

    New code may have written data or a schema that the old reader cannot understand. Expand-and-contract preserves an overlap period before obsolete state is removed. Identify when contraction ends safe rollback and what forward repair remains. Reversing traffic does not reverse every stored or external effect.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 20 / C5

    Which duties remain with a team using a managed database?

    Schema, access, retention, application transaction use, acknowledgment choices, and validation of recovery still require owners. Provider tasks vary by contract. Test maintenance, throttling, failover, and credential changes instead of assuming “managed” covers every application correctness need.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 20 / S1

    Scale-down kills a worker holding an unrecorded job. What was missing?

    Durable accepted-work identity and a safe drain or transfer protocol. Stop new claims, persist progress, and let another valid owner recover as required. Killing a process cannot preserve work that existed only in its memory, regardless of how well the platform schedules replacements.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 20 / S2

    A feature is disabled after writing a new data format. What risk remains?

    Old code and clients may still read the new state. A flag changes exposure, not stored compatibility or past effects. Keep migration and reader support explicit, including what rollback or forward repair is supported after the new data exists.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 20 / S3

    Why do two successfully scheduled replicas not necessarily form a correct shared service?

    Each may use an unrelated local database or incompatible configuration. Placement establishes running instances, not common state ownership. Define the shared or coordinated data model, identity, and failure behaviour before distributing requests across them.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 20 / D1

    A blue-green release shares one database and removes a column needed by the old version. Review its rollback plan.

    Parallel app environments do not make shared state reversible. Use compatible expansion and overlap-safe readers, backfill and verify, then retire old readers before contraction. Mark the end of safe rollback and the forward repair path. Test representative mixed-version traffic.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 20 / I1

    Plan and test an expand-and-contract release with old and new readers.

    Add compatible state, deploy overlap-safe readers, backfill with bounded progress, and verify. Retire old readers before removing obsolete schema. Test rollback before that point and identify what requires forward repair afterward. Expose representative traffic to a canary, including important expensive paths.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 20 / T1

    How can rollback restore old code while leaving incompatible data or effects?

    Old code can return while new schemas, values, provider calls, and published messages remain. Maintain compatibility during overlap and identify the point where contraction ends safe rollback. Some outcomes need forward repair or compensation. Restoring an artifact cannot reverse every state transition it previously performed.

    ← Return to question

    Unit 21 · Performance, Cost Optimization, and System Validation

    UNIT 21 / C1

    What must accompany a reusable benchmark result?

    Workload, data distribution, hardware or capacity, versions, warmup, concurrency, duration, success definition, variability, and relevant failures. A function microbenchmark cannot establish full application throughput. Preserve enough setup to reproduce and interpret the claim rather than presenting one number without its conditions.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 21 / C2

    How can coordinated omission hide waiting?

    A generator waits for a slow reply before issuing later work that independent real arrivals would already have submitted. Some queueing and delay disappear from the observed population. Choose a generator model matching the workload and record offered, completed, failed, and abandoned work.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 21 / C3

    Why is a short measured throughput maximum not a safe production target?

    Real operation includes variance, maintenance, background work, and required failure capacity. Near saturation, extra arrivals sharply worsen waiting or rejection. Locate the useful knee and reserve margin against the actual objective rather than running indefinitely at one short benchmark's ceiling.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 21 / C4

    Why can cost per attempt hide increasing cost per useful outcome?

    Retries and failures can enlarge the attempt denominator without producing additional completed orders or documents. Define successful business outcomes and the accounting period, while retaining technical breakdowns. Compare candidates with equivalent correctness and service objectives.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 21 / C5

    What should an architecture fitness function protect?

    A meaningful required property such as module dependencies, tenant isolation, compatibility, or tested recovery. It should permit harmless implementation changes and be updated when a valid architecture decision changes the requirement. Its pass establishes only its covered evidence, not universal correctness.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 21 / S1

    An index fixes the slow query. Why might sharding have been a poorer first step?

    Sharding changes ownership, routing, transactions, and migration while the avoidable scan may remain. A targeted implementation fix can address the measured mechanism with less risk. Architectural change is justified when the underlying limit actually requires it, not because it sounds more scalable.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 21 / S2

    What does killing a process only before work begins fail to test?

    It misses gaps such as commit before reply, output write before completion record, or resumed work after lease expiry. Inject faults at the boundary in question and check both serving and required state. Successful restart alone does not establish that accepted work survived.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 21 / S3

    Source and destination counts match but tenant owners differ. Why did validation miss it?

    A count compares quantity, not identity or meaning. Compare keys, versions, relationships, ownership, and business invariants as appropriate. State whether the check examines all records or samples. Migration, replay, and recovery need evidence that the right data reached the right scope.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 21 / D1

    A faster and cheaper benchmark configuration omits failures and disables authorisation. Can it replace the original design?

    It tests a different workload and service contract. Restore mandatory correctness and access checks, include failed and waiting work, disclose setup, and compare useful outcomes under the original requirements. A favourable number cannot compensate for removing the properties the service must provide.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 21 / I1

    Compare the three fictional architectures against equal requirements and costs.

    cost_options totals 371, 551, and 1,402 monthly units. Keep these inputs separate from measured capacity and reliability. Use the constructed latency and independent-component examples only within their assumptions, then state which real tests would establish each candidate meets the original workload and service goals.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 21 / T1

    When could a more expensive architecture be simpler to operate overall?

    Compare total work for people as well as the invoice. A managed service may reduce patching, backup, or recovery burden while adding charges and leaving application responsibilities. Evaluate the same correctness and service goals with explicit staffing assumptions. Choose the design the team can understand, change, and recover reliably.

    ← Return to question

    Unit 22 · End-to-End Design, Architecture Reviews, and Evolution

    UNIT 22 / C1

    A short-link click count is temporarily behind, while two buyers are trying to claim one seat. Why can these operations use different consistency rules?

    The delayed count can often be corrected by processing identified click events later. During the delay, the displayed total is less fresh, but no exclusive resource has necessarily been allocated twice.

    A seat claim must decide who owns the seat before confirmation. If two callers both win and the records converge later, the service has already broken its promise. State each operation's observable rule and failure behaviour: delayed aggregation may suit the count, while the claim needs one coordinated ownership decision.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / C2

    A chat service returns a persisted receipt, then the recipient disconnects before receiving a live frame. What has the receipt established, and how should delivery recover?

    The receipt establishes that the accepted message is retained under the stated storage contract. It does not establish that a recipient device received the frame or that a person read the message.

    The returning device fetches history after its known sequence, detects gaps, and recognises repeated messages by identity. Device-delivery and human-read evidence are tracked separately. This makes a missed live frame recoverable without changing the meaning of the persistence receipt.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / C3

    Worker A pauses at epoch 7. Its lease expires, and worker B receives epoch 8. Why does the lease alone not guarantee one external execution?

    Lease expiry changes who currently has permission to work; it does not stop A's paused process. A can resume and perform an action alongside B. An atomic current-epoch check rejects A's local completion, preserving local progress.

    The external receiver needs supported stable effect identity or enforced fencing to protect its own boundary. Fencing requires the receiver to reject stale authority; merely attaching an epoch is insufficient. An effect accepted before authority changed may still require reconciliation. Neither the lease nor the local completion check by itself establishes one external execution.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / C4

    Two document replicas finish with equal text. What else must be checked before calling the collaborative editor correct?

    Equal text establishes only that final comparison for that history. The replicas may both contain an unauthorised edit, invalid rich-text structure, incorrect Unicode treatment, or broken undo behaviour.

    First check convergence under the chosen protocol and its supported operation context. Then test access, structural validity, identity-based repetition, and reconnect from snapshots and retained history. Include offline clients whose access has changed. These properties need separate evidence; convergence does not supply them automatically.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / C5

    An extraction worker finishes without an exception. What further conditions may be needed before a document-processing workflow is complete?

    The output must be usable, permitted, and linked to its exact source and pipeline versions. It may still need structural validation, human review, or publication. A worker finishing only establishes progress through that attempt.

    Track extraction, review decisions, and publication separately. Preserve the evidence, actor, and version needed to explain the result. If deletion or authority changes before publication, current-state checks must still prevent stale output from becoming available. Define complete in terms of the required output journey.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / S1

    A payment succeeds after its seat hold has expired. Another buyer may now own the seat. What may the booking service safely do?

    Read the current authoritative ownership and apply the documented recovery policy. The service may reacquire the seat only through a valid claim if it is still available. Otherwise, it must follow a refund or another supported resolution; the successful payment cannot justify issuing against another buyer's confirmed seat.

    Keep the provider operation identity and reconcile the financial result. Expiry does not erase a charge that happened externally. Seat ownership and payment recovery must both be resolved without allowing one to overwrite the other's evidence.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / S2

    A provider charges successfully, the process stops before recording its reply, and the client retries. How can the service avoid another logical charge?

    Persist intent and stable provider operation identity before submission. On retry, recover that operation rather than inventing a new key. Use the provider's supported safe-repeat or status protocol and reconcile its existing effect before considering another submission.

    Apply verified evidence through an idempotent local transition that creates one valid balanced posting set. The local key and transaction protect local records; they cannot impose unsupported deduplication on an arbitrary provider. If available evidence cannot resolve the effect yet, retain uncertainty instead of declaring failure and charging afresh.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / S3

    An epoch-7 extraction worker finishes after the document is deleted or its attempt is superseded. What must stop the old artifact from being published?

    At the authoritative completion boundary, check current epoch, input version, and live deletion state together with the state change. Reject the artifact's completion if those conditions no longer hold. A check performed only before computation can become stale while the worker runs.

    Publication and derived serving paths must respect the same current lifecycle state. Sending a cancellation message is insufficient because the worker may already be running, paused, or unreachable. The persisted conditional transition supplies the local protection independently of worker timing.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / D1

    Review a short-link service at 100,000 redirects/s when its cache becomes unavailable. What assumption has changed, and what must the design demonstrate?

    With a warm 90% hit ratio, only 10% of 100,000 redirects/s reaches the source: 10,000 reads/s before retries or coalescing. Cache loss removes that assumption, so fallback demand can approach the full offered rate.

    Define bounded origin admission and the permitted response when capacity is exhausted. Test cold-cache capacity, hot links, and recovery while preserving expiry and revocation rules. Extra cache replicas can reduce some failures, but do not establish safe fallback or immediate invalidation. Record the supported degraded outcome and the evidence for it.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / I1

    Choose one case study and implement its failure exercise. Which invariant will you check, where will you interrupt execution, and what recovered state should result?

    Name the exact protected boundary and an observable invariant before writing the test. For example, a short-link creation may commit its mapping and operation result, lose the reply, then return that same mapping on a repeated key without a second creation. A seat exercise can instead check that an old expiry never releases a newer reservation.

    Inject the interruption at the relevant boundary and inspect recovered records, including repeats or stale work. Explain why the mechanism enforces the result. Use the provided fixtures as examples, while keeping external guarantees within the actual mock, provider, or editing-protocol contract. A passing local exercise does not establish unsupported external behaviour.

    ← Return to question
    UNIT 22 / T1

    You can fund another region, tested restores, or stronger reconciliation first. How would you choose which work reduces the most important risk?

    Start with the most harmful unmet requirement and a failure history showing the gap. If the sole copy can be destroyed, reconciliation cannot recreate its missing bytes. If provider effects have no recoverable identity, another region repeats the same uncertainty. A restore test addresses a different question: whether saved data can become a usable recovered system.

    Compare the risk reduced, operating work added, and evidence each option can provide. Record why the selected change addresses the present gap and what observation would justify reconsidering the choice. Additional infrastructure is useful when it repairs the required failure behaviour.

    THE REFERENCE DESK

    A searchable glossary

    Definitions and concept summaries link directly to their complete treatment, including individual patterns.

    Abstract Factory
    Creates a compatible family of collaborators through one selected construction interface. Read the lesson →
    Abstraction
    Presenting the operations a caller needs while hiding implementation details; the contract still states the behaviour the caller relies on. Read the lesson →
    Abstraction, encapsulation, polymorphism, inheritance
    Abstraction presents needed behaviour; encapsulation controls representation; polymorphism permits compatible implementations; inheritance specialises a relationship. Read the lesson →
    ACID properties
    ACID separates atomicity, invariant preservation, isolation, and conditional durability; application rules still need correct expression. Read the lesson →
    Active-active vs active-passive
    Active-active and active-passive assign serving roles for a particular function, each needing tested transitions. Read the lesson →
    Adapter
    Translates an existing interface or representation into a caller’s required behavioural contract. Read the lesson →
    Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy
    Structural patterns organise interface translation, composition, grouping, added behaviour, simplified access, sharing, and mediation to a target. Read the lesson →
    ADR
    Architecture Decision Record: a short record of a design choice, why it was made, its consequences, and when to reconsider it. Read the lesson →
    Aggregates, entities, value objects, domain services
    An aggregate groups changes requiring one consistency boundary, with a root controlling its members' transitions. Read the lesson →
    Alert design and alert fatigue
    Useful alerts identify actionable harm or impending objective loss with an owner and response. Read the lesson →
    Amdahl's Law and bottlenecks
    Amdahl's Law bounds fixed-work speedup when part of the job remains sequential. Read the lesson →
    Anti-corruption layers
    An anti-corruption layer translates external meanings so they do not silently redefine the local model. Read the lesson →
    API documentation and discoverability
    Useful API documentation explains complete success and failure histories beyond machine-readable message shape. Read the lesson →
    API fundamentals and interface contracts
    An API is a behavioural communication contract, including identity, effects, failures, timing, and supported change. Read the lesson →
    API gateways and BFF
    Gateways provide shared boundary policy; BFFs adapt interactions to particular client needs. Read the lesson →
    API security and common vulnerabilities
    API security follows how accepted input is used, including ownership, injection, resource, and destination risks. Read the lesson →
    API versioning and compatibility
    Compatibility preserves supported meanings and client behaviour across a planned transition. Read the lesson →
    Application architecture
    The organization and interaction of application responsibilities and their dependency rules. Read the lesson →
    Architecture fitness functions
    Architecture fitness checks protect required properties without freezing irrelevant implementation details. Read the lesson →
    At-most-once and at-least-once processing
    At-most-once can lose required effects; at-least-once can repeat them and therefore needs safe effect handling. Read the lesson →
    Audit trails
    Audit trails record scoped actors, actions, and actual outcomes while protecting integrity and sensitive context. Read the lesson →
    Authentication vs authorization
    Authentication establishes identity; authorisation grants a particular action on a resource under policy. Read the lesson →
    Authentication vs authorization at API boundaries
    Authentication identifies a caller; authorisation checks the permitted action on the particular resource. Read the lesson →
    Autoscaling
    Autoscaling must include useful signals, startup, draining, durable work, downstream limits, and spending bounds. Read the lesson →
    Autoscaling metrics
    Autoscaling reacts to workload signals with delay, bounds, warmup, and downstream-capacity constraints. Read the lesson →
    Availability
    Whether a system can provide the required service when needed. A measurement must define which requests and results count. Read the lesson →
    Availability vs durability
    Availability concerns useful serving; durability concerns committed data surviving the specified failure model. Read the lesson →
    Availability, reliability, durability, consistency
    Availability, durability, reliability, and consistency concern different serving, persistence, correctness, and observation requirements. Read the lesson →
    Average vs median vs p95/p99 latency
    Means and percentiles describe different features of a timing distribution; combined percentiles require appropriate underlying data. Read the lesson →
    B-tree/B+tree and hash indexing
    Ordered trees support ranges and equality; hash indexes target equality under their implementation's rules. Read the lesson →
    Backpressure
    A mechanism that communicates or enforces downstream capacity limits on upstream work. Read the lesson →
    Backpressure and replay
    Backpressure and replay need capacity budgets, retained identity, and useful completion indicators. Read the lesson →
    Backup, recovery, and durability

    OLTP vs OLAP
