    On-call and runbooks
    On-call needs useful alerts, access, escalation, rehearsed runbooks, and service ownership that reduces recurring toil. Read the lesson →
    Onion Architecture
    Onion Architecture organises inward policy dependencies; concrete contracts matter more than diagram shape. Read the lesson →
    Ordering guarantees
    Publication, delivery, execution, and effect order can differ when work proceeds concurrently. Read the lesson →
    PACELC as a useful extension
    PACELC highlights partition choices and ordinary latency/consistency costs as a design lens, not a complete protocol. Read the lesson →
    Pages, records, indexes, and buffer pools
    Pages organise records; buffer pools cache pages, while query locality determines which work can be avoided. Read the lesson →
    Pagination, filtering, sorting
    Pagination bounds query and response work using defined order, filtering, size, and access rules. Read the lesson →
    Partial failures
    Partial failure permits one participant's effect to succeed while another fails to observe or record it. Read the lesson →
    Partitioning and sharding
    Sharding distributes partitions among owners, adding routing, query, transaction, and movement requirements. Read the lesson →
    Partitions, consumer groups, offsets
    Partitions provide ordered lanes; consumer groups and offsets track ownership and progress within those lanes. Read the lesson →
    Password hashing
    Password hashing uses a purpose-built salted work mechanism with maintained implementations and deployment-appropriate parameters. Read the lesson →
    Paxos: conceptual foundations
    Paxos preserves chosen decisions through numbered proposals and required prior evidence across intersecting majorities. Read the lesson →
    Peak vs average load
    Peak load and its duration can differ substantially from an evenly distributed daily average. Read the lesson →
    Performance budgets
    Performance budgets allocate acceptable end-to-end costs under a workload and remain targets until measured. Read the lesson →
    Performance tuning vs architecture changes
    Tuning changes implementation costs; architecture changes alter major ownership or placement and need proportionate evidence. Read the lesson →
    Physical vs logical clocks
    Physical clocks estimate time; logical clocks represent ordering relationships without necessarily measuring seconds. Read the lesson →
    Platform engineering basics
    Platform engineering offers reusable operating capabilities whose limits and ownership remain visible to developer users. Read the lesson →
    Poison messages
    Poison messages need diagnosis and controlled quarantine rather than unlimited identical retries. Read the lesson →
    Polyglot persistence and its operational costs
    Polyglot persistence combines engines for useful capabilities while adding operating and cross-store coordination work. Read the lesson →
    Primary/replica architectures
    Primary/replica topology needs explicit write authority, acknowledgment, promotion, and stale-owner protection. Read the lesson →
    Privacy, retention, and deletion
    Privacy lifecycle spans collection, access, correction, retention, deletion, and historical recovery of copies. Read the lesson →
    Producers, consumers, brokers
    Producers, brokers, and consumers acknowledge different stages that must be named to reason about ownership. Read the lesson →
    Profiling
    Profiling locates runtime work or waits under measured conditions, which must be related to user outcomes. Read the lesson →
    Profiling and benchmarking
    Profiles locate runtime work; benchmarks compare controlled conditions with disclosed workloads, versions, variation, and outcomes. Read the lesson →
    Program vs process vs thread
    A program is saved instructions. A process runs them. Threads within a process execute work and can share data. Read the lesson →
    Prototype
    Creates an object by copying configured state under explicit sharing and ownership rules. Read the lesson →
    Proxy
    Represents a target interface while controlling access, creation, or location with explicit cost and failure behaviour. Read the lesson →
    Public vs internal APIs
    Internal APIs still cross trust, version, and failure boundaries; public APIs add explicit audience and support commitments. Read the lesson →
    Query and application performance diagnosis
    Diagnosis separates waiting from execution and tests proposed bottleneck mechanisms against evidence. Read the lesson →
    Query planning and EXPLAIN
    A query planner chooses physical execution using estimates; compare plans with actual work where safely supported. Read the lesson →
    Queue saturation and throughput ceilings
    Saturation limits useful completion; added arrivals become waiting or rejection, requiring operating margin. Read the lesson →
    Queueing and overload
    Queues absorb temporary mismatch but sustained overload requires admission, capacity, or workload changes. Read the lesson →
    Queues vs logs vs pub/sub
    Queues distribute work, logs retain ordered history, and pub/sub follows its stated subscription and retention contract. Read the lesson →
    Quorum
    A set of participants whose responses meet a protocol’s decision rule. Intersection alone does not establish all read or write correctness properties. Read the lesson →
    Quorum-based systems
    A quorum is a permitted decision set within a protocol whose members preserve the required evidence. Read the lesson →
    Quorums and read/write trade-offs
    Quorum intersection is a fixed-set property; version, durability, concurrency, and membership rules determine its use. Read the lesson →
    Race conditions and critical sections
    Both callers read zero before either writes. Protecting the whole read–modify–write sequence lets two increments produce two. Read the lesson →
    Raft: terms, elections, log replication, commit
    Raft combines term-based elections, log freshness, replication, commitment, and membership rules to preserve history. Read the lesson →
    Range partitioning vs hash partitioning
    Range placement supports ordered locality; hashing spreads keys, with different scan and hot-key trade-offs. Read the lesson →
    Rate limiting
    Rate limiting applies a scoped pace and burst rule with an explicit state-failure policy. Read the lesson →
    Rate limits and quotas
    Rate limits control pace and bursts; quotas cap accumulated use under defined scope and failure rules. Read the lesson →
    Read replicas and read/write splitting
    Read/write splitting must respect observation and transaction needs, not merely classify by SQL verb. Read the lesson →
    Read-heavy vs write-heavy systems
    A read/write ratio counts work at a specified boundary; one user action can cause many physical operations. Read the lesson →
    Read-your-writes and monotonic reads
    Read-your-writes and monotonic reads preserve particular session observations across supported routing and recovery paths. Read the lesson →
    Rebalancing
    Rebalancing transfers current data and authority while preserving concurrent writes, routing, validation, and recovery. Read the lesson →
    Reconciliation after partial failure
    Reconciliation compares intended and observed outcomes and repairs partial failure through safe identified operations. Read the lesson →
    RED and USE methods
    RED focuses on serving rate, errors, and duration; USE examines resource utilisation, saturation, and errors. Read the lesson →
    Redis-like data structures
    Redis-like data structures offer specific operations; local command atomicity does not automatically cover a larger workflow. Read the lesson →
    Redundancy
    Redundancy requires independent failure exposure, valid state, usable takeover, and enough surviving capacity. Read the lesson →
    Refactoring and recognizing code smells
    Refactoring improves structure while preserving the intended observable behaviour. Read the lesson →
    Referential integrity
    Referential integrity protects valid relationships using mechanisms appropriate to the ownership and transaction boundary. Read the lesson →
    Regression testing
    Regression tests preserve important behaviour while allowing deliberate contract changes and tolerating measured noise appropriately. Read the lesson →
    Relational databases and SQL
    Relational storage models facts with keys and constraints; SQL expresses operations whose physical cost needs investigation. Read the lesson →
    Replication
    Replication maintains copies under explicit acknowledgment, authority, lag, and recovery rules. Read the lesson →
    Replication lag
    Replica receipt, persistence, and apply progress can differ and support different freshness or recovery claims. Read the lesson →
    Repository
    Offers application-oriented persistence operations through a contract defining transactions, bounds, errors, and lifetimes. Read the lesson →
    Repository, Unit of Work, Specification, CQRS, and dependency boundaries
    Repository, Unit of Work, Specification, and CQRS clarify data access, commit ownership, predicates, and distinct read/write models. Read the lesson →
    Request scopes, session scopes, and custom scopes
    Scopes define resource lifetimes for requests, sessions, or jobs; their meanings need explicit ownership and cleanup. Read the lesson →
    Request/response schemas
    Schemas describe structure; validation also checks business meaning, size limits, and safe error behaviour. Read the lesson →
    Resource exhaustion and backpressure
    If arrivals exceed completions, waiting work grows. Backpressure makes the producer respond to the receiving side’s limited capacity. Read the lesson →
    Resource modeling
    Resource modelling gives business objects and operations stable identities and meaningful lifecycles. Read the lesson →
    REST, GraphQL, gRPC, RPC
    REST, GraphQL, and RPC styles organise interaction differently; none alone supplies safe retries or compatibility. Read the lesson →
    Retries and dead-letter queues
    Retry and dead-letter policies need bounds, useful error context, ownership, and a safe repair/replay path. Read the lesson →
    Retries and timeouts
    Retries spend bounded time and capacity and need safe repetition, particularly for uncertain effects. Read the lesson →
    Retries, exponential backoff, jitter
    Retries spend bounded capacity and time, with backoff, jitter, classification, and safe effect identity. Read the lesson →
    Retry storms
    Retry storms amplify failure traffic; timing randomisation alone does not bound total attempts. Read the lesson →
    Reverse proxies vs forward proxies
    A forward proxy acts for clients. A reverse proxy receives requests in front of application servers. Read the lesson →
    Role-based and attribute-based access control
    RBAC assigns scoped role permissions; ABAC evaluates trusted attributes, with enforcement and testing required for either. Read the lesson →
    Rollbacks and database migrations
    Rollback depends on compatible state; expand-and-contract maintains a supported overlap before removing old structures. Read the lesson →
    Rolling, blue-green, and canary deployments
    Rolling, blue-green, and canary exposure need representative verification, compatible state, and sufficient transition capacity. Read the lesson →
    Root-cause investigation
    Cause investigation distinguishes triggers from contributing mechanisms and tests explanations beyond correlation. Read the lesson →
    Row-oriented vs column-oriented storage
    Row and column layouts group physical values differently to support different read and update patterns. Read the lesson →
    RPO
    Recovery Point Objective: an objective for the amount of data loss measured in time. Read the lesson →
    RTO
    Recovery Time Objective: an objective for restoring service after disruption. Read the lesson →
    RTO and RPO
    RTO targets recovery time; RPO targets acceptable data-loss exposure in time. Read the lesson →
    Safety vs liveness
    Safety excludes bad outcomes; liveness requires progress under specified environmental conditions. Read the lesson →
    Saga
    A coordinated sequence of local transactions with compensating actions; compensation need not be a perfect inverse. Read the lesson →
    Sagas and compensating transactions
    Sagas coordinate local steps and supported compensations with durable progress and explicit uncertainty. Read the lesson →
    Sampling and telemetry cost
    Sampling and retention balance diagnostic questions, privacy, cardinality, and telemetry capacity. Read the lesson →
    Scale-out economics
    Scale economics includes surviving capacity, coordination, transfer, baseline resources, and operating effort per useful outcome. Read the lesson →
    Scaling writes vs scaling reads
    Read scaling can reuse copies; write scaling must divide or reduce ownership work while preserving invariants. Read the lesson →
    Scheduling and context switching
    The scheduler chooses a ready thread. A context switch saves one thread’s execution state and restores another’s. Read the lesson →
    Scheduling and service discovery
    Scheduling selects eligible resources; discovery advertises endpoints whose readiness and shared-state behaviour still need handling. Read the lesson →
    Scheduling, leases, and worker coordination
    Scheduling separates stable due occurrences from attempts, with atomic creation, time, overlap, and stale-worker rules. Read the lesson →
    Schema evolution
    Schema evolution must preserve supported interpretation of stored events, historical data, and delayed readers. Read the lesson →
    Search engines and inverted indexes
    An inverted index maps analysed terms to document postings, with source and access metadata for safe serving. Read the lesson →
    Search indexes
    Search indexes are retrieval representations with source-version, freshness, access, and rebuild obligations. Read the lesson →
    Search ingestion and reindexing
    Reindexing builds and validates a new generation while catching up edits and deletes before serving switches. Read the lesson →
    Secrets management
    Secrets need controlled distribution, ownership, rotation, revocation, and protection from accidental exposure. Read the lesson →
    Secure-by-design reviews
    Secure reviews follow sensitive operations and changed conditions through every required enforcement boundary. Read the lesson →
    Security vs usability trade-offs
    Security and usability need a workable safe journey without trading away mandatory isolation or correctness. Read the lesson →
    Sequential and causal consistency
    Sequential consistency preserves participant program order; causal consistency preserves dependencies while allowing unrelated orders to differ. Read the lesson →
    Serializability
    A transactional correctness condition requiring equivalence to some serial execution; real-time order is a separate issue. Read the lesson →
    Serializability vs linearizability
    Serializability concerns transaction equivalence; strict serializability additionally respects real-time constraints. Read the lesson →
    Serializable execution and serializability
    Serializability concerns serial transaction equivalence; linearizability also concerns operation real-time precedence. Read the lesson →
    Serverless and function-oriented architectures
    Serverless execution delegates platform work while retaining limits, state, identity, and retry requirements. Read the lesson →
    Serverless compute
    Serverless delegates selected platform duties while retaining limits, durable state, identity, and safe retries. Read the lesson →
    Service discovery
    Service discovery supplies possible destinations. A destination can stop after the list is obtained, so callers must handle that change. Read the lesson →
    Sessions, cookies, tokens
    Sessions, tokens, and cookies have different state and transport roles with explicit validation and revocation rules. Read the lesson →
    Shared memory vs message passing
    Shared memory lets callers change the same value. Message passing can give one owner control of that value. Read the lesson →
    Single points of failure
    A single point of failure can be any shared dependency defeating the required service or recovery. Read the lesson →
    Singleton
    Restricts instance access within a specified program or container boundary, without implying global uniqueness or safe mutation. Read the lesson →
    SLI / SLO / SLA
    Indicator: measured behavior. Objective: target for that behavior. Agreement: an explicit service agreement, potentially with consequences. Read the lesson →
    SLI, SLO, SLA, and error budgets
    An SLI measures behaviour, an SLO targets it over a window, and an SLA states agreement obligations. Read the lesson →
    SLIs, SLOs, error budgets
    SLIs measure behaviour; SLOs target it; error-budget burn compares observed shortfall with its allowance. Read the lesson →
    SLO-based reliability decisions
    SLO evidence guides reliability investment without hiding critical low-volume harm inside a broad denominator. Read the lesson →
    SOLID principles, including their limitations
    SOLID offers guidelines for responsibilities, useful extension, substitution, focused interfaces, and dependency direction. Read the lesson →
    Specification
    Names a reusable eligibility or selection predicate whose later state-changing use may need atomic revalidation. Read the lesson →
    Split-brain prevention and fencing tokens
    Fencing epochs reject stale authority only when receivers enforce them atomically with protected effects. Read the lesson →
    Split-brain situations
    Split brain creates conflicting authorities; stale actors need prevention or enforcement at the protected effect boundary. Read the lesson →
    Stale-while-revalidate
    Stale-while-revalidate serves an allowed older value while refresh proceeds, with a limit on unusable age. Read the lesson →
    State
    Organises behaviour around a lifecycle whose guarded transitions follow entity history. Read the lesson →
    Stateless vs stateful services
    Stateless instances keep no required per-client conversation only locally, while using appropriate external state owners. Read the lesson →
    Status codes and error models
    Protocol status and business state can differ: a created resource may still represent pending work. Read the lesson →
    Sticky sessions
    Sticky sessions preserve affinity while adding load-skew and recovery consequences for locally held state. Read the lesson →
    Storage, memory, bandwidth, and CPU estimates
    Estimate requests, bytes, memory, CPU, and transfer separately using explicit workload assumptions. Read the lesson →
    Strategy
    Supplies an interchangeable algorithm or policy behind a stable behavioural contract. Read the lesson →
    Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Chain of Responsibility, Template Method, Iterator, Mediator, Memento, Visitor
    Behavioural patterns organise algorithms, notifications, intentions, state transitions, traversal, and coordination at chosen extension points. Read the lesson →
    Stream processing fundamentals
    Stream processing needs keyed state, event/processing time, lateness, corrections, and recoverable progress. Read the lesson →
    Streaming APIs and long-running operations
    Long-running and streaming APIs need explicit ownership, progress, cancellation, buffering, and recovery contracts. Read the lesson →
    Strong consistency and eventual consistency
    Eventual convergence needs stated repair assumptions and conflict semantics; “strong” needs a named precise model. Read the lesson →
    Strongly consistent metadata services
    Consistent metadata services own small control decisions, with explicit consequences when new decisions cannot proceed. Read the lesson →
    Structured logging
    Structured logs give fields stable meanings, bounded size, safe content, and explicit event boundaries. Read the lesson →
    Supply-chain security
    Supply-chain controls protect inputs, builds, artifacts, credentials, deployment, and compromised-release response. Read the lesson →
    Sustainability and resource efficiency
    Resource efficiency removes unnecessary work and transfer while broader sustainability claims require actual supporting evidence. Read the lesson →
    Synchronous vs asynchronous communication
    Asynchronous submission separates acceptance from completion and needs an owner for the intervening work. Read the lesson →
    Synchronous vs asynchronous execution
    A synchronous interface returns completion before the caller proceeds; an asynchronous interface separates starting from receiving the result. Read the lesson →
    Synchronous vs asynchronous replication
    Synchronous replication waits for named milestones; asynchronous acknowledgment can precede another durable copy. Read the lesson →
    Tail latency analysis
    Tail analysis connects timing distributions and representative paths without incorrectly averaging percentile summaries. Read the lesson →
    Tail latency and latency budgets
    A request needing many results can be delayed by its slowest dependency; budget the complete path. Read the lesson →
    TCP vs UDP vs QUIC
    TCP carries an ordered byte stream; UDP carries datagrams; QUIC supplies secure streams over UDP. The application still interprets the data. Read the lesson →
    Technical vs business boundaries
    Business boundaries group capabilities; technical layers organise mechanisms within or across them. Read the lesson →
    Tell, Don't Ask
    Tell, Don't Ask favours sending intentions to the owner that can protect the relevant state rule. Read the lesson →
    Template Method
    Preserves a process skeleton while allowing selected implementation steps to vary. Read the lesson →
    Testability and design for change
    Testable design gives controlled inputs and visible outcomes; substitutes and real integration tests establish different evidence. Read the lesson →
    The fallacies of distributed computing
    Distributed-computing fallacies expose hidden assumptions about networks, cost, topology, trust, and administration. Read the lesson →
    Thread pools and worker pools
    A pool limits active workers. A separate queue limit controls waiting jobs. Restart recovery also needs saved job records. Read the lesson →
    Thread safety and immutability
    Immutable records stay unchanged. Their mutable collection still needs rules for concurrent access. Read the lesson →
    Threat modeling
    Threat modelling connects assets, actors, abuse paths, and impact to controls and concrete tests. Read the lesson →
    Throughput
    Completed work per unit time under a specified workload and success definition. Read the lesson →
    Time, clocks, and event ordering
    Physical timestamps, elapsed durations, and causal order answer different questions and need suitable clocks or protocols. Read the lesson →
    Time-series databases
    Time-series data combines measurements, times, and dimensions with explicit cardinality, lateness, and retention handling. Read the lesson →
    Timeouts
    Timeouts bound waiting; overall deadlines include acquisition and stage waits without proving remote nonexecution. Read the lesson →
    TLS and HTTPS
    TLS checks peer identity and protects messages in transit. The application separately checks permission to use a resource. Read the lesson →
    Trace IDs, span IDs, context propagation
    Trace context links observations across calls or messages and must not be treated as authorisation. Read the lesson →
    Trade-off
    A choice that accepts one cost or limitation to gain another benefit, judged against the requirements. Read the lesson →
    Transaction commit and rollback
    Commit accepts a transaction under the engine protocol; rollback abandons uncommitted work and cannot reverse unrelated remote effects. Read the lesson →
    Transactional outbox
    Recording a state change and publication intent in one local transaction, then relaying the intent; duplicate delivery still requires handling. Read the lesson →
    Transactions across multiple operations
    Related statements need an explicit common transaction when their invariant requires one all-or-nothing change. Read the lesson →
    Transient, scoped, singleton, and framework-specific lifetimes
    Transient, scoped, and singleton describe reuse within defined framework boundaries, not universal global identity or safety. Read the lesson →
    Trust boundaries
    Trust boundaries mark changes in identity, authority, and confidence that require appropriate validation. Read the lesson →
    Trust boundary
    A point across which identity, privilege, or confidence in input changes. Read the lesson →
    TTL and cache expiration
    TTL limits intended residence after insertion, not necessarily the source age of the inserted fact. Read the lesson →
    Twelve-Factor App principles
    Twelve-Factor practices guide repeatable service operation while workload-specific correctness and recovery remain required. Read the lesson →
    Unit of Work
    Owns related local changes under one commit and cleanup boundary. Read the lesson →
    Unit, integration, contract, end-to-end, and performance tests
    Test scopes provide different evidence; choose checks by failures they can detect rather than a mandatory count ratio. Read the lesson →
    User journeys and workload characteristics
    A workload describes the operations users cause, their frequency, payloads, and dependent work. Read the lesson →
    Vector indexes: introductory architecture only
    Vector indexes retrieve similarity candidates from embeddings; scores establish neither truth nor access permission. Read the lesson →
    Vertical vs horizontal scaling
    Vertical scaling enlarges a node; horizontal scaling adds nodes, with gains limited by the work that can divide. Read the lesson →
    Virtual machines vs containers
    VMs virtualise hardware with guest systems; typical containers share a host kernel, with actual isolation and failure scope verified. Read the lesson →
    Visitor
    Adds operations across a known structure, trading easier new operations for more work when element types change. Read the lesson →
    Webhooks and delivery acknowledgments
    Webhooks are asynchronous deliveries requiring authenticity, stable event identity, and defined acknowledgment behaviour. Read the lesson →
    WebSockets, Server-Sent Events, and polling
    Polling repeatedly asks for updates. SSE sends server events; WebSockets allows both ends to send. Missed updates still need recovery. Read the lesson →
    What data storage must guarantee
    Storage guarantees state accepted outcomes, observation rules, ownership, retention, and recovery under specified failures. Read the lesson →
    What makes a distributed system difficult
    Distributed participants observe only parts of an operation, so legal outcomes need explicit message and recovery protocols. Read the lesson →
    When caching is harmful
    Caching can be harmful when it saves little, weakens scope, hides origin limits, or adds excessive lifecycle work. Read the lesson →
    When not to use microservices
    Microservice extraction needs concrete benefits and operating capability sufficient to justify its added coordination cost. Read the lesson →
    Why caching works
    Caching saves repeated work when reuse outweighs access, storage, and maintenance costs under the required semantics. Read the lesson →
    Wide-column stores
    Wide-column designs commonly combine partition keys with ordered dimensions, requiring bounded partitions and query-driven modelling. Read the lesson →
    Workflow engines
    Workflow engines persist coordination under a programming model while external activities still need safe effect contracts. Read the lesson →
    Write-ahead logging
    Write-ahead logging preserves recovery information before corresponding data pages, under configured persistence rules. Read the lesson →
    Zero-trust principles
    Zero-trust principles avoid implicit permission from location alone and make trust evidence and limits explicit. Read the lesson →

    THE FORMULA REFERENCE

    Symbols with assumptions

    Every indexed model is introduced in the lessons. Inputs and guarantee boundaries accompany the notation.

    State transition

    T(S, c) → (S′, result)

    Identify valid state changes and preserved invariants. This abstracts away implementation and failures.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Weighted preference

    score(a) = Σ wᵢ sᵢ(a) / Σ wᵢ

    Use nonnegative weights with positive total. Compare only feasible designs. Scores are illustrative judgments, not benchmark results.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Request rate

    λ = daily users × requests per user per day / 86,400

    An average workload estimate. Peak factors must be assumed or measured separately.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Little’s Law

    L = λ W

    Long-run stable averages with consistent boundaries and units. It is not a universal p99 prediction.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Amdahl’s Law

    speedup(N) = 1 / [(1 − p) + p/N]

    Idealized fixed workload and parallel fraction p; excludes extra coordination overhead unless modeled.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Storage growth

    bytes/day = records/day × bytes/record × retained copies

    Account separately for indexes, compression, retention, metadata, and headroom.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Error allowance

    allowed bad events = (1 − target fraction) × eligible events

    Valid for an event-based SLO; time-based objectives need their own denominator.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Token refill

    tokens′ = min(capacity, tokens + refill_rate × elapsed)

    Admission consumes tokens atomically. Distributed clocks and state ownership need additional design.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Quorum intersection

    R + W > N

    An intersection condition for reads and writes on a fixed replica set. Not by itself a proof of linearizability.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Cost per outcome

    cost / successful business outcomes

    Define accounting period and include capacity, storage, networking, telemetry, and operational work where relevant.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Ideal M/M/1 mean residence

    W = S / (1 − rho)

    S is mean service time and rho is utilization, below one. This single-server model assumes Poisson arrivals and independent exponential service times. W includes waiting and service; it is a mean, so it cannot predict p99.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Fan-out slow probability

    P(any slow) = 1 − (1 − p)^N

    Requires independent equal-probability call outcomes in this model. Shared failures can correlate tails.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Retry amplification

    maximum attempts = a^L

    a allowed attempts at each of L nested independently retrying layers; actual execution can terminate earlier.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Busy-capacity worksheet

    instances = ceil(peak RPS / (assumed capacity × utilization target))

    Capacity is an explicit hypothetical or tested input; other bottlenecks and surviving failure capacity remain separate.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Error-budget burn

    burn = observed bad fraction / allowed bad fraction

    Use the same eligible-event denominator and a positive allowance.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Cache service-time average

    E[T] = h × T_hit + (1 − h) × T_miss

    A simple service-time mixture, excluding queue effects, dependence, and tail inference.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Backlog growth

    growth/s = arrival/s − completion/s

    Sustained positive growth requires rejection, reduction, or more useful capacity; a bigger queue only changes waiting.

    Derivation and worked example →

    Raw daily storage

    bytes/day = records/s × bytes/record × 86400

    Add indexes, history, metadata, replication, retention, compression and migration separately.

    Derivation and worked example →

    What the evidence means

    Content checks establish presence, exact syllabus allocation, figures, references, and assessment. Executable examples test bounded arithmetic and local invariants. Browser checks test reading, interactions, layouts, offline behavior, and print assembly. The book does not report illustrative objectives as measured production achievements or toy protocols as reviewed production consensus, security, or financial integrations.

    The original request is retained in BRIEF.txt. Additional optional case subjects are suggestions beyond the twelve mandatory worked designs, not omitted required chapters.
